parameter space of the pencil, so each point \(p\in C\) contributes at most one
member of the pencil.

Hence the number of cubics in a generic pencil tangent to \(C\) equals the
number of points \(p\in C\) for which those three linear conditions are
simultaneously satisfied.  This number can be computed by intersecting Chern
classes of the relevant bundles on \(C\); the result is the well‑known formula
for the “tangency divisor’’ on a linear system of plane curves of degree \(d\)
to a fixed smooth curve of degree \(e\):

\[
\deg(\Delta)= d\,e\,(d+e-2).
\]

Here \(d=3\) (cubics) and \(e=7\).  Therefore

\[
\deg(\Delta)= 3\cdot 7\,(3+7-2)=21\cdot 8=168.
\]

Thus the divisor class of \(\Delta\) in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\) is
\(168\) times the hyperplane class.

\[
\boxed{168}
\]

For a smooth plane curve \(C\subset \mathbf P^{2}\) of degree \(e=7\) the genus is  

\[
g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{6\cdot5}{2}=15 .
\]

A pencil of cubics (a line in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\)) restricts to a map  

\[
\phi : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1},
\]

because a cubic meets \(C\) in \(3e = 21\) points (counted with multiplicity).  
Hence \(\phi\) is a morphism of degree  

\[
d = 3e = 21 .
\]

The divisor \(\Delta\) records those cubics in the pencil that are tangent to \(C\); these are precisely the ramification points of \(\phi\).  
For a map \(f : C \to \mathbf P^{1}\) of degree \(d\) the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives  

\[
\deg \operatorname{Ram}(f)= 2g(C)-2 - d\,(2g(\mathbf P^{1})-2)
                        = 2g(C)-2 + 2d .
\]

Substituting \(g(C)=15\) and \(d=21\),

\[
\deg \operatorname{Ram}(f)= 2\cdot 15 - 2 + 2\cdot 21 = 30 - 2 + 42 = 70 .
\]

Thus a generic line (pencil) in the space of plane cubics meets the divisor \(\Delta\) in \(70\) points, so the class of \(\Delta\) in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\cong \mathbf P^{9}\) is

\[
[\Delta]= 70 \, H,
\]

where \(H\) is the hyperplane class.

\[
\boxed{70}
\]

problems.skill: Divisor class of tangency to a fixed curve
problems.problem:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a fixed smooth plane curve of degree \(e=9\).  
Consider the complete linear system \(|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(5)|\); its projectivization is a projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\).  

Inside \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\) let \(D\) be the divisor consisting of those degree‑\(5\) curves that are tangent to \(C\) at some (unspecified) point of intersection.  

The degree of \(D\) equals the number of members of a general pencil of quintic curves that are tangent to \(C\).  
Compute this degree.

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The pencil of quintic curves defines a morphism  

\[
f : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(d = 5\cdot 9 = 45\) (the intersection number of a quintic with the degree‑9 curve \(C\)).  
For a pencil, the curves that are tangent to \(C\) correspond exactly to the ramification points of this map: a member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\) iff the fibre of \(f\) over the corresponding point of \(\mathbf P^{1}\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\) at \(p\).

The total ramification degree of a map \(f : C \to \mathbf P^{1}\) of degree \(d\) is given by the Riemann–Hurwitz formula  

\[
\deg R = 2g(C)-2 + 2d,
\]

where \(g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}\) is the genus of \(C\).  
For \(e=9\),

\[
g(C)=\frac{(9-1)(9-2)}{2}= \frac{8\cdot7}{2}=28 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 28 - 2 + 2\cdot 45 = 54 + 90 = 144 .
\]

In a general pencil all ramification points are simple, so each ramification point gives a distinct member of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\). Therefore the divisor \(D\) in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|\) has degree equal to \(\deg R = 144\).

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)|\) has dimension  

\[
N+1 = \binom{5+2}{2}=21 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbb P^{N}= \mathbb P^{20}.
\]

Fix a smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e=9\).  
Its genus is  

\[
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{8\cdot 7}{2}=28 .
\]

Restricting \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\) to \(C\) gives a line bundle of degree  

\[
d = 5e = 45 .
\]

A general pencil (a \(\mathbb P^{1}\subset \mathbb P^{20}\)) of quintics yields a \(g^{1}_{45}\) on \(C\):
a linear series of degree \(45\) and dimension \(1\).

A member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the corresponding divisor on \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\); i.e. the map \(C \xrightarrow{\;g^{1}_{45}\;} \mathbb P^{1}\) is ramified at that point.

For a \(g^{r}_{d}\) on a curve of genus \(g\) the total ramification divisor has degree (Plücker formula)

\[
\deg R = (r+1)\bigl(d+r(g-1)\bigr).
\]

Here \(r=1\), \(d=45\), \(g=28\):

\[
\deg R = 2\bigl(45 + (28-1)\bigr)=2(45+27)=2\cdot72 = 144 .
\]

For a general pencil the ramification is simple, so each ramification point gives a distinct branch point on the \(\mathbb P^{1}\). Hence the number of members of the pencil that are tangent to \(C\) equals the number of branch points, which is \(\deg R = 144\).

Therefore the divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{20}\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{144}.
\]

The pencil of quintic curves gives a \(g^{1}_{45}\) on the smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(9\) (genus \(g=\frac{(9-1)(9-2)}2 =28\)).  
For a generic pencil the associated map  

\[
f:C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}
\]

has degree \(d=45\) and only simple ramification points.  
By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula  

\[
2g-2 = d\cdot(-2)+\sum_{p}(e_p-1),
\]

so the total ramification weight is  

\[
\sum_{p}(e_p-1)=2g-2+2d.
\]

With \(g=28\) and \(d=45\),

\[
2g-2+2d = 2\cdot28-2+2\cdot45 = 56-2+90 = 144 .
\]

Each simple ramification point corresponds to a member of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\). Hence the divisor \(D\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

For a smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e=9\) the genus is  

\[
g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{8\cdot 7}{2}=28 .
\]

A quintic curve meets \(C\) in  

\[
d = 5\cdot e = 45
\]

points (counted with multiplicities).  
A general pencil of quintics gives a two–dimensional subspace  
\(V\subset H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5))\).  
Restricting the sections to \(C\) yields a map  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1},
\qquad p \mapsto \bigl[\,s_{0}(p):s_{1}(p)\,\bigr],
\]

where \(s_{0},s_{1}\) generate the pencil.  
Since the pencil is general we may assume it has no base points on \(C\); thus \(\varphi\) is a morphism of degree  

\[
\deg\varphi = d = 45 .
\]

A member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the fibre of \(\varphi\) over some point contains a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\), i.e. when \(\varphi\) is ramified at that point.  
Hence the number of members of a generic pencil that are tangent to \(C\) equals the total ramification of \(\varphi\).

For a map \(f:C\to\mathbb P^{1}\) the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives  

\[
2g(C)-2 = \deg f\;(2g(\mathbb P^{1})-2) + R,
\]

where \(R\) is the total ramification.  Since \(g(\mathbb P^{1})=0\),

\[
R = 2g(C)-2 + 2\deg f .
\]

Substituting \(g(C)=28\) and \(\deg f =45\),

\[
R = 2\cdot 28 - 2 + 2\cdot 45 = 56 - 2 + 90 = 144 .
\]

For a generic pencil all ramification points are simple, so each contributes one member of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\).

Therefore the degree of the divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{N}\) is  

\[
\boxed{144}.
\]

The divisor \(D\subset |{\mathcal O}_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|\cong \mathbf P^{20}\) consists of those quintic curves which are tangent to the fixed smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e=9\).  

For a plane curve \(C\) the condition “a member of the linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(d)|\) is tangent to \(C\)” is the discriminant of the complete linear series \(|\mathcal O_{C}(d)|\) on \(C\).  

If a smooth curve of genus \(g\) is embedded in projective space by a line bundle of degree \(n\), the class (degree) of its dual variety – i.e. the degree of the discriminant hypersurface in the corresponding projective space of sections – is  

\[
\operatorname{deg}=2n+2g-2 .
\]

Here the line bundle is \(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\).  
Its degree is  

\[
n = \deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)=5\cdot e =5\cdot 9 =45 .
\]

The genus of a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\) is  

\[
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{8\cdot 7}{2}=28 .
\]

Hence

\[
\deg D = 2n+2g-2 = 2\cdot45 + 2\cdot28 -2 = 90 + 56 -2 = 144 .
\]

Thus a general pencil of quintic curves contains exactly \(144\) members that are tangent to the fixed degree‑9 curve \(C\).

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The pencil of quintics restricts to a \(g^{1}_{45}\) on the smooth plane curve  

\[
C:\; \deg C = e = 9 ,\qquad g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}=28 .
\]

For a pencil (a map \(f:C\to\mathbb P^{1}\)) of degree  

\[
d = \deg (Q\cap C)=5\cdot 9 =45,
\]

the points where a member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) are exactly the ramification points of \(f\).
By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula for a map \(f:C\to\mathbb P^{1}\),

\[
2g-2 = d\,(2\cdot0-2)+\deg R \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\deg R = 2d+2g-2 .
\]

Substituting \(d=45\) and \(g=28\),

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot45 + 2\cdot28 - 2 = 90 + 56 - 2 = 144 .
\]

For a general pencil the ramification is simple, so each ramification point corresponds to a distinct tangential quintic. Hence the degree of the divisor \(D\) (the number of members of a generic pencil tangent to \(C\)) equals \(144\).

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{20}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)|\) consists of those quintic curves that have a point of tangency with the fixed smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e=9\).

For a point \(p\in C\) the condition “\(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)” imposes two independent linear conditions on the space \(V=H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5))\) (vanishing at \(p\) and the vanishing of the derivative in the tangent direction of \(C\)).  
Thus the subspace of quintics tangent at \(p\) is a linear subspace \(P(W_{p})\subset\mathbb P(V)\) of codimension \(2\) (\(\dim P(W_{p})=18\)).

Let \(U\subset V\) be the 2‑dimensional vector space corresponding to a general pencil of quintics (a line \(\ell\subset\mathbb P(V)\)).  
For a point \(p\in C\) the pencil meets the subspace \(P(W_{p})\) iff the natural map  

\[
U \longrightarrow V/W_{p}\cong Q_{p}
\]

has a non‑trivial kernel.  
The quotient \(Q:=V/W\) is a rank‑2 vector bundle on \(C\).  
The determinant of the map \(U\to Q\) gives a section of the line bundle \(\det Q\) on \(C\); its zeros are precisely the points \(p\) where the pencil contains a curve tangent to \(C\) at \(p\).

Hence the number of such members in a generic pencil equals \(\deg(\det Q)\).

---

### Computing \(\det Q\)

Write \(L=\mathcal O_{C}(5)\).  
We have the exact sequence of jet bundles on the curve \(C\):

\[
0\longrightarrow \Omega_{C}\otimes L \longrightarrow J^{1}(L) \longrightarrow L \longrightarrow 0 .
\]

The subspace \(W_{p}\) consists of sections whose value at \(p\) is zero and whose derivative in the tangent direction of \(C\) vanishes; therefore  

\[
V/W \;\cong\; L\;\oplus\;(\Omega_{C}\otimes L).
\]

For a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\) we have \(\Omega_{C}\cong K_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(e-3)\).  
Thus

\[
V/W \;\cong\; \mathcal O_{C}(5)\;\oplus\; \mathcal O_{C}(e-3+5)=\mathcal O_{C}(5)\oplus\mathcal O_{C}(e+2).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\det Q \;\cong\; \mathcal O_{C}\bigl(5+(e+2)\bigr)=\mathcal O_{C}(e+7).
\]

The degree of \(\mathcal O_{C}(k)\) on a plane curve of degree \(e\) is \(k\cdot e\).  
Hence  

\[
\deg(\det Q)= (e+7)\,e.
\]

---

### Applying \(e=9\)

\[
\deg D = (9+7)\times 9 = 16 \times 9 = 144 .
\]

Thus a general pencil of quintic curves contains exactly **144** members that are tangent to the fixed smooth plane curve of degree 9.

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{N}\) is the image of the incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(Q,p)\mid p\in C,\; Q\text{ passes through }p,\;
\text{and }Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions “\(Q(p)=0\)” and “the gradient of \(Q\) at \(p\) is proportional to the gradient of \(C\) at \(p\)” are three independent linear conditions on the space of quintics \(\mathbb P^{20}\).  
Hence the fibre of the projection \(I\to C\) is a \(\mathbb P^{17}\); \(I\) is a \(\mathbb P^{17}\)-bundle over the curve \(C\).

Let \(\mathcal L= \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(1)\boxtimes\mathcal O_{C}(5)\) on the product
\(S=\mathbb P^{1}\times C\).  
A pencil of quintics corresponds to a section of \(\mathcal L\); its zero‑locus
\(D\subset S\) is a smooth curve of class \((1,5)\) (degree \(1\) on \(\mathbb P^{1}\) and
degree \(5\) on \(C\)).  

Denote by \(s\) the class of a fibre \(\mathbb P^{1}\times\{pt\}\) and by
\(f\) the class of a fibre \(\{pt\}\times C\); then \([D]=s+5f\).
On \(S\) we have  

\[
K_{S}= -2f+(2g(C)-2)s,\qquad g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}2=28 .
\]

Using the adjunction formula,

\[
\begin{aligned}
2g(D)-2 &= (K_{S}+D)\cdot D  \\
        &=\bigl((-2f+54s)+(s+5f)\bigr)\cdot(s+5f) \\
        &= (52s+3f)\cdot(s+5f)=278 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(g(D)=140\).  
The projection \(\pi:D\to\mathbb P^{1}\) has degree  

\[
d=\deg(\pi)=\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)=5e=45 .
\]

Riemann–Hurwitz gives the total ramification

\[
R = 2g(D)-2 + 2d = 278 + 90 = 368 .
\]

A ramification point of \(\pi\) occurs exactly when the fibre (the divisor of
intersection of the corresponding quintic with \(C\)) has a double point,
i.e. when the quintic is tangent to \(C\).  
For a general pencil all ramification points are simple, so the number of
tangent members equals \(R\).

Hence the degree of the divisor \(D\) in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)|\) is  

\[
\boxed{368}.
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{N}\) parametrizes quintic curves that are tangent to the fixed smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e=9\).

For a point \(p\in C\) the condition that a quintic \(Q\) be tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) means that the section of \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\) defining \(Q\) vanishes to order at least \(2\) at \(p\) when restricted to \(C\).
Hence, for each \(p\) the subspace of sections satisfying this condition has codimension \(2\) in
\(V=H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\bigr)\).

Let \(L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)|_{C}\); it is a line bundle of degree  

\[
\deg L = 5\cdot e = 5\cdot 9 = 45 .
\]

Consider the first jet bundle \(J^{1}(L)\) on \(C\); there is an exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes \Omega_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

For a fixed pencil \(W\subset V\) (\(\dim W =2\)) we have a map of vector bundles on \(C\)

\[
\phi : W\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L).
\]

A point \(p\) gives a member of the pencil tangent to \(C\) exactly when \(\phi\) drops rank at \(p\).
Thus the set of such points is the degeneracy divisor of a map between two rank‑2 bundles.
By the Thom–Porteous formula its class is  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)-c_{1}\bigl(W\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\bigr)
     =c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr),
\]

since \(W\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\) is trivial.

From the exact sequence above  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(L\otimes\Omega_{C})
                         =2c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(\Omega_{C}).
\]

Now \(\deg c_{1}(L)=45\).  
For a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\) the genus is \(g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}\); here  

\[
g=\frac{(9-1)(9-2)}{2}=28,
\]
so the canonical bundle \(K_{C}=\Omega_{C}\) has degree  

\[
\deg K_{C}=2g-2=2\cdot28-2=54.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\deg c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=2\cdot45+54=90+54=144.
\]

For a generic pencil the map \(I\to D\) is birational, so the degree of the divisor \(D\) equals this number.

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|\) restricts to the curve \(C\) as a linear series  

\[
g^{1}_{d}\qquad\text{with }d = \deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\!\mid_{C}\bigr)=5\cdot 9 = 45 .
\]

A generic pencil inside \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|\) gives a base‑point‑free \(g^{1}_{45}\) on the smooth plane curve \(C\).  
A member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the corresponding divisor on \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\); this is a ramification point of the map  

\[
f : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

defined by the pencil.

For a degree‑\(d\) map \(f\) from a smooth curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\), the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives the total ramification

\[
\sum_{P\in C}(e_P-1)=2d+2g-2 .
\]

In a general pencil all ramification points are simple (\(e_P=2\)), so the number of members of the pencil that are tangent to \(C\) equals this total ramification.

* Genus of a smooth plane curve of degree \(e=9\):

\[
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{8\cdot 7}{2}=28 .
\]

* Degree of the map: \(d = 45\).

Hence  

\[
\text{degree}(D)=2d+2g-2 = 2\cdot 45 + 2\cdot 28 - 2 = 90 + 56 - 2 = 144 .
\]

Thus the divisor \(D\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

problems.skill: Divisor class of tangency to a fixed curve
problems.problem:
Let \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)|\) denote the complete linear system of plane curves of degree \(5\); its projectivization is the projective space \(\mathbb P^{20}\).  
Fix a smooth plane cubic curve \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\).  
Define \(D\subset\mathbb P^{20}\) to be the divisor consisting of those quintic curves \(Q\) for which there exists a point \(p\in C\) such that the intersection multiplicity \(\operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2\) (i.e. \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)).  

Using the incidence correspondence and the adjunction formula, compute the degree of the divisor \(D\) in \(\mathbb P^{20}\).  

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid p\in C,\; Q\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)| ,\;
\operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2\}
\]

is a projective bundle over \(C\).  
For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions  

* \(Q(p)=0\) (the curve passes through \(p\)),  
* the first derivative of \(Q\) along the tangent of \(C\) at \(p\) vanishes  

are two independent linear conditions on the space \(H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(5))\) (dimension \(21\)).  
Hence the fibre over \(p\) is a \(\mathbf P^{18}\).  
Thus  

\[
I\simeq \mathbf P(K)\qquad\text{with}\qquad \operatorname{rk}K=19,
\]

where \(K\) is the kernel of the jet‑evaluation map  

\[
H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(5))\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\longrightarrow 
J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr).
\]

On the smooth cubic \(C\) (genus \(g=1\)) we have  

\[
J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)\cong \mathcal O_{C}(5)\oplus\mathcal O_{C}(5),
\qquad\deg\mathcal O_{C}(5)=5\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=5\cdot3=15 .
\]

Hence \(\deg J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(5)) =30\) and, because the source bundle is trivial,
\[
c_{1}(K) = -c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(5))\bigr) = -30 .
\]

Let \(\xi = c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P(K)}(1)\bigr)\) and \(\pi :\mathbf P(K)\to C\) be the projection.
The divisor \(D\subset \mathbf P^{20}\) is the image of \(I\); its degree equals  

\[
\deg D = \int_{\mathbf P(K)} \xi^{19}.
\]

In the Chow ring of a projective bundle over a curve we have the relation  

\[
\xi^{19}=c_{1}(K)\,\xi^{18}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\deg D = \int_{\mathbf P(K)} \pi^{*}c_{1}(K)\,\xi^{18}
        = \bigl(\deg c_{1}(K)\bigr)\int_{\mathbf P(K)}\xi^{18}
        = (-30)\cdot (-1)=30,
\]

because \(\int_{\mathbf P(K)}\xi^{18}=1\) (push‑forward of \(\xi^{18}\) to \(C\) gives the fundamental
class of \(C\)).  

Equivalently, for a general pencil of quintics the induced map  
\(C\stackrel{\;|\mathcal O_{C}(5)|}{\longrightarrow}\mathbf P^{1}\) has degree \(15\); by the
Riemann–Hurwitz formula its total ramification is \(30\), which is exactly the number of
pencils members tangent to \(C\).

Hence the divisor \(D\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{20}\) is the image of the incidence  

\[
I=\{(Q,p)\mid p\in C,\; \operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2\}
\subset \mathbb P^{20}\times C .
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the condition \(\operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2\) means that the restriction of the quintic to \(C\) has a **double zero** at \(p\).  
Let  

\[
L = \mathcal O_{C}(5)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\!\mid _C ,\qquad \deg L = 5\cdot 3 = 15 .
\]

The space of sections of \(L\) is \(H^{0}(C,L)\) of dimension \(15\); the restriction map  

\[
H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)) \longrightarrow H^{0}(C,L)
\]

is surjective with a \(6\)-‑dimensional kernel, so \(|L|\cong \mathbb P^{14}\) is the image of the linear projection
\(\pi:\mathbb P^{20}\dashrightarrow \mathbb P^{14}\).

Thus \(D\) is the pull‑back via \(\pi\) of the discriminant divisor
\[
\Delta =\{\,\text{sections of }L\text{ having a double zero on }C\,\}\subset \mathbb P^{14}.
\]

Hence \(\deg D = \deg \Delta\).

---

### Degree of the discriminant on an elliptic curve

For a smooth curve \(C\) of genus \(1\) and a line bundle \(L\) of degree \(d\ge 3\), the embedding given by \(|L|\) is an **elliptic normal curve** of degree \(d\) in \(\mathbb P^{d-1}\).  
The discriminant \(\Delta\) is precisely the dual variety of this embedded curve, i.e. the set of hyperplanes tangent to the curve.  
A classical result (e.g. Hartshorne, *Exercise IV.3.5*) states that the dual variety of an elliptic normal curve of degree \(d\) is a hypersurface of degree \(2d\).

In our case \(d=\deg L =15\); therefore  

\[
\deg \Delta = 2d = 2\cdot 15 = 30 .
\]

Since the projection \(\pi\) is linear, the pull‑back of a hypersurface of degree \(30\) has the same degree in \(\mathbb P^{20}\). Consequently  

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

For a quintic curve \(Q\subset \mathbf P^{2}\) write  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_{C}(5)=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\!\mid _{C}.
\]

Because \(C\) is a smooth cubic, \(\deg L =5\cdot 3 =15\) and, since \(C\) has genus
\(g=1\),

\[
h^{0}(L)=\deg L =15 .
\]

---

### 1.  From quintics to divisors on \(C\)

The restriction map  

\[
\rho:H^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\bigr)\longrightarrow
H^{0}(L)
\]

is surjective.  Its kernel consists of the sections that contain the cubic
\(C\); it is the image of \(H^{0}(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2))\) (dimension
\(6\)).  Hence we have an exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2))\; ( \dim =6)
\longrightarrow H^{0}(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5))\; ( \dim =21)
\stackrel{\rho}{\longrightarrow} H^{0}(L)\; ( \dim =15)\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Thus the linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|\cong \mathbf P^{20}\)
projects linearly onto \(|L|\cong \mathbf P^{14}\).

For a quintic \(Q\) the divisor \(Q\cap C\) is the zero‑scheme of the
section \(\rho(Q)\in H^{0}(L)\); it is a divisor of degree \(15\) on \(C\).

---

### 2.  The discriminant on \(|L|\)

A section \(s\in H^{0}(L)\) gives a reduced divisor on \(C\) iff it has no
zero of multiplicity \(\ge 2\).  
The locus in \(|L|\) where a section acquires a double zero is the **discriminant
divisor** \(\Delta\subset |L|\).

Let \(J^{1}(L)\) be the first jet bundle of \(L\) on the smooth curve \(C\);
it fits into  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes \Omega_{C}^{1}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)
\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

The incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(s,p)\in |L|\times C\mid s(p)=0,\; ds(p)=0\}
\]

is the zero‑locus of a regular section of the rank‑2 bundle
\(J^{1}(L)\otimes\mathcal O_{|L|}(1)\).  Hence  

\[
[I]=c_{2}\!\bigl(J^{1}(L)\otimes\mathcal O_{|L|}(1)\bigr)
      =c_{2}(J^{1}(L))+c_{1}(J^{1}(L))\cdot h ,
\]

where \(h=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{|L|}(1))\).  Pushing forward to \(|L|\) gives  

\[
[\Delta]=c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr).
\]

For a line bundle of degree \(d\) on a curve of genus \(g\),

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=2d+2g-2 .
\]

(Indeed \(c_{1}(J^{1}(L))=c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(L\otimes\Omega^{1}_{C})
               =d+(d+2g-2)=2d+2g-2\).)

Here \(d=\deg L =15\) and \(g=1\); therefore  

\[
\deg\Delta = 2\cdot 15 + 2\cdot 1 -2 = 30 .
\]

Thus the discriminant is a hypersurface of degree \(30\) in \(|L|\cong
\mathbf P^{14}\).

---

### 3.  Pull‑back to the space of quintics

The linear projection \(\rho:\mathbf P^{20}\dashrightarrow \mathbf P^{14}\)
is given by a \(15\times 21\) matrix of constants.  Pulling back a homogeneous
polynomial of degree \(30\) on \(\mathbf P^{14}\) yields a homogeneous
polynomial of the same degree on \(\mathbf P^{20}\).  Consequently the
pre‑image \(\rho^{-1}(\Delta)\) is a divisor \(D\subset \mathbf P^{20}\) of
degree \(30\).

Equivalently, intersecting \(D\) with a generic line (a pencil of quintics)
counts the number of members of the pencil whose restriction to \(C\) has a
double zero; this number is precisely \(\deg\Delta =30\).

---

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The divisor  

\[
D=\{\,Q\in \mathbb P^{20}\mid \exists p\in C \text{ with } \operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2 \,\}
\]

is the pull‑back of the discriminant hypersurface of the linear system
\(|\mathcal O_{C}(5)|\).

---

### 1.  Restriction to the cubic  

The restriction map  

\[
\rho : H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\bigr)
      \longrightarrow H^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)
\]

has kernel of dimension \(6\) (because \(h^{0}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5))=21\) and
\(h^{0}(\mathcal O_{C}(5))=15\)).  
Hence we obtain a linear projection  

\[
\bar\rho : \mathbb P^{20}\; \dashrightarrow\; \mathbb P^{14}
\qquad(\mathbb P^{14}= \mathbb P H^{0}(C,\mathcal O_{C}(5))).
\]

A quintic \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at some point iff the restricted
section \(\rho(Q)\in \mathbb P^{14}\) has a double zero on \(C\).
Thus  

\[
D=\bar\rho^{-1}(\Delta ),
\]

where \(\Delta\subset\mathbb P^{14}\) is the discriminant hypersurface of the
complete linear series \(|\mathcal O_{C}(5)|\).

---

### 2.  Degree of the discriminant on the cubic  

The line bundle \(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\) has degree  

\[
\deg \mathcal O_{C}(5)=5\cdot\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=5\cdot 3 = 15 .
\]

For a smooth curve \(C\) of genus \(g\) embedded by a complete linear series
\(g^{r}_{d}\) (\(d=\deg L\)), the class (degree) of its dual curve – i.e. the
degree of the discriminant hypersurface in \(\mathbb P^{r}\) – is  

\[
\operatorname{deg}\Delta = 2d + 2g - 2 .
\]

Here \(g=1\) (the cubic is an elliptic curve) and \(d=15\); consequently  

\[
\operatorname{deg}\Delta = 2\cdot 15 + 2\cdot 1 - 2 = 30 .
\]

---

### 3.  Pull‑back to \(\mathbb P^{20}\)

The projection \(\bar\rho\) is given by a linear map, so
\(\bar\rho^{*}\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{14}}(1)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{20}}(1)\).
Therefore the pull‑back of the hypersurface \(\Delta\) has the same degree:

\[
\deg D = \deg \Delta = 30 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

Let  

\[
\mathbb P^{20}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|
\]

be the linear system of plane quintics and fix a smooth cubic curve  

\[
C\subset\mathbf P^{2},\qquad \deg C =3 ,\; g(C)=1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The divisor \(D\)

For a point \(p\in C\) let  

\[
\Lambda _p=\{\,Q\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)|\;|\;Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }p \,\}.
\]

The condition “\(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)” means  

* \(Q(p)=0\) (the curve passes through \(p\));
* the differential of \(Q\) restricted to the tangent line of \(C\) at \(p\) vanishes.

Both are **linear** conditions on the space \(H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(5))\) of dimension \(21\).  
Hence for each fixed \(p\) the set \(\Lambda _p\) is a linear subspace of codimension \(2\), i.e. a \(\mathbf P^{18}\).

Define the incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\in C\times\mathbf P^{20}\mid Q\in\Lambda _p\}.
\]

The projection \(\pi_{2}:I\to\mathbf P^{20}\) has image exactly the divisor \(D\).  
Thus \(D\) is the image of a \(\mathbf P^{18}\)-bundle over the curve \(C\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Intersecting \(D\) with a general line in \(\mathbf P^{20}\)

The degree of a divisor in \(\mathbf P^{20}\) equals the number of its points
meeting a **general linear subspace of codimension 1**, i.e. a line
\(\ell\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\subset\mathbf P^{20}\).

Take a general 2‑dimensional subspace  

\[
V\subset H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(5)),\qquad \dim V =2,
\]

and let \(\ell =\mathbf P(V)\).  The members of the pencil \(V\) are the
quintics parametrised by \(\ell\).

Restrict a quintic \(Q\) to the cubic curve \(C\):
\[
Q|_{C}\in H^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr).
\]

Because \(\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=3\), we have  

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)=5\cdot 3 = 15 .
\]

Hence the pencil \(V\) induces a **linear series**  

\[
g^{1}_{15}\;=\; \bigl|\,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr|_{V}
\]

on the smooth cubic \(C\) (an elliptic curve, genus \(g=1\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Ramification of the induced \(g^{1}_{15}\)

For a linear series \(g^{r}_{d}\) on a smooth curve of genus \(g\) the total
ramification is given by the Plücker formula  

\[
\operatorname{Ram}(g^{r}_{d}) = (r+1)\bigl(d+r(g-1)\bigr).
\]

Here \(r=1,\; d=15,\; g=1\), therefore  

\[
\operatorname{Ram}(g^{1}_{15}) = 2\bigl(15 + (1-1)\bigr)=2\cdot 15 = 30 .
\]

A ramification point of the map \(C\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}\) defined by the pencil is precisely a point \(p\in C\) where the divisor \(Q|_{C}\) has a double point, i.e. where the corresponding quintic \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\).

For a **general** pencil the ramification points are simple and distinct,
so each ramification point gives a different member of the pencil that is
tangent to \(C\). Consequently the pencil meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly
\(30\) points (counted with multiplicity).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Degree of \(D\)

Since a general line \(\ell\subset\mathbf P^{20}\) meets \(D\) in \(30\) points,
the divisor class of \(D\) is \(30H\) where \(H\) is the hyperplane class.
Hence  

\[
\deg D = 30 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{20}\) consists of those quintic curves which are tangent to the fixed smooth cubic \(C\) at some point.  

Let  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid p\in C,\; Q\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)|,\; \operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2\}
\subset C\times \mathbb P^{20}
\]

and denote by \(\pi_2:I\to \mathbb P^{20}\) the projection.  
For a general quintic \(Q\) the intersection \(Q\cap C\) consists of \(5\cdot 3=15\) distinct points, so a generic fibre of \(\pi_2\) contains at most one point; thus \(\pi_2\) is birational onto its image \(D\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Incidence as a zero–locus

On \(C\times\mathbb P^{20}\) the universal quintic divisor has class  

\[
L = \operatorname{pr}_1^{*}\mathcal O_{C}(5)\;\otimes\; \operatorname{pr}_2^{*}\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{20}}(1).
\]

A section \(s\) of \(L\) evaluates a quintic at a point of \(C\).  
The condition that \(s\) vanish to order \(\ge 2\) at a point \(p\) is equivalent to the vanishing of the section of the first jet bundle \(J^{1}(L)\). Hence  

\[
I = Z\bigl( s_{J^{1}(L)}\bigr) ,\qquad 
[I]=c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Chern class of \(J^{1}(L)\)

For a smooth curve we have the exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes\Omega^{1}_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow0 .
\]

Because \(C\) is a smooth plane cubic, \(\Omega^{1}_{C}\cong \mathcal O_{C}\) (genus \(1\)), so \(L\otimes\Omega^{1}_{C}\cong L\).  
Thus \(J^{1}(L)\) is an extension of \(L\) by itself and  

\[
c\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c(L)^{2}=(1+c_{1}(L))^{2}
\Longrightarrow c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c_{1}(L)^{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(c_{1}(L)\)

Let \(f\) be the pull‑back of a point divisor on \(C\) (\(\deg f =1\) on \(C\)), and let \(H\) be the pull‑back of the hyperplane class from \(\mathbb P^{20}\).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr) &= \deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)\,f = 5\cdot\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(1)\bigr)f
                                   = 5\cdot 3\,f = 15f,\\
c_{1}(L) &= 15f + H .
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The class \(c_{2}(J^{1}(L))\)

\[
c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c_{1}(L)^{2} = (15f+H)^{2}=225f^{2}+30fH+H^{2}=30\,fH+H^{2},
\]
because \(f^{2}=0\) on a curve.

Hence the component of codimension two involving \(fH\) has coefficient **30**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Degree of \(D\)

The degree of a divisor in \(\mathbb P^{20}\) is  

\[
\deg D = \int_{\mathbb P^{20}} H^{19}\,[D]
       = \int_{C\times\mathbb P^{20}} H^{19}\,c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr).
\]

Only the term \(30\,fH\) contributes, giving  

\[
\deg D = 30 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{30}
\]

Let  

\[
V=H^{0}\bigl(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\bigr),\qquad \dim V =21 .
\]

For the fixed smooth cubic \(C\) put  

\[
L=\mathcal O_{C}(5)=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\!\mid _{C},\qquad 
\deg L =5\cdot 3 =15 .
\]

The restriction map \(V\to H^{0}(C,L)\) is surjective; indeed  

\[
h^{0}(C,L)=\deg L =15,
\qquad \dim V-h^{0}(C,L)=6,
\]

and the kernel consists of the conics multiplied by the equation of \(C\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Incidence variety  

Define  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid p\in C,\; Q\in \mathbf P(V),\; 
\operatorname{mult}_{p}(Q\cap C)\ge 2\}.
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the condition “\(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)” is
two linear conditions on the sections in \(V\); therefore the fibre  

\[
I_{p}= \{Q\mid (p,Q)\in I\}\subset \mathbf P(V)
\]

is a projective subspace \(\mathbf P^{18}\).
Consequently  

\[
\pi_{1}:I\longrightarrow C
\]

is a \(\mathbf P^{18}\)-bundle; \(\dim I =1+18=19\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The vector bundle description  

Let  

\[
\mathcal V = V\otimes \mathcal O_{C}\qquad(\text{rank }21).
\]

Evaluation of a section and its first derivative on \(C\) gives the **first jet
bundle** of \(L\),

\[
0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow \mathcal V 
\stackrel{\mathrm{ev}}{\longrightarrow} J^{1}(L)\longrightarrow 0,
\]

where  

* \(J^{1}(L)\) has rank \(2\) and degree  
  \(\deg J^{1}(L)=\deg L+\deg(L\otimes\Omega_{C})=15+15=30\);
* \(F\) is a rank‑\(19\) vector bundle, and  
  \(\deg F = -\deg J^{1}(L) = -30\).

The projective bundle \(\mathbf P(F)\) parametrises the pairs \((p,Q)\) with the
required tangency, i.e.  

\[
I \simeq \mathbf P(F),\qquad \xi:=c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P(F)}(1)\bigr).
\]

The pull‑back of the hyperplane class \(H\) from \(\mathbf P^{20}= \mathbf P(V)\)
to \(I\) is exactly \(\xi\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing the degree of the divisor  

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbf P^{20}\) is the image of \(I\) under the second
projection \(\pi_{2}:I\to \mathbf P^{20}\).  
Because for a general tangent quintic the tangency point is unique,
\(\pi_{2}\) is generically one‑to‑one, so  

\[
\deg D = \int_{I} \xi^{19}.
\]

For a projective bundle \(\pi:\mathbf P(F)\to C\) with \(\operatorname{rank}F=r\)
the push‑forward formula (see Fulton, *Intersection Theory*) is  

\[
\pi_{*}\bigl(\xi^{r-1+m}\bigr)=(-1)^{m}\,c_{m}(F),\qquad m\ge 0.
\]

Here \(r=19\) and we need \(m=1\) because \(r-1+m = 19\). Hence  

\[
\int_{\mathbf P(F)}\xi^{19}= \int_{C}(-c_{1}(F))
      = -\deg F = -(-30)=30 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Result  

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The restriction of a quintic to the smooth cubic \(C\) gives a line bundle  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\big|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(5)
\]

of degree  

\[
\deg L = 5\cdot \deg C =5\cdot 3 = 15 .
\]

Since \(C\) is a plane cubic, it has genus \(g=1\) and canonical bundle
\(K_{C}\simeq\mathcal O_{C}\).

---

### 1.  The discriminant on \(|L|\)

Consider the projective space of sections  

\[
\mathbf P\bigl(H^{0}(C,L)\bigr)=\mathbf P^{14},
\qquad \dim H^{0}(C,L)=\deg L =15 .
\]

A section \(s\) has a multiple zero at some point of \(C\) iff its
first jet \(j^{1}s\) vanishes somewhere.  
The bundle of first jets fits into  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes K_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)
\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Thus \(J^{1}(L)\) is a rank‑2 vector bundle on the curve with  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(L\otimes K_{C})
= \deg L + \deg (L\otimes K_{C})
= 15+0 =15 .
\]

The locus in \(\mathbf P^{14}\) where a section has a vanishing jet is
the degeneracy locus of a map of vector bundles of rank \(2\); its class
is \(c_{1}(J^{1}(L))\).  Hence the discriminant hypersurface in
\(|L|\) has degree  

\[
\deg(\text{discriminant}) = \int_{C} c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=15 .
\]

---

### 2.  Pull‑back to the space of quintics

The restriction map  

\[
\rho : \mathbf P\bigl(H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5))\bigr)
     =\mathbf P^{20}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{14}=|L|
\]

is a linear projection (its kernel has dimension \(5\)).  
The divisor \(D\subset\mathbf P^{20}\) is precisely the pull‑back
\(\rho^{-1}(\text{discriminant})\).  Pull‑back by a linear projection does
not change the degree, so

\[
\deg D = \deg(\text{discriminant}) = 15 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{15}
\]

The restriction map  

\[
r:H^{0}\bigl(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(5)\bigr)\longrightarrow 
H^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)
\]

is linear.  
Since \(\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=3\), we have  

\[
\mathcal O_{C}(5)=\mathcal O_{C}(1)^{\otimes 5},\qquad 
\deg \mathcal O_{C}(5)=5\cdot 3=15 .
\]

For a smooth elliptic curve the space of sections of a line bundle of degree
\(d\) has dimension \(d\); hence  

\[
h^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)=15,\qquad 
\dim |\,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\,| =14 .
\]

Thus \(r\) gives a linear projection  

\[
\pi:\mathbf P^{20}\dashrightarrow \mathbf P^{14}
\]

with centre the \(\mathbf P^{5}\) of quintics containing \(C\).

A quintic \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at some point \(p\) iff the restricted
section \(r(Q)\in |\,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\,|\) has a double zero at \(p\).
Hence the divisor \(D\subset\mathbf P^{20}\) is the pull‑back by \(\pi\) of the
discriminant divisor  

\[
\Delta\subset \mathbf P^{14}
\]

consisting of sections of \(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\) with a multiple zero.

The curve \(C\) embedded by \(|\mathcal O_{C}(5)|\) is an elliptic normal curve
of degree \(d=15\) in \(\mathbf P^{14}\).  Its dual variety is a hypersurface,
and the classical result on elliptic normal curves states that the degree of
the dual (the discriminant) equals \(2d\).  Consequently  

\[
\deg \Delta = 2\cdot 15 = 30 .
\]

Because \(\pi\) is linear, pulling back a homogeneous polynomial of degree
\(30\) on \(\mathbf P^{14}\) yields a homogeneous polynomial of the same degree
on \(\mathbf P^{20}\).  Therefore  

\[
\deg D = \deg \Delta = 30 .
\]

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{20}\) consists of those quintic curves whose restriction to the fixed smooth cubic \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\).
For a quintic \(Q\) the divisor \(Q\cap C\) on \(C\) has degree  

\[
\deg (Q\cap C)=5\cdot 3 =15 .
\]

Hence the restriction map  

\[
H^{0}\big(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\big)\;\longrightarrow\;
H^{0}\big(C,\mathcal O_{C}(5)\big)
\]

gives a complete linear series \(|\mathcal O_{C}(5)|\) of degree \(15\) and dimension \(14\) on the elliptic curve \(C\) (a \(g^{14}_{15}\)).  

A generic pencil of quintics corresponds, via this restriction, to a generic \(g^{1}_{15}\) on \(C\); i.e. a morphism  

\[
\phi : C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}
\]

of degree \(d=15\).  
Points of the pencil where the quintic is tangent to \(C\) are precisely the ramification points of \(\phi\) (the divisor on the pencil where the divisor on \(C\) acquires a double point).

For a map \(C\to\mathbb P^{1}\) the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives  

\[
\deg R = 2d + 2g - 2,
\]

where \(R\) is the ramification divisor and \(g\) the genus of \(C\).  
Since \(C\) is an elliptic curve, \(g=1\); thus  

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 15 + 2\cdot 1 - 2 = 30 .
\]

A generic pencil has only simple ramification, so each ramification point contributes weight \(1\). Consequently a generic line in \(\mathbb P^{20}\) meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly \(30\) points.

Therefore the degree of the divisor \(D\) in \(\mathbb P^{20}\) is  

\[
\boxed{30}
\]
