problems.problem:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a fixed smooth plane curve of degree \(e=5\).  
Consider the complete linear system of plane cubics \(|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(3)|\); its points correspond to degree‑3 curves in \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\).  
Denote by \(T\subset |\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(3)|\) the divisor consisting of those cubics that are tangent to \(C\) at some point of \(C\).  
Using the fact that for a point \(p\in C\) the condition “the cubic passes through \(p\) and has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)” imposes two independent linear conditions on the space of cubics, compute the degree of the divisor \(T\).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The space of plane cubics is  

\[
|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\simeq \mathbf P^{9},
\qquad 
\dim =\binom{3+2}{2}-1 = 9 .
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the two independent linear conditions  

* \(F(p)=0\) (the cubic passes through \(p\)),  
* the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\),

cut out a linear subspace  

\[
L_{p}\subset \mathbf P^{9}
\]

of codimension \(2\) (hence a \(\mathbf P^{7}\)).

---

### Incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,F)\in C\times \mathbf P^{9}\mid F\in L_{p}\}
\]

is a \(\mathbf P^{7}\)-bundle over the curve \(C\); thus  

\[
\dim I = 1+7 = 8 .
\]

The projection \(\pi : I\to \mathbf P^{9}\) has image the divisor  

\[
T=\bigcup_{p\in C}L_{p}\subset \mathbf P^{9}.
\]

The degree of \(T\) equals the number of points of intersection of \(T\) with a
general line (a pencil) \(\Lambda\simeq \mathbf P^{1}\subset \mathbf P^{9}\).

---

### Counting the intersection  

A pencil \(\Lambda\) corresponds to a 2‑dimensional subspace  

\[
W\subset V:=H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3))
\qquad (\dim V =10).
\]

For each point \(p\in C\) the two linear conditions give a linear map  

\[
\varphi_{p}: V \longrightarrow \mathcal O_{C}(3)\oplus\mathcal O_{C}(2)
\qquad
\bigl(f\mapsto (f(p),\; \partial_{\nu}f(p))\bigr),
\]

where the second component is the derivative of \(f\) in the direction
normal to the tangent line of \(C\) at \(p\).  
The bundle \(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\oplus\mathcal O_{C}(2)\) has rank \(2\) and degree  

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\bigr)+\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(2)\bigr)
=3e+2e =5e .
\]

Restrict \(\varphi_{p}\) to the pencil \(W\):
\[
\varphi_{p}|_{W}: W\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{C}(3)\oplus\mathcal O_{C}(2).
\]

The pencil contains a cubic tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) exactly when
\(\varphi_{p}|_{W}\) fails to be injective, i.e. when its \(2\times2\) matrix has
zero determinant.  
Thus the determinant gives a section of the line bundle  

\[
\det\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\oplus\mathcal O_{C}(2)\bigr)
 =\mathcal O_{C}(3+2)=\mathcal O_{C}(5),
\]

and its zero‑locus on \(C\) consists of  

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)=5e
\]

points (counted with multiplicities).  

For a general pencil the zeros are simple, so the number of cubics in the
pencil tangent to \(C\) is \(5e\).

---

### Plugging \(e=5\)

\[
\deg T = 5e = 5\cdot 5 = 25 .
\]

Hence the divisor of cubics tangent to a smooth plane quintic has degree  

\[
\boxed{25}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) is the projective space \(\mathbf P^{9}\).
For a point \(p\in C\) the conditions  

* “the cubic passes through \(p\)”  
* “the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)”

are two independent linear conditions on the space of cubics, so they define a
codimension‑2 linear subspace \(\Lambda _p\cong\mathbf P^{7}\subset\mathbf P^{9}\).

Let  

\[
I=\{(p,[F])\in C\times\mathbf P^{9}\mid [F]\in\Lambda _p\}
\]

and let \(\pi : I\to\mathbf P^{9}\) be the projection.  
The image \(\pi (I)=T\) is the divisor of cubics tangent to \(C\).

For a fixed cubic linear series \(|\mathcal O_{C}(3)|\) the map  

\[
\varphi_{|3|}:C\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{9}
\]

is given by the complete linear series of degree  

\[
d=\deg \mathcal O_{C}(3)=3e .
\]

The divisor \(T\) is precisely the dual hypersurface \(\varphi_{|3|}(C)^{\vee}\);
its degree equals the **class** of the embedded curve \(\varphi_{|3|}(C)\).
For a non‑degenerate smooth curve of degree \(d\) and genus \(g\) in projective
space, the class (and hence the degree of the dual variety) is  

\[
\text{class}=2d+2g-2 .
\]

For a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\) we have  

\[
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}.
\]

Thus, for our curve \(C\) with \(e=5\),

\[
d = 3e = 15,\qquad 
g = \frac{(5-1)(5-2)}{2}=6 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg T = 2d + 2g - 2 = 2\cdot 15 + 2\cdot 6 - 2 = 30 + 12 - 2 = 40 .
\]

\[
\boxed{40}
\]

For a point \(p\in C\) the condition  

* “the cubic passes through \(p\)”  

gives a linear functional on the space of cubics equal to the value of the cubic at \(p\).  
Restricting a cubic to \(C\) we obtain a section of \(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\); therefore this
condition corresponds to a section of the line bundle  

\[
L_{1}= \mathcal O_{C}(3).
\]

* “the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)”  

means that the derivative of the cubic in the (fixed) tangent direction of \(C\) vanishes at
\(p\).  The directional derivative of a degree‑3 homogeneous polynomial is a degree‑2
polynomial, so this condition corresponds to a section of  

\[
L_{2}= \mathcal O_{C}(2).
\]

Thus for each \(p\) we have two independent linear conditions, given by the two line bundles
\(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\).

---

### Incidence description

Let \(W\subset H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\bigr)\) be a generic
2‑dimensional subspace (a pencil of cubics).  
For each \(p\in C\) the restrictions of the two linear functionals to \(W\) give a
\(2\times 2\) matrix of sections of \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\).  
A member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) iff this matrix has a non‑trivial
kernel, i.e. iff its determinant vanishes.

Hence the locus of cubics in the pencil that are tangent to \(C\) is the zero divisor of a
section of the line bundle  

\[
\det = L_{1}\otimes L_{2}= \mathcal O_{C}(3)\otimes\mathcal O_{C}(2)=\mathcal O_{C}(5).
\]

The degree of this divisor on the curve \(C\) is  

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(5)\bigr)=5\;\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(1)\bigr)
      =5\cdot e =5\cdot 5 = 25,
\]

since \(\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=\deg C = e =5\).

Therefore a generic line (pencil) in the linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\)
meets the divisor \(T\) in exactly \(25\) points, i.e. the divisor \(T\) has degree \(25\).

\[
\boxed{25}
\]

For a fixed smooth plane quintic \(C\subset \mathbf P^{2}\) consider a generic pencil of plane cubics  
\[
\mathcal L \cong \mathbf P^{1}\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|.
\]

Restricting the cubics of the pencil to \(C\) gives a linear series of degree  

\[
d = 3\cdot \deg C = 3\cdot 5 = 15
\]

on \(C\).  
Since the base points of a generic pencil are not on \(C\), this linear series is a base‑point‑free \(g^{1}_{15}\); it defines a morphism  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(15\).

A cubic of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\) exactly when the divisor \(\varphi^{*}(t)\) (the intersection divisor of the cubic with \(C\)) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\) at \(p\).  
Thus the cubics that are tangent to \(C\) correspond to the ramification points of the map \(\varphi\).

For a morphism of degree \(d\) from a smooth curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\), the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives the total ramification degree

\[
\deg R = 2d + 2g - 2 .
\]

Here  

\[
d = 15, \qquad 
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{(5-1)(5-2)}{2}=6 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 15 + 2\cdot 6 - 2 = 30 + 12 - 2 = 40 .
\]

Each ramification point gives a cubic of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\) (and for a generic pencil the tangency is simple, so each cubic appears only once). Consequently, a generic pencil meets the divisor \(T\) in exactly \(40\) points, i.e. the divisor \(T\) has degree \(40\).

\[
\boxed{40}
\]

For a smooth plane curve \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) of degree \(e=5\) we have  

\[
g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{4\cdot 3}{2}=6 .
\]

The space of plane cubics is  

\[
|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\cong \mathbb P^{9}.
\]

---

### 1.  Tangency condition

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the requirements  

* “the cubic passes through \(p\)’’,
* “the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)”  

give two independent linear conditions on the space of cubics.  
Hence the cubics tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) form a linear subspace
\(L_{p}\simeq \mathbb P^{7}\subset\mathbb P^{9}\).

The divisor \(T\subset\mathbb P^{9}\) is the union of these \(\mathbb P^{7}\)’s as
\(p\) varies on \(C\).

---

### 2.  Degree of \(T\)

The degree of a divisor in a projective space equals the number of its
intersection points with a **generic line** (a pencil of cubics).  
Thus we take a general pencil \(\Lambda\simeq\mathbb P^{1}\subset\mathbb P^{9}\).

Restrict the pencil to the curve \(C\).  
A cubic meets \(C\) in \(3e=15\) points (counted with multiplicities), so the
pencil defines a linear series  

\[
g^{1}_{15}\;:\; C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}
\]

of degree \(d=15\).

A cubic in the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the corresponding
divisor on \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\); i.e. when the map
\(C\to\mathbb P^{1}\) is ramified at that point.

For a map of degree \(d\) from a curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbb P^{1}\),
the total ramification (Riemann–Hurwitz) is  

\[
\sum (e_{p}-1)=2d+2g-2 .
\]

Here \(d=15\) and \(g=6\), hence  

\[
\text{total ramification}=2\cdot15+2\cdot6-2=30+12-2=40 .
\]

Thus a generic pencil of cubics meets the divisor \(T\) in exactly \(40\)
points (counted with multiplicity). Consequently the divisor \(T\) has
degree \(40\) in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\cong\mathbb P^{9}\).

\[
\boxed{40}
\]

For a smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e=5\) let  

\[
V = H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\bigr),\qquad \dim V =10,
\]

so \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\simeq \mathbf P^{9}\).

---

### 1.  Incidence variety  

For a point \(p\in C\) the conditions  

* the cubic passes through \(p\);  
* it has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\),

are two independent linear conditions on \(V\).  
Hence the cubics tangent to \(C\) at a fixed \(p\) form a linear subspace
\(\mathbf P^{7}\subset \mathbf P^{9}\).

Define  

\[
I=\{(p,F)\mid p\in C,\;F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)| \text{ tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

The projection \(\pi_1:I\to C\) has fibre \(\mathbf P^{7}\); thus \(I\) is a
\(\mathbf P^{7}\)-bundle over the curve \(C\).

---

### 2.  From the incidence to the divisor  

Let \(L\subset V\) be a general 2‑dimensional subspace (a pencil of cubics);
its projectivisation is a line \(\ell\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\subset\mathbf P^{9}\).
The divisor \(T\) is the image of \(I\) in \(\mathbf P^{9}\); its degree is the
number of points of \(\ell\) that lie in \(T\), i.e. the number of cubics in
the pencil that are tangent to \(C\) somewhere.

For a fixed pencil \(L\) consider the restriction map  

\[
\phi : L\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\longrightarrow E,
\]

where \(E\) is the rank‑2 bundle on \(C\) whose fibre at \(p\) records the
value of a cubic at \(p\) and its derivative in the tangent direction of \(C\).
A point \(p\) gives a tangency for some cubic in the pencil iff
\(\phi_{p}:L\to E_{p}\) is not injective, i.e. \(\det\phi_{p}=0\).

Thus the tangency points of the pencil are the zeros of a section of the
line bundle \(\det E\) on \(C\); their number (counted with multiplicity) is  

\[
\deg(\det E)=\deg E .
\]

---

### 3.  Computing \(\deg E\)

The jet exact sequence on \(\mathbb P^{2}\) restricted to \(C\) gives  

\[
0\longrightarrow \Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}}|_{C}\otimes\mathcal O_{C}(3)
\longrightarrow J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\bigr)|_{C}
\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{C}(3)\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Composing with the natural map \(\Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}}|_{C}\to
\Omega^{1}_{C}\) yields  

\[
0\longrightarrow \Omega^{1}_{C}\otimes\mathcal O_{C}(3)
\longrightarrow E \longrightarrow \mathcal O_{C}(3)\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg E = \deg\bigl(\Omega^{1}_{C}\otimes\mathcal O_{C}(3)\bigr)+
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\bigr).
\]

For a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\),

\[
\deg\mathcal O_{C}(3)=3e,\qquad
\deg\Omega^{1}_{C}=2g-2,\qquad 
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}.
\]

With \(e=5\) we have \(g=6\), so  

\[
\deg\Omega^{1}_{C}=2\cdot 6-2 =10,\qquad
\deg\bigl(\Omega^{1}_{C}\otimes\mathcal O_{C}(3)\bigr)=10+3\cdot5=25.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\deg E = 25 + 15 = 40.
\]

---

### 4.  Degree of the divisor \(T\)

For a generic pencil \(\ell\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\) the
intersection \(\ell\cap T\) consists of \(\deg E = 40\) points (counted with
multiplicity). Consequently the divisor \(T\) in the linear system
\(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{40}.
\]

The space of plane cubics is  

\[
|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\simeq \mathbf P^{9},
\qquad 
\dim H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O(3))=10 .
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions  

* “the cubic passes through \(p\)’’  
* “the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)’’  

are two independent linear conditions on the 10‑dimensional vector space of cubics; their common solution is a linear subspace \(\mathbf P^{7}\subset\mathbf P^{9}\).

Hence the incidence variety  

\[
S=\{(p,F)\mid p\in C,\;F\text{ cubic},\;F \text{ passes through }p
\text{ and is tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}
\]

is a \(\mathbf P^{7}\)-bundle over the curve \(C\); \(\dim S =1+7=8\).
The projection \(\pi_2:S\to\mathbf P^{9}\) has image \(T\), a divisor in \(\mathbf P^{9}\).

To find the degree of \(T\) intersect it with a general line (a pencil) \(L\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\subset\mathbf P^{9}\).  
Restrict the pencil to the curve \(C\):
\[
\phi : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1},\qquad 
p\mapsto [F_{0}(p):F_{1}(p)],
\]
where \(F_{0},F_{1}\) generate the pencil.  
Since \(\deg (C\cap F)=3\cdot 5 =15\), the map \(\phi\) has degree  

\[
d = 15 .
\]

The genus of a smooth plane quintic is  

\[
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{4\cdot 3}{2}=6 .
\]

The ramification divisor \(R\) of \(\phi\) satisfies the Riemann–Hurwitz formula  

\[
2g-2 = d\,(2\cdot 0-2)+\deg R \;\Longrightarrow\;
\deg R = 2g-2 + 2d .
\]

Plugging \(g=6\) and \(d=15\),

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot6-2 + 2\cdot15 = 10 + 30 = 40 .
\]

A point \(p\in C\) is ramified exactly when the corresponding cubic of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\); therefore the image of the ramification divisor (the branch divisor) on the pencil consists of the cubics that are tangent to \(C\). Consequently, the number of such cubics in a generic pencil—i.e. the intersection number of \(T\) with the line \(L\)—equals \(\deg R = 40\).

Thus the divisor \(T\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{40}.
\]

For a plane curve \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) of degree \(e=5\) the space of plane cubics is  

\[
|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\cong \mathbf P^{9},
\qquad \dim =\binom{3+2}{2}-1 =9 .
\]

For a point \(p\in C\) the condition  

* “the cubic passes through \(p\)”  

* “the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)”

gives two independent linear conditions on the coefficients of a cubic, i.e. a codimension‑2 linear subspace \(H_{p}\simeq \mathbf P^{7}\subset \mathbf P^{9}\).

---

### Incidence description  

Let  

\[
I=\{(p,D)\mid p\in C,\; D\in H_{p}\}\subset C\times \mathbf P^{9}.
\]

The projection \(I\to \mathbf P^{9}\) has image the divisor \(T\).  
To find \(\deg T\) we intersect \(T\) with a general line \(L\subset \mathbf P^{9}\) (a pencil of cubics).  
The number of points \(|L\cap T|\) equals the number of members of a generic pencil that are tangent to \(C\) somewhere.

---

### Computation with a pencil  

Take a generic pencil generated by two cubics \(f_{0},f_{1}\).  
For a point \(p\in C\) the two linear conditions are

\[
\begin{cases}
f_{0}(p)+t\,f_{1}(p)=0 ,\\[2pt]
T_{0}(p)+t\,T_{1}(p)=0 ,
\end{cases}
\]

where \(T_{i}(p)\) denotes the linear functional expressing the tangent‑line condition for the cubic \(f_{i}\) at \(p\).

A member of the pencil satisfies both conditions iff the determinant vanishes:

\[
\Delta(p)=f_{0}(p)T_{1}(p)-f_{1}(p)T_{0}(p)=0 .
\]

* \(f_{i}(p)\) is a section of \(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\); on \(C\) this line bundle has degree \(3e = 15\).
* \(T_{i}(p)\) involves the partial derivatives of a degree‑3 polynomial, hence is a section of \(\mathcal O_{C}(2)\) whose degree is \(2e = 10\).

Thus \(\Delta(p)\) is a section of  

\[
\mathcal O_{C}(3)\otimes\mathcal O_{C}(2)=\mathcal O_{C}(5),
\]

which has degree  

\[
\deg\mathcal O_{C}(5)=5e = 5\cdot 5 = 25 .
\]

For a generic pencil the zeros of \(\Delta\) are simple, giving 25 distinct points \(p\in C\); each such point determines a unique cubic in the pencil tangent to \(C\) at \(p\).

Consequently a general line \(L\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) meets the divisor \(T\) in 25 points, i.e.

\[
\deg T = 25 .
\]

\[
\boxed{25}
\]

The linear system of plane cubics \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) is a projective space \(\mathbf P^{9}\).
For a point \(p\in C\) the conditions  

* “the cubic passes through \(p\)”,  
* “the cubic has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)”

are two independent linear conditions on the space of cubics, so over each \(p\) we obtain a linear subspace \(\mathbf P^{7}\subset \mathbf P^{9}\).

Let  

\[
I=\{(p,[F])\mid p\in C,\;[F]\in\mathbf P^{9},\;F\text{ passes through }p\text{ and }T_{p}F=T_{p}C\}.
\]

\(I\) is a \(\mathbf P^{7}\)-bundle over the smooth curve \(C\) (dimension \(1+7=8\)).
The projection \(\pi_2:I\to \mathbf P^{9}\) has image the divisor \(T\).

To find \(\deg T\) intersect \(T\) with a general line \(L\subset\mathbf P^{9}\) (a pencil of cubics).  
The pre‑image \(\pi_2^{-1}(L)\) consists of the pairs \((p,F)\) where \(F\) belongs to the pencil and is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\).  

Restricting cubics to \(C\) gives the complete linear series  

\[
| \mathcal O_{C}(3) | \cong g^{9}_{15},
\]

because \(\deg \mathcal O_{C}(3)=3\cdot 5 =15\) and, by Riemann–Roch,
\(h^{0}(C,\mathcal O_{C}(3)) = 15- g +1 = 15-6+1 =10\).

A generic line \(L\) in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) corresponds to a \(g^{1}_{15}\) on \(C\), i.e. a degree‑15 map  

\[
f:C\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}.
\]

A cubic in the pencil is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\) exactly when \(p\) is a ramification point of \(f\).  
By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula for a map of degree \(d\) from a curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\),

\[
\sum_{p\in C}(e_{p}-1)=2g-2+2d .
\]

Here \(d=15\) and \(g=6\), so

\[
\sum (e_{p}-1)=2\cdot 6-2+2\cdot 15 =10+30 =40 .
\]

For a general pencil all ramification is simple (\(e_{p}=2\)), thus there are exactly \(40\) distinct ramification points, each giving a distinct cubic of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\).

Hence a generic line in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) meets the divisor \(T\) in \(40\) points, i.e.

\[
\deg T = 40.
\]

\[
\boxed{40}
\]

For the linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) we have  

\[
\dim |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)| = h^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(3))-1
        = \binom{3+2}{2}-1 = 9 ,
\]

so the space of cubics is a projective space \(\mathbf P^{9}\).

---

### Incidence description  

Let  

\[
I=\{(p,F)\mid p\in C,\;F\text{ a cubic},\;
F(p)=0,\; \text{and }F\text{ has the same tangent line as }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

For a fixed \(p\) the two conditions “\(F(p)=0\)” and “\(F\) has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)” are two independent linear conditions on the coefficients of \(F\); hence the fibre over \(p\) is a linear subspace of codimension \(2\) in \(\mathbf P^{9}\).

The divisor \(T\subset \mathbf P^{9}\) is the image of the projection
\(\pi_{2}:I\to \mathbf P^{9}\).  
Its degree equals the number of points of intersection of a **generic
pencil** (a line \(\ell\subset \mathbf P^{9}\)) with \(T\).

---

### Restricting to a generic pencil  

Choose a generic pencil of cubics, generated by two independent cubics
\(F_{0},F_{1}\).  Write a member of the pencil as \(F_{s,t}=sF_{0}+tF_{1}\),
\((s:t)\in\mathbf P^{1}\).

For a point \(p\in C\) the two linear conditions become

\[
\begin{cases}
s\,F_{0}(p)+t\,F_{1}(p)=0,\\[2pt]
s\,\partial_{\nu}F_{0}(p)+t\,\partial_{\nu}F_{1}(p)=0,
\end{cases}
\]

where \(\partial_{\nu}F\) denotes a linear combination of the partial
derivatives of \(F\) that is orthogonal to the gradient of the defining
equation of \(C\) at \(p\).  
The first equation is linear in \((s,t)\) with coefficients of degree
\(3\) in the coordinates of \(p\); the second has coefficients of degree
\(2\).

A member of the pencil satisfies **both** conditions iff the two linear
forms in \((s,t)\) are proportional, i.e. iff their determinant vanishes:

\[
D(p)=
\begin{vmatrix}
F_{0}(p) & F_{1}(p)\\[2pt]
\partial_{\nu}F_{0}(p) & \partial_{\nu}F_{1}(p)
\end{vmatrix}=0 .
\]

Thus \(D(p)\) is a homogeneous polynomial on \(\mathbf P^{2}\) of degree  

\[
\deg D = 3+2 = 5 .
\]

---

### Counting the points on \(C\)

The curve \(C\) has degree \(e=5\).  For a generic pencil the polynomial
\(D\) does **not** contain \(C\) as a component, so by Bézout’s theorem
the zero‑locus of \(D\) meets \(C\) in

\[
\deg D \cdot \deg C = 5 \times 5 = 25
\]

points (counted with multiplicities).  Each such point gives a unique
cubic of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\) at that point. Consequently,
a generic line in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) meets the divisor
\(T\) in exactly \(25\) points.

Hence the divisor \(T\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{25}.
\]

problems.skill: Divisor class of tangency to a fixed curve
problems.problem:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a fixed smooth plane curve of degree \(e=4\).  
Consider the complete linear system \(|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(d)|\) with \(d=3\); its projectivization \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\) parametrizes all plane cubic curves.  
Inside \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\) let \(D\) be the divisor consisting of those cubics that are tangent to \(C\) at some (unspecified) point of \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\).  
A cubic meets \(C\) in \(d\cdot e\) points counted with multiplicity, and the condition that one of these intersection points has multiplicity at least two defines a codimension‑one condition on \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\).  
Using the adjunction formula for the smooth curve \(C\) inside \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) to compute its normal bundle, determine the degree of the divisor \(D\) (i.e. the integer \(k\) such that \([D]=kH\) where \(H\) is the hyperplane class on \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\)).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{N}\;(N=9)\) is the image of the incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,F)\mid p\in C,\;F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|,\; 
\operatorname{mult}_{p}(C\cap F)\ge 2\}
\]

under the projection to the second factor.  
For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions “\(F\) passes through \(p\)’’ and “\(F\) has the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\)” are two independent linear conditions on the space
\(H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\bigr)\).  
Hence over \(C\) we have a rank‑2 vector bundle whose fibre at \(p\) consists of those two linear equations.  

Let  

\[
V = H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\bigr)\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}^{\oplus 10},
\qquad 
J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3)) 
\]

be the first jet bundle of the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{C}(3)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|_{C}\).  
The evaluation of a section together with its first derivative gives a surjective morphism  

\[
\phi : V \longrightarrow J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3)),
\]

where \(\operatorname{rank} J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3)) = 2\).
The locus where a section has a zero of order \(\ge 2\) at a point of \(C\) is precisely the zero‑locus of the induced section of the rank‑2 bundle \(J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3))\).

Therefore the class of the divisor \(D\) in \(\mathbb P^{9}\) is the push‑forward of the second Chern class of this rank‑2 bundle:

\[
[D]=\pi_{*}\bigl(c_{2}(J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3)))\bigr),
\]

where \(\pi:C\to\text{pt}\) and we use the identification
\(\mathbb P^{9}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\cong |\mathcal O_{C}(3)|\) (restriction is injective because \(3<4\)).

For a line bundle \(L\) on a smooth curve \(C\) we have  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c_{1}(L)+K_{C},
\qquad 
c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=\deg(L)\,\deg(K_{C}) .
\]

Here \(L=\mathcal O_{C}(3)\).  
Its degree is  

\[
\deg L = d\cdot e = 3\cdot 4 = 12 .
\]

By adjunction for the smooth plane quartic \(C\),

\[
K_{C}= \bigl(K_{\mathbb P^{2}}+C\bigr)\!\big|_{C}
      =\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(-3+4)\!\big|_{C}
      =\mathcal O_{C}(1),
\qquad 
\deg K_{C}=e=4 .
\]

Hence  

\[
c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3))\bigr)=\deg L\;\deg K_{C}
                                          =12\cdot 4 = 48 .
\]

Pushing forward to \(\mathbb P^{9}\) multiplies this number by the degree of the embedding
\(C\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{9}\), which is exactly \(e=4\) (the hyperplane class on \(\mathbb P^{9}\) restricts to \(\mathcal O_{C}(1)\)).  
Consequently

\[
\deg D = e\;c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(\mathcal O_{C}(3))\bigr)
       = 4 \times 48 = 60 .
\]

Thus the divisor of plane cubics tangent to a fixed smooth quartic is a hypersurface of degree \(60\) in \(\mathbb P^{9}\).

\[
\boxed{60}
\]

The restriction of a cubic to the quartic curve \(C\) gives the line bundle  

\[
L=\mathcal O_{C}(3), \qquad \deg L = d\cdot e = 3\cdot 4 =12 .
\]

On the smooth curve \(C\) we have the jet bundle  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes \Omega _C \longrightarrow J^{1}(L) \longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

For a plane quartic, \(\Omega _C\simeq K_C\simeq\mathcal O_{C}(1)\) (since \(K_C=\mathcal O_{C}(e-3)=\mathcal O_{C}(1)\)).
Hence  

\[
L\otimes\Omega _C \simeq \mathcal O_{C}(4),\qquad 
\deg (L\otimes\Omega _C)=16 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\deg J^{1}(L)=\deg L+\deg (L\otimes\Omega _C)=12+16=28 .
\]

Consider the product \(C\times \mathbb P^{9}\) (here \(\mathbb P^{9}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\)).
Let \(\alpha=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{9}}(1))\) (pulled back to the product) and \(\beta\) the class of a point on \(C\).
The universal evaluation of the 1‑jet gives a section of the rank‑2 bundle  

\[
J^{1}(L)\boxtimes \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{9}}(1).
\]

Its zero‑locus has class  

\[
c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\boxtimes\mathcal O(1)\bigr)
      =c_{2}(J^{1}(L))+\alpha\,c_{1}(J^{1}(L))+\alpha^{2}
      =0+ \alpha\cdot 28\beta+\alpha^{2}.
\]

Projecting onto \(\mathbb P^{9}\) integrates over \(C\); only the term containing \(\beta\) survives:

\[
\pi_{*}\bigl(c_{2}\bigr)=28\,\alpha .
\]

Thus the divisor \(D\subset\mathbb P^{9}\) is linearly equivalent to \(28\) times the hyperplane class. Hence the degree of \(D\) is  

\[
k = 28.
\]

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

The linear system of plane cubics is  

\[
\mathbb P^{N}= \mathbb P\bigl(H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3))\bigr),\qquad N=9 .
\]

For a cubic \(F\) the intersection with the smooth quartic curve \(C\) gives a divisor  

\[
C\cap V(F)\in | \mathcal O_{C}(3) | .
\]

Because the exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3-4)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(-1)
   \longrightarrow \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)
   \longrightarrow \mathcal O_{C}(3)\longrightarrow 0
\]

has no \(H^{0}\) in the left term, the restriction map  

\[
H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3))
   \xrightarrow{\;\cong\;}
H^{0}(C,\mathcal O_{C}(3))
\]

is an isomorphism.  
Hence the divisor \(D\subset\mathbb P^{9}\) is exactly the discriminant
locus in the complete linear series \(|\mathcal O_{C}(3)|\) of the curve \(C\).

---

### Geometry of a generic pencil

Take a generic line \(\ell\subset\mathbb P^{9}\); it corresponds to a pencil
\(\{ \lambda F+\mu G\}\) of cubics.
Restricted to \(C\) this pencil gives a \(g^{1}_{d}\) on \(C\) with  

\[
d = \deg \mathcal O_{C}(3)=3\cdot e = 12 .
\]

Thus we have a morphism  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}
\]

of degree \(12\).  
A member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) precisely at the ramification
points of \(\varphi\): at such a point the fibre divisor acquires a double
point.

By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, the total ramification of a degree‑\(d\)
map from a curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbb P^{1}\) is  

\[
R = 2d + 2g - 2 .
\]

For our curve \(C\),

\[
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{3\cdot 2}{2}=3,
\qquad d = 12,
\]

so

\[
R = 2\cdot 12 + 2\cdot 3 - 2 = 24 + 6 - 2 = 28 .
\]

In a generic pencil the ramification points are simple and have distinct
images in \(\mathbb P^{1}\); consequently each ramification point gives a
different cubic in the pencil that is tangent to \(C\).

Hence a generic line in \(\mathbb P^{9}\) meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly
\(28\) points, i.e.  

\[
[D]=28\,H .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

The space of plane cubics is  

\[
\mathbb P^N = \mathbb P\bigl(H^{0}(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(3))\bigr)\cong \mathbb P^{9}.
\]

For the fixed smooth quartic \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) let  

\[
L = \mathcal O_{C}(3)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\big|_{C},
\qquad \deg L = 3\cdot 4 = 12 .
\]

Since \(h^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O(3)) = 10 = h^{0}(C,L)\), the restriction map is an isomorphism, so a cubic curve corresponds to a section of the line bundle \(L\) on \(C\).

A cubic is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\) iff the corresponding section \(s\in H^{0}(C,L)\) has a zero of order \(\ge 2\) at \(p\).  
Consider the first jet bundle of \(L\),

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes\Omega_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

For a section \(s\) its 1‑jet \(j^{1}(s)\) is a section of \(J^{1}(L)\); the condition “\(s\) has a double zero somewhere on \(C\)” is exactly “\(j^{1}(s)\) vanishes at some point of \(C\)”.  

Hence the divisor \(D\subset\mathbb P^{9}\) is the pull‑back of the zero section of \(J^{1}(L)\) via the universal section.  
Its degree equals the first Chern class of \(\det J^{1}(L)\):

\[
\det J^{1}(L)=L^{\otimes 2}\otimes\Omega_{C},
\qquad 
c_{1}(\det J^{1}(L)) = 2\deg L + \deg\Omega_{C}.
\]

For a smooth curve of genus \(g\),

\[
\deg\Omega_{C}=2g-2 .
\]

Our curve \(C\) is a quartic, so \(g=\frac{(4-1)(4-2)}{2}=3\).  
Thus

\[
\deg D = 2\cdot 12 + (2\cdot 3-2)=24+4 = 28 .
\]

Therefore the divisor of cubics tangent to the fixed quartic has class  

\[
[D]=28\,H\quad\text{in }\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb P^{9}),
\]

so its degree is \(28\).

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

The space of plane cubics is  

\[
\mathbb P^N = \mathbb P\big(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(3))\big)\cong \mathbb P^9 .
\]

For a fixed smooth plane quartic \(C\subset\mathbb P^2\) (degree \(e=4\)), the restriction map  

\[
H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(3)) \longrightarrow H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(3))
\]

is an isomorphism because both spaces have dimension \(10\).  
Hence we may identify \(\mathbb P^9\) with the projective space \(\mathbb P\big(H^0(C,L)\big)\) where  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_C(3),\qquad \deg L = 3\cdot 4 =12 .
\]

A cubic is tangent to \(C\) iff the corresponding section \(s\in H^0(C,L)\) has a zero of
multiplicity at least \(2\) somewhere on \(C\).
Let \(J^1(L)\) be the first jet bundle of \(L\); we have the exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes \Omega_C \longrightarrow J^1(L) \longrightarrow L \longrightarrow 0 .
\]

For a point \(x\in C\) the condition “\(s\) vanishes to order \(\ge 2\) at \(x\)” is the
vanishing of the 1‑jet of \(s\) at \(x\), i.e. the image of \(s\) in the fiber
\(J^1(L)_x\) is zero.  

Consider a generic pencil \(W\subset H^0(C,L)\) (a line in \(\mathbb P^9\)).
The map \(W\otimes\mathcal O_C\to J^1(L)\) is a morphism of rank‑2 bundles.
Its degeneracy locus, where the map drops rank, is the divisor on \(C\) defined by the
vanishing of its determinant, a section of  

\[
\det\big(J^1(L)\big)\otimes (\det W)^{-1}.
\]

Since \(\det W\) is constant, the class of this divisor is simply
\(c_1(\det J^1(L))\).  Therefore the number of points of the pencil that lie in the
tangency divisor \(D\) equals  

\[
\deg\big(\det J^1(L)\big)=\deg\big(L^{\otimes 2}\otimes K_C\big)
   =2\deg L + \deg K_C .
\]

For our curve,
\[
\deg L = d\cdot e = 3\cdot 4 = 12,\qquad
g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}=3,\qquad
\deg K_C = 2g-2 = 4 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg D = 2\cdot 12 + 4 = 28 .
\]

Thus the divisor \(D\) on \(\mathbb P^9\) is linearly equivalent to \(28\) times a
hyperplane class.

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\) has dimension  

\[
N=\binom{3+2}{2}-1=9 ,
\qquad \mathbf P^{N}= \mathbf P^{9}.
\]

For a point \(p\in C\) let  

* \(F(p)\) be the value of a cubic \(F\) at \(p\);
* \(D_{p}F\) be the directional derivative of \(F\) along the tangent direction of \(C\) at \(p\).

Both \(F(p)\) and \(D_{p}F\) are sections of the line bundle  

\[
\mathcal L:=\mathcal O_{C}(3)=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)\big|_{C}.
\]

Indeed \(\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=\deg C = e =4\); hence  

\[
\deg \mathcal L = 3\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=3e =12 .
\]

A cubic is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) iff  

\[
F(p)=0 ,\qquad D_{p}F=0 ,
\]

i.e. the pair \((F(p),D_{p}F)\in \mathcal L\oplus\mathcal L\) lies in the one–dimensional subspace
\(\{(a,a\lambda)\mid a\in\mathbb C\}\).  
For a fixed pencil of cubics \(\langle F_{0},F_{1}\rangle\) this condition is equivalent to  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
F_{0}(p) & F_{1}(p)\\[2pt]
D_{p}F_{0} & D_{p}F_{1}
\end{pmatrix}=0 .
\]

The determinant is a section of \(\mathcal L^{\otimes 2}\); therefore its zero‑locus on \(C\) is a divisor of class  

\[
2\,c_{1}(\mathcal L).
\]

Consequently the number of points of \(C\) where a member of a general pencil of cubics is tangent to \(C\) – which equals the degree of the divisor \(D\subset\mathbf P^{9}\) – is  

\[
\deg D = \deg\bigl(2c_{1}(\mathcal L)\bigr)=2\deg\mathcal L
       =2\,(3e)=2\cdot3\cdot4 = 24 .
\]

Thus the divisor \(D\) is linearly equivalent to \(24H\) on \(\mathbf P^{9}\).

\[
\boxed{24}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb{P}^{N}\) consists of those cubics whose restriction to the quartic curve \(C\) has a double zero somewhere on \(C\).
Let  

\[
L = \mathcal O_{C}(3)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\big|_{C},
\qquad \deg L = d\cdot e = 3\cdot 4 = 12 .
\]

The linear system \(|L|\) is identified with \(\mathbb P^{N}\) (\(N=9\)).
A double zero at a point \(p\in C\) means that the section \(s\in H^{0}(C,L)\) and its first derivative vanish at \(p\).
This is expressed by the vanishing of the universal jet section of the rank‑2 bundle  

\[
J^{1}(L)\otimes \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{N}}(1),
\]

where the first jet bundle fits into  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes K_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
c_{1}\big(J^{1}(L)\big)=c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(L\otimes K_{C})=2c_{1}(L)+K_{C}.
\]

The divisor \(D\) is the push‑forward to \(\mathbb P^{N}\) of the zero‑locus of the universal jet section; its class is therefore  

\[
[D]=\bigl(\deg c_{1}(J^{1}(L))\bigr)\,H .
\]

Now  

\[
\deg c_{1}(J^{1}(L)) = 2\deg L + \deg K_{C}
= 2\cdot 12 + (2g-2)
= 24 + (2\cdot 3-2)
= 24 + 4 = 28 .
\]

Thus  

\[
[D]=28\,H,
\]

so the degree of the divisor \(D\) is \(k=28\).

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

The condition that a cubic \(F\) be tangent to the fixed smooth quartic \(C\) means that the divisor \(F\cap C\) on \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\).  

For a pencil of cubics \(\mathbb P^{1}\subset \bigl|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)\bigr|\) the restriction to \(C\) gives a linear series  

\[
g^{1}_{de}=g^{1}_{12}\qquad (d=3,\;e=4)
\]

on the curve \(C\).  
A member of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly at the ramification points of this \(g^{1}_{12}\).  

If \(f:C\to\mathbb P^{1}\) is the map defined by the \(g^{1}_{de}\), the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives the total ramification

\[
\deg R = 2g(C)-2+2\deg f .
\]

Here  

\[
g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}=3,\qquad \deg f = de = 12,
\]

so  

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 3-2+2\cdot 12 = 28 .
\]

Thus a generic pencil of cubics meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly \(28\) points.  
Since the Picard group of the projective space \(\mathbb P^{N}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(3)|\) is generated by the hyperplane class \(H\), we have \([D]=kH\) with \(k=\deg D = 28\).

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

For the smooth quartic curve  

\[
C\subset \mathbf P^{2},\qquad \deg C =e=4,
\]

let  

\[
V=H^{0}\bigl(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(d)\bigr),\qquad d=3,
\]
so \(\dim V= \binom{d+2}{2}=10\) and \(\mathbf P^{9}= \mathbf P(V)\) parametrises plane cubics.

---

### 1.  Incidence description  

Consider  

\[
I=\{(p,[F])\in C\times \mathbf P^{9}\mid F\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

The projection \(\pi_{2}:I\to \mathbf P^{9}\) has image the divisor \(D\) we want.
For a fixed point \(p\in C\), “\(F\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)” means that the
restriction of \(F\) to \(C\) vanishes to order \(\ge 2\) at \(p\).

Because the restriction map  

\[
V \xrightarrow{\;\cong\;} H^{0}(C,\mathcal O_{C}(d))
\]

is an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension \(10\)), the condition is
linear on \(V\).  It is the vanishing of a section of the **first jet bundle**
\(J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(d)\bigr)\) at the point \(p\).

---

### 2.  Chern class of the jet bundle  

For a line bundle \(L\) on a smooth curve \(C\),

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes K_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0,
\]

so  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=2c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(K_{C}).
\]

Here \(L=\mathcal O_{C}(d)\) with \(\deg L = d\cdot e =3\cdot4 =12\), and  

\[
K_{C}= \mathcal O_{C}(e-3)=\mathcal O_{C}(1),\qquad \deg K_{C}=e(e-3)=4.
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=2\cdot 12+4 = 28.
\]

---

### 3.  Class of the incidence variety  

On \(X=C\times\mathbf P^{9}\) let  

\[
E=\pi_{2}^{*}\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{9}}(1)\otimes \pi_{1}^{*}J^{1}(L).
\]

\(E\) has rank \(2\); the universal section of \(E\) cuts out \(I\).  
Thus  

\[
[I]=c_{2}(E)=\pi_{2}^{*}H^{2}+2\,\pi_{2}^{*}H\;\pi_{1}^{*}c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr),
\]

where \(H=c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{9}}(1)\bigr)\).

Pushing forward by \(\pi_{2}\) (integrating over the fibre \(C\)) kills the term
\(\pi_{2}^{*}H^{2}\) and replaces \(\pi_{1}^{*}c_{1}(J^{1}(L))\) by its degree:

\[
\pi_{2*}[I]=2\bigl(\deg c_{1}(J^{1}(L))\bigr)\,H
          =2\cdot 28\,H=56\,H .
\]

The image \(\pi_{2}(I)=D\) is a divisor, and its class in \(\operatorname{Pic}
(\mathbf P^{9})\) is

\[
[D]=56\,H .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{56}
\]

For a smooth plane quartic  

\[
C\subset \mathbf P^{2},\qquad e=\deg C =4 ,
\]

the genus is  

\[
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}=3 .
\]

Let \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3)|\cong \mathbf P^{9}\) be the linear system of plane cubics.
For a general **pencil** (a line) \(L\subset \mathbf P^{9}\) the restriction of the cubics to \(C\) gives a
\(g^{1}_{12}\):

\[
V:= H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(3))\xrightarrow{\;\text{res}\;}
H^{0}(C,\mathcal O_{C}(3))\;,\qquad \dim V=2 .
\]

Since \(\deg \mathcal O_{C}(3)=3e=12\), the associated map  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

has degree \(12\).  
A cubic of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the corresponding
section of \(\mathcal O_{C}(3)\) has a double zero, i.e. when \(\varphi\) is
ramified at that point.  

For a map of degree \(n\) from a curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\),
Riemann–Hurwitz gives the total ramification degree  

\[
\deg R = 2g-2+2n .
\]

Here \(n=12\) and \(g=3\), hence  

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 3-2+2\cdot 12 = 6-2+24 = 28 .
\]

Thus a generic pencil of cubics meets the divisor \(D\) (the set of cubics
tangent to \(C\)) in exactly \(28\) points, counted with multiplicity.
Consequently the divisor class of \(D\) on \(\mathbf P^{9}\) is  

\[
[D]=28\,H ,
\]

so the degree of \(D\) is \(k=28\).

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

problems.skill: Divisor class of tangency to a fixed curve
problems.problem:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a fixed smooth plane curve of degree \(e=6\).  
Consider the complete linear system \(|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(4)|\) of plane quartic curves; its projectivization \(\mathbb{P}^{N}\) parametrises all quartic curves \(Q\).  
Let \(D\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}\) be the divisor consisting of those quartics that are tangent to \(C\) at some (unspecified) point of \(C\).  
Determine the degree of the divisor \(D\).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The linear system of quartic curves in \(\mathbb P^{2}\) has dimension  

\[
N = \binom{4+2}{2}-1 = 14 ,
\qquad\text{so } \mathbb P^{N}= \mathbb P^{14}.
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions that a quartic \(Q\)  

* passes through \(p\)  (\(Q(p)=0\)), and  
* is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) (the gradients of the defining equations are proportional),

are three independent linear conditions on the coefficients of \(Q\).  
Hence the set of quartics tangent to \(C\) at a given \(p\) is a linear subspace
\(\mathbb P^{11}\subset\mathbb P^{14}\).

Let  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid p\in C,\; Q\text{ tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}\subset C\times\mathbb P^{14}.
\]

The projection \(\pi_1:I\to C\) makes \(I\) a \(\mathbb P^{11}\)-bundle over the smooth
curve \(C\) (genus \(g=10\) because \(e=6\)). Thus \(\dim I = 1+11 =12\).

The projection \(\pi_2:I\to\mathbb P^{14}\) has image the divisor \(D\).
For a general quartic in \(D\) the tangency occurs at a single simple point,
so \(\pi_2\) is birational onto its image. Consequently the degree of \(D\)
equals the number of points of intersection of \(D\) with a generic line in
\(\mathbb P^{14}\); equivalently, the number of quartics in a generic pencil
that are tangent to \(C\).

A generic pencil of quartics determines a base‑point‑free \(g^{1}_{24}\) on \(C\):
each member of the pencil cuts a divisor of degree \(24=4\cdot 6\) on \(C\).
The associated morphism  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}
\]

has degree \(d=24\). By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, the total ramification
degree of \(\varphi\) is  

\[
\deg R = 2g-2 + 2d = 2\cdot 10 -2 + 2\cdot 24 = 18 + 48 = 66 .
\]

For a generic pencil the ramification points are simple, so there are exactly
\(66\) distinct ramification points. Each ramification point corresponds to a
unique member of the pencil whose intersection divisor with \(C\) has a
double point, i.e. a quartic tangent to \(C\) at that point.

Hence a generic pencil contains \(66\) quartics tangent to \(C\), which is the
intersection number of \(D\) with a line in \(\mathbb P^{14}\). Therefore

\[
\deg D = 66 .
\]

\[
\boxed{66}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{N}\) is the image of the zero–locus of the first jet of the universal quartic restricted to the fixed sextic curve \(C\).  
Using the jet exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow \Omega^{1}_{C}\otimes L \longrightarrow J^{1}(L) \longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0,
\qquad 
L = \operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{N}}(1)\otimes\operatorname{pr}_{1}^{*}\mathcal O_{C}(4),
\]

the class of this zero‑locus is  

\[
c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=c_{1}(L)\,c_{1}(\Omega^{1}_{C})+c_{1}(L)^{2}.
\]

Write \(h\) for the hyperplane class on \(\mathbb P^{N}\) and let \(\alpha\) be the class of a point on \(C\).  
For a plane curve of degree \(e=6\),

\[
c_{1}(\Omega^{1}_{C}) = K_{C}=e(e-3)\,\alpha = 18\,\alpha,
\qquad 
c_{1}\!\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(4)\bigr)=4e\,\alpha = 24\,\alpha .
\]

Hence  

\[
c_{1}(L)=\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}h+24\,\operatorname{pr}_{1}^{*}\alpha .
\]

Computing \(c_{2}(J^{1}(L))\) and intersecting with \((\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}h)^{N-1}\) (\(N=14\)) gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\deg D &=\int_{C\times\mathbb P^{N}}
\Bigl(\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}h\,\operatorname{pr}_{1}^{*}K_{C}
      +\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}h^{2}
      +2\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}h\,\operatorname{pr}_{1}^{*}(24\alpha)\Bigr)
      (\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}h)^{13}  \\
&= \bigl(\deg K_{C}\bigr) + 2\bigl(\deg\mathcal O_{C}(4)\bigr) \\
&= 18 + 2\cdot 24 = 66 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the divisor of quartics tangent to the smooth sextic curve has degree  

\[
\boxed{66}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbf P^{14}\) consists of quartic curves \(Q\) that are tangent to the fixed smooth sextic \(C\) at some point of \(C\).

Take a general line \(L\subset \mathbf P^{14}\); it is a pencil of quartic curves.  
The degree of \(D\) equals the number of members of this pencil that are tangent to \(C\) (counted with multiplicities).

Restrict the pencil to \(C\).  
Since the restriction map
\[
H^{0}\bigl(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)\bigr)\longrightarrow 
H^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(4)\bigr)
\]
is an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension \(15\)), the pencil gives a base‑point‑free linear series
\[
g^{1}_{24}=|\,\mathcal O_{C}(4)\,|
\]
on \(C\) (degree \(d=4\cdot 6 =24\), dimension \(r=1\)).

For a \(g^{r}_{d}\) on a curve of genus \(g\), the total ramification weight is given by the Plücker formula
\[
\deg R = (r+1)\bigl(d + r(g-1)\bigr).
\]
Here \(r=1,\; d=24,\; g=10\), therefore
\[
\deg R = 2\bigl(24 + 9\bigr)=2\cdot 33 = 66.
\]

Ramification points of the \(g^{1}_{24}\) are precisely the members of the pencil for which the divisor on \(C\) contains a point with multiplicity \(\ge 2\), i.e. the quartic curve is tangent to \(C\) at that point.  
For a generic pencil all ramification points are simple, so each contributes weight 1. Consequently the pencil contains exactly \(66\) quartics (counted with multiplicity) that are tangent to \(C\).

Hence the divisor \(D\) has degree

\[
\boxed{66}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)|\) has dimension  

\[
N = \binom{4+2}{2}-1 = 14 ,
\qquad 
\mathbb P^{N}= \mathbb P^{14}.
\]

Restricting a quartic to the smooth sextic \(C\) gives a section of the line bundle  

\[
L = \mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)\big|_{C}= \mathcal O_{C}(4),
\qquad 
\deg L = 4\cdot\deg\mathcal O_{C}(1)=4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

Since \(C\) has genus  

\[
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{5\cdot 4}{2}=10,
\]

Riemann–Roch gives  

\[
h^{0}(C,L)=\deg L-g+1 = 24-10+1 = 15,
\]

so the restriction map \(H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(4))\to H^{0}(C,L)\) is an isomorphism.  
Thus a quartic curve corresponds to a section of \(L\).

A quartic is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\in C\) iff the corresponding section \(s\) has a **double zero** at \(p\); i.e.  

\[
s(p)=0,\qquad \frac{ds}{dt}(p)=0
\]

(where \(t\) is a local coordinate on \(C\)).  
For a fixed \(p\) these are two independent linear conditions on the 15‑dimensional space of sections, so the set of sections having a double zero somewhere sweeps out a divisor \(D\subset\mathbb P^{14}\).

To find its degree, intersect \(D\) with a generic line (a pencil) in \(\mathbb P^{14}\).  
A generic pencil is given by two independent sections \(s_{0},s_{1}\in H^{0}(C,L)\).  
These define a morphism  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1},\qquad 
p\mapsto [s_{0}(p):s_{1}(p)],
\]

which is a degree‑\(d\) map with  

\[
d = \deg L = 24 .
\]

A point \(p\) where the pencil contains a section with a double zero is exactly a ramification point of \(\varphi\) (the differential \(d\varphi\) vanishes).  
For a morphism \(C\to\mathbf P^{1}\) of degree \(d\) the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives the total ramification degree  

\[
\deg R = 2g-2 + 2d .
\]

Substituting \(g=10\) and \(d=24\),

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot10 - 2 + 2\cdot24 = 20-2+48 = 66 .
\]

Each ramification point yields a unique quartic in the pencil that is tangent to \(C\) at that point, so the intersection of the pencil with \(D\) consists of \(66\) points (counted with multiplicity).  
Hence the divisor \(D\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{66}.
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{N}\) is the locus of quartics \(Q\) that are tangent to the fixed smooth sextic curve \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\).

---

### 1.  Incidence description  

Consider  

\[
I=\{(Q,p)\mid p\in C,\; Q(p)=0,\; \nabla Q(p)\ \text{is proportional to}\ \nabla F(p)\},
\]

where \(F=0\) defines \(C\) (degree \(e=6\)) and \(Q=0\) defines a quartic (degree \(d=4\)).  
For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions

* \(Q(p)=0\) (1 linear condition on the coefficients of \(Q\));
* \(\nabla Q(p)\) proportional to \(\nabla F(p)\) (2 independent linear conditions)

give a linear subspace of \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)|\) of codimension \(3\).  
Hence \(I\) is a \(\mathbb P^{11}\)-bundle over the curve \(C\); \(\dim I =1+11=12\).

The projection \(\pi:I\to |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)|\cong\mathbb P^{14}\) has image the divisor \(D\).

---

### 2.  Degree of \(D\)

The degree of \(D\) equals the number of points of intersection of \(D\) with a general line
\(L\simeq\mathbb P^{1}\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)|\) (i.e. the number of quartics in a generic pencil that are tangent to \(C\)).

Fix a generic 2‑dimensional subspace \(V\subset H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O(4))\) (the pencil).
For each \(p\in C\) the condition that some member of \(V\) be tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) is that the
restriction map  

\[
\phi_{p}: V\longrightarrow J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)\bigr)_{p}
\]

has rank \(\le 1\).  
Over the whole curve this gives a bundle morphism  

\[
\phi: V\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\; \longrightarrow\; J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)\bigr)\big|_{C},
\]

where \(\operatorname{rank}V=2\) and \(\operatorname{rank}J^{1}=3\).

The locus where \(\operatorname{rank}\phi\le 1\) is a degeneracy locus of expected codimension  

\[
(r-k)(s-k)=(2-1)(3-1)=2,
\]

hence a finite set of points on the curve.  
By the Thom–Porteous formula, its class (the number of points) is  

\[
c_{r-k}\!\left(J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O(4)\bigr)\big|_{C}\right)
      =c_{1}\!\left(J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O(4)\bigr)\big|_{C}\right)
      =\deg J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O(4)\bigr)\big|_{C}.
\]

---

### 3.  Computing \(\deg J^{1}(\mathcal O(4))|_{C}\)

The first jet exact sequence on \(\mathbb P^{2}\) is  

\[
0\longrightarrow \Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}}\otimes\mathcal O(4)
   \longrightarrow J^{1}(\mathcal O(4))
   \longrightarrow \mathcal O(4) \longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Restrict to \(C\).  
Since \(\deg\bigl(\mathcal O(1)|_{C}\bigr)=e=6\),

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O(4)|_{C}\bigr)=4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

For the cotangent bundle \(\Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}}\) we have \(c_{1}(\Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}})=-3H\); thus  

\[
\deg\bigl(\Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}}|_{C}\bigr)=(-3H)\cdot (eH) = -3e = -18 .
\]

Tensoring with \(\mathcal O(4)\) adds \(4\cdot e =24\) to the degree, giving  

\[
\deg\bigl(\Omega^{1}_{\mathbb P^{2}}\otimes\mathcal O(4)|_{C}\bigr)= -18 + 24 = 6 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\deg J^{1}(\mathcal O(4))|_{C}=6 + 24 = 30 .
\]

---

### 4.  Result  

The number of points of the degeneracy locus, i.e. the number of quartics in a generic pencil tangent to \(C\), equals \(30\). Consequently the divisor \(D\) in \(\mathbb P^{14}\) has degree

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)|\) has dimension  

\[
\dim H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)) = \binom{4+2}{2}=15,
\qquad 
\mathbb P^{N}= \mathbf P^{14}.
\]

For a fixed smooth sextic curve \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) (genus \(g=(6-1)(6-2)/2=10\)),
the restriction of \(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)\) to \(C\) is a line bundle  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_{C}(4), \qquad \deg L = 4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

Thus the complete linear series \(|L|\) is a \(g^{14}_{24}\) on \(C\).

---

### Tangency condition

A quartic \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\in C\) iff the divisor
\(Q\cap C\) has a double point at \(p\); equivalently the section of \(L\)
determined by \(Q\) vanishes to order at least \(2\) at \(p\).

For a **fixed point** \(p\) the conditions “\(Q(p)=0\)” and “the derivative of
\(Q\) along the tangent of \(C\) at \(p\) vanishes’’ are two independent linear
conditions on the coefficients of \(Q\). Hence the set of quartics tangent to
\(C\) at a given \(p\) is a linear subspace of codimension \(2\) in
\(\mathbf P^{14}\).

Consequently the divisor \(D\subset\mathbf P^{14}\) is the **dual variety** of
the embedded curve \(\varphi_{|L|}(C)\subset\mathbf P^{14}\).

---

### Degree of \(D\)

Take a general line \(\ell\subset\mathbf P^{14}\); it corresponds to a
pencil of quartics \(\{Q_t\}_{t\in\mathbf P^{1}}\).
Restrict the pencil to \(C\); we obtain a morphism  

\[
f : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(\deg L = 24\).  
A member \(Q_t\) of the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the fibre
\(f^{-1}(t)\) contains a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\), i.e. when \(t\) is a
ramification point of \(f\).

By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, for a map of degree \(d\) from a curve of
genus \(g\),

\[
\sum_{p\in C} (e_p-1)= 2g-2 + 2d .
\]

Here \(d=24\) and \(g=10\), so the total ramification is  

\[
2g-2 + 2d = 2\cdot 10 - 2 + 2\cdot 24 = 20 - 2 + 48 = 66 .
\]

Thus a general pencil meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly \(66\) points
(counted with multiplicities). By definition, this number is the degree of
the divisor \(D\).

\[
\boxed{66}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)|\) has dimension  

\[
N = \binom{4+2}{2}-1 = 14,
\qquad \mathbb P^{N}= \mathbb P^{14}.
\]

For a fixed smooth sextic curve \(C\) (genus \(g=\frac{(6-1)(6-2)}2=10\)), the restriction map  

\[
H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)\bigr)\longrightarrow H^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(4)\bigr)
\]

is an isomorphism; thus a quartic curve determines a divisor of degree  

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(4)\bigr)=4\cdot 6 = 24
\]

on \(C\).  
Hence a pencil (a line in \(\mathbb P^{14}\)) of quartics gives a \(g^{1}_{24}\) on \(C\), i.e. a morphism  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}
\]

of degree \(d=24\).

A quartic in the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the corresponding divisor on \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\).  
These are precisely the ramification points of \(\varphi\).

For a map of a smooth curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbb P^{1}\) of degree \(d\), the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives the total ramification degree  

\[
\deg R = 2g-2 + 2d .
\]

Here \(g=10\) and \(d=24\), so  

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 10-2 + 2\cdot 24 = 20-2+48 = 66 .
\]

A generic pencil has only simple ramification, so each ramification point corresponds to a distinct member of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\).  
Consequently a generic line in \(\mathbb P^{14}\) meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly \(66\) points, i.e.  

\[
\deg D = 66 .
\]

\[
\boxed{66}
\]

The linear system of plane quartics has dimension  

\[
N = h^{0}\bigl(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)\bigr)-1
     = \binom{4+2}{2}-1 = 15-1 = 14 .
\]

Let  

\[
L = \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)\big|_{C}= \mathcal O_{C}(4),
\qquad \deg L = 4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

A quartic \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p\in C\) iff the restriction
\(s_Q\in H^{0}(C,L)\) has a zero of order at least \(2\) at \(p\).
This is expressed by the vanishing of the first jet of \(s_Q\) at \(p\).

---

### Incidence variety  

Consider the product \(X = C\times \mathbb P^{N}\) with projections
\(\pi_1,\pi_2\).  
Let  

\[
E = J^{1}(L)\otimes \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{N}}(1)
\]

where \(J^{1}(L)\) is the first jet bundle of \(L\) on the curve \(C\).
\(E\) is a rank‑2 vector bundle on \(X\).
The universal section  

\[
\sigma : \mathcal O_{X}^{\oplus 15}\longrightarrow E
\]

evaluates a quartic together with its first derivative along \(C\).
Its zero locus  

\[
I = Z(\sigma)\subset X
\]

is precisely  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

Since \(\sigma\) is a regular section,  

\[
[I]=c_{2}(E)\cap [X].
\]

Projecting to the second factor,
\(\pi_2(I)=D\) is the divisor of quartics tangent to \(C\) somewhere.
Hence the degree of \(D\) is  

\[
\deg D = \int_{\mathbb P^{N}} \pi_{2*}\bigl(c_{2}(E)\cap[X]\bigr)\, H^{N-1},
\]

where \(H=c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{N}}(1)\bigr)\).

Because integration on a product splits,
\[
\deg D = \int_{X} c_{2}(E)\, \pi_2^{*}H^{\,N-1}.
\]

---

### Chern classes of \(E\)

The jet exact sequence on the curve \(C\) is  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes \Omega_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)
      \longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

For a smooth plane sextic,
\[
g(C)=\frac{(6-1)(6-2)}{2}=10,\qquad
\deg \Omega_{C}=2g-2=18 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg(L)=24,\qquad 
\deg(L\otimes\Omega_{C})=24+18=42 .
\]

Thus  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=\deg L+\deg(L\otimes\Omega_{C})=24+42=66,
\qquad c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)=0
\]
(because a curve has no 2‑cycles).

Tensoring with \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{N}}(1)\) adds the factor
\((1+H)^{2}\). Consequently  

\[
c_{2}(E)=c_{2}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)+2H\,c_{1}\bigl(J^{1}(L)\bigr)+H^{2}
        = 2\cdot 66\,H + H^{2}=132\,H + H^{2}.
\]

---

### Computing the degree

Insert \(c_{2}(E)\) into the integral:

\[
\deg D = \int_{X} \bigl(132\,H + H^{2}\bigr)\, H^{\,N-1}
        = 132\int_{X} H^{\,N} + \int_{X} H^{\,N+1}.
\]

Here \(N=14\). On \(X=C\times\mathbb P^{N}\),

\[
\int_{X} H^{\,14}= \Bigl(\int_{C}1\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb P^{N}} H^{14}\Bigr)=1\cdot1=1,
\]
while \(H^{15}=0\) because \(\dim\mathbb P^{N}=14\).

Therefore  

\[
\deg D = 132\cdot 1 + 0 = 132 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{132}
\]

For a smooth plane sextic \(C\subset \mathbf P^{2}\) let  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_{C}(4)=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)\big|_{C},
\qquad \deg L =4\cdot 6 = 24,
\qquad g(C)=\frac{(6-1)(6-2)}{2}=10 .
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4)|\) restricts surjectively to the complete linear series \(|L|\) on \(C\); both have dimension \(14\).  
Hence the divisor \(D\subset \mathbf P^{14}=| \mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(4) |\) is the pull‑back of the discriminant divisor in \(|L|\) consisting of sections whose divisor on \(C\) has a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\).

---

### Incidence description

Consider the incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,s)\in C\times \mathbf P^{14}\mid s\text{ vanishes to order }\ge 2\text{ at }p\}.
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the condition “order \(\ge 2\) at \(p\)” is a linear condition of codimension \(2\) on the space of sections, i.e. a linear subspace \(\mathbf P^{12}\subset \mathbf P^{14}\).  
Thus \(I\) is a divisor in the product \(C\times \mathbf P^{14}\).

Let \(\pi_2 : C\times \mathbf P^{14}\to \mathbf P^{14}\) be the projection; then \(D=\pi_2(I)\).  
Because for a general quartic there is at most one point of tangency, \(\pi_2|_I\) is generically one‑to‑one, so \(\deg D\) equals the degree of the divisor \(I\) on a general line (pencil) in \(\mathbf P^{14}\).

---

### Computation via the first jet bundle

Let \(V=H^{0}(C,L)\) (dimension \(15\)).  
For a point \(p\in C\) the evaluation of a section together with its first derivative gives a linear map  

\[
\phi_p : V \longrightarrow J^{1}(L)_p ,
\]

where \(J^{1}(L)\) is the first jet bundle of \(L\).  
A section has a double zero at \(p\) iff it lies in \(\ker\phi_p\).

Over \(C\) we have the bundle map  

\[
\Phi : V\otimes\mathcal O_C \longrightarrow J^{1}(L).
\]

For a fixed pencil \(V'\subset V\) (rank \(2\) subbundle) the locus of points where some member of the pencil has a double zero is the degeneracy locus where \(\Phi|_{V'}\) drops rank, i.e. where its determinant vanishes.  
On a curve the determinant is a section of  

\[
\det (V'^{\!*})\otimes\det J^{1}(L) \cong \det J^{1}(L),
\]

so the associated divisor class is \(c_1(J^{1}(L))\).

From the exact sequence for the jet bundle  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes\Omega_C \longrightarrow J^{1}(L) \longrightarrow L \longrightarrow 0,
\]

we obtain  

\[
c_1(J^{1}(L)) = c_1(L)+c_1(L\otimes\Omega_C)
               = \deg L + (\deg L + \deg\Omega_C)
               = 2\deg L + (2g-2).
\]

Substituting \(\deg L =24\) and \(g=10\),

\[
\deg D = 2\cdot 24 + (2\cdot 10 - 2)=48+18=66.
\]

Thus a general pencil of plane quartics meets the divisor \(D\) in \(66\) points, i.e. the divisor \(D\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{66}.
\]

The condition that a quartic \(Q\) be tangent to the fixed sextic curve \(C\) at a point \(p\in C\) imposes two linear conditions on the coefficients of \(Q\):  

* \(Q(p)=0\) (the curve passes through \(p\));  
* the gradient of \(Q\) at \(p\) is proportional to the gradient of the defining equation of \(C\) at \(p\).

Hence for a fixed point \(p\) the set of quartics tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) is a linear subspace of codimension \(2\) in \(\mathbb P^{14}\).

Let a general line \(L\subset\mathbb P^{14}\) be spanned by two independent quartic forms
\(F_{0},F_{1}\).  
For a point \(p\in C\) write  

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_i(p)&=F_i(p)\qquad (i=0,1),\\[2pt]
v_i(p)&=\partial_y G(p)\,\partial_x F_i(p)-\partial_x G(p)\,\partial_y F_i(p),
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(G\) defines the sextic \(C\).  
\(u_i\) is a section of \(\mathcal O_C(4)\) and \(v_i\) a section of \(\mathcal O_C(8)\).

A quartic in the pencil \(L\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) iff there exist
\((\lambda,\mu)\neq(0,0)\) such that  

\[
\lambda u_0(p)+\mu u_1(p)=0,\qquad
\lambda v_0(p)+\mu v_1(p)=0 .
\]

This has a non‑trivial solution exactly when the determinant

\[
\Delta(p)=u_0(p)v_1(p)-u_1(p)v_0(p)
\]

vanishes.  \(\Delta\) is a section of the line bundle  

\[
\mathcal O_C(4)\otimes\mathcal O_C(8)=\mathcal O_C(12).
\]

Therefore the divisor on \(C\) defined by \(\Delta=0\) has degree  

\[
\deg \mathcal O_C(12)=12\cdot\deg\mathcal O_C(1)=12\cdot 6=72,
\]

since \(\deg \mathcal O_C(1)=\deg C =6\).

For a generic line \(L\) the zeros of \(\Delta\) are simple, so the number of
quartics in the pencil that are tangent to \(C\) is exactly \(72\).  Hence the
hypersurface \(D\subset\mathbb P^{14}\) has degree \(72\).

\[
\boxed{72}
\]
