problems.problem:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a fixed smooth plane curve of degree \(e=5\).  
Consider the complete linear system of plane conics \(|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{2}}(2)|\); its projectivization is a projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) with hyperplane class \(h\).  
Denote by \(D\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\) the divisor consisting of those conics that are tangent to \(C\) at some (unspecified) point of \(C\).  
Using the universal conic and the fact that tangency imposes one additional linear condition beyond passing through a point of \(C\), compute the degree of the divisor \(D\) (i.e. the number of points in the intersection of \(D\) with a general line in \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\)).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
For the universal conic  

\[
\mathcal U=\{(x,Q)\in\mathbf P^{2}\times\mathbf P^{5}\mid Q(x)=0\}
\]

let  

* \(L\) be the pull‑back of the hyperplane class from \(\mathbf P^{2}\);
* \(H\) be the pull‑back of the hyperplane class from \(\mathbf P^{5}\).

\[
[\mathcal U]=2L+H\qquad(\text{bidegree }(2,1)).
\]

---

### Incidence defining tangency  

A conic \(Q\) is tangent to the fixed smooth quintic \(C\) at a point \(p\) iff  

1. \(p\in C\)                      \(eL\)   (with \(e=5\));
2. \(Q(p)=0\)                     \((2L+H)\);
3. the tangent line of \(Q\) at \(p\) coincides with that of \(C\).

The third condition is linear in the coefficients of \(Q\); its coefficients are the
partial derivatives \(\partial C/\partial x_i(p)\), which are homogeneous of degree \(e-1=4\) in the coordinates of \(p\).  
Since \(\partial Q(p)\) is linear in the coordinates of \(p\), the condition
\(\partial Q(p)\wedge\partial C(p)=0\) has bidegree \((5,1)\); its class is  

\[
5L+H .
\]

Hence the incidence variety \(I\subset\mathbf P^{2}\times\mathbf P^{5}\) of
\((p,Q)\) with \(Q\) tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) has class  

\[
[I]=eL\;(2L+H)\;(5L+H)
      =e\bigl(10L^{3}+7L^{2}H+LH^{2}\bigr).
\]

---

### Push‑forward to \(\mathbf P^{5}\)

The projection \(\pi_2:\mathbf P^{2}\times\mathbf P^{5}\to\mathbf P^{5}\) has
fibres \(\mathbf P^{2}\).  For a product class \(L^{a}H^{b}\),

\[
\pi_{2*}(L^{a}H^{b})=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\Bigl(\int_{\mathbf P^{2}}L^{2}\Bigr)H^{b}=H^{b}, & a=2,\\[4pt]
0, & a\neq2 .
\end{cases}
\]

Only the term with \(L^{2}H\) survives:

\[
\pi_{2*}[I]=e\cdot 7\,H =5\cdot 7\,H =35\,H .
\]

Thus the divisor \(D\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) of conics tangent to \(C\) is
linearly equivalent to \(35\) times a hyperplane; its degree (the number of
points of intersection with a general line in \(\mathbf P^{5}\)) is  

\[
\boxed{35}.
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb P^{5}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2)|\) consists of conics that are tangent to the fixed smooth quintic curve \(C\).

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conditions  

* “the conic passes through \(p\)” – one linear condition,  

* “the conic is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)” – one additional linear condition  

give a linear subspace \(\mathbb P^{3}\subset \mathbb P^{5}\).  
Hence \(D\) is the image of the incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid p\in C,\; Q\text{ tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}\subset C\times\mathbb P^{5}
\]

and \(D\) is a hypersurface in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

---

### Intersecting with a general line  

Take a general line \(L\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) (a pencil of conics).  
Restrict the complete linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2)|\) to \(C\).  
Since \(\deg C =5\),

\[
\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(2)\bigr)=2\cdot5=10 .
\]

The restriction gives a \(g^{4}_{10}\) on \(C\).  
A line \(L\) in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) gives a one‑dimensional sub‑linear series,
i.e. a \(g^{1}_{10}\) (a morphism \(\varphi:C\to\mathbb P^{1}\) of degree \(10\)).

For a \(g^{1}_{d}\) the ramification divisor has degree (Riemann–Hurwitz)

\[
\deg R = 2g-2 + 2d,
\]

where \(g\) is the genus of \(C\) and \(d\) the degree of the map.
For a smooth plane quintic,
\[
g=\frac{(5-1)(5-2)}{2}=6,\qquad d=10 .
\]

Hence

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 6 - 2 + 2\cdot 10 = 12 - 2 + 20 = 30 .
\]

A ramification point of \(\varphi\) is exactly a point where the corresponding
conic in the pencil meets \(C\) with multiplicity at least \(2\), i.e. where the
conic is tangent to \(C\).  

Thus a general pencil of conics meets the divisor \(D\) in \(30\) points,
counted with multiplicity. Consequently the degree of the divisor \(D\) is

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

The divisor \(D\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) consists of conics that are tangent to the fixed smooth quintic curve \(C\).  
For a general pencil (a line) of conics the number of members that are tangent to \(C\) equals the degree of \(D\).

Restrict a general pencil of conics to the curve \(C\).  
Each conic meets \(C\) in \(2e=10\) points (counted with multiplicities).  
Thus the pencil defines a \(g^{1}_{10}\) on \(C\).  

For a map \(f:C\to\mathbb P^{1}\) of degree \(d\) the total ramification is

\[
\deg R = 2g(C)+2d-2 .
\]

Here \(g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}2 =6\) (since \(e=5\)) and \(d=10\). Hence

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 6 + 2\cdot 10 - 2 = 12 + 20 - 2 = 30 .
\]

A ramification point of the \(g^{1}_{10}\) corresponds exactly to a conic of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\) at that point.  
For a general pencil each tangent conic is simply tangent at a single point, so the number of tangent conics in the pencil equals the degree of the ramification divisor, i.e. \(30\).

Therefore the divisor \(D\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The divisor \(D\subset \mathbb{P}^{5}\) parametrises conics that are tangent to the fixed smooth quintic curve \(C\).
A general line \(L\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\) corresponds to a pencil of plane conics.
For a conic \(Q\) in the pencil we have  

\[
Q\cap C = 10 \text{ points (counted with multiplicities)},
\]

because \(\deg Q =2\) and \(\deg C =5\).

Hence the pencil defines a morphism  

\[
f : C \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1},
\qquad p\mapsto \text{the member of the pencil containing }p .
\]

The degree of this map is the number of intersection points of a general conic with \(C\), i.e.  

\[
\deg f = 2\cdot 5 = 10 .
\]

A conic in the pencil is tangent to \(C\) exactly when the fibre of \(f\) over the corresponding point of \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) contains a point of multiplicity \(\ge 2\); in other words, when \(f\) is ramified at that point of \(C\).

For a smooth plane quintic the genus is  

\[
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}= \frac{4\cdot 3}{2}=6 .
\]

Applying the Riemann–Hurwitz formula to \(f\),

\[
\sum_{p\in C} (e_{p}-1)= 2g-2 + 2\deg f
        = 2\cdot 6 -2 + 2\cdot 10 = 30 ,
\]

where \(e_{p}\) is the ramification index at \(p\).  For a general pencil all ramification points are simple, so the total number of ramification points (i.e. tangencies) is \(30\).

Therefore a general line in \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) meets the divisor \(D\) in \(30\) points, and the degree of \(D\) is

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

The restriction of a pencil of conics to the smooth plane quintic \(C\) gives a linear series of degree  

\[
\deg (Q|_C)=2\cdot e = 10 .
\]

Hence a general pencil defines a morphism  

\[
\varphi : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(d =10\).  
For a map of a smooth curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\) the total ramification is, by Riemann–Hurwitz,

\[
R = 2g-2 + 2d .
\]

For a plane curve of degree \(e\) we have  

\[
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2},\qquad d = 2e .
\]

Thus  

\[
R = 2\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2} -2 + 4e
   = (e-1)(e-2) -2 + 4e
   = e^{2}+e = e(e+1).
\]

Each simple ramification point corresponds to a conic in the pencil that is tangent to \(C\) at that point, and for a general pencil these ramification points are all simple and occur at distinct conics. Consequently the number of conics in a general pencil that are tangent to \(C\) equals the total ramification \(R\).

For \(e =5\),

\[
R = 5\cdot (5+1)=30 .
\]

Hence the divisor \(D\subset \mathbf P^{5}\) of conics tangent to the quintic curve has degree  

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

The linear system of plane conics \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2)|\) is \(\mathbf P^{5}\) with hyperplane class \(h\).
For a fixed smooth quintic curve \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) (\(e=5\)) consider  

\[
D=\{\,Q\in\mathbf P^{5}\mid Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at some point}\,\}.
\]

---

### 1.  Tangency condition

For a point \(p\in C\) the set of conics tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) is obtained by imposing  

* the conic passes through \(p\)  (\(1\) linear condition),  
* the conic has the same tangent direction as \(C\) at \(p\)  (\(1\) extra linear condition).

Hence for each \(p\) we get a linear subspace of \(\mathbf P^{5}\) of codimension \(2\); i.e. a \(\mathbf P^{3}\).

Let  

\[
\mathcal I=\{(p,Q)\in C\times \mathbf P^{5}\mid Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

\(\mathcal I\) is a \(\mathbf P^{3}\)-bundle over \(C\); the projection \(\pi_2:\mathcal I\to \mathbf P^{5}\) has image \(D\).

---

### 2.  Restriction of the conic linear system to \(C\)

Restricting conics to \(C\) gives a linear series on \(C\)

\[
| \mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2) |_{C}=g^{4}_{10},
\]

because  

\[
\deg(\mathcal O_{C}(2)) = 2e =10,\qquad
g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}2 =6,\qquad
h^{0}(\mathcal O_{C}(2)) =10-6+1 =5,
\]

so the projective dimension is \(4\).

A **pencil** of conics corresponds to a \(g^{1}_{10}\) on \(C\); its members intersect \(C\) in a divisor of degree \(10\).

---

### 3.  Tangency in a pencil = ramification of the \(g^{1}_{10}\)

For a map \(f:C\to\mathbf P^{1}\) defined by a \(g^{1}_{d}\) the total ramification is, by Riemann–Hurwitz,

\[
\deg R = 2d+2g-2 .
\]

Here \(d=10\) and \(g=6\), therefore

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 10 + 2\cdot 6 -2 = 20+12-2 = 30 .
\]

A ramification point of the \(g^{1}_{10}\) is exactly a point \(p\in C\) where the corresponding conic of the pencil is **tangent** to \(C\) at \(p\).  
For a general pencil all ramification points are simple, so each ramification point gives a distinct conic of the pencil that is tangent to \(C\).

Consequently a **general line** \(L\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) (i.e. a pencil of conics) meets the divisor \(D\) in exactly \(30\) points.

---

### 4.  Degree of \(D\)

Since \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^{5})=\mathbb Z\cdot h\) and the degree of a divisor is its intersection with a general line, we have  

\[
D \sim a\,h,\qquad a = D\cdot L = 30 .
\]

Thus the degree of the divisor of conics tangent to a fixed smooth quintic curve is  

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

For a smooth plane quintic  

\[
C\subset \mathbf P^{2},\qquad \deg C=e=5,
\]

the linear system of conics is  

\[
| \mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2) | \cong \mathbf P^{5},
\]

with hyperplane class \(h\).

---

### 1.  Tangency condition as a discriminant

Restrict a conic \(Q\) to the curve \(C\).  
From the exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(-3)\longrightarrow 
\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2)\longrightarrow 
\mathcal O_{C}(2)\longrightarrow 0
\]

and \(h^{0}(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(-3))=0\) we obtain an **isomorphism**

\[
H^{0}\!\bigl(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2)\bigr)
\;\xrightarrow{\;\cong\;}\;
H^{0}\!\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(2)\bigr).
\]

Thus a conic determines a section of the line bundle  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_{C}(2)=\mathcal O_{C}(e-3)=K_{C},
\]

which is the **canonical bundle** of \(C\).  
Hence the space of conics is identified with the projective space
\(\mathbf P\bigl(H^{0}(C,K_{C})\bigr)=\mathbf P^{5}\).

The zero‑divisor of a section of \(K_{C}\) is a canonical divisor of
degree  

\[
\deg K_{C}=2g-2=10\qquad (g=\text{genus of }C=6).
\]

A conic is **tangent** to \(C\) at a point \(p\) exactly when the
corresponding section of \(K_{C}\) vanishes to order at least \(2\) at
\(p\); i.e. the canonical divisor has a double point.  
Thus \(D\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) is the discriminant locus of the linear
series \(|K_{C}|=g^{5}_{10}\).

---

### 2.  Class of the discriminant of a \(g^{r}_{d}\)

For a linear series \(g^{r}_{d}\) on a smooth curve, the discriminant
(the set of sections having a double zero) is a divisor in the projective
space \(\mathbf P^{r}\) whose class is

\[
(r+1)(d-r)\,h .
\]

(See e.g. Harris, *Algebraic Geometry*, Example 2.5.)

In our situation  

\[
r = 5,\qquad d = 10,
\]

so the class of \(D\) is  

\[
(5+1)(10-5)\,h = 6\cdot5\,h = 30\,h .
\]

Hence the degree of the divisor \(D\) – the number of points in the
intersection of \(D\) with a general line in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) – is

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

The incidence variety  

\[
I=\{(p,Q)\mid p\in C,\; Q\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2)|,\; p\in Q,\; Q \text{ tangent to }C \text{ at }p\}
\]

is a \(\mathbf P^{3}\)-bundle over the smooth curve \(C\); for a fixed \(p\) the conditions “\(Q\) passes through \(p\)” and “\(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\)” are two independent linear conditions on the 6‑dimensional space of conics, leaving a \(\mathbf P^{3}\).

Projecting \(I\) to \(\mathbf P^{5}=|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2)|\) gives the divisor  

\[
D\subset \mathbf P^{5}
\]

of conics tangent to \(C\).

---

### Intersecting \(D\) with a general line

A general line \(L\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) corresponds to a pencil of conics \(\{Q_t\}_{t\in\mathbf P^{1}}\).  
Restrict this pencil to the curve \(C\):

\[
Q_t|_{C}\in |\mathcal O_{C}(2)|
\]

Because for a plane quintic \(C\) we have \(K_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2)\), the complete linear system \(|\mathcal O_{C}(2)|\) is the canonical series \(g^{5}_{10}\).  
A line in \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2)|\) gives a **pencil** \(g^{1}_{10}\) on \(C\); i.e. a morphism  

\[
f : C \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree  

\[
d = \deg (\mathcal O_{C}(2)) = 2\cdot e = 10 .
\]

The points of the pencil for which the conic is tangent to \(C\) are precisely the ramification points of \(f\).  
For a map of degree \(d\) from a smooth curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\), the total ramification degree is given by Riemann–Hurwitz:

\[
\deg R = 2g-2+2d .
\]

Here \(g(C)=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}=6\) and \(d=10\), so

\[
\deg R = 2\cdot 6 - 2 + 2\cdot 10 = 12 - 2 + 20 = 30 .
\]

For a general pencil the ramification is simple, hence there are exactly \(30\) distinct conics in the pencil that are tangent to \(C\).

Thus a general line in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) meets the divisor \(D\) in \(30\) points, i.e.  

\[
\deg D = 30 .
\]

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

The space of conics is  

\[
\mathbb P^5 = \mathbb P\bigl(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2))\bigr),\qquad 
\dim H^0(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2)) =6 .
\]

Restrict a conic to the fixed smooth quintic curve \(C\).  
Put  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_C(2),\qquad \deg L = 2\cdot 5 =10 ,\qquad 
g(C)=\frac{(5-1)(5-2)}2 =6 .
\]

The restriction map  

\[
\rho : H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2))\longrightarrow 
H^0(C,L)
\]

is surjective; \(\dim H^0(C,L)=5\) (Riemann–Roch) and \(\ker\rho\) is 1‑dimensional.

For a point \(p\in C\) the condition that a conic be tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) is that the
restricted section lies in  

\[
H^0\bigl(C,L(-2p)\bigr)\subset H^0(C,L),
\]

which has codimension \(2\).  Hence for each \(p\) we obtain a linear subspace
\(\mathbb P^3\subset \mathbb P^5\) of conics tangent to \(C\) at \(p\).

Let  

\[
Q:=\frac{H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2))}{H^0\bigl(C,L(-2p)\bigr)}
\]

be the rank‑2 bundle on \(C\) whose fibre is the space of jets of sections of \(L\) at \(p\).
This is the first jet bundle \(J^1(L)\) and fits into the exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes\Omega_C \longrightarrow J^1(L)\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\det J^1(L)=L\otimes (L\otimes\Omega_C)=L^{\otimes 2}\otimes\Omega_C .
\]

Its degree is  

\[
\deg\bigl(\det J^1(L)\bigr)=2\deg L+\deg\Omega_C
=2\cdot 10 + (2g-2)=20+10=30 .
\]

For a general line \(\ell\subset\mathbb P^5\) (a pencil of conics) the condition that a
member of the pencil be tangent to \(C\) is that the 2‑dimensional subspace
defining \(\ell\) intersect the fibre of \(Q\) non‑trivially.  The number of such
intersection points equals \(\deg(\det Q)=30\).

Hence the divisor \(D\subset\mathbb P^5\) of tangent conics has degree  

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

The complete linear system of conics is  

\[
| \mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2) |\simeq \mathbf P^{5},
\qquad h = c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{5}}(1)\bigr).
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\) the conics that are tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) are those that  

* pass through \(p\) (one linear condition), and  
* have the same tangent line as \(C\) at \(p\) (one more linear condition).

Hence for each \(p\) we obtain a linear subspace of codimension \(2\) in \(\mathbf P^{5}\); its class is \(h^{2}\).

Let  

\[
X=\{(p,Q)\in C\times\mathbf P^{5}\mid Q\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ at }p\}.
\]

The projection \(\pi_{2}:X\to\mathbf P^{5}\) has image the divisor \(D\).  
On \(C\times\mathbf P^{5}\) the class of \(X\) is  

\[
[X]=[C]\cdot h^{2}=e\,\alpha\; h^{2},
\]

where \(\alpha=\pi_{1}^{*}(\text{hyperplane class of }\mathbf P^{2})\) and \(e=\deg C=5\).

Pushing forward to \(\mathbf P^{5}\),

\[
[D]=\pi_{2*}\bigl(e\,\alpha\,h^{2}\bigr)=e\;(\pi_{2*}\alpha)\;h^{2}.
\]

Since \(\pi_{2*}\alpha\) integrates \(\alpha\) over the fibre \(C\), we obtain  

\[
\int_{C}\alpha = \deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(1)\bigr)=e.
\]

Thus  

\[
[D]=e^{2}\,h = 5^{2}h = 30\,h .
\]

Consequently the degree of the divisor \(D\) (the intersection number with a general line in \(\mathbf P^{5}\)) is  

\[
\boxed{30}.
\]

problems.skill: Naive Bézout count for multiple tangency conditions
problems.problem:
Let \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(9)|\) denote the complete linear system of plane curves of degree \(d=9\); it is a projective space of dimension \(\binom{9+2}{2}-1\).  

Fix two smooth plane curves:
\[
C_{1}\subset\mathbb P^{2}\quad\text{of degree }e_{1}=3,
\qquad
C_{2}\subset\mathbb P^{2}\quad\text{of degree }e_{2}=4.
\]

For each \(i=1,2\), let \(D_{i}\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(9)|\) be the divisor consisting of those degree‑\(9\) curves that are tangent to \(C_{i}\) at some point of \(\mathbb P^{2}\).

1. Compute the degree of the divisor \(D_{1}\).  
2. Compute the degree of the divisor \(D_{2}\).  
3. Using Bézout’s theorem, give the naive count (i.e. the product of the degrees) of the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\), which represents the number of degree‑\(9\) curves tangent simultaneously to both \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\).

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
**Step 1.  The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\).**  

\[
\dim |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|=\binom{9+2}{2}-1=\binom{11}{2}-1=55-1=54 .
\]

Thus a divisor \(D_i\) in this projective space is a hypersurface; its degree equals the number of members of a *generic pencil* (a one‑dimensional linear subsystem) that satisfy the defining condition.

---

### 1. Degree of \(D_{1}\) (tangency to the cubic \(C_{1}\))

Fix a generic pencil \(\{F_t\}_{t\in\mathbf P^{1}}\) of degree‑9 curves.  
Restrict the pencil to the smooth cubic \(C_{1}\).  
Because \(C_{1}\) has degree \(e_{1}=3\), each curve \(F_t\) meets \(C_{1}\) in  

\[
9\cdot e_{1}=9\cdot 3=27
\]

points (counted with multiplicity).  
Hence the pencil gives a map  

\[
\phi : C_{1}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(d e_{1}=27\).  
A member \(F_t\) of the pencil is tangent to \(C_{1}\) exactly when two of the
intersection points coalesce, i.e. when \(\phi\) is ramified at the corresponding point of \(C_{1}\).

For a map of degree \(n\) from a smooth curve of genus \(g\) to \(\mathbf P^{1}\), the total ramification degree is given by the Riemann–Hurwitz formula  

\[
\deg R = 2g-2+2n .
\]

The cubic \(C_{1}\) has genus  

\[
g_{1}= \frac{(e_{1}-1)(e_{1}-2)}{2}= \frac{2\cdot1}{2}=1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\deg R_{1}=2\cdot1-2+2\cdot(9\cdot3)=0+54=54 .
\]

Consequently a generic pencil meets \(D_{1}\) in \(54\) members, so  

\[
\boxed{\deg D_{1}=54}.
\]

---

### 2. Degree of \(D_{2}\) (tangency to the quartic \(C_{2}\))

Now \(e_{2}=4\).  
The same reasoning gives a map  

\[
\phi : C_{2}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(9\cdot4=36\).  
The genus of a smooth quartic is  

\[
g_{2}= \frac{(4-1)(4-2)}{2}= \frac{3\cdot2}{2}=3 .
\]

Applying Riemann–Hurwitz,

\[
\deg R_{2}=2\cdot3-2+2\cdot(9\cdot4)=6-2+72=76 .
\]

Hence a generic pencil meets \(D_{2}\) in \(76\) members, i.e.

\[
\boxed{\deg D_{2}=76}.
\]

---

### 3. Naïve count of curves tangent to **both** \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\)

Since \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) are hypersurfaces in the 54‑dimensional projective space
\(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\), the expected number of points in their intersection,
obtained by Bézout’s theorem, is the product of their degrees:

\[
\#(D_{1}\cap D_{2})_{\text{naïve}} = \deg D_{1}\,\deg D_{2}=54 \times 76 = 4104 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{4104}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) has dimension  

\[
\dim = \binom{9+2}{2}-1 = 55-1 = 54 .
\]

For a fixed smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e\) the condition that a degree‑\(9\) curve be tangent to \(C\) at some point is the ramification divisor of the \(g^{1}_{9e}\) on \(C\) cut out by the pencil of degree‑\(9\) curves.  
For a base‑point‑free linear series \(g^{1}_{n}\) on a smooth curve of genus \(g\) the total ramification degree is (Plücker formula)

\[
\deg(\text{ram}) = 2n + 2g - 2 .
\]

Here \(n = 9e\) and the genus of a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\) is  

\[
g = \frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}.
\]

---

### 1.  Degree of \(D_{1}\) (\(e_{1}=3\))

\[
g(C_{1}) = \frac{(3-1)(3-2)}{2}=1,\qquad n = 9\cdot 3 = 27.
\]

\[
\deg D_{1}= 2\cdot 27 + 2\cdot 1 - 2 = 54 .
\]

---

### 2.  Degree of \(D_{2}\) (\(e_{2}=4\))

\[
g(C_{2}) = \frac{(4-1)(4-2)}{2}=3,\qquad n = 9\cdot 4 = 36.
\]

\[
\deg D_{2}= 2\cdot 36 + 2\cdot 3 - 2 = 76 .
\]

---

### 3.  Naive count of \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\)

Assuming the two divisors intersect transversely, the number of degree‑\(9\) curves tangent to both \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) is the product of their degrees:

\[
\#(D_{1}\cap D_{2}) = \deg D_{1}\cdot \deg D_{2}= 54 \times 76 = 4104 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4104}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) is a projective space \(\mathbf P^{54}\).

---

### 1.  Degree of \(D_{1}\)

Let \(C_{1}\) be a smooth plane cubic (\(e_{1}=3\)).  
Consider the incidence variety  

\[
I_{1}= \{(p,F)\mid p\in C_{1},\;F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|,\;F\text{ tangent to }C_{1}\text{ at }p\}.
\]

Projecting to \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) gives the divisor \(D_{1}\).
For a fixed point \(p\in C_{1}\) the condition “\(F\) is tangent to \(C_{1}\) at \(p\)” is two independent linear conditions on the coefficients of \(F\) (vanishing of the value and of the derivative in the tangent direction).  

Hence, for a **generic pencil** \(\Lambda\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) the points of tangency are the zeros of the determinant of the map  

\[
\Lambda\otimes\mathcal O_{C_{1}}\longrightarrow J^{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|_{C_{1}}\bigr),
\]

where \(J^{1}\) is the first jet bundle.  
On a smooth curve \(C\) we have  

\[
\det J^{1}(L)=L^{\otimes 2}\otimes \Omega_{C},
\]

so for \(L=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|_{C_{1}}\),

\[
\deg\bigl(\det J^{1}(L)\bigr)=2\deg L+\deg\Omega_{C_{1}}.
\]

Now \(\deg L = 9\,e_{1}=27\) and for a plane curve of degree \(e\) the canonical bundle has degree \(\deg\Omega_{C}=e(e-3)\).  
Thus  

\[
\deg D_{1}=2\cdot 27 + 3(3-3)=54.
\]

---

### 2.  Degree of \(D_{2}\)

The same computation with \(e_{2}=4\) gives  

\[
\deg L = 9\cdot 4 = 36,\qquad 
\deg\Omega_{C_{2}} = 4(4-3)=4,
\]

\[
\deg D_{2}=2\cdot 36 + 4 = 76.
\]

---

### 3.  Naïve count of \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\)

Treating the two divisors as hypersurfaces in \(\mathbf P^{54}\), the expected number of points in their intersection (the product of the degrees) is  

\[
\deg D_{1}\cdot\deg D_{2}=54 \times 76 = 4104.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{4104}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) has  

\[
\dim |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|=\binom{9+2}{2}-1=54 .
\]

For a fixed smooth plane curve \(C\) of degree \(e\) the divisor  

\[
D(C)=\{\,F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\mid F\text{ is tangent to }C\text{ somewhere}\,\}
\]

is obtained by requiring that the intersection divisor \(F\cap C\) (of total degree \(9e\) by Bézout) contain a point of multiplicity at least \(2\).
If we intersect a **generic pencil** of degree‑\(9\) curves with \(C\), we obtain a family of effective divisors of degree \(9e\) on the smooth curve \(C\).  
The discriminant of this family (the locus where the divisor ceases to be reduced) is a divisor on the pencil whose degree equals the class of the discriminant of a degree‑\(9e\) linear series on a smooth curve.  
For a linear series of degree \(m\) on a smooth curve the discriminant has degree  

\[
m\,(m-2e+2)=m\,(m+e-2),
\]

where \(e\) is the degree of the curve that gives the series.  
Putting \(m=9e\) we obtain

\[
\deg D(C)=9e\,(9+e-2)=9e\,(7+e).
\]

---

### 1.  \(C_{1}\) has degree \(e_{1}=3\)

\[
\deg D_{1}=9\cdot 3\,(9+3-2)=27\cdot 10=270 .
\]

### 2.  \(C_{2}\) has degree \(e_{2}=4\)

\[
\deg D_{2}=9\cdot 4\,(9+4-2)=36\cdot 11=396 .
\]

### 3.  Naïve count of curves tangent to **both** \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\)

The intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) in the projective space \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) is expected to consist of  

\[
\deg D_{1}\times \deg D_{2}=270\times 396=106\,920
\]

points, i.e. that many degree‑\(9\) curves would be tangent simultaneously to \(C_{1}\) and to \(C_{2}\).

\[
\boxed{106920}
\]

The divisor of degree‑\(9\) curves tangent to a fixed smooth curve \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) of degree \(e\) is the discriminant of the restriction map  

\[
H^{0}\bigl(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)\bigr)\longrightarrow H^{0}\bigl(C,\mathcal O_{C}(9)\bigr),
\]

which is a linear map.  
On the curve \(C\) the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{C}(9)\) has degree \(9e\).  
For a line bundle of degree \(n\) on a smooth curve, the discriminant divisor in the projective space of its sections has degree \(2n-2\).  
Hence the degree of the divisor of tangency is  

\[
\deg D = 2\cdot (9e)-2 = 18e-2 .
\]

---

1. For \(C_{1}\) with \(e_{1}=3\):
\[
\deg D_{1}=18\cdot 3-2 = 54-2 = 52 .
\]

2. For \(C_{2}\) with \(e_{2}=4\):
\[
\deg D_{2}=18\cdot 4-2 = 72-2 = 70 .
\]

3. The naïve Bézout count for the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) is the product of the two degrees:

\[
\deg(D_{1}\cap D_{2}) = 52 \times 70 = 3640 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3640}
\]

The linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) has dimension  

\[
N=\binom{9+2}{2}-1= \binom{11}{2}-1 =55-1 =54 .
\]

For a fixed smooth plane curve \(C_i\) of degree \(e_i\) let  

\[
D_i=\{\,F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)| \mid F \text{ is tangent to } C_i \text{ at some point}\,\}.
\]

---

### Degree of \(D_i\)

Take a generic pencil \(\mathcal L\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) (a line in the projective space).  
For each curve \(F\in\mathcal L\) the intersection \(F\cap C_i\) is a divisor of degree  

\[
n = \deg(F)\deg(C_i)=9\,e_i
\]

on the smooth curve \(C_i\).  
Thus the pencil defines a morphism  

\[
\phi_i : C_i \longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}
\]

of degree \(n\).  
A curve \(F\) from the pencil is tangent to \(C_i\) exactly when two points of the fibre
\(\phi_i^{-1}(t)\) coincide, i.e. when \(\phi_i\) is ramified at the corresponding point of \(C_i\).

Hence the number of tangencies that occur in a generic pencil equals the total ramification
of \(\phi_i\). By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula for a map of degree \(n\) from a curve of genus
\(g(C_i)\),

\[
\sum_{p\in C_i}(e_p-1)=2g(C_i)-2+2n .
\]

Therefore the degree of the divisor \(D_i\) (the number of tangency points in a generic pencil) is  

\[
\boxed{\deg D_i = 2g(C_i)-2+2\cdot 9e_i } .
\]

Now compute for the two given curves.

*For \(C_1\) (a smooth cubic, \(e_1=3\)):*  

\[
g(C_1)=\frac{(3-1)(3-2)}{2}=1,\qquad n=9\cdot3=27,
\]
\[
\deg D_1 = 2\cdot1-2+2\cdot27 = 0+54 = \boxed{54}.
\]

*For \(C_2\) (a smooth quartic, \(e_2=4\)):*  

\[
g(C_2)=\frac{(4-1)(4-2)}{2}=3,\qquad n=9\cdot4=36,
\]
\[
\deg D_2 = 2\cdot3-2+2\cdot36 = 6-2+72 = \boxed{76}.
\]

---

### Naïve count of \(D_1\cap D_2\)

Assuming the divisors intersect transversely, the expected number of degree‑9 curves that are
simultaneously tangent to both \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) is the product of the degrees:

\[
\deg(D_1\cap D_2)=\deg D_1\cdot\deg D_2 = 54 \times 76 = \boxed{4104}.
\]

Thus the required numerical answer is  

\[
\boxed{4104}
\]

For a smooth plane curve \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) of degree \(e\) let  

\[
L:=\mathcal O_{C}(d)=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(d)\big|_{C},
\qquad 
\deg L = d\,e .
\]

The complete linear system \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(d)|\) has dimension  

\[
N=\binom{d+2}{2}-1 .
\]

A curve \(F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(d)|\) is tangent to \(C\) at a point
\(p\in C\) iff the restriction \(F|_{C}\) vanishes to order \(\ge 2\) at \(p\).
Thus we must study the locus of sections of \(L\) having a double zero
somewhere on \(C\).

---

### Jet‑bundle description  

Consider the first jet bundle of \(L\) on the smooth curve \(C\)

\[
0\longrightarrow L\otimes K_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L)
\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow 0 ,
\]

where \(K_{C}\) is the canonical bundle of \(C\).  
\(J^{1}(L)\) is a rank‑2 vector bundle with

\[
\det J^{1}(L)=L\otimes(L\otimes K_{C}) = L^{2}\otimes K_{C}.
\]

Let \(V=H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(d))\) (so \(\dim V=N+1\)).
Restricting sections to \(C\) gives a surjective map \(V\otimes\mathcal O_{C}
\to L\). Composing with the jet map we obtain

\[
\phi : V\otimes\mathcal O_{C}\longrightarrow J^{1}(L).
\]

For a fixed point \(p\in C\), the subspace of sections whose jet at \(p\)
vanishes is a codimension‑2 linear subspace of \(V\).  
Consequently, the divisor \(D\subset\mathbf P(V)\) consisting of sections
having a double zero somewhere on \(C\) is the degeneracy locus of \(\phi\).

If we intersect \(D\) with a generic pencil (a \(\mathbf P^{1}\subset\mathbf P(V)\)),
the induced map \(\mathcal O_{C}^{\;2}\to J^{1}(L)\) drops rank exactly at the
zeros of a section of \(\det J^{1}(L)=L^{2}\otimes K_{C}\).  
Hence the number of points of intersection of a generic pencil with \(D\) –
i.e. the degree of \(D\) – equals the degree of the line bundle \(L^{2}\otimes
K_{C}\):

\[
\boxed{\deg D = \deg\big(L^{2}\otimes K_{C}\big)=2\deg L + \deg K_{C}}.
\]

For a smooth plane curve of degree \(e\),

\[
\deg L = d\,e,\qquad
\deg K_{C}=2g-2,\qquad 
g=\frac{(e-1)(e-2)}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\deg D = 2(d e) + (2g-2)=2de + 2g -2 .
\]

---

### Applying to the two given curves  

*For \(C_{1}\) (a cubic, \(e_{1}=3\)):*  

\[
g_{1}= \frac{(3-1)(3-2)}{2}=1,\qquad
\deg D_{1}=2\cdot 9\cdot 3 + 2\cdot 1-2 = 54+2-2 = \boxed{54}.
\]

*For \(C_{2}\) (a quartic, \(e_{2}=4\)):*  

\[
g_{2}= \frac{(4-1)(4-2)}{2}=3,\qquad
\deg D_{2}=2\cdot 9\cdot 4 + 2\cdot 3-2 = 72+6-2 = \boxed{76}.
\]

---

### Naïve count of simultaneous tangency  

Bézout’s theorem suggests that the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) in the
projective space \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\) has degree equal to the
product of the two divisor degrees:

\[
\deg(D_{1}\cap D_{2}) = \deg D_{1}\,\deg D_{2}= 54 \times 76 = \boxed{4104}.
\]

Hence the naïve (product) count of degree‑\(9\) curves tangent to both the
cubic \(C_{1}\) and the quartic \(C_{2}\) is **4104**.

\[
\boxed{4104}
\]

The linear system of degree‑\(9\) plane curves is  

\[
|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)|\cong \mathbf P^{N},\qquad 
N=\binom{9+2}{2}-1 = 54 .
\]

For a fixed smooth plane curve \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) of degree \(e\) we consider  

\[
D(C)=\{\,F\in |\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(9)| \mid
F \text{ is tangent to } C \text{ at some point}\,\}.
\]

---

### 1‑2.  Degree of \(D(C)\)

Let \(p\in C\).  Choose local coordinates with \(p=(0,0)\) and
\(C\) given by the smooth equation \(y=0\).
A degree‑\(9\) curve is given locally by a homogeneous polynomial
\(f(x,y)\) of degree \(9\).
The intersection multiplicity of \(f=0\) with \(C\) at \(p\) is the
order of vanishing of \(f(x,0)\) at \(x=0\).
Thus \(F\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(p\) iff  

\[
f(0,0)=0 ,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=0 .
\]

These are **two independent linear conditions** on the coefficients of
\(f\).  
For a fixed point \(p\) they cut out a linear subspace of codimension
\(2\) in the vector space \(H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O(9))\); in the
projective space \(|\mathcal O(9)|\) this gives a hyperplane.

Let \(C\) be parametrised by a point of the curve; as \(p\) moves along
\(C\) the corresponding hyperplanes sweep out a divisor \(D(C)\) in
\(|\mathcal O(9)|\).  The degree of that divisor equals the number of
curves in a generic **pencil** of degree‑\(9\) curves that are tangent to
\(C\).

Restrict a degree‑\(9\) curve to \(C\).  The restriction is a divisor of
degree  

\[
\deg\bigl(F|_{C}\bigr)=9\cdot e .
\]

A pencil of curves gives a pencil of such divisors on \(C\).  The
condition that a divisor of degree \(n=9e\) on a smooth curve has a
double point is the classical discriminant condition, whose degree in
the projective space of sections is  

\[
n\,(n-1)= (9e)\bigl(9e-1\bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\deg D(C)= (9e)(9e-1)} .
\]

Now apply this to the two given curves.

* For \(C_{1}\) with \(e_{1}=3\):

\[
\deg D_{1}= (9\cdot 3)(9\cdot 3-1)=27\cdot 26 = 702 .
\]

* For \(C_{2}\) with \(e_{2}=4\):

\[
\deg D_{2}= (9\cdot 4)(9\cdot 4-1)=36\cdot 35 = 1260 .
\]

---

### 3.  Naïve count of \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\)

In a projective space, the expected number of points in the
intersection of two divisors is the product of their degrees
(Bézout’s theorem).  Thus the naïve count of degree‑\(9\) curves that are
tangent to **both** \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) is  

\[
\deg D_{1}\cdot\deg D_{2}=702 \times 1260 = 884\,520 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{884520}
\]

The divisor \(D_i\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(9)|\) consists of degree‑\(9\) curves that are tangent to the fixed smooth curve \(C_i\) of degree \(e_i\).

For a fixed point \(p\in C_i\) the condition “the curve passes through \(p\) and is tangent to \(C_i\) at \(p\)” imposes two independent linear conditions on the space of degree‑\(9\) curves.  
Varying the point \(p\) (a one‑dimensional family) gives a divisor in the projective space \(|\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(9)|\).

Intersect this divisor with a generic line (a pencil of degree‑\(9\) curves).  
For a pencil generated by two forms \(F_0,F_1\) of degree \(9\), the condition that some member of the pencil is tangent to \(C_i\) at a point \(p\) is the vanishing of the determinant  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
F_0(p) & F_1(p)\\[2pt]
\partial_{\!t}F_0(p) & \partial_{\!t}F_1(p)
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

where \(\partial_t\) denotes differentiation in the tangent direction of \(C_i\) at \(p\).
The first row has degree \(9\); the second row has degree \(8\). Hence the determinant is a homogeneous polynomial of degree  

\[
9+8 = 2\cdot 9-1 = 17 .
\]

Thus, for a generic pencil the points \(p\) satisfying the tangency condition are the intersection of a degree‑\(17\) curve with \(C_i\). By Bézout’s theorem the number of such points (counted with multiplicities) is  

\[
\deg D_i = 17\;e_i .
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg D_1 = 17\cdot 3 = 51,\qquad 
\deg D_2 = 17\cdot 4 = 68 .
\]

The naive count of the intersection \(D_1\cap D_2\) is the product of the two degrees:

\[
\#(D_1\cap D_2)_{\text{naive}} = 51 \times 68 = 3468 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3468}
\]

The divisor \(D_i\subset |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(9)|\) consists of degree‑\(9\) curves that have a point of tangency with the fixed smooth curve \(C_i\) of degree \(e_i\).
For a point \(p\in C_i\) the tangency imposes two independent linear conditions on the space of degree‑\(9\) homogeneous polynomials, so over \(C_i\) we obtain a \(\mathbb P^{N-2}\)-bundle (\(N=\dim |\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(9)|=54\)).  
Projecting to the linear system gives a hypersurface, whose degree equals the number of curves in a generic pencil that are tangent to \(C_i\).

Using the discriminant of sections of the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{C_i}(9)\) on the curve \(C_i\), the degree of this hypersurface is  

\[
\deg D_i = 2\deg\bigl(\mathcal O_{C_i}(9)\bigr) + 2g(C_i)-2
        = 2\cdot 9e_i + (e_i-1)(e_i-2)-2
        = e_i\bigl(2\cdot 9 + e_i -3\bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
\deg D_1 = 3\bigl(18+0\bigr)=54,\qquad
\deg D_2 = 4\bigl(18+1\bigr)=76.
\]

The naive count of the intersection \(D_1\cap D_2\) is the product of the two degrees:

\[
\#(D_1\cap D_2)_{\text{naive}} = 54 \times 76 = 4104.
\]

\[
\boxed{4104}
\]

problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \(V=\mathbb{P}^{5}\) be the projective space that parametrises plane conics.  

* \(H_{1}\subset V\) is the hyperplane consisting of conics that pass through a fixed point \(P\); it has degree \(1\).  
* \(Q\subset V\) is the quadric hypersurface of conics that are tangent to a fixed line \(\ell\); it has degree \(2\).  
* \(C\subset V\) is a cubic hypersurface consisting of conics that are singular at another fixed point \(Q\); it has degree \(3\).

If the three hypersurfaces met transversely, the length of their intersection would be the product of the degrees, namely \(1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6\).  
In fact the intersection is not transverse because \(Q\) and \(C\) share a common component \(Z\), which is a line in \(V\) (hence \(\deg Z = 1\)).  
The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(Z\) has rank \(1\) and its first Chern class satisfies \(\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1\).  

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the number of smooth conics that satisfy all three conditions (i.e., the corrected length of the intersection after removing the excess contribution).  

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The expected intersection product of the three divisor classes is  

\[
\deg (H_1\cdot Q\cdot C)=1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because the quadric \(Q\) and the cubic \(C\) share the line \(Z\subset V\) (a component of codimension 4 instead of the expected codimension 3), there is an excess contribution.  

For the excess component \(Z\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) has rank  

\[
\operatorname{rk}E = \text{codim}_V Z - 3 = 1 ,
\]

and its first Chern class satisfies  

\[
\int_Z c_1(E)=1 .
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of \(Z\) to the intersection product is  

\[
c_1(E)\cap[Z] = \int_Z c_1(E)=1 .
\]

Hence the corrected degree (the number of smooth conics satisfying all three conditions) is  

\[
6 - 1 = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The three hypersurfaces  

\[
H_{1},\; Q,\; C\subset V=\mathbb P^{5}
\]

are all codimension‑1.  
If they met transversely the refined intersection product would be a
\(0\)-cycle of degree  

\[
\deg(H_{1})\deg(Q)\deg(C)=1\cdot 2\cdot 3=6 .
\]

Because \(Q\) and \(C\) are not transverse they share a common
component  

\[
Z\subset Q\cap C ,\qquad  Z\cong \mathbb P^{1},
\]

so the intersection \(Q\cap C\) is not proper.  
For the excess component \(Z\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) has rank
\(1\) and  

\[
\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

---

### Excess‑intersection contribution

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says that the contribution of the
excess component \(Z\) to the refined intersection product is  

\[
c(E)\cap[Z]=\bigl(1+c_{1}(E)\bigr)\cap[Z]
\]

and, since \(\dim Z=1\) and \(\operatorname{rk}E=1\),

\[
\deg\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)=\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

Thus the non‑transverse part contributes a \(0\)-cycle of degree \(1\).

---

### Corrected number of isolated points

The total refined intersection product has degree \(6\).  Removing the
excess contribution of degree \(1\) leaves only the isolated points,
i.e. the smooth conics satisfying the three conditions:

\[
\#\{\text{smooth conics}\}=6-1=5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The expected number of solutions for three transverse hypersurfaces would be  

\[
\deg H_{1}\cdot\deg Q\cdot\deg C = 1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because \(Q\) and \(C\) share the line \(Z\subset V\), the intersection is not transverse.  
For the excess component \(Z\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) has rank 1 and  

\[
\int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of the excess component to the refined intersection product equals this integral, i.e. \(1\).  

Hence the refined intersection number (the total length of the intersection) splits as  

\[
\text{(smooth isolated points)} \;+\; \underbrace{1}_{\text{excess contribution}} = 6 .
\]

Therefore the number of smooth conics satisfying all three conditions is  

\[
6-1 = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The three hypersurfaces in the parameter space \(V=\mathbf P^{5}\) have codimension \(1\).  
If they met transversely, the refined intersection product would be  

\[
[H_{1}]\cdot[Q]\cdot[C]=1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6,
\]

i.e. a 0‑dimensional cycle of length \(6\).

Because the quadric \(Q\) (tangent to the fixed line \(\ell\)) and the cubic \(C\) (singular at the fixed point \(Q\)) share a common component,
\[
Z = Q\cap C \qquad (\text{a line in }V),
\]
the intersection is not transverse.  
The excess‑intersection formula (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*) tells us that the contribution of this common component to the refined product is

\[
j_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap[Z]\bigr),
\]

where \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on \(Z\) (rank \(1\)).  
We are given  

\[
\int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

Thus the excess contribution to the 0‑dimensional intersection number is exactly \(1\).

Hence the corrected length of the intersection, i.e. the number of **smooth** conics satisfying the three conditions, is obtained by subtracting the excess contribution from the transverse count:

\[
\text{number of smooth conics}= 6 - 1 = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The expected number of conics satisfying the three conditions would be  

\[
\deg H_{1}\cdot\deg Q\cdot\deg C = 1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because the quadric \(Q\) and the cubic \(C\) share the line \(Z\subset V\) as a common component, the intersection is not transverse.  
For the excess component \(Z\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) has rank \(1\) and  

\[
\int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of the excess component to the zero‑dimensional intersection class is exactly \(\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1\).  
Hence the number of isolated (zero‑dimensional) points, i.e. the smooth conics satisfying all three conditions, is  

\[
6 - 1 = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The three hypersurfaces have expected intersection number  

\[
\deg H_{1}\cdot\deg Q\cdot\deg C = 1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because the quadric \(Q\) and the cubic \(C\) share the line  

\[
Z\subset V ,\qquad \deg Z = 1 ,
\]

the actual intersection contains an excess component \(Z\).

For the excess component the excess normal bundle \(E\) has rank \(1\) and  

\[
\int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

By Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, the contribution of the excess component to the intersection product is the top Chern class of \(E\) integrated over \(Z\):

\[
\text{excess contribution}= \int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

Hence the corrected number of isolated points (the smooth conics satisfying the three conditions) is

\[
6 - 1 = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The three hypersurfaces in the projective space  

\[
V=\mathbf P^{5}
\]

are  

* \(H_{1}\) – a hyperplane, \(\deg H_{1}=1\);
* \(Q\) – a quadric, \(\deg Q =2\);
* \(C\) – a cubic, \(\deg C =3\).

If they intersect transversely the 0‑dimensional intersection class would be  

\[
[H_{1}]\cdot[Q]\cdot[C]=1\cdot 2\cdot 3 =6\;[{\rm pt}].
\]

---

### Excess component  

\(Q\) and \(C\) are not transverse: they share a common component  

\[
Z\subset Q\cap C,
\]

where \(Z\cong\mathbf P^{1}\) (a line in \(V\)).  
For the intersection of the three hypersurfaces the excess normal bundle
\(E\) on \(Z\) has  

* rank \(\operatorname{rk}E =1\);
* first Chern class satisfying \(\displaystyle\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1\).

Hence  

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E).
\]

---

### Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula  

For three divisors the refined intersection product is  

\[
[H_{1}]\cdot[Q]\cdot[C]\;=\;6[{\rm pt}]\;-\;
\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)\cap[H_{1}].
\]

The excess contribution is obtained by capping the class \(c(E)\cap[Z]\)
with the remaining divisor \(H_{1}\).

* \([Z]\cap[H_{1}]\) is the intersection of a line with a hyperplane,
  giving **one** point.
* \(c_{1}(E)\cap[Z]\) is a 0‑cycle whose degree is  
  \(\displaystyle\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1\).

Therefore  

\[
\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)\cap[H_{1}]
   =([Z]\cap[H_{1}]) + (c_{1}(E)\cap[Z])
   = 1 + 1 = 2\;[{\rm pt}].
\]

---

### Corrected number of smooth conics  

Subtracting the excess contribution from the transverse count gives  

\[
\text{number of smooth conics}= 6-2 = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The three hypersurfaces have classes  

\[
[H_{1}]=h,\qquad [Q]=2h,\qquad [C]=3h\qquad (h=\text{hyperplane class in } \mathbb{P}^{5}),
\]

so the expected intersection product is  

\[
[H_{1}]\cdot[Q]\cdot[C]=h\cdot 2h\cdot 3h = 6\,h^{3}.
\]

If the intersection were transverse, the length (the degree of the resulting 0‑cycle) would be the product of the degrees, i.e. \(6\).

Because \(Q\) and \(C\) share the line \(Z\subset V\) (a component of excess dimension), Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of this component to the 0‑cycle is  

\[
\int_{Z} c(E)=\int_{Z}\bigl(1+c_{1}(E)\bigr)=\underbrace{\int_{Z}1}_{\deg Z=1}+ \underbrace{\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)}_{=1}=2 .
\]

Only the term of codimension 3 (the 0‑dimensional part) contributes to the length, namely \(\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1\).

Hence the excess contribution that must be removed from the naïve count is \(1\).

\[
\text{Corrected length}=6-1=5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The expected transverse intersection number of the three hypersurfaces is  

\[
\deg(H_{1})\cdot\deg(Q)\cdot\deg(C)=1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because \(Q\) and \(C\) share the line \(Z\subset V\), the actual intersection contains an excess component.  
For a component \(Z\) of excess dimension, Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of \(Z\) to the intersection product is  

\[
\int_{Z} c_{r}(E),
\]

where \(r\) is the rank of the excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(Z\).  
Here \(r=1\) and we are given  

\[
\int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1 .
\]

Hence the excess contribution of the line \(Z\) is \(1\).

The corrected length, i.e. the number of points of the intersection that are not accounted for by the excess component, is therefore  

\[
6 - 1 = 5 .
\]

Thus there are **5 smooth conics** satisfying all three conditions.

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The three hypersurfaces in  

\[
V=\mathbf P^{5}
\]

have codimension \(1\) each, so a transverse intersection would have codimension  

\[
1+1+1 = 3 ,
\]

hence would be a zero‑dimensional scheme of length  

\[
\deg H_{1}\cdot\deg Q\cdot\deg C = 1\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because the quadric \(Q\) and the cubic \(C\) share the line  

\[
Z\subset V ,\qquad \deg Z =1 ,
\]

the intersection is not transverse.  
For the excess component \(Z\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) has  

* rank \(=1\),
* \(\displaystyle \int_{Z} c_{1}(E)=1\).

---

### Excess‑intersection contribution

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says that the contribution of an excess component \(Z\) to the refined intersection product is  

\[
c_{e}(E)\cap[Z],
\]

where \(e\) is the excess (here \(e=1\) because \(\operatorname{rank}E=1\)).  
Since \(c_{1}(E)\) is a divisor class on the line \(Z\),

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap[Z]=\int_{Z}c_{1}(E)\;[{\rm pt}]
\]

which is a point counted with multiplicity \(\displaystyle \int_{Z}c_{1}(E)=1\).

Thus the excess component contributes **1** to the naive count of six points.

---

### Corrected number of points

\[
\text{Number of smooth conics}= 6 \;-\; 1 = 5 .
\]

Hence, after removing the excess contribution, there are five smooth conics that pass through the fixed point \(P\), are tangent to the fixed line \(\ell\), and are singular at the fixed point \(Q\).

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \(V=\mathbb{P}^{5}\) be the projective space that parametrises plane conics.  
Inside \(V\) consider two effective divisors:

* \(D_{1}\) is the divisor of conics that are tangent to a fixed smooth cubic curve \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) at a fixed point \(P\in C\); its class is \(4H\) (so \(\deg D_{1}=4\)).  
* \(D_{2}\) is the discriminant divisor consisting of singular conics; its class is \(3H\) (so \(\deg D_{2}=3\)).

The naïve Bézout number for the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) is therefore \(4\cdot 3 = 12\).  
However \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) meet non‑transversely along the line \(L\subset V\) parametrising the double lines \(2\ell\) where \(\ell\) is the line tangent to \(C\) at \(P\).  The excess normal bundle \(E\) of the intersection, restricted to \(L\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}\), is a line bundle of degree \(5\) (so \(c_{1}(E)=5\)).  

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the corrected intersection number, i.e. the number of conics that are both tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) and singular, counted with multiplicity.  Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The ambient space is  

\[
V=\mathbb P^{5},\qquad \dim V =5 .
\]

The two divisors are  

\[
D_{1}\sim 4H ,\qquad D_{2}\sim 3H .
\]

Hence the naïve Bézout number (the degree of the codimension‑2 cycle
\(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\)) is  

\[
\deg(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}) = 4\cdot 3 = 12 .
\]

---

### Excess component

The intersection is not transverse: the line  

\[
L\simeq\mathbb P^{1}\subset V
\]

parametrises the double lines \(2\ell\) where \(\ell\) is the line tangent
to the cubic \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\).
Along \(L\) the two divisor hypersurfaces meet with excess.
The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(L\) is a line bundle of degree  

\[
c_{1}(E)=5 .
\]

Thus  

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E)=1+5h,
\]

where \(h\) generates \(A^{1}(L)\cong\mathbb Z\).

---

### Fulton’s excess–intersection formula  

For a component \(Z\) of the intersection we have  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}] = i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr),
\]

where \(i:Z\hookrightarrow V\).
Applying this to the excess component \(L\),

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap[L]\bigr)=i_{*}\bigl((1+5h)\cap[L]\bigr)
      = i_{*}\bigl([L]\bigr)+5\,i_{*}\bigl(h\cap[L]\bigr).
\]

The first term \([L]\) has codimension \(4\) in \(V\); it does **not**
contribute to the degree of the codimension‑2 intersection.
The second term contributes a class of codimension \(2\) whose degree is

\[
\int_{L} 5h =5 .
\]

Hence the excess component adds \(5\) to the intersection number.

---

### Corrected intersection number  

\[
\boxed{\;12\;+\;5\;=\;17\;}
\]

Therefore, the number of conics that are simultaneously tangent to the
cubic \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\) and singular, counted with the
appropriate multiplicities, is  

\[
\boxed{17}
\]

The two divisor classes are  

\[
[D_{1}]=4H ,\qquad [D_{2}]=3H\qquad\text{in }A^{1}(\mathbf P^{5}),
\]

so the naïve Bézout number (the degree of the product of the classes) is  

\[
\deg\bigl([D_{1}]\cdot [D_{2}]\bigr)= (4H)(3H)H^{3}=12 .
\]

Because \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) intersect non‑transversely along the line  

\[
L\cong\mathbf P^{1}\subset \mathbf P^{5},
\]

the refined intersection product must be corrected by Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula.  
For a component \(L\) of excess dimension \(e=1\) the contribution is  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c_{e}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr).
\]

The excess normal bundle \(E\) restricted to \(L\) is a line bundle of degree \(5\); hence  

\[
c_{1}(E)=5\in A^{1}(L).
\]

Thus  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L]=5\cdot\text{(a point on }L),
\]

so the contribution of the excess component to the 0‑cycle is \(5\) points.

Let \(\alpha\) denote the class of the proper (transverse) part of the intersection.  
Taking degrees after intersecting with three generic hyperplanes (i.e. computing the
enumerative number) we have  

\[
\deg(\alpha)+\deg\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=12 .
\]

Since \(\deg(c_{1}(E)\cap [L])=5\), we obtain  

\[
\deg(\alpha)=12-5=7 .
\]

Therefore the corrected enumerative count — the number of conics that are both
tangent to the cubic \(C\) at \(P\) and singular, counted with multiplicity — is

\[
\boxed{7}.
\]

The intersection product of the two divisor classes is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]=(4H)(3H)=12H^{2}.
\]

After intersecting with three further general hyperplanes (class \(H^{3}\)) the naïve Bézout number is  

\[
12H^{2}\cdot H^{3}=12 .
\]

Because \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) meet non‑transversely along the line \(L\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\), we must correct this count using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula.

For the component \(L\) the excess normal bundle is a line bundle \(E\) with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=\deg E =5 .
\]

The contribution of \(L\) to the 0‑dimensional intersection after intersecting with the three hyperplanes is  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\cdot H^{3}=5\cdot 1 =5 ,
\]

since a line meets three general hyperplanes in a single point.

Hence the isolated (proper) part of the intersection contributes  

\[
12-5 = 7
\]

points (counted with multiplicity).  
Therefore the corrected intersection number – the total number of conics that are both tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) and singular, counted with multiplicity – is

\[
\boxed{7}
\]

The intersection product of the two divisor classes is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}] = (4H)\cdot(3H)=12 .
\]

Because \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) meet non‑transversely along the line \(L\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}\), Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula must be applied.  

For the excess component \(L\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=\deg E =5 .
\]

The contribution of \(L\) to the refined intersection product is  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap [L]\bigr)= i_{*}\bigl((1+c_{1}(E))\cap [L]\bigr)
      = i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr) ,
\]

which is a \(0\)-cycle of degree \(\deg E =5\).

Hence the corrected intersection number (the number of conics that are both tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) and singular, counted with multiplicity) is  

\[
12 \;+\; 5 \;=\; 17 .
\]

\[
\boxed{17}
\]

The naïve Bézout count for the intersection of the two divisors is  

\[
\deg D_{1}\cdot\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 3 = 12 .
\]

Because \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) meet non‑transversely along the line  

\[
L \cong \mathbb{P}^{1},
\]

the excess–intersection formula of Fulton must be applied.  
For the component \(L\) the excess normal bundle \(E\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=5 .
\]

The contribution of this component to the refined intersection product is the degree of \(c_{1}(E)\) on \(L\); i.e. a correction term of \(5\).

Hence the actual number of conics that are both tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) and singular is

\[
12 - 5 = 7 .
\]

\[
\boxed{7}
\]

The naïve Bézout number for the two divisors is  

\[
\deg D_{1}\cdot\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 3 = 12 .
\]

Because the divisors share the line \(L\subset V\) as a common component, the intersection is not transverse.  
Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of the excess component \(L\) is

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=\deg\bigl(c_{1}(E)\bigr)=\deg(E)=5 .
\]

Hence the corrected intersection number (the count of singular conics tangent to \(C\) at \(P\), with multiplicities) is the naïve count minus the excess contribution:

\[
12 - 5 = 7 .
\]

\[
\boxed{7}
\]

The two divisors are  

\[
D_{1}\sim 4H ,\qquad D_{2}\sim 3H\qquad (H=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{5}}(1))).
\]

If they intersect transversally the intersection number would be  

\[
\deg(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}) = (4H)(3H)H^{3}=12 .
\]

Because the intersection contains the line  

\[
L\simeq\mathbb P^{1}\subset V
\]

of double lines \(2\ell\) (where \(\ell\) is the tangent line to \(C\) at \(P\)), the intersection is not proper.  
Let  

\[
Z=D_{1}\cap D_{2}=L\cup\{\text{isolated points}\}.
\]

The excess normal bundle of the inclusion \(L\hookrightarrow D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) has  

\[
\operatorname{rk}E=1,\qquad c_{1}(E)=5 .
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]
   = i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr) ,
\]
where \(i:Z\hookrightarrow V\).  
Since \(c(E)=1+c_{1}(E)\),

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)
   = i_{*}\bigl([Z]\bigr) \;+\; i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap[L]\bigr).
\]

Now intersect with three general hyperplanes (i.e. with \(H^{3}\)) to obtain a zero‑cycle:

* The class \([L]\) meets three generic hyperplanes in one point, so  
  \(\deg([L]\cdot H^{3}) = 1\).

* The term \(c_{1}(E)\cap[L]\) is a zero‑cycle on \(L\) of degree \(\deg c_{1}(E)=5\).

Hence the contribution of the whole component \(L\) to the intersection number is  

\[
1 + 5 = 6 .
\]

The naïve Bézout count \(12\) already includes the “ordinary’’ contribution \(1\) from the line, but it does **not** include the extra contribution \(5\) coming from the excess bundle.  
Therefore the number of **isolated** conics (the ones that are not on the line \(L\)) is

\[
12 - 5 = 7 .
\]

Thus the corrected intersection number – the total number of conics that are tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) and singular, counted with multiplicity – is  

\[
\boxed{7}
\]

The two divisors are  

\[
D_{1}\sim 4H ,\qquad D_{2}\sim 3H\qquad\text{in }V=\mathbf P^{5},
\]

so the naïve Bézout number is  

\[
\deg D_{1}\cdot\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 3 = 12 .
\]

Because the line  

\[
L\cong\mathbf P^{1}\subset V
\]

parametrising the double lines \(2\ell\) (with \(\ell\) tangent to \(C\) at \(P\)) is contained in the scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\), the intersection is not transverse.  

For a component \(L\) of the intersection, Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]
   \;=\; i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap [L]\bigr)\;+\;(\text{contributions from the isolated points}),
\]

where \(i:L\hookrightarrow V\) and \(E\) is the excess normal bundle.  
The rank of \(E\) equals the excess codimension  

\[
e=\bigl(\operatorname{codim}D_{1}+\operatorname{codim}D_{2}\bigr)
    -\operatorname{codim}L
   = (1+1)-4 = -2,
\]

so the only relevant term is the top Chern class \(c_{1}(E)\) (because \(L\) is one‑dimensional).  
We are told  

\[
c_{1}(E)=\deg E = 5 .
\]

Hence the contribution of the whole line \(L\) to the intersection product is  

\[
\int_{L}c_{1}(E)=5 .
\]

Subtracting this excess contribution from the naïve Bézout number leaves the contribution of the isolated (proper) intersection points:

\[
\#\bigl(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\bigr)_{\text{corrected}}
   = 12 \;-\; 5 = 7 .
\]

Thus the number of conics that are simultaneously tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) and singular, counted with multiplicity, is  

\[
\boxed{7}
\]

The excess–intersection formula of Fulton gives  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]=i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap [L]\bigr),
\]

where \(i:L\hookrightarrow V\) and \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on the excess component \(L\cong\mathbf P^{1}\).

For a line \(L\) the only term of \(c(E)\) that contributes to a \(0\)-cycle after pushing forward is the first Chern class:

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E),\qquad \deg c_{1}(E)=\deg E=5 .
\]

Hence the contribution of the excess component to the intersection number is  

\[
\int_{L} c_{1}(E)=5 .
\]

The naïve Bézout number for the intersection of the two divisors is  

\[
\deg D_{1}\cdot\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 3=12 .
\]

Subtracting the excess contribution gives the corrected (enumerative) count of isolated conics that satisfy both conditions:

\[
\text{corrected number}=12-5=7 .
\]

Thus there are **seven** conics that are tangent to the cubic \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\) and are singular, when counted with multiplicity.

\[
\boxed{7}
\]

The two divisors \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) on the smooth variety \(V=\mathbf P^{5}\) have classes  

\[
[D_{1}]=4H ,\qquad [D_{2}]=3H .
\]

If they intersect transversally their intersection number would be  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]=4\cdot 3 =12 .
\]

However the actual intersection contains the line  

\[
L\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\subset V ,
\]

the locus of double lines \(2\ell\) where \(\ell\) runs through the lines through the fixed point \(P\).  
Thus the intersection has an **excess component** \(L\) of dimension \(1\) (where the expected
dimension of the intersection is \(0\)).  

For a component \(Z\) of excess dimension, Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]
= [\text{expected 0‑dim part}]
+ c_{e}(E)\cap[Z],
\]

where \(e=\operatorname{rank}E\) is the excess codimension and \(E\) is the excess normal bundle
restricted to \(Z\).

Here \(Z=L\) and the excess bundle \(E\) is a line bundle on \(L\) with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=\deg E =5 .
\]

Hence  

\[
c_{e}(E)\cap[Z]=c_{1}(E)\cap[L]=\deg(E)=5,
\]

which contributes a \(0\)-cycle of degree \(5\) coming from the line \(L\).

Therefore the contribution from the isolated points (the actual finite set of conics that are
both singular and tangent) is obtained by subtracting this excess contribution from the naïve
Bézout number:

\[
\text{corrected intersection number}
= 12 - 5 = 7 .
\]

\[
\boxed{7}
\]
