problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \(V=\mathbb{P}^{5}\) be the projective space parametrising plane conics.  
Fix a line \(L\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\).  Denote by \(D_{1}\subset V\) the divisor consisting of conics tangent to \(L\); it is a hypersurface of degree \(2\).  Let \(D_{2}\subset V\) be the discriminant hypersurface of singular conics; it has degree \(3\).  
The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) contains a component \(C\) consisting of the reducible conics that contain \(L\); this component is a linear plane \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\subset V\) of degree \(1\).  
The normal bundle of \(D_{1}\) in \(V\) restricts to \(C\) as \(\mathcal{O}_{C}(2)\), so \(c_{1}\!\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=2\).  
Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the number of isolated points in the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) (i.e. the contribution to the refined intersection product after removing the excess coming from \(C\)).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The two hypersurfaces  

\[
D_{1},\;D_{2}\subset V=\mathbf P^{5}
\]

have classes  

\[
[D_{1}]=2H ,\qquad [D_{2}]=3H\qquad (H=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{V}(1))).
\]

Hence  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]= (2H)(3H)=6H^{2}\in A_{3}(V)
\]

is the total refined intersection class of \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\).

---

### The excess component \(C\)

The component \(C\subset D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) is a linear plane \(\mathbf P^{2}\subset \mathbf P^{5}\);
its class is  

\[
[C]=H^{3}\in A_{2}(V).
\]

The normal bundle of the divisor \(D_{1}\) restricted to \(C\) is  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\simeq\mathcal O_{C}(2),\qquad c_{1}=2H .
\]

Since \(D_{2}\) is a degree‑\(3\) hypersurface,  

\[
N_{D_{2}}V|_{C}\simeq\mathcal O_{C}(3).
\]

For the linear plane \(C\subset V\) we have  

\[
N_{C}V\simeq\mathcal O_{C}(1)^{\oplus 3},\qquad c_{1}(N_{C}V)=3H .
\]

From the exact sequences  

\[
0\to N_{C}D_{1}\to N_{C}V\to\mathcal O_{C}(2)\to0,\qquad
0\to N_{C}D_{2}\to N_{C}V\to\mathcal O_{C}(3)\to0,
\]

we obtain  

\[
c_{1}(N_{C}D_{1})=3H-2H = H,\qquad
c_{1}(N_{C}D_{2})=3H-3H =0 .
\]

The **excess bundle** on \(C\) is the quotient  

\[
E = N_{C}V\big/ \bigl(N_{C}D_{1}\oplus N_{C}D_{2}\bigr),
\]

so  

\[
c_{1}(E)=c_{1}(N_{C}V)-c_{1}(N_{C}D_{1})-c_{1}(N_{C}D_{2})
        =3H-H-0 =2H .
\]

Thus \(E\simeq\mathcal O_{C}(2)\) and \(\operatorname{rk}E=1\).

---

### Contribution of \(C\) to the refined product

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives the contribution of the component \(C\) as  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [C]\bigr)
      = i_{*}\bigl(2H\cap H^{3}\bigr)
      =2\, i_{*}\bigl(H^{4}\bigr),
\]

where \(i:C\hookrightarrow V\).  
Since \(H^{4}\) on a plane is the class of a line, the above class is \(2\) times a line lying in \(C\).

When we intersect the whole refined product with three general hyperplanes
(\(H^{3}\)), a line meets those hyperplanes in exactly one point, so the
contribution of \(C\) to the number of points is \(2\).

---

### Number of isolated points

The total degree of the refined product is obtained by intersecting
\(6H^{2}\) with three hyperplanes:

\[
6H^{2}\cdot H^{3}=6 .
\]

Subtracting the contribution coming from the excess component \(C\) gives

\[
\#\text{isolated points}=6-2 = 4 .
\]

Hence the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) contains **four isolated points**
once the excess component \(C\) is removed.

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The two divisors  

\[
D_{1},D_{2}\subset V=\mathbf P^{5}
\]

have classes  

\[
[D_{1}]=2H ,\qquad [D_{2}]=3H\qquad (H=\text{hyperplane class}).
\]

Hence  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot [D_{2}]=6H^{2}.
\]

Since \(\dim V =5\), the 0‑dimensional degree of this class (i.e. the total number of points counted with multiplicities in a general three‑fold linear section) is  

\[
\deg (6H^{2}\cdot H^{3}) =6 .
\]

So **six** points are counted by the refined intersection product of \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\).

The scheme‑theoretic intersection contains the excess component  

\[
C\simeq\mathbf P^{2}\subset V ,
\]

which is a linear plane of degree \(1\).  
Along \(C\) the normal bundle of \(D_{1}\) in \(V\) restricts to  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\cong \mathcal O_{C}(2),
\qquad c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=2 .
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of the component \(C\) to the refined product is  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)\;\cap\;[C]
      = 2\,[C] .
\]

Since \([C]\) is a plane of degree \(1\), this contribution corresponds to **two** isolated points (counted with multiplicity).

Subtracting this excess contribution from the total degree gives the number of genuine isolated points in the intersection:

\[
\text{isolated points}= 6-2 = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The two hypersurfaces in the smooth ambient space \(V=\mathbf P^{5}\) are  

\[
D_{1}\sim 2H ,\qquad D_{2}\sim 3H ,
\]

where \(H\) denotes the hyperplane class on \(V\).  
Hence their (ordinary) intersection product in \(A_{3}(V)\) is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}] = (2H)(3H)=6H^{2}.
\]

The degree of this 0‑cycle (i.e. the number of points counted with multiplicity) is the product of the degrees of the two hypersurfaces:

\[
\deg\bigl([D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]\bigr)=2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) is not pure‑dimensional: besides the expected 3‑dimensional component it contains the linear plane  

\[
C\simeq\mathbf P^{2}\subset V ,
\]

which is a component of excess codimension.  
To remove its contribution we use Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula.

---

### Excess bundle on \(C\)

Inside \(V\) the normal bundle of the divisor \(D_{1}\) is the line bundle  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V \cong \mathcal O_{V}(2)_{|D_{1}} .
\]

Restricting to \(C\) we obtain  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\;\cong\;\mathcal O_{C}(2) .
\]

Thus the excess bundle on \(C\) is the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{C}(2)\) whose total Chern class is  

\[
c\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=1+2h ,
\]

where \(h=c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{C}(1)\bigr)\) is the hyperplane class on the plane \(C\).

---

### Contribution of \(C\) to the refined intersection

The refined intersection class contributed by \(C\) is  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C})\cap [C]\bigr)
   = i_{*}\bigl((1+2h)\cap [C]\bigr).
\]

Since \([C]\) is a 2‑dimensional class, only the term of degree \(2\) in the Chern class survives:

\[
(2h)\cap [C]=2\;h^{2}\cap [C].
\]

On a plane \(\int_{C}h^{2}=1\). Hence the numerical contribution of the component \(C\) is  

\[
\int_{C}2h^{2}=2 .
\]

---

### Isolated points

The total intersection number is \(6\). Subtracting the excess contribution coming from \(C\) gives the number of isolated points (the remaining 0‑dimensional part of the intersection):

\[
\#\text{ isolated points}=6-2=4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The total refined intersection number of two hypersurfaces of degrees \(2\) and \(3\) in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is  

\[
\deg(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}) = 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

The component \(C\simeq \mathbf P^{2}\) contributes via the excess‑intersection formula.  

* Normal bundle of \(D_{1}\) restricted to \(C\): \(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}= \mathcal O_{C}(2)\) with total Chern class \(c(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}) = 1+2h\).
* \(C\) is a linear \(\mathbf P^{2}\subset \mathbf P^{5}\); its normal bundle in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is \(N_{C}V = \mathcal O_{C}(1)^{\oplus 3}\).
* Since \(D_{2}\) is a degree‑\(3\) hypersurface containing \(C\), we have an exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow N_{C}D_{2}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{C}(1)^{\oplus 3}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{C}(3)\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
c(N_{C}D_{2}) = \frac{c(\mathcal O(1)^{\oplus 3})}{c(\mathcal O(3))}
               = \frac{(1+h)^{3}}{1+3h}= 1+3h^{2}.
\]

The excess bundle on \(C\) is the virtual bundle  

\[
E = N_{D_{1}}V|_{C} - N_{C}D_{2},
\qquad
c(E)=\frac{c(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C})}{c(N_{C}D_{2})}
     =\frac{1+2h}{1+3h^{2}}
     =1+2h-3h^{2}.
\]

Therefore the contribution of \(C\) to the refined intersection product is  

\[
j_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap [C]\bigr)= [C] + 2h\cap[C] - 3h^{2}\cap[C].
\]

Only the zero‑dimensional part matters for the degree; \(h^{2}\cap[C]\) is a point class of degree \(1\) on the plane \(C\).  
Hence the contribution of \(C\) to the degree is \(-3\).

Let \(N\) be the number of isolated (zero‑dimensional) points in \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\).  
Then  

\[
6 = (\text{contribution of }C) + N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
N = 6 - (-3) = 9 .
\]

Thus there are \(9\) isolated points in the intersection after removing the excess component.

\[
\boxed{9}
\]

The Chow ring of \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is  

\[
A^{*}(\mathbb P^{5})=\mathbb Z[H]/(H^{6}),\qquad H=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{5}}(1)).
\]

For a hypersurface of degree \(d\) the class is \(dH\).  
Hence  

\[
[D_{1}]=2H ,\qquad [D_{2}]=3H .
\]

The refined intersection product of the two divisors is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]= (2H)(3H)=6H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbb P^{5}) .
\]

The class \(6H^{2}\) has degree \(6\); geometrically it means that a
general linear subspace \(\Lambda\cong\mathbb P^{2}\) (intersection of three
general hyperplanes) meets \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) in \(6\) points, counted with
multiplicity.

The component  

\[
C\simeq\mathbb P^{2}\subset D_{1}\cap D_{2}
\]

has codimension \(3\) in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) (so it is of higher codimension than
the expected codimension \(2\)).  
For such a component the excess‑intersection bundle is  

\[
0\longrightarrow N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\oplus N_{D_{2}}V|_{C}\longrightarrow
N_{C}V\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow 0,
\]

with  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2),\qquad
N_{D_{2}}V|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(3),\qquad
N_{C}V\cong\mathcal O_{C}(1)^{\oplus 3}.
\]

Thus  

\[
c(E)=\frac{c(N_{C}V)}{c(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C})c(N_{D_{2}}V|_{C})}
      =\frac{(1+H)^{3}}{(1+2H)(1+3H)}=1+2H-3H^{2}.
\]

Only the term of codimension \(2\) (i.e. the \(H^{2}\)-term) would affect the
class in \(A^{2}(\mathbb P^{5})\), but the factor \(-3H^{2}\) is supported on
\(C\) (dimension \(2\)), so after pushing forward it lies in
\(A^{3}(\mathbb P^{5})\) of codimension \(3\) or higher. Consequently the
excess component \(C\) contributes **nothing** to the codimension‑2 part of the
refined product.

Therefore the refined intersection product is entirely given by the
expected term \(6H^{2}\).  After removing the excess component \(C\), the
remaining part consists of isolated points whose total multiplicity equals
the degree of this class:

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The divisor classes in \(A^{*}( \mathbf P^{5})\) are generated by the hyperplane class \(H\) with  
\[
A^{*}(\mathbf P^{5})=\mathbf Z[H]/(H^{6}),\qquad \deg H^{5}=1 .
\]

* \(D_{1}\) is a quadric hypersurface, so \([D_{1}]=2H\).  
* \(D_{2}\) is a cubic hypersurface, so \([D_{2}]=3H\).

Hence the refined intersection product of the two divisors is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot [D_{2}]= (2H)(3H)=6H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbf P^{5}).
\]

---

### The excess component \(C\)

\(C\subset \mathbf P^{5}\) is a linear plane, therefore  

\[
[C]=H^{3}\in A^{3}(\mathbf P^{5}).
\]

The normal bundle of \(D_{1}\) in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) restricts to \(C\) as  

\[
N_{D_{1}}\mathbf P^{5}\big|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2),
\]
so \(c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}\mathbf P^{5}|_{C}\bigr)=2H|_{C}\).

For the excess‑intersection formula (Fulton, §6.3) the contribution of the component \(C\) to the refined product is  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(N_{D_{1}}\mathbf P^{5}|_{C})\cap [C]\bigr)
   = i_{*}\bigl(2H\cap H^{3}\bigr)=2H^{4}\in A^{4}(\mathbf P^{5}).
\]

---

### Isolated (zero‑dimensional) part

The refined product \(6H^{2}\) lives in codimension 2.  
To obtain a zero‑cycle we intersect with a general linear subspace of codimension 3, i.e. with \(H^{3}\):

\[
\deg\bigl(6H^{2}\cdot H^{3}\bigr)=6 .
\]

The excess contribution becomes a zero‑cycle after intersecting \(2H^{4}\) with a general hyperplane \(H\):

\[
\deg\bigl(2H^{4}\cdot H\bigr)=2 .
\]

Therefore the degree (i.e. the number) of the isolated points in the intersection, after removing the excess coming from \(C\), is  

\[
6-2 = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The two hypersurfaces  

\[
D_{1},D_{2}\subset V=\mathbb P^{5}
\]

have divisor classes  

\[
[D_{1}]=2H,\qquad [D_{2}]=3H\qquad (H=\text{hyperplane class}).
\]

Hence their refined intersection product in the Chow ring of \(V\) is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]= (2H)(3H)=6H^{2}\in A^{2}(V).
\]

To obtain a number we intersect further with three general hyperplanes
\(H^{3}\); the degree is  

\[
\deg\big(6H^{2}\cdot H^{3}\big)=6 .
\]

Thus a complete intersection of \(D_{1},D_{2}\) with three general
hyperplanes consists of \(6\) points counted with multiplicities.

The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) contains the
linear plane  

\[
C\simeq\mathbb P^{2}\subset V,
\]

which is an excess component.  
For the excess component the Fulton excess‑intersection formula gives
the contribution

\[
c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)\cap [C].
\]

We are told \(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2)\); hence  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=2H|_{C}.
\]

Since \(\deg([C])=1\) (the plane has degree 1), the 0‑dimensional
contribution of \(C\) is  

\[
\deg\bigl(2H|_{C}\cap [C]\bigr)=2\cdot 1 =2 .
\]

Therefore the isolated (0‑dimensional) part of the intersection
contributes the remaining degree:

\[
\text{number of isolated points}=6-2=4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The two hypersurfaces in \(V=\mathbf P^{5}\) are  

\[
[D_{1}]=2h ,\qquad [D_{2}]=3h ,\qquad h=c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{V}(1)\bigr).
\]

Hence the total refined intersection product in the Chow group of \(V\) is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot [D_{2}]= (2h)(3h)=6h^{2}.
\]

The degree of this class (intersection with \(h^{3}\)) is  

\[
\deg\bigl(6h^{2}\bigr)=6,
\]

so a transverse intersection of the two divisors would consist of six isolated points.

---

### The excess component \(C\)

The scheme‑theoretic intersection contains the linear plane  

\[
C\simeq\mathbf P^{2}\subset V ,
\qquad [C]=h^{3},\qquad \deg C =1 .
\]

Along \(C\) the normal bundle of the divisor \(D_{1}\) is  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2),
\qquad c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=2 .
\]

By Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, the contribution of the component
\(C\) to the refined product is the class  

\[
c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)\,[C]=2\,[C].
\]

Since \([C]=h^{3}\) and \(\deg h^{3}=1\), the excess component contributes  

\[
\deg\bigl(2\,[C]\bigr)=2\cdot 1 = 2
\]

to the total intersection number.

---

### Isolated points

Subtracting the excess contribution from the total degree gives the number of
isolated points (the 0‑dimensional part of the refined intersection product):

\[
\#\text{isolated points}=6-2=4.
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The ambient space is  

\[
V=\mathbb P^{5}= \operatorname{Proj}\,k[x_{0},\dots ,x_{5}]
\]

which parametrises plane conics.  

* \(D_{1}\subset V\) : conics tangent to a fixed line \(L\).  
  It is a hypersurface of degree \(2\).

* \(D_{2}\subset V\) : the discriminant (singular conics).  
  It is a hypersurface of degree \(3\).

Hence  

\[
[D_{1}]=2h,\qquad [D_{2}]=3h\qquad (h=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{V}(1))).
\]

The expected codimension of the intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{codim}D_{1}+\operatorname{codim}D_{2}=1+1=2,
\]

so we expect a 3‑dimensional variety.  
Inside the scheme–theoretic intersection there is a component  

\[
C\simeq\mathbb P^{2}\subset V
\]

consisting of the reducible conics that contain the line \(L\).  
\(C\) has codimension \(3\) in \(V\); therefore the excess codimension is  

\[
e=\operatorname{codim}C-\bigl(\operatorname{codim}D_{1}+\operatorname{codim}D_{2}\bigr)=3-2=1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Excess‑intersection contribution of \(C\)

For a regular embedding \(i:D_{1}\hookrightarrow V\) the normal bundle is  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V \cong \mathcal O_{V}(2),
\]

and its restriction to \(C\) is  

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2),\qquad 
c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=2 .
\]

Because the excess codimension is \(e=1\), the excess bundle is exactly this line bundle, and Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives the contribution of the component \(C\) to the refined intersection product:

\[
\bigl(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}\bigr)_{C}=c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)\cap [C]
=2\,[\text{point}] .
\]

Thus the component \(C\) accounts for a 0‑cycle of degree \(2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Isolated points

The total refined intersection product of the two hypersurfaces in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]
= (2h)\cdot(3h)=6h^{2}.
\]

Intersecting further with three general hyperplanes (i.e. with \(h^{3}\)) gives a 0‑cycle of degree  

\[
6h^{5}=6 .
\]

Hence the whole intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) contributes \(6\) points (counted with multiplicities).  
Subtracting the contribution coming from the excess component \(C\) leaves the number of **isolated** points:

\[
\#\text{isolated points}=6-2=4 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The two divisors have degrees  

\[
\deg D_{1}=2 ,\qquad \deg D_{2}=3 .
\]

Hence, if they intersect properly the refined intersection product would have degree  

\[
\deg(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}) = 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Because the component  

\[
C\simeq \mathbf P^{2}\subset V
\]

appears in the scheme‑theoretic intersection, we must subtract its excess contribution.  
For the excess component \(C\) the excess normal bundle is just the restriction of the normal bundle of \(D_{1}\) to \(C\):

\[
N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\cong\mathcal O_{C}(2),\qquad c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr)=2 .
\]

The contribution of \(C\) to the refined intersection product is

\[
\int_{C} c_{1}\bigl(N_{D_{1}}V|_{C}\bigr) = \int_{C} 2h = 2,
\]

where \(h\) is the hyperplane class on the plane \(C\) and \(\int_{C}h^{2}=1\).

Therefore the number of isolated points (the part of the intersection not coming from \(C\)) is  

\[
6 - 2 = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \(M\simeq\mathbb{P}^{9}\) be the projective space parametrising plane quartic curves. Inside \(M\) consider two effective divisors:

* \(D_{t}\) consisting of quartics tangent to a fixed line \(\ell\); its degree is \(\deg D_{t}=4\).
* \(D_{s}\) consisting of singular quartics; its degree is \(\deg D_{s}=6\).

The expected intersection number of \(D_{t}\) and \(D_{s}\) is the product \(4\cdot 6 = 24\). However, the two divisors meet non‑transversely at the single point \(x\in M\) corresponding to the quartic that is singular at a point of \(\ell\) and whose tangent cone contains \(\ell\). At this point the excess normal bundle \(E\) is a line bundle on \(\{x\}\) whose first Chern class has degree \(3\).

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the correction term that must be subtracted from the naïve count \(24\), and give the resulting corrected intersection number.

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The two divisors \(D_t\) and \(D_s\) have classes  

\[
[D_t]=4H ,\qquad [D_s]=6H\qquad (H=\text{hyperplane class on } \mathbf P^{9}),
\]

so a naïve intersection would give  

\[
4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

Because the intersection is not transverse, Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula must be used.  
Let  

\[
Y = D_t\cap D_s = \{x\}
\]

be the (zero‑dimensional) excess component.  
The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(Y\) has rank \(1\) and its first Chern class satisfies  

\[
c_1(E)=3\;[x].
\]

For a zero‑dimensional excess component the contribution of the excess to the refined intersection product is the degree of the top Chern class of \(E\):

\[
\deg\bigl(c_1(E)\bigr)=3 .
\]

Thus the refined intersection number is

\[
\text{(naïve)}\;-\;\deg\bigl(c_1(E)\bigr)=24-3=21 .
\]

Hence the corrected intersection number is  

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The two divisors \(D_t\) and \(D_s\) have degrees  

\[
\deg D_t = 4 ,\qquad \deg D_s = 6 .
\]

If they met transversely, their intersection number would be  

\[
4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

Because the intersection is not transverse, there is an excess normal bundle  
\(E\) supported at the single point \(x\).  For a point, Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says that the contribution of the excess is the degree of the top Chern class of \(E\):

\[
\text{excess contribution}= \int_{\{x\}} c_1(E)=\deg c_1(E).
\]

We are told \(\deg c_1(E)=3\).  Hence the naïve count \(24\) includes an extra \(3\) coming from this excess intersection.  Subtracting this correction term gives the true intersection number:

\[
\boxed{24-3 = 21}.
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of the non‑transverse component \(x\) is the top Chern class of the excess normal bundle \(E\) evaluated on \(\{x\}\).

* \(E\) is a line bundle on the point \(\{x\}\).
* Its first Chern class has degree \(\deg c_{1}(E)=3\).

Hence the excess contribution that must be **subtracted** from the naïve count \(4\cdot 6 = 24\) is  

\[
\text{correction term}= \deg c_{1}(E)=3 .
\]

Therefore the corrected intersection number is  

\[
24 - 3 = 21 .
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula says that the contribution of the non‑transverse point \(x\) is given by the top Chern class of the excess normal bundle \(E\):
\[
c_{1}(E) \in A^{1}(\{x\}) .
\]

Since \(E\) is a line bundle on the zero‑dimensional scheme \(\{x\}\) whose first Chern class has degree  

\[
\deg c_{1}(E)=3,
\]

the excess contribution that must be removed from the naïve product \(4\cdot 6 = 24\) is exactly \(3\).

Hence the corrected intersection number is  

\[
24-3 = 21 .
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The naive count of the intersection is  

\[
4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

Because the two divisors meet non‑transversely at the single point \(x\), Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of this point is corrected by the top Chern class of the excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(\{x\}\).

Here \(E\) is a line bundle on the point, so its rank is \(1\).  
The top Chern class is simply \(c_{1}(E)\).  
We are given that  

\[
\deg c_{1}(E)=3 .
\]

Thus the correction term that must be **subtracted** from the naïve count is \(3\).

\[
\text{Corrected intersection number}=24-3=21 .
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula states  

\[
[D_t]\cdot[D_s]=i_*\bigl(c_{e}(E)\cap [x]\bigr),
\]

where \(e\) is the rank of the excess bundle \(E\).  
Here \(D_t\) and \(D_s\) are divisors, so the excess bundle has rank \(e=1\).  
For a point \(x\) the only non‑zero Chern class of a line bundle is its first Chern class, and we are told  

\[
\deg c_{1}(E)=3 .
\]

Hence the refined intersection contribution of the point \(x\) is  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [x]=3\,[x].
\]

The naïve intersection number is the product of the degrees of the two divisors:

\[
4\cdot 6 = 24 .
\]

Since the true contribution of the point is \(3\), the excess part that has been over‑counted is  

\[
24-3 = 21 .
\]

Subtracting this correction term from the naïve count gives the **corrected intersection number**

\[
24-21 = 3 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula of Fulton says that for the (possibly non‑transverse) intersection  

\[
D_{t}\cap D_{s}= \{x\},
\]

the refined intersection class is  

\[
[D_{t}]\cdot[D_{s}] \;=\; c(E)\cap [x],
\]

where \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on the component \(\{x\}\).

* Here \(E\) is a line bundle, so  

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E).
\]

* The first Chern class has degree \(\deg c_{1}(E)=3\).

Hence  

\[
c(E)\cap [x]= (1+c_{1}(E))\cap [x]=[x]+3\,[x],
\]

so the excess contribution beyond the ordinary transverse contribution “\(1\)” is **\(3\)**.

The naïve product of the divisor degrees gives  

\[
\deg D_{t}\cdot\deg D_{s}=4\cdot6 = 24 .
\]

To obtain the correct intersection number we must subtract the excess contribution \(3\):

\[
\text{corrected intersection number}=24-3 = 21 .
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula says that at the point \(x\) the contribution to the intersection product is  

\[
c(E)\cap [x]=\bigl(1+c_{1}(E)\bigr)\cap [x]
\]

Since \(E\) is a line bundle on the point \(\{x\}\) with \(\deg c_{1}(E)=3\),

\[
c(E)\cap [x]=[x]+3[x]=4[x].
\]

The naïve product of the divisor classes gives \(4\cdot 6 = 24\) points.  
Because the true contribution at \(x\) is \(4\) rather than the naïve contribution of \(1\), the excess contributes an extra \(3\) that must be removed from the naïve count.

\[
\text{correction term}=3,\qquad
\text{corrected intersection number}=24-3=21.
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula tells us that the contribution of the non‑transverse point \(x\) is the top Chern class of the excess normal bundle \(E\).  
Since \(E\) is a line bundle on the point \(\{x\}\) with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=\deg(E)=3,
\]

the excess contribution is \(3\).

The naïve product of the divisor classes gives \(4\cdot 6 = 24\).  
Subtracting the excess contribution yields the actual intersection number:

\[
24 - 3 = 21 .
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula says that for a component \(Z\) where the intersection is not transverse the contribution is  

\[
\int_{Z} c(E)\cap [Z] .
\]

Here \(Z=\{x\}\) is a point and the excess normal bundle \(E\) has rank 1 with  

\[
\deg c_{1}(E)=3 .
\]

Thus  

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E),\qquad 
\int_{\{x\}}c(E)=1+3=4 .
\]

The naïve product of the divisor classes gives the number \(4\cdot6=24\), which counts the point \(x\) with multiplicity 1.  
Because the true contribution of \(x\) is \(4\), we must subtract the excess amount  

\[
\text{correction}=4-1 = 3 .
\]

Hence the corrected intersection number is  

\[
24-3 = 21 .
\]

\[
\boxed{21}
\]

problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \(V=\mathbb{P}^{9}\) be the projective space that parametrises plane cubic curves, and let \(H\) denote the hyperplane class on \(V\).

* \(\Delta\subset V\) is the discriminant hypersurface consisting of singular cubics; its class is \(12H\) (i.e. \(\deg\Delta=12\)).
* \(\Sigma\subset V\) is the divisor of cubics that are singular at a fixed point \(P\in\mathbb{P}^{2}\); its class is \(3H\) (so \(\Sigma\simeq\mathbb{P}^{8}\)).
* The scheme–theoretic intersection \(\Delta\cap\Sigma\) is not proper because \(\Sigma\) lies inside the singular locus of \(\Delta\).  
  The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(\Sigma\) is a line bundle with first Chern class \(c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}\).

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the refined intersection product \(\Delta\cdot\Sigma\) (i.e. the corrected intersection number after accounting for the excess).  

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The excess‑intersection formula states that for a regular embedding  
\(i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow V\) and a closed subscheme \(\Delta\subset V\) with
\(Z=\Sigma\cap\Delta\) (here \(Z=\Sigma\) because \(\Sigma\subset\Delta\)),
the refined Gysin map is  

\[
i^{!}[\Delta]=c(E)\cap[Z],
\]

where \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on \(Z\).

Here  

* \(\Sigma\) is a divisor of class \(3H\) (so \(\dim\Sigma =8\));
* \(\Delta\) is a divisor of class \(12H\);
* the excess normal bundle on \(\Sigma\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Thus  

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E)=1+4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Cap‑product with the fundamental class \([\Sigma]\) gives  

\[
c(E)\cap[\Sigma]=[\Sigma]+4H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma].
\]

Only the codimension‑1 part survives in the refined intersection
\(\Delta\cdot\Sigma\); therefore  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = 4\,H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma].
\]

Since \(H|_{\Sigma}\) generates \(A^{1}(\Sigma)\cong\mathbb{Z}\), the refined
intersection product is \(4\) times the hyperplane class on \(\Sigma\).

Hence the corrected intersection number is  

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The expected codimension of the intersection of two divisors in the smooth variety  
\(V=\mathbb P^{9}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{codim}\Delta+\operatorname{codim}\Sigma=1+1=2 .
\]

But \(\Sigma\subset\Delta\) (every cubic singular at the fixed point \(P\) is
singular, hence lies in the discriminant).  
Thus  

\[
\Delta\cap\Sigma = \Sigma ,\qquad 
\operatorname{codim}(\Delta\cap\Sigma)=1 .
\]

Hence the excess codimension is  

\[
e = (1+1)-1 = 1 .
\]

The excess normal bundle on the intersection is a line bundle \(E\) with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

---

### Excess‑intersection formula  

For a proper intersection the refined product would be
\(c(E)\cap [\Delta\cap\Sigma]\).  
Since \(E\) has rank \(1\),

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E)=1+4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

The term of codimension \(1\) (the only non‑zero contribution) is  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap[\Sigma]=4H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma].
\]

Thus the refined intersection product is the divisor class  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = 4\,H|_{\Sigma}\;\in A_{7}(\Sigma).
\]

---

### Numerical intersection number  

\(\Sigma\simeq\mathbb P^{8}\) with hyperplane class \(h=H|_{\Sigma}\).
The degree of the divisor \(4h\) is obtained by intersecting it with
\(h^{7}\):

\[
\deg(\Delta\cdot\Sigma)=\int_{\Sigma} 4h\;h^{7}=4\int_{\Sigma}h^{8}=4\cdot1=4 .
\]

Hence the corrected (refined) intersection number of \(\Delta\) and \(\Sigma\) is  

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula (Fulton, Thm. 6.3) says that for two regular embeddings  

\[
i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow V ,\qquad j:\Delta\hookrightarrow V
\]

with (scheme‑theoretic) intersection \(W=\Sigma\cap\Delta\) the refined intersection product is  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma \;=\; c(E)\;\cap\;[W],
\]

where \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on \(\Sigma\).

Here  

* \(\Sigma\) is a divisor of class \(3H\) in \(V=\mathbf P^{9}\);
* \(\Delta\) is a divisor of class \(12H\);
* the excess normal bundle \(E\) is a line bundle on \(\Sigma\) with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Thus  

\[
c(E)=1+4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Since \(W=\Sigma\) (set‑theoretically the whole \(\Sigma\) lies in the singular locus of \(\Delta\)), we have  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = (1+4H|_{\Sigma})\cap[\Sigma]
                 = 4H|_{\Sigma}\in A_{7}(V).
\]

To obtain a number we intersect this class with the remaining hyperplane classes so that the total codimension is \(9\):

\[
\deg(\Delta\cdot\Sigma)=\int_{\Sigma} 4H|_{\Sigma}\, H^{7}
          =4\int_{\mathbf P^{8}} H^{8}=4\cdot 1 =4 .
\]

Hence the refined (excess‑corrected) intersection number is  

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The Chow ring of the ambient projective space is  

\[
A^{*}(V)=\mathbb Z[H]/(H^{10}),\qquad \deg H^{9}=1 .
\]

---

### 1.  Restriction of the divisor classes to \(\Sigma\)

\[
\Delta|_{\Sigma}=12H|_{\Sigma}=12h ,\qquad 
\Sigma\hookrightarrow V\text{ has }c_{1}(N_{\Sigma/V})=3h .
\]

Here \(h:=H|_{\Sigma}\) generates \(A^{*}(\Sigma)=\mathbb Z[h]/(h^{9})\).

---

### 2.  Excess normal bundle  

The excess bundle is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4h\;\Longrightarrow\;c(E)=1+4h .
\]

---

### 3.  Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula  

For the regular embeddings \(\Sigma\hookrightarrow V\) and \(\Delta\hookrightarrow V\),

\[
i^{!}[\Delta]=c(E)\cap (\Delta|_{\Sigma})\in A_{7}(\Sigma).
\]

Hence  

\[
c(E)\cap (\Delta|_{\Sigma})=(1+4h)\cdot 12h=12h+48h^{2}.
\]

The term \(12h\) has codimension 1 on \(\Sigma\) (dimension 7), while the term \(48h^{2}\) has codimension 2 (dimension 6).  
Both appear in the refined Gysin image.

---

### 4.  Push‑forward to \(V\)

The inclusion \(i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow V\) satisfies \(i_{*}(h^{k})=H^{k+1}\) because \(\Sigma\) is a divisor. Therefore  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(12h+48h^{2}\bigr)=12H^{2}+48H^{3}.
\]

Thus the refined intersection product in \(A_{7}(V)\) is  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = 12H^{2}+48H^{3}.
\]

---

### 5.  Obtaining a number (degree)

To get a numerical intersection number we intersect further with seven general hyperplanes, i.e. we compute  

\[
\int_{V} (\Delta\cdot\Sigma)\, H^{7}
   = \int_{V} (12H^{2}+48H^{3}) H^{7}
   = 12\int_{V} H^{9}+48\int_{V} H^{10}.
\]

Since \(H^{10}=0\) on \(\mathbb P^{9}\) and \(\int_{V} H^{9}=1\),

\[
\int_{V} (\Delta\cdot\Sigma)\, H^{7}=12.
\]

Hence the corrected intersection number is **12**.

\[
\boxed{12}
\]

The excess‑intersection formula says that for the regular embeddings  

\[
i:\Delta\hookrightarrow V ,\qquad j:\Sigma\hookrightarrow V ,
\]

with \(Y=\Delta\cap\Sigma\) and excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(\Sigma\),

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma \;=\; c(E)\;\cap\;[\,\Sigma\,]\in A_{7}(\Sigma).
\]

Here \(E\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = c_{1}(E)\cap[\Sigma]=4H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma].
\]

To obtain a number we intersect further with enough hyperplanes to get a
zero‑cycle.  Since \(\dim\Sigma =8\),

\[
\deg(\Delta\cdot\Sigma)=\int_{\Sigma} 4H|_{\Sigma}\; H^{7}|_{\Sigma}
      =4\int_{\Sigma} H^{8}|_{\Sigma}.
\]

On \(\Sigma\simeq\mathbb{P}^{8}\) we have \(\int_{\Sigma} H^{8}=1\). Therefore  

\[
\deg(\Delta\cdot\Sigma)=4.
\]

So the refined intersection product equals \(4\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The expected codimension of the intersection of the two divisors \(\Delta\) and \(\Sigma\) in the smooth variety \(V=\mathbf P^{9}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{codim}\Delta+\operatorname{codim}\Sigma =1+1 =2 .
\]

Because \(\Sigma\subset \operatorname{Sing}(\Delta)\) we actually have  

\[
\Delta\cap\Sigma = \Sigma ,
\qquad\operatorname{codim}(\Delta\cap\Sigma)=1 .
\]

Hence the excess codimension is  

\[
e = (1+1)-1 = 1 .
\]

The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(\Sigma\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Fulton's excess‑intersection formula gives  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = c_{e}(E)\cap[\Delta\cap\Sigma]
                  = c_{1}(E)\cap[\Sigma]
                  = 4H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma].
\]

Since \([\Sigma]=3H\) in \(A_{8}(V)\),

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = 4H\cdot (3H)=12H^{2}\in A_{7}(V).
\]

To obtain the numerical intersection number we intersect further with \(H^{7}\) (so that the total codimension is \(9\)):

\[
\deg(\Delta\cdot\Sigma)=\int_{V}12H^{2}\,H^{7}=12\int_{V}H^{9}=12\cdot1=12 .
\]

Thus the refined (corrected) intersection product is the class \(12H^{2}\), whose degree is \(12\).

\[
\boxed{12}
\]

The expected codimension of the intersection of the two divisors  

\[
\Delta \;( \operatorname{codim}=1),\qquad 
\Sigma \;( \operatorname{codim}=1)
\]

in the smooth variety \(V=\mathbf P^{9}\) is  

\[
1+1 = 2 .
\]

In fact \(\Sigma\subset \Delta\), so the scheme‑theoretic intersection is  

\[
Z = \Delta\cap\Sigma = \Sigma ,
\]

which has codimension \(1\).  
Hence the excess codimension is  

\[
e = (1+1)-1 = 1 .
\]

The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(\Sigma\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives the refined product  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma \;=\; c_{1}(E)\;\cap\;[\Sigma]
\]

as a class of codimension \(2\) in \(V\).

Since \([\Sigma]=3H\) (the divisor class of \(\Sigma\) in \(V\)), we obtain  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = (4H)\cdot(3H)=12\,H^{2}\in A^{2}(V).
\]

To get the numerical intersection number we intersect further with \(H^{7}\) (because \(\dim V=9\)):

\[
\int_{V} 12\,H^{2}\,H^{7}=12\int_{V} H^{9}=12\cdot 1=12 .
\]

Thus the corrected (refined) intersection number is  

\[
\boxed{12}
\]

The excess–intersection formula says  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma \;=\; c(E)\cap [\Delta\cap\Sigma]\in A_{*}(\Sigma),
\]

where \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on \(\Sigma\).
Because \(\Sigma\subset\Delta\) (the whole divisor \(\Sigma\) consists of singular cubics),
the ordinary intersection \(\Delta\cap\Sigma\) is just \(\Sigma\) itself.  
Thus the refined product reduces to the top Chern class of \(E\) intersected with \(\Sigma\):

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma = c_{1}(E)\cap [\Sigma].
\]

On \(\Sigma\simeq\mathbf P^{8}\) the hyperplane class is \(h=H|_{\Sigma}\) and we are given  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}=4h .
\]

To obtain a number we intersect further with \(h^{7}\) (the remaining powers needed to reach a 0‑cycle on \(\mathbf P^{8}\)):

\[
\deg(\Delta\cdot\Sigma)=\int_{\Sigma} c_{1}(E)\,h^{7}
      =\int_{\mathbf P^{8}} 4h\;h^{7}
      =4\int_{\mathbf P^{8}} h^{8}=4\cdot 1=4 .
\]

Hence the refined intersection product (the corrected intersection number) is  

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The two subvarieties are  

* \( \Delta \subset V=\mathbf P^{9}\) – a hypersurface of class \(12H\);  
* \( \Sigma \subset V\) – a divisor of class \(3H\) (indeed \(\Sigma\simeq\mathbf P^{8}\)).

Both are regular embeddings of codimension \(1\) in the smooth variety \(V\).  
Since every cubic singular at the fixed point \(P\) is singular, we have the scheme‑theoretic inclusion  

\[
\Sigma \subset \Delta .
\]

Hence the scheme‑theoretic intersection \(\Delta\cap\Sigma\) is just \(\Sigma\) itself, which has codimension \(1\) in \(V\) instead of the expected codimension \(2\).  
The excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(\Sigma\) has rank  

\[
r = (\operatorname{codim}\Delta)+(\operatorname{codim}\Sigma)-\operatorname{codim}(\Delta\cap\Sigma)
   = 1+1-1 = 1,
\]

and we are given  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

---

### Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula  

For regular embeddings \(i:\Delta\hookrightarrow V\) and \(j:\Sigma\hookrightarrow V\) with excess bundle \(E\),

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma \;=\; c_{r}(E)\;\cap\;[\Delta\cap\Sigma].
\]

Here \(r=1\), so \(c_{r}(E)=c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}\), and \([\Delta\cap\Sigma]=[\Sigma]\). Thus  

\[
\Delta\cdot\Sigma \;=\; (4H|_{\Sigma})\;\cap\;[\Sigma].
\]

---

### Computing the numerical degree  

On \(\Sigma\simeq\mathbf P^{8}\), the restriction \(H|_{\Sigma}\) is the hyperplane class of \(\mathbf P^{8}\).  
Intersecting \(4H|_{\Sigma}\) with the fundamental class of \(\Sigma\) gives a codimension‑2 cycle of degree  

\[
4\; \bigl(\deg(\Sigma)\bigr)=4\cdot 1 = 4,
\]

because a linear subspace \(\mathbf P^{8}\subset\mathbf P^{9}\) has degree \(1\).

Hence the refined (excess‑corrected) intersection product is the class represented by a degree‑\(4\) cycle, and its numerical value is \(4\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The ambient space is  

\[
V=\mathbf P^{9},\qquad A^{*}(V)=\mathbf Z[H]/(H^{10}),\qquad \deg H^{9}=1 .
\]

Both \(\Delta\) and \(\Sigma\) are divisors, so  

\[
[\Delta]=12H,\qquad [\Sigma]=3H .
\]

Because every cubic singular at the fixed point \(P\) is singular, we have  

\[
\Sigma\subset \Delta .
\]

Hence the scheme‑theoretic intersection is \(\Delta\cap\Sigma=\Sigma\) and the intersection is not proper.  
The excess bundle \(E\) on \(\Sigma\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=4H|_{\Sigma}.
\]

---

### Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula  

If \(X,Y\subset V\) meet with excess bundle \(E\) and \(Z=X\cap Y\), then  

\[
X\cdot Y \;=\; i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)\in A_{*}(V),
\]

where \(i:Z\hookrightarrow V\) is the inclusion.  
Here \(c(E)=1+c_{1}(E)=1+4H|_{\Sigma}\).

Thus  

\[
c(E)\cap[\Sigma]=[\Sigma]+4H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma].
\]

Pushing forward to \(V\),

\[
i_{*}[\Sigma]=3H,\qquad 
i_{*}\bigl(4H|_{\Sigma}\cap[\Sigma]\bigr)=4H\cdot[\Sigma]=4H\cdot3H=12H^{2}.
\]

The refined intersection product \(\Delta\cdot\Sigma\) is the component of codimension  

\[
\operatorname{codim}\Delta+\operatorname{codim}\Sigma=1+1=2,
\]

so we keep the \(H^{2}\)‑term:

\[
\boxed{\Delta\cdot\Sigma = 12\,H^{2}}.
\]

The numerical intersection number (the degree of this class) is the coefficient of \(H^{2}\), namely **12**.

\[
\boxed{12}
\]

problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \(L\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a fixed line, and let  

* \(A\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a smooth cubic curve that does **not** contain \(L\);  
* \(B\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) be a smooth quartic curve that does **not** contain \(L\) and meets \(A\) transversely.

Define the reducible divisors  

\[
D_{1}=L\cup A\qquad (\deg D_{1}=4),\qquad 
D_{2}=L\cup B\qquad (\deg D_{2}=5).
\]

The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) contains the common component \(L\) and, away from \(L\), consists of the isolated points where \(A\) meets \(B\).  

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the excess intersection contribution coming from the component \(L\) to the intersection product \(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}\).  Give this excess contribution as a single integer.  

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
First compute the total intersection number of the two divisors in \(\mathbf P^{2}\).

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]=\deg D_{1}\,\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 5=20 .
\]

---

### 1.  Isolated contributions (away from \(L\))

The only isolated points of \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) are the points where the smooth cubic \(A\) meets the smooth quartic \(B\).  
Since \(A\) and \(B\) intersect transversely,

\[
\#(A\cap B)=3\cdot 4 =12,
\]

and each contributes multiplicity \(1\). Hence the contribution coming from these isolated points is

\[
12 .
\]

---

### 2.  Excess contribution from the common component \(L\)

Let  

* \(X=\mathbf P^{2}\) (smooth, \(\dim X =2\)),  
* \(Y=D_{1}\) and \(Z=D_{2}\) (Cartier divisors, \(\operatorname{codim}=1\)),  
* \(W=L=Y\cap Z\) (a line, \(\operatorname{codim}=1\)).

The expected codimension of the intersection is \(2\); the actual component \(W\) has codimension \(1\), so the excess codimension is  

\[
e = \operatorname{codim}Y+\operatorname{codim}Z-\operatorname{codim}W =1+1-1 =1 .
\]

The excess bundle \(E\) on \(W\) is defined by the exact sequence (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*, §6.3)

\[
0\longrightarrow N_{W/X}\longrightarrow N_{Y/X}|_{W}\oplus N_{Z/X}|_{W}\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Compute the normal bundles:

* \(N_{W/X}=N_{L/\mathbf P^{2}}\cong\mathcal O_{L}(1)\)  (a line in \(\mathbf P^{2}\)).
* \(N_{Y/X}= \mathcal O_{X}(D_{1})\) and its restriction to \(L\) is \(\mathcal O_{L}(D_{1})\cong\mathcal O_{L}(4)\).
* \(N_{Z/X}= \mathcal O_{X}(D_{2})\) and its restriction to \(L\) is \(\mathcal O_{L}(D_{2})\cong\mathcal O_{L}(5)\).

Thus the exact sequence becomes  

\[
0\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{L}(1)\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{L}(4)\oplus\mathcal O_{L}(5)\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Taking degrees gives  

\[
\deg E = \deg\mathcal O_{L}(4)+\deg\mathcal O_{L}(5)-\deg\mathcal O_{L}(1)=4+5-1=8 .
\]

Since \(e=1\), the excess contribution of the component \(L\) to the intersection product is  

\[
c_{e}(E)\cap [L]=c_{1}(E)\cap [L]=\deg E = 8 .
\]

---

### 3.  Check

\[
\text{total }20 = \underbrace{12}_{A\cap B\text{ points}}+\underbrace{8}_{\text{excess from }L},
\]

as required.

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The intersection product of the two divisors is  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}]= (L+A)\cdot(L+B)=L\cdot L+L\cdot B+A\cdot L+A\cdot B .
\]

In \(\mathbb P^{2}\) we have  

* \(L\cdot L = 1\) (self–intersection of a line),  
* \(L\cdot B = \deg L\cdot\deg B = 1\cdot4 = 4\),  
* \(A\cdot L = \deg A\cdot\deg L = 3\cdot1 = 3\),  
* \(A\cdot B = 3\cdot4 = 12\) (they meet transversely).

Hence  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}] = 1+4+3+12 = 20 .
\]

The points away from the common component \(L\) contribute the 19 points coming from
\(A\cap B\) (12 points), \(L\cap A\) (3 points) and \(L\cap B\) (4 points).  
The remaining contribution comes from the excess intersection along the common
component \(L\); by Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula this contribution is exactly the self‑intersection number \(L\cdot L\).

Therefore the excess contribution from the component \(L\) is  

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

The intersection product on the smooth surface \(\mathbb P^{2}\) is  

\[
D_1\cdot D_2=(L+A)\cdot(L+B)=L\cdot L+L\cdot B+A\cdot L+A\cdot B .
\]

Because the curves are smooth and meet transversely,
\[
\begin{aligned}
L\cdot L &= 1,\\
L\cdot B &= \deg L\cdot\deg B =1\cdot 4 =4,\\
A\cdot L &= \deg A\cdot\deg L =3\cdot 1 =3,\\
A\cdot B &= \deg A\cdot\deg B =3\cdot 4 =12 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
D_1\cdot D_2 = 1+4+3+12 = 20 .
\]

The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_1\cap D_2\) has the common component \(L\); away from \(L\) the only isolated points are the transverse intersections of \(A\) with \(B\), i.e. the \(12\) points counted by \(A\cdot B\).

Therefore the excess contribution coming from the component \(L\) must supply the remaining part of the total intersection number:

\[
\text{excess from }L = D_1\cdot D_2 - (A\cdot B)=20-12 = 8 .
\]

Thus the excess intersection contribution from \(L\) is  

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The total intersection number in \(\mathbb P^{2}\) is  

\[
D_{1}\cdot D_{2}= (L+A)(L+B)=L^{2}+L\cdot B+A\cdot L+A\cdot B
               =1+4+3+12=20 .
\]

The transverse intersection points of \(A\) and \(B\) give \(12\) (since \(\deg A\cdot\deg B=3\cdot4\)).  
Hence the remaining contribution, which comes from the common component \(L\), must be  

\[
20-12 = 8 .
\]

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, the excess bundle on \(L\) has  

\[
c_{1}(E)=c_{1}(N_{D_{1}}|_{L})+c_{1}(N_{D_{2}}|_{L})-c_{1}(N_{L/\mathbb P^{2}})
        =4+5-1 = 8,
\]

so \(\int_{L}c_{1}(E)=8\).

Thus the excess contribution from the component \(L\) is  

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The divisors  

\[
D_{1}=L\cup A ,\qquad D_{2}=L\cup B
\]

are effective Cartier divisors on the smooth surface \(\mathbf P^{2}\); hence the
embeddings  

\[
i_{1}:D_{1}\hookrightarrow \mathbf P^{2},\qquad i_{2}:D_{2}\hookrightarrow \mathbf P^{2}
\]

are regular of codimension 1.

The expected codimension of the intersection of two codimension‑1 subvarieties is
\(2\).  Because \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) contains the whole line \(L\) (dimension 1),
the intersection has **excess** codimension  

\[
e = 2-1 = 1 .
\]

For a component \(Z\) of the intersection (here \(Z=L\)), Fulton’s excess‑intersection
formula states that the contribution of \(Z\) to the refined intersection product
\(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}\) is  

\[
c_{e}(E)\cap [Z],
\]

where the **excess bundle** is  

\[
E = \frac{N_{Z/D_{1}}\oplus N_{Z/D_{2}}}{N_{Z/\mathbf P^{2}}}
      \;=\; N_{D_{1}/\mathbf P^{2}}\!\big|_{Z}\;\oplus\;
           N_{D_{2}/\mathbf P^{2}}\!\big|_{Z}\; \big/ \;
           N_{Z/\mathbf P^{2}} .
\]

Because \(Z=L\) and the inclusions \(L\subset D_{1},\,L\subset D_{2}\) are
components rather than codimension‑1 embeddings, the normal bundles
\(N_{L/D_{1}}\) and \(N_{L/D_{2}}\) are zero.  Hence the excess bundle reduces to  

\[
E = \frac{N_{D_{1}/\mathbf P^{2}}|_{L}\;\oplus\; N_{D_{2}/\mathbf P^{2}}|_{L}}
           {N_{L/\mathbf P^{2}}}.
\]

For a divisor \(D\) on a smooth surface, \(N_{D/\mathbf P^{2}} \cong
\mathcal O_{D}(D)\).  Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{D_{1}/\mathbf P^{2}}|_{L} &\cong \mathcal O_{L}(D_{1}) 
   = \mathcal O_{L}(4), &&\deg =4,\\
N_{D_{2}/\mathbf P^{2}}|_{L} &\cong \mathcal O_{L}(D_{2}) 
   = \mathcal O_{L}(5), &&\deg =5,\\
N_{L/\mathbf P^{2}} &\cong \mathcal O_{L}(1), &&\deg =1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(E\) is a line bundle of degree  

\[
\deg E = 4+5-1 = 8 .
\]

Since the excess codimension is \(e=1\), the top Chern class is \(c_{1}(E)\),
and its cap with \([L]\) gives a 0‑cycle of degree \(\deg E\).

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The excess‑intersection contribution comes from the common component  

\[
Z=L\subset \mathbb P^{2}.
\]

For the two Cartier divisors  

\[
D_{1}=L+A ,\qquad D_{2}=L+B ,
\]

the normal bundles of \(L\) in the divisors are  

\[
N_{L/D_{1}} \cong \mathcal O_{L}(A)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(3),\qquad 
N_{L/D_{2}} \cong \mathcal O_{L}(B)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(4),
\]

while the normal bundle of \(L\) in the ambient surface is  

\[
N_{L/\mathbb P^{2}}\cong \mathcal O_{L}(1).
\]

The excess bundle is  

\[
E=\frac{N_{L/D_{1}}\oplus N_{L/D_{2}}}{N_{L/\mathbb P^{2}}}\;,
\qquad 
\operatorname{rank}E=1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
c(E)=\frac{c(N_{L/D_{1}})c(N_{L/D_{2}})}{c(N_{L/\mathbb P^{2}})}
      =\frac{(1+3h)(1+4h)}{1+h}=1+6h,
\]

where \(h\) denotes the hyperplane class on \(L\simeq\mathbb P^{1}\).
The top Chern class of \(E\) is \(c_{1}(E)=6h\).  Intersecting with \([L]\) gives a
zero‑cycle of degree  

\[
\deg\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=6 .
\]

Thus the excess‑intersection contribution of the component \(L\) to the
intersection product \(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}\) is the integer  

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The ambient surface is the smooth projective plane  

\[
M=\mathbf P^{2}.
\]

\(D_{1}=L\cup A\) and \(D_{2}=L\cup B\) are effective Cartier divisors of
degrees  

\[
\deg D_{1}=1+3=4 ,\qquad \deg D_{2}=1+4=5 .
\]

For two divisors on a smooth surface the total intersection number is the
product of the degrees (Bézout’s theorem)

\[
D_{1}\cdot D_{2}= \deg D_{1}\,\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 5 =20 .
\]

The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) consists of  

* the common component \(L\);  
* the isolated points where the smooth curves \(A\) and \(B\) meet away from
\(L\).

Because \(A\) and \(B\) are smooth and intersect transversely, they meet in  

\[
\deg A\cdot\deg B = 3\cdot 4 =12
\]

distinct points.  Since the line \(L\) does **not** lie on either \(A\) or
\(B\), a general choice makes none of these 12 points lie on \(L\).  Hence
the isolated (proper) intersection contribution is exactly the 12 reduced
points, each with multiplicity \(1\):

\[
\text{contribution from } A\cap B\text{ (away from }L) =12 .
\]

The excess contribution is what remains in the total intersection number
after the proper part has been removed:

\[
\text{excess from }L = D_{1}\cdot D_{2} - 12 =20-12 =8 .
\]

Thus the excess‑intersection class on the component \(L\) has degree \(8\),
so the excess contribution to the intersection product \(D_{1}\cdot D_{2}\)
is the integer  

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The total intersection product of the two divisors in \(\mathbb P^{2}\) is  

\[
D_{1}\cdot D_{2}= \deg D_{1}\,\deg D_{2}=4\cdot 5 = 20\;[\text{pt}].
\]

Away from the common component \(L\) the intersection consists of the transverse points
\(A\cap B\).  By Bézout,
\[
\#(A\cap B)=3\cdot 4 = 12 ,
\]
so these give a contribution of \(12\) to the 0‑cycle.

The remaining contribution comes from the excess intersection along the component \(L\).
For a Cartier divisor \(D\) on a smooth surface,
\[
N_{D/\mathbb P^{2}} \cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(D)\big|_{D}.
\]

Hence on the line \(L\cong\mathbb P^{1}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{D_{1}}|_{L}&\cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(4)\big|_{L}\cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(4),\\
N_{D_{2}}|_{L}&\cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(5)\big|_{L}\cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(5),\\
N_{L}&\cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(1)\big|_{L}\cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(1).
\end{aligned}
\]

The excess normal bundle is  

\[
E = \frac{N_{D_{1}}|_{L}\oplus N_{D_{2}}|_{L}}{N_{L}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\det E = N_{D_{1}}|_{L}\otimes N_{D_{2}}|_{L}\otimes N_{L}^{-1}
      \cong \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(4+5-1)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(8).
\]

Thus \(E\) is a line bundle of degree \(8\) on \(L\).  
The excess contribution is the top Chern class of \(E\) pushed forward to a point:

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L]=\deg(E)=8 .
\]

Therefore the excess intersection contribution from the component \(L\) is  

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The two divisors are  

\[
D_{1}=L+A ,\qquad D_{2}=L+B .
\]

Both are effective Cartier divisors on the smooth surface \(V=\mathbf P^{2}\).  
Their expected codimension of intersection is  

\[
\operatorname{codim}D_{1}+\operatorname{codim}D_{2}=1+1=2,
\]

so we would expect a 0‑dimensional intersection.  
Because they share the component \(L\) (a curve), the actual intersection has
excess dimension \(e=1\).

---

### The excess bundle on \(L\)

For a Cartier divisor \(D\) on a smooth variety, the normal bundle of the
divisor is the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{V}(D)\) restricted to the divisor.
Thus  

\[
N_{D_{1}/V}|_{L}= \mathcal O_{V}(L)|_{L}=N_{L/V},\qquad 
N_{D_{2}/V}|_{L}= \mathcal O_{V}(L)|_{L}=N_{L/V},
\]

because on \(L\) only the factor \(L\) of the divisor \(L+A\) (resp. \(L+B\))
vanishes; the other component \(A\) (resp. \(B\)) meets \(L\) transversely
and does **not** contribute to the normal bundle.

Hence the excess bundle on the component \(L\) is  

\[
E = \frac{N_{D_{1}/V}|_{L}\;\oplus\; N_{D_{2}/V}|_{L}}{N_{L/V}}
   = \frac{N_{L/V}\oplus N_{L/V}}{N_{L/V}}
   \cong N_{L/V}.
\]

Since \(L\cong \mathbf P^{1}\) and \(N_{L/V}\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{1}}(1)\),
\[
c_{1}(E)=c_{1}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{1}}(1)\bigr)
\]
has degree \(1\).

---

### Excess contribution to the intersection product

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says that the contribution of the
component \(L\) to the refined intersection product is  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L],
\]

which is a 0‑cycle of degree \(\deg c_{1}(E)=1\).

Thus the excess intersection contribution coming from the common component
\(L\) is the integer **1**.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

The intersection product in \(\mathbb P^{2}\) satisfies  

\[
[D_{1}]\cdot[D_{2}] = (\deg D_{1})(\deg D_{2}) = 4\cdot 5 = 20 .
\]

The only isolated components of the scheme‑theoretic intersection \(D_{1}\cap D_{2}\) are the transverse points where the smooth cubic \(A\) meets the smooth quartic \(B\).  
Since \(A\) and \(B\) intersect transversely,  

\[
A\cdot B = 3\cdot 4 = 12
\]

points (each with multiplicity 1).

Thus the remaining contribution to the intersection product must come from the common component \(L\).  
Let \(Y=L\). The excess normal bundle is  

\[
E = \frac{N_{D_{1}}\mathbb P^{2}|_{L}\;\oplus\; N_{D_{2}}\mathbb P^{2}|_{L}}
           {N_{L}\mathbb P^{2}} .
\]

Because each divisor \(D_i\) is Cartier,  

\[
N_{D_{i}}\mathbb P^{2}|_{L}= \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(D_i)\big|_{L}
      =\mathcal O_{L}(1)\otimes\mathcal O_{L}(\deg D_i-1) .
\]

Hence  

\[
N_{D_{1}}|_{L}= \mathcal O_{L}(4),\qquad 
N_{D_{2}}|_{L}= \mathcal O_{L}(5),\qquad 
N_{L}= \mathcal O_{L}(1).
\]

Therefore  

\[
E \cong \frac{\mathcal O_{L}(4)\oplus\mathcal O_{L}(5)}{\mathcal O_{L}(1)}
      \cong \mathcal O_{L}(8),
\]

so \(\operatorname{rank}E =1\) and  

\[
c_{1}(E)=8 \in A^{1}(L).
\]

The excess contribution of the component \(L\) to the intersection product is  

\[
\deg\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=8 .
\]

Since the isolated points contribute \(12\) and the total product must be \(20\), this also confirms the excess contribution.

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

problems.skill: Excess‑intersection correction via Fulton’s excess intersection formula
problems.problem:
Let \( \mathbb{P}^{4} \) be equipped with homogeneous coordinates \([x_{0}:\dots:x_{4}]\) and let \(H\) denote the hyperplane class.  

1. Let \(X\subset \mathbb{P}^{4}\) be a hypersurface of degree \(4\) whose singular locus contains the line  
\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong \mathbb{P}^{1}.
\]  
2. Let \(Y\subset \mathbb{P}^{4}\) be a hypersurface of degree \(5\) that contains the same line \(L\).  

The scheme‑theoretic intersection \(X\cap Y\) has expected codimension \(2\), but because both hypersurfaces contain the line \(L\) there is an excess component supported on \(L\).  

Assume that the excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(L\) (the bundle that appears in Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula) is a line bundle of degree \(7\) on \(L\) (i.e. \(c_{1}(E)=7\cdot [\text{pt}]\) when integrated over \(L\)).  

Using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, compute the degree of the refined intersection product \([X]\cdot[Y]\) in \(A^{2}(\mathbb{P}^{4})\); equivalently, determine the number of points (counted with multiplicity) obtained by intersecting \(X\) and \(Y\) and then intersecting the result with two general hyperplanes.  

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The Chow ring of \(\mathbf P^{4}\) is  

\[
A^{*}(\mathbf P^{4})=\mathbb Z[H]/(H^{5}),\qquad \deg(H^{2})=1 .
\]

The divisor classes of the hypersurfaces are  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H .
\]

If the two hypersurfaces met properly, their intersection product would be  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot 5H =20\,H^{2},
\]

so after intersecting with two general hyperplanes we would obtain \(20\) points.

Because both hypersurfaces contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong\mathbf P^{1},
\]

the actual scheme‑theoretic intersection \(Z=X\cap Y\) has an excess component \(L\).
Let  

\[
i:L\hookrightarrow X\cap Y
\]

be the inclusion.  
The excess normal bundle on \(L\) is a line bundle of degree \(7\); hence  

\[
c(E)=1+7\,[\text{pt}] \in A^{*}(L).
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives  

\[
i^{!}[Y]=c(E)\cap[Z]=[Z]_{\text{proper}} \;+\; 7\,[\text{pt}]_{L},
\]

where \([Z]_{\text{proper}}\) is the fundamental class of the
2‑dimensional component of the intersection and \(7\,[\text{pt}]_{L}\) is the
contribution coming from the excess line.

To obtain a class in \(A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4})\) we intersect with two general
hyperplanes \(H^{2}\).  
Since a line meets two general hyperplanes in a single point,  

\[
\deg\bigl(7\,[\text{pt}]_{L}\cdot H^{2}\bigr)=7 .
\]

Hence the proper component must contribute  

\[
20-7 = 13
\]

points. Adding the two contributions we recover the total refined
intersection degree

\[
\deg\bigl([X]\cdot[Y]\bigr)=13+7 = 20 .
\]

Thus the number of points (counted with multiplicity) obtained by first
intersecting \(X\) and \(Y\) and then intersecting the result with two
general hyperplanes is  

\[
\boxed{20}
\]

The classes of the two hypersurfaces are  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H\qquad\text{in }A^{1}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]

so their product in the Chow ring is  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot5H =20\,H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4}).
\]

To see how the excess component \(L\) contributes, apply Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula.  
Let \(Z=L\) (a line, \(\dim Z =1\)).  
The excess normal bundle on \(Z\) is a line bundle with  

\[
c_{1}(E)=7\,[\text{pt}],\qquad\int_{L}c_{1}(E)=7 .
\]

Thus the excess contribution is  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)=i_{*}\bigl([Z]+c_{1}(E)\cap[Z]\bigr)
   = [L] + 7\,[\text{pt}].
\]

The term \([L]\) has codimension \(3\) (it does not affect the class in \(A^{2}\)), while the zero‑dimensional term contributes \(7\) points after intersecting with two general hyperplanes.

Hence the remaining (proper) part of the intersection must supply the remaining
\(20-7=13\) points.  Altogether, after intersecting \(X\cap Y\) with two general hyperplanes we obtain  

\[
13+7 = 20
\]

points (counted with multiplicity).  

Therefore the degree of the refined intersection product \([X]\cdot[Y]\) in \(A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4})\) is

\[
\boxed{20}
\]

The Chow ring of \(\mathbf P^{4}\) is  

\[
A^{*}(\mathbf P^{4})=\mathbb Z[H]/(H^{5}),\qquad \deg(H^{4})=1 .
\]

For the two hypersurfaces  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H \;\in A^{1}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]

the **expected** intersection product is  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]_{\text{exp}} = (4H)(5H)=20\,H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4}).
\]

If we intersect this class with two general hyperplanes we obtain  

\[
20\,H^{2}\cdot H^{2}=20\,H^{4},
\qquad \deg(20\,H^{4})=20 .
\]

Because both hypersurfaces contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong\mathbf P^{1},
\]

there is an excess component.  
The excess bundle \(E\) on \(L\) has rank \(e=1\) and first Chern class  

\[
c_{1}(E)=7\,[\text{pt}] \quad\text{on }L .
\]

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula gives the correction term
\[
i_{*}\big(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\big)\in A_{0}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]
where \(i:L\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^{4}\).  
Since \(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\) is a \(0\)-cycle of degree \(7\) on the line,
its push‑forward is a \(0\)-cycle of degree \(7\) in \(\mathbf P^{4}\).

When we further intersect with two general hyperplanes, the class
\(i_{*}\big(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\big)\) meets the hyperplanes in exactly those
points of \(L\) cut out by the hyperplanes, contributing the same degree
\(7\).

Hence the total degree of the refined intersection product after cutting
by two hyperplanes is  

\[
\deg\big([X]\cdot[Y]\big)= 20 + 7 = 27 .
\]

\[
\boxed{27}
\]

The classes of the two hypersurfaces are  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H \qquad\text{in }A^{1}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]

so if they met properly the refined intersection product would be  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot 5H =20\,H^{2}.
\]

Because both hypersurfaces contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong\mathbf P^{1},
\]

the intersection has an excess component supported on \(L\).  
For a smooth excess component \(L\) the excess‑intersection formula (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*, Theorem 6.3) gives  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=[X\cap Y]_{\text{proper}}+ i_{*}\bigl(c(E)\cap [L]\bigr),
\]

where \(i:L\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^{4}\) and \(E\) is the excess normal bundle on \(L\).

The excess bundle is assumed to be a line bundle of degree \(7\) on \(L\); hence  

\[
c(E)=1+c_{1}(E),\qquad c_{1}(E)=7\,[\text{pt}] \text{ on }L .
\]

Only the term \(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\) contributes to codimension‑2 cycles (points).  
Since \([L]\) has degree \(1\) after intersecting with two general hyperplanes, we obtain  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=7\;\text{points}.
\]

Therefore the refined intersection product in codimension 2 is  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=20\;\text{points}+7\;\text{points}=27\;\text{points}.
\]

Hence the degree of \([X]\cdot[Y]\) (the number of points, counted with multiplicity, after intersecting with two general hyperplanes) is  

\[
\boxed{27}
\]

The two hypersurfaces  

\[
X\in |4H| ,\qquad Y\in |5H|
\]

are Cartier divisors in the smooth variety \(\mathbf P^{4}\).
Hence their divisor classes are  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H\quad\text{in }A^{1}(\mathbf P^{4}).
\]

---

### 1.  Expected intersection  

If the intersection were proper, the refined product would be  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot 5H = 20 H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]

and after intersecting with two further general hyperplanes we would obtain  

\[
\deg\bigl(( [X]\cdot[Y])\; H^{2}\bigr)=20 .
\]

---

### 2.  The excess component  

Both hypersurfaces contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong \mathbf P^{1}.
\]

Consequently the scheme‑theoretic intersection \(X\cap Y\) has an **embedded** component \(L\) of codimension \(3\) (dimension \(1\)).  
For this component the excess‑intersection bundle is a line bundle  

\[
E\;=\; \mathcal O_{L}(7),\qquad \deg E =7 .
\]

In Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula, the contribution of an embedded component of codimension \(c\) to a product of codimension \(a+b\) is the top Chern class of the excess bundle capped with the component.  
Here \(a=b=1\) and the excess bundle has rank \(1\); therefore the contribution of \(L\) to the **0‑dimensional** part (i.e. after intersecting with two hyperplanes) is  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L]=\deg E = 7 .
\]

Thus the line supplies \(7\) points (counted with multiplicity) to the final zero‑cycle.

---

### 3.  Residual proper intersection  

The total class in \(A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4})\) must still be \(20H^{2}\); hence after removing the \(7\) points contributed by \(L\) the remaining (proper) intersection contributes  

\[
20-7 = 13
\]

points.

---

### 4.  Degree of the refined product  

Adding the two contributions we obtain the degree of the refined intersection product after intersecting with two general hyperplanes:

\[
\boxed{20}
\]

So there are **20 points (counted with multiplicity)** in the refined intersection of the quartic \(X\) and the quintic \(Y\) after intersecting with two generic hyperplanes.

For a hypersurface of degree \(d\) in \(\mathbb {P}^{4}\) its class in the Chow ring is  

\[
[X]=dH ,\qquad [Y]=eH .
\]

Here  

\[
d=4,\qquad e=5 .
\]

Hence in the Chow ring  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=(4H)(5H)=20H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbb {P}^{4}).
\]

The degree of a codimension‑2 class is obtained by intersecting it with two general hyperplanes, i.e. with \(H^{2}\).  
Since \(H^{4}=1\) in \(\mathbb {P}^{4}\),

\[
\deg\bigl([X]\cdot[Y]\bigr)=20H^{4}=20 .
\]

Geometrically we can see the same number using Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula.  
The intersection \(X\cap Y\) has an excess component \(L\cong\mathbb P^{1}\).  
The excess normal bundle on \(L\) is a line bundle of degree \(7\); therefore  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L]
\]

is a zero‑cycle on \(L\) of degree \(7\).  
Intersecting the residual (proper) surface component of \(X\cap Y\) with two general hyperplanes gives \(13\) points, and the excess component contributes the additional \(7\) points, so the total number of points is  

\[
13+7 = 20 .
\]

Thus the refined intersection product has degree  

\[
\boxed{20}
\]

The hypersurfaces \(X\) and \(Y\) are Cartier divisors in \(\mathbb P^{4}\) with classes  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H .
\]

The expected codimension of their intersection is \(2\).  
Because both contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong \mathbf P^{1},
\]

the actual intersection has an excess component \(L\).  
Let  

\[
E = N_{X/\mathbb P^{4}}|_{L}\big/ N_{L/Y}
\]

be the excess normal bundle; we are told \(\deg E = c_{1}(E)=7\).

---

### Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula  

For the regular embedding \(i\colon X\hookrightarrow \mathbb P^{4}\) we have  

\[
i^{!}[Y]=c\!\big(N_{X/\mathbb P^{4}}\big)\;\cap\; s(E)\;\cap\;[L],
\]

where \(s(E)=c(E)^{-1}\) is the Segre class of the excess bundle.

On the line \(L\) the hyperplane class restricts to the class \(h\) of a point,
with \(h^{2}=0\).  

\[
c\!\big(N_{X/\mathbb P^{4}}\big)=1+4h ,\qquad 
c(E)=1+7h\;\Longrightarrow\;
s(E)=\frac{1}{1+7h}=1-7h .
\]

Hence  

\[
c(N_{X/\mathbb P^{4}})\,s(E)=(1+4h)(1-7h)=1-3h .
\]

Applying this to \([L]\) gives  

\[
i^{!}[Y]=(1-3h)\cap [L]=[L]-3\;(\text{point}) .
\]

Pushing forward to \(\mathbb P^{4}\) we obtain a class whose component of
codimension \(2\) is exactly the product of the divisor classes:

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot5H = 20\,H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbb P^{4}).
\]

---

### Degree after intersecting with two general hyperplanes  

Intersecting with two further hyperplanes corresponds to multiplying by
\(H^{2}\).  Using \(H^{4}=1\) on \(\mathbb P^{4}\),

\[
\deg\big( [X]\cdot[Y]\; \cap H^{2}\big)=
\int_{\mathbb P^{4}} 20 H^{2}\, H^{2}=20\int_{\mathbb P^{4}} H^{4}=20 .
\]

Thus the refined intersection product has degree **20**; equivalently,
after cutting \(X\cap Y\) by two general hyperplanes we obtain 20 points
counted with multiplicity.

\[
\boxed{20}
\]

The classes of the hypersurfaces are  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H\qquad\text{in }A^{1}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]

where \(H\) is the hyperplane class.  
Hence the expected (naïve) product in the Chow ring is  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot 5H =20\,H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4}).
\]

Because both hypersurfaces contain the line \(L\), the intersection \(X\cap Y\) has an
excess component supported on \(L\).  
Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says that the refined product is

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]\;=\;(X\cap Y)_{\text{proper}} \;+\;
i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr),
\]

where \(i:L\hookrightarrow \mathbf P^{4}\) and \(E\) is the excess normal bundle.
The excess bundle is a line bundle of degree \(7\) on \(L\); therefore  

\[
c_{1}(E)\cap [L]=7\,[\text{pt}],
\]

i.e. it contributes \(7\) points (with multiplicity).

Thus, after intersecting \(X\cap Y\) with two general hyperplanes, the total
number of points counted with multiplicity is the degree of the class
\(20H^{2}\), namely

\[
\deg\bigl([X]\cdot[Y]\bigr)=20 .
\]

So the refined intersection product has degree **20**.

\[
\boxed{20}
\]

The classes of the two hypersurfaces in the Chow ring of \(\mathbf P^{4}\) are  

\[
[X]=4H ,\qquad [Y]=5H ,\qquad H=\text{hyperplane class}.
\]

If the two divisors met transversally the refined product would be  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=4H\cdot5H =20\,H^{2}\in A^{2}(\mathbf P^{4}),
\]

so the expected number of points after intersecting with two general
hyperplanes would be \(20\).

Because both hypersurfaces contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong\mathbf P^{1},
\]

the actual intersection has an excess component \(L\) of codimension
\(3\) (instead of the expected codimension \(2\)).  
The excess normal bundle on \(L\) is a line bundle of degree  

\[
\deg E = c_{1}(E)=7 .
\]

---

### Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula  

Let \(i:L\hookrightarrow \mathbf P^{4}\) be the inclusion.
For two regularly embedded codimension‑\(1\) subschemes the excess
bundle has rank  

\[
e = (1+1)-\operatorname{codim}(L)=2-3=1 .
\]

The excess contribution to the refined product is  

\[
i_{*}\bigl(c_{e}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)=i_{*}\bigl(c_{1}(E)\cap [L]\bigr)
      = i_{*}\bigl(7\,[\text{pt}]\bigr).
\]

Thus the refined product splits as  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=\underbrace{Z}_{\text{proper surface class}}
            \;+\; i_{*}\bigl(7\,[\text{pt}]\bigr),
\]

where \(Z\) is the class of the residual surface of codimension \(2\).

Taking degrees (i.e. intersecting with two general hyperplanes, which
means multiplying by \(H^{2}\)) we obtain  

\[
\deg\bigl([X]\cdot[Y]\bigr)=\deg(Z\cdot H^{2})+\deg\bigl(i_{*}(7[\text{pt}])\bigr)
                         =\deg(Z\cdot H^{2})+7 .
\]

But the total refined product must equal the product of the divisor
classes, whose degree is \(20\). Hence  

\[
\deg(Z\cdot H^{2}) = 20-7 = 13,
\]

and the total number of points (including the excess contribution) is  

\[
\boxed{20}.
\]

The Chow ring of \(\mathbf P^{4}\) is  

\[
A^{*}(\mathbf P^{4})=\mathbf Z[H]/(H^{5}),\qquad H=[\text{hyperplane}].
\]

For a hypersurface of degree \(d\) we have \([X]=dH\).

---

### 1.  Expected contribution  

\[
[X]\cdot[Y]=(4H)\cdot(5H)=20\,H^{2}.
\]

Intersecting the class \(20H^{2}\) with two further general hyperplanes \(H^{2}\) gives  

\[
20H^{2}\cdot H^{2}=20\;(\text{points}),
\]

i.e. the ordinary intersection of a degree‑4 and a degree‑5 hypersurface would consist of \(20\) points.

---

### 2.  Excess component on the line \(L\)

Both hypersurfaces contain the line  

\[
L=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}\cong\mathbf P^{1},
\qquad [L]=H^{3}.
\]

Because \(L\) has codimension \(3\) while the expected codimension of \(X\cap Y\) is \(2\), there is an excess component of **excess codimension**  

\[
e=\operatorname{codim}L-(\operatorname{codim}X+\operatorname{codim}Y)=3-2=1 .
\]

Hence the excess normal bundle \(E\) on \(L\) has rank \(e=1\).  
We are told that \(\deg E = c_{1}(E)=7\).

Fulton’s excess‑intersection formula says that the contribution of this component to the refined product is  

\[
c_{e}(E)\cap [L]=c_{1}(E)\cap [L]=7\,[\text{pt\ on }L].
\]

Thus, after intersecting with two general hyperplanes, the line contributes  

\[
7\;(H^{2}\cdot L)=7\cdot 1 =7\; \text{points}.
\]

---

### 3.  Total number of points

\[
\text{total points}= \underbrace{20}_{\text{expected surface}}+
\underbrace{7}_{\text{excess line}} = 27 .
\]

Hence the degree of the refined intersection product \([X]\cdot[Y]\) (i.e. the number of points obtained after intersecting with two general hyperplanes) is  

\[
\boxed{27}
\]
