problems.problem:
Let \(\nu:\mathbb{P}^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{5}\) be the Veronese embedding of degree 2, sending a point \([x:y:z]\) to the class of the quadratic monomials \([x^{2}:xy:xz:y^{2}:yz:z^{2}]\).  
Identify a plane conic \(C\) with the point \([a_{0}:a_{1}:a_{2}:a_{3}:a_{4}:a_{5}]\in\mathbb{P}^{5}\) corresponding to the homogeneous quadratic form  

\[
a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0 .
\]

Fix a line \(L\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) given by the linear equation \(\ell(x,y,z)=\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0\), and a point \(P=[p_{x}:p_{y}:p_{z}]\) lying on \(L\) (so \(\alpha p_{x}+\beta p_{y}+\gamma p_{z}=0\)).  

A conic \(C\) passes through \(P\) precisely when the quadratic form evaluates to zero at \(P\); this gives a linear equation in the coefficients \(a_{i}\).  

The conic \(C\) is tangent to the line \(L\) at the point \(P\) exactly when, in addition to passing through \(P\), the gradient of the quadratic form at \(P\) is a scalar multiple of the normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) of the line. This tangency condition yields one further independent linear equation in the \(a_{i}\).

How many independent linear equations in the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) are imposed simultaneously by requiring that a conic passes through the fixed point \(P\) and is tangent to the fixed line \(L\) at \(P\)?

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
For a conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2},
\]

the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) are homogeneous coordinates in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

---

### 1.  Passing through \(P\)

Evaluating the quadratic form at the point \(P=[p_x:p_y:p_z]\) gives  

\[
a_{0}p_x^{2}+a_{1}p_xp_y+a_{2}p_xp_z+a_{3}p_y^{2}+a_{4}p_yp_z+a_{5}p_z^{2}=0 .
\]

This is a **single linear equation** in the six unknowns \(a_i\).

---

### 2.  Tangency to the line \(L\)

The gradient of \(Q\) is  

\[
\nabla Q=
\bigl(2a_{0}x+a_{1}y+a_{2}z,\; a_{1}x+2a_{3}y+a_{4}z,\; a_{2}x+a_{4}y+2a_{5}z\bigr).
\]

At \(P\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
G_1 &= 2a_{0}p_x + a_{1}p_y + a_{2}p_z,\\
G_2 &= a_{1}p_x + 2a_{3}p_y + a_{4}p_z,\\
G_3 &= a_{2}p_x + a_{4}p_y + 2a_{5}p_z .
\end{aligned}
\]

For the line \(L:\ell(x,y,z)=\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0\) the normal vector is  
\(N=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\).

Tangency at \(P\) means that \(G\) is a scalar multiple of \(N\):
\[
G = \lambda N \quad\text{for some }\lambda\in\mathbb C .
\]

Thus we have three equations  

\[
\begin{cases}
2a_{0}p_x + a_{1}p_y + a_{2}p_z = \lambda\alpha,\\
a_{1}p_x + 2a_{3}p_y + a_{4}p_z = \lambda\beta,\\
a_{2}p_x + a_{4}p_y + 2a_{5}p_z = \lambda\gamma .
\end{cases}
\]

The unknown \(\lambda\) can be eliminated; the condition “\(G\) is colinear with \(N\)” gives **two independent linear relations** among the \(a_i\) (the three equations are linearly dependent because they all involve the same \(\lambda\)).

---

### 3.  Total number of independent linear conditions

* one linear condition from “\(C\) passes through \(P\)”,  
* two independent linear conditions from the tangency requirement.

Hence the simultaneous requirement that a conic pass through the fixed point \(P\) and be tangent to the fixed line \(L\) at \(P\) imposes  

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

independent linear equations on the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

The conic is given by the quadratic form  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}.
\]

---

### 1.  Condition “\(C\) passes through \(P\)”

Evaluating \(Q\) at the point \(P=[p_x:p_y:p_z]\) gives  

\[
a_{0}p_{x}^{2}+a_{1}p_{x}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{x}p_{z}+a_{3}p_{y}^{2}+a_{4}p_{y}p_{z}+a_{5}p_{z}^{2}=0 .
\]

This is a single linear equation in the six coefficients \(a_{0},\dots ,a_{5}\).

---

### 2.  Condition “\(C\) is tangent to \(L\) at \(P\)”

The gradient of \(Q\) is  

\[
\nabla Q=(2a_{0}x+a_{1}y+a_{2}z,\; a_{1}x+2a_{3}y+a_{4}z,\;
           a_{2}x+a_{4}y+2a_{5}z).
\]

At \(P\) we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_x Q(P) &= 2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z},\\
\partial_y Q(P) &= a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z},\\
\partial_z Q(P) &= a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the line \(L\) with normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) to be tangent to \(C\) at \(P\) we need  

\[
\nabla Q(P)=\lambda(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)
\]

for some scalar \(\lambda\).  
Eliminating the scalar \(\lambda\) gives the two linear relations  

\[
\begin{cases}
\beta\bigl(2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z}\bigr)
      -\alpha\bigl(a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z}\bigr)=0,\\[4pt]
\gamma\bigl(a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z}\bigr)
      -\beta\bigl(a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}\bigr)=0 .
\end{cases}
\]

These are **two** independent linear equations in the coefficients \(a_i\).

---

### 3.  Total number of independent linear conditions

* One linear equation comes from the requirement \(Q(P)=0\).
* The tangency condition contributes **one** additional independent linear equation (the two equations above are linearly dependent once the point‑condition is already imposed).

Hence, simultaneously imposing “\(C\) passes through \(P\)” and “\(C\) is tangent to \(L\) at \(P\)” yields  

\[
\boxed{2}
\]

independent linear equations on the vector \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

The conic is given by  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}.
\]

---

### 1.  Passing through the fixed point \(P\)

\(Q(P)=0\) gives one linear equation in the coefficients \(a_i\).

---

### 2.  Tangency to the line \(L\) at \(P\)

The gradient of \(Q\) is  

\[
\nabla Q=(2a_{0}x+a_{1}y+a_{2}z,\; a_{1}x+2a_{3}y+a_{4}z,\; a_{2}x+a_{4}y+2a_{5}z).
\]

At \(P=[p_x:p_y:p_z]\),

\[
\nabla Q(P)=\bigl(2a_{0}p_x+a_{1}p_y+a_{2}p_z,\;
a_{1}p_x+2a_{3}p_y+a_{4}p_z,\;
a_{2}p_x+a_{4}p_y+2a_{5}p_z\bigr).
\]

Tangency means \(\nabla Q(P)\) is parallel to the normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) of \(L\); i.e. there exists a scalar \(\lambda\) such that  

\[
\nabla Q(P)=\lambda (\alpha,\beta,\gamma).
\]

These are three linear equations in the seven unknowns \((a_0,\dots ,a_5,\lambda)\).  
For a generic point \(P\) the three rows are linearly independent, so the rank of this system is \(3\). Hence the solution space has dimension \(7-3=4\); eliminating the auxiliary variable \(\lambda\) leaves **two independent linear relations among the coefficients \(a_i\)**.

---

### 3.  Total number of independent linear conditions

* one condition from \(Q(P)=0\);
* two independent conditions from the tangency requirement.

Therefore the simultaneous requirement “\(C\) passes through \(P\) and is tangent to \(L\) at \(P\)” imposes  

\[
1+2 = 3
\]

independent linear equations on the six coefficients \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\).

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) with homogeneous coordinates \([a_{0}:a_{1}:a_{2}:a_{3}:a_{4}:a_{5}]\).

* Passing through \(P=[p_{x}:p_{y}:p_{z}]\) gives the linear condition  

\[
a_{0}p_{x}^{2}+a_{1}p_{x}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{x}p_{z}+a_{3}p_{y}^{2}+a_{4}p_{y}p_{z}+a_{5}p_{z}^{2}=0 .
\]

* Tangency to the line \(L : \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0\) at \(P\) requires the gradient of the quadratic form at \(P\),

\[
\bigl(2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z},\,
      a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z},\,
      a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}\bigr),
\]

to be a scalar multiple of the normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\). This yields one further linear equation in the \(a_i\).

For a generic choice of \(P\) and \(L\) the two equations are linearly independent, so together they impose **two independent linear conditions** on the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

\[
\boxed{2}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space \(\mathbb P^{5}\) of the six coefficients  
\((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) of a homogeneous quadratic form, so a conic is represented by a point
\([a_{0}:\dots :a_{5}]\).

---

### 1.  Passing through the fixed point \(P\)

For \(P=[p_{x}:p_{y}:p_{z}]\) the condition \(Q(P)=0\) is  

\[
a_{0}p_{x}^{2}+a_{1}p_{x}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{x}p_{z}+a_{3}p_{y}^{2}+a_{4}p_{y}p_{z}+a_{5}p_{z}^{2}=0 .
\]

This is a **single linear equation** in the coefficients \(a_i\).

---

### 2.  Tangency to the line \(L\) at \(P\)

The line \(L\) has equation \(\ell(x,y,z)=\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0\); its normal vector is
\((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\).

The gradient of the quadratic form \(Q\) is  

\[
\nabla Q=
\bigl(2a_{0}x+a_{1}y+a_{2}z,\; a_{1}x+2a_{3}y+a_{4}z,\; a_{2}x+a_{4}y+2a_{5}z\bigr).
\]

At the point \(P\) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_x Q(P)&=2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z},\\
\partial_y Q(P)&=a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z},\\
\partial_z Q(P)&=a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Tangency means that this gradient is **parallel** to the normal vector of \(L\); i.e. there exists a scalar \(\lambda\) such that  

\[
\nabla Q(P)=\lambda(\alpha,\beta,\gamma).
\]

Eliminating the unknown \(\lambda\) gives two independent linear relations among the
\(a_i\):

\[
\begin{cases}
\bigl(2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z}\bigr)\beta-
\bigl(a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z}\bigr)\alpha =0,\\[4pt]
\bigl(2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z}\bigr)\gamma-
\bigl(a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}\bigr)\alpha =0 .
\end{cases}
\]

Thus tangency contributes **two** independent linear equations.

---

### 3.  Total number of independent linear conditions

- Passing through \(P\): 1 equation.  
- Tangency to \(L\) at \(P\): 2 independent equations.

Hence the simultaneous requirement “\(C\) passes through \(P\) and is tangent to \(L\) at \(P\)” imposes  

\[
1+2 = 3
\]

independent linear equations on the coefficient vector \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^{5}\) (six coefficients \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\) up to scaling).  

*Passing through \(P\).*  
Evaluating the quadratic form at \(P=[p_x:p_y:p_z]\) gives  

\[
a_0p_x^{2}+a_1p_xp_y+a_2p_xp_z+a_3p_y^{2}+a_4p_yp_z+a_5p_z^{2}=0,
\]

which is a single homogeneous linear equation in the \(a_i\).

*Tangency to \(L\) at \(P\).*  
The gradient of the quadratic form is  

\[
\nabla Q=(2a_0x+a_1y+a_2z,\;a_1x+2a_3y+a_4z,\;a_2x+a_4y+2a_5z).
\]

At \(P\) we require \(\nabla Q(P)\) to be a scalar multiple of the normal vector
\(N=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) of the line \(L\):
\[
\nabla Q(P)=\lambda N .
\]

Writing the three components gives three linear equations in the \(a_i\) together with the unknown scalar \(\lambda\). Because \(\lambda\) is free, these three equations are linearly dependent; they impose **one** additional independent linear condition on the coefficients (the condition that the component of \(\nabla Q(P)\) orthogonal to \(N\) vanishes).

Hence the combined requirement “\(C\) passes through \(P\) and is tangent to \(L\) at \(P\)” imposes  

\[
1\;(\text{point condition})\;+\;1\;(\text{tangency condition})\;=\;2
\]

independent linear equations on \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\).

\[
\boxed{2}
\]

The condition that the conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0
\]

passes through the fixed point \(P=[p_x:p_y:p_z]\) is  

\[
Q(P)=a_{0}p_x^{2}+a_{1}p_xp_y+a_{2}p_xp_z+a_{3}p_y^{2}+a_{4}p_yp_z+a_{5}p_z^{2}=0,
\]

which is a single linear equation in the coefficients \(a_i\).

The gradient of \(Q\) is  

\[
\nabla Q = \bigl(2a_{0}x + a_{1}y + a_{2}z,\;
               a_{1}x + 2a_{3}y + a_{4}z,\;
               a_{2}x + a_{4}y + 2a_{5}z \bigr).
\]

Evaluated at \(P\) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_x Q(P) &= 2a_{0}p_x + a_{1}p_y + a_{2}p_z,\\
\partial_y Q(P) &= a_{1}p_x + 2a_{3}p_y + a_{4}p_z,\\
\partial_z Q(P) &= a_{2}p_x + a_{4}p_y + 2a_{5}p_z .
\end{aligned}
\]

Tangency of \(C\) to the line \(L:\ell(x,y,z)=\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0\) at \(P\) means that the gradient at \(P\) is parallel to the normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\); i.e.

\[
\nabla Q(P)=\lambda (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)
\]

for some scalar \(\lambda\).  This gives the three equations  

\[
\begin{cases}
2a_{0}p_x + a_{1}p_y + a_{2}p_z = \lambda \alpha,\\[2pt]
a_{1}p_x + 2a_{3}p_y + a_{4}p_z = \lambda \beta,\\[2pt]
a_{2}p_x + a_{4}p_y + 2a_{5}p_z = \lambda \gamma .
\end{cases}
\]

The unknown \(\lambda\) can be eliminated, leaving two independent linear relations among the \(a_i\) (for instance by taking the cross‑product \(\nabla Q(P)\times(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=0\)).  

Hence the tangency condition contributes **two** independent linear equations, while the point‑passing condition contributes **one** more.

\[
\text{Total independent linear equations} = 1 + 2 = 3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The condition “the conic passes through \(P\)” is  

\[
a_{0}p_{x}^{2}+a_{1}p_{x}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{x}p_{z}+a_{3}p_{y}^{2}+a_{4}p_{y}p_{z}+a_{5}p_{z}^{2}=0,
\]

which is a single linear equation in the six coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

For tangency we need the gradient of the quadratic form at \(P\) to be a scalar multiple of the normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) of the line \(L\).  
The gradient is  

\[
\nabla Q(P)=\bigl(2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z},
\;a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z},
\;a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}\bigr).
\]

Thus there exists a scalar \(\lambda\) such that  

\[
\begin{cases}
2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z}= \lambda\alpha,\\[2pt]
a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z}= \lambda\beta,\\[2pt]
a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z}= \lambda\gamma .
\end{cases}
\]

Eliminating the auxiliary variable \(\lambda\) leaves two independent linear relations among the \(a_i\) (the three equations are linearly dependent because they express that two vectors are parallel).

Hence the tangency condition contributes **two** independent linear equations, and together with the point‑passing condition we have  

\[
1\;(\text{point})\;+\;2\;(\text{tangency}) \;=\; 3
\]

independent linear equations on \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The condition that a conic passes through the fixed point \(P\) is the single linear equation  

\[
a_{0}p_{x}^{2}+a_{1}p_{x}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{x}p_{z}+a_{3}p_{y}^{2}+a_{4}p_{y}p_{z}+a_{5}p_{z}^{2}=0 .
\]

For tangency at \(P\) we require that the gradient of the quadratic form at \(P\) be parallel to the normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) of the line \(L\).  
Writing the gradient components at \(P\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_x Q(P) &= 2a_{0}p_{x}+a_{1}p_{y}+a_{2}p_{z},\\
\partial_y Q(P) &= a_{1}p_{x}+2a_{3}p_{y}+a_{4}p_{z},\\
\partial_z Q(P) &= a_{2}p_{x}+a_{4}p_{y}+2a_{5}p_{z},
\end{aligned}
\]

the parallelism means that there exists a scalar \(\lambda\) such that  

\[
\bigl(\partial_x Q(P),\partial_y Q(P),\partial_z Q(P)\bigr)=\lambda(\alpha,\beta,\gamma).
\]

These three equations involve the unknown \(\lambda\); eliminating \(\lambda\) leaves two independent linear relations among the coefficients \(a_i\).  
Hence the tangency condition contributes **one additional** independent linear equation beyond the one already given by “passing through \(P\)”.

Therefore the total number of independent linear equations imposed on \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) by requiring a conic to pass through \(P\) and be tangent to \(L\) at \(P\) is  

\[
\boxed{2}
\]

For a conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2},
\]

the coefficients \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\) are homogeneous coordinates of a point in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

---

### 1.  Passing through the fixed point \(P\)

Evaluating \(Q\) at \(P=[p_x:p_y:p_z]\) gives  

\[
a_{0}p_x^{2}+a_{1}p_xp_y+a_{2}p_xp_z+a_{3}p_y^{2}+a_{4}p_yp_z+a_{5}p_z^{2}=0 .
\]

This is a **single linear equation** in the six unknowns \(a_i\).

---

### 2.  Tangency to the line \(L\) at \(P\)

The line \(L\) has normal vector \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\).  
The gradient of \(Q\) is  

\[
\nabla Q=(\partial_x Q,\partial_y Q,\partial_z Q)
       =(2a_{0}x+a_{1}y+a_{2}z,\; a_{1}x+2a_{3}y+a_{4}z,\; a_{2}x+a_{4}y+2a_{5}z).
\]

At the point \(P\) we require \(\nabla Q(P)\) to be **parallel** to \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\); i.e. there exists a scalar \(\lambda\) such that  

\[
\begin{cases}
2a_{0}p_x + a_{1}p_y + a_{2}p_z = \lambda\alpha,\\[2pt]
a_{1}p_x + 2a_{3}p_y + a_{4}p_z = \lambda\beta,\\[2pt]
a_{2}p_x + a_{4}p_y + 2a_{5}p_z = \lambda\gamma .
\end{cases}
\]

These are three linear equations in the seven unknowns \((a_0,\dots ,a_5,\lambda)\).  
Because \(\lambda\) is free, the system imposes **two independent linear relations** among the \(a_i\).

Equivalently, the condition “vectors are parallel’’ can be expressed by the vanishing of the cross product  

\[
\nabla Q(P)\times(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=0,
\]

which yields three scalar equations, but only two of them are independent (the third follows from the first two when \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\neq(0,0,0)\)).

---

### 3.  Total number of independent linear conditions

- 1 condition from \(Q(P)=0\);
- 2 independent conditions from the tangency requirement.

Hence the total number of independent linear equations imposed on \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\) is  

\[
1+2 = 3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

problems.skill: Veronese embedding of conics and translation of tangency to hyperplane sections
problems.problem:
Let \(\nu:\mathbb{P}^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{5}\) be the Veronese embedding of degree 2, sending a point \([x:y:z]\) to \([x^{2}:xy:xz:y^{2}:yz:z^{2}]\).  Under this embedding a plane conic \(D\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) corresponds to a hyperplane \(H_{D}\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\) with  
\[
D=\nu^{-1}\bigl(H_{D}\cap \nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\bigr).
\]

Fix a smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) and choose a point \(P\in C\).  Also fix a point \(Q\in\mathbb{P}^{2}\) that does **not** lie on \(C\).  A hyperplane \(H\) defines a conic \(D\) as above.  

Using the fact that a hyperplane section of the Veronese surface \(\nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\) is tangent to the surface at \(\nu(P)\) precisely when the hyperplane contains the tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\), determine how many independent linear conditions on the coefficients of \(H\) are imposed by the two requirements:

1. \(D\) is tangent to \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\);
2. \(D\) passes through the fixed point \(Q\).

In other words, compute the codimension of the resulting linear subspace inside the space of all hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is the dual projective space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\!*}\); its vector space of coefficients has dimension \(6\) (up to scaling the projective dimension is \(5\)).

---

### 1.  Tangency condition at the fixed point \(P\)

A conic \(D\) is tangent to the fixed smooth conic \(C\) at \(P\) iff the corresponding hyperplane \(H\) contains the tangent plane to the Veronese surface at \(\nu(P)\):
\[
T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset H .
\]

The tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\) is a projective plane, i.e. a linear subspace of \(\mathbf P^{5}\) of dimension \(2\).  
In the underlying \(6\)-dimensional vector space it is a \(3\)-dimensional linear subspace \(V\).

A linear form \(L\) (the equation of a hyperplane) vanishes on \(V\) iff its coefficients satisfy **three independent linear equations** (the coefficients of the three independent directions in \(V\) must be zero).  
Hence the tangency condition imposes **3 independent linear conditions** on the coefficients of \(H\).

---

### 2.  Passing through the fixed point \(Q\)

For the conic \(D\) to pass through \(Q\) we need
\[
\nu(Q)\in H .
\]
Thus the linear form defining \(H\) must vanish at the single point \(\nu(Q)\). This is one additional independent linear equation on the coefficients of \(H\).

Because \(Q\notin C\), \(\nu(Q)\) is not contained in the tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\); therefore this condition is not a consequence of the three obtained above.

---

### 3.  Total codimension

The two requirements together give  

\[
\underbrace{3}_{\text{tangency}} \;+\; \underbrace{1}_{\text{passing through }Q}
= 4
\]

independent linear conditions on the coefficients of a hyperplane in \(\mathbf P^{5}\).

Thus the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both conditions has codimension **4** inside the space of all hyperplanes.

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) is the dual projective space \((\mathbb{P}^{5})^{*}\), which has dimension \(5\).  
A linear condition on the coefficients of a hyperplane corresponds to a linear equation in the \(6\)-dimensional vector space of linear forms; the codimension of the subspace of hyperplanes satisfying the condition equals the number of independent linear equations.

---

### 1.  Tangency at the fixed point \(P\)

Let \(P=[x_{0}:y_{0}:z_{0}]\).  
The tangent plane to the Veronese surface \(\nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\) at \(\nu(P)\) is a 2‑dimensional linear subspace of \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
Requiring a hyperplane \(H\) to contain this tangent plane means that the defining linear form \(\ell\) of \(H\) must vanish on the whole 3‑dimensional vector subspace that lifts the tangent plane.  

Vanishing on a subspace of dimension \(3\) imposes **three independent linear equations** on the coefficients of \(\ell\).  
Thus tangency at \(P\) contributes **3 conditions**.

---

### 2.  Passing through the fixed point \(Q\)

The condition that the conic \(D\) passes through \(Q\) is equivalent to requiring that the hyperplane contain the point \(\nu(Q)\).  
This adds **one linear equation** \(\ell(\nu(Q))=0\).

Since \(Q\notin C\), the point \(\nu(Q)\) does **not** lie in the tangent plane at \(\nu(P)\); consequently this equation is independent of the three obtained in step 1.

---

### Total codimension

\[
\text{codimension}=3\;(\text{tangency})+1\;(\text{through }Q)=4 .
\]

Hence the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has codimension **4** inside the full space of hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is the dual projective space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{*}\); it has projective dimension  

\[
\dim (\mathbf P^{5})^{*}=5 .
\]

A hyperplane \(H\) is given by a linear form  

\[
L(a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})=a_{0}X_{0}+a_{1}X_{1}+ \dots + a_{5}X_{5}=0,
\]

so the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) form a point of a \(6\)-dimensional vector space.  
Linear conditions on the hyperplane correspond to linear equations on these coefficients.

---

### 1.  Tangency to \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\)

Let \(P\in C\).  
The Veronese surface \(\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset \mathbf P^{5}\) is a smooth surface.  
Its tangent plane at \(\nu(P)\) is a **projective plane**, i.e. a linear subspace of \(\mathbf P^{5}\) of dimension \(2\).  

In vector terms the tangent plane corresponds to a \(3\)-dimensional linear subspace \(V\subset \mathbf k^{6}\) (the 6‑dimensional vector space underlying \(\mathbf P^{5}\)).  

A hyperplane \(H\) is tangent to \(\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\) at \(\nu(P)\) **iff** its defining linear form \(L\) vanishes on the whole tangent plane, i.e. \(L|_{V}=0\).

The set of linear forms that vanish on a \(3\)-dimensional subspace has dimension  

\[
\dim \{L\mid L|_{V}=0\}=6-\dim V = 6-3 = 3 .
\]

Hence the requirement “\(D\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(P\)” imposes **three independent linear conditions** on the coefficients of \(H\).

---

### 2.  Passing through a fixed external point \(Q\)

The condition that the conic \(D\) (i.e. the hyperplane section) contains the point \(Q\) is simply  

\[
f(Q)=0,
\]

where \(f\) is the quadratic form corresponding to \(H\).  
This is a single linear equation in the coefficients of \(L\).  
Thus it contributes **one independent linear condition**.

---

### 3.  Total codimension

The two sets of conditions are independent (the point \(\nu(Q)\) does not lie in the tangent plane at \(\nu(P)\) because \(Q\notin C\)).  
Therefore the total number of independent linear conditions is  

\[
3\;(\text{tangency})\;+\;1\;(\text{through }Q)=4.
\]

Consequently the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has codimension \(4\) inside the 5‑dimensional space of all hyperplanes.

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

For a hyperplane  

\[
H:\; a_0X_0+a_1X_1+a_2X_2+a_3X_3+a_4X_4+a_5X_5=0\qquad (X=\nu[x:y:z])
\]

the vector of coefficients \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\) is defined up to a non‑zero scalar; hence the space of all hyperplanes in \(\mathbf P^5\) is a projective space \(\mathbf P^5\) (dimension 5).

---

### Condition (2): \(D\) passes through \(Q\)

If \(Q=[q_0:q_1:q_2]\) then \(\nu(Q)=[q_0^2,q_0q_1,q_0q_2,q_1^2,q_1q_2,q_2^2]\) must satisfy the equation of \(H\):

\[
a_0q_0^2+a_1q_0q_1+a_2q_0q_2+a_3q_1^2+a_4q_1q_2+a_5q_2^2=0 .
\]

This is one linear equation in the coefficients \(a_i\); it contributes **one** independent linear condition.

---

### Condition (1): \(D\) is tangent to \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\)

Let \(P=[p_0:p_1:p_2]\).  
The tangent plane to the Veronese surface \(\nu(\mathbf P^2)\) at \(\nu(P)\) is a projective plane
\[
\Pi_P = T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbf P^2)\subset\mathbf P^5 .
\]

For a hyperplane \(H\) the curve \(D\) is the intersection \(H\cap \nu(\mathbf P^2)\).  
The tangent line to \(D\) at \(P\) is \(\Pi_P\cap H\); similarly the tangent line to the fixed conic \(C\) is \(\Pi_P\cap H_C\) where \(H_C\) is the hyperplane corresponding to \(C\).

The two conics are tangent at \(P\) exactly when these two lines coincide, i.e.

\[
\Pi_P\cap H = \Pi_P\cap H_C .
\]

Thus the restriction of the linear functional defining \(H\) to the 3‑dimensional vector space
\(W=\text{span}(\Pi_P)\) must be a scalar multiple of the restriction of the fixed functional
defining \(H_C\).

The space of all restrictions \(\phi|_W\) is a 3‑dimensional vector space \(W^{*}\).  
Requiring \(\phi|_W\) to lie in the 1‑dimensional subspace \(\langle \phi_C|_W\rangle\) imposes a codimension
\(3-1 = 2\) linear condition on \(\phi\).

Hence tangency at \(P\) contributes **two** independent linear conditions.

---

### Total codimension

The two sets of conditions are independent (the point \(Q\) does not lie on \(C\), so its linear equation is not a combination of the tangency equations).  

\[
\text{codimension}= 2\;(\text{tangency}) + 1\;(\text{passing through }Q)=\boxed{3}.
\]

The hyperplane \(H\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) corresponds to a quadratic form  

\[
G(x,y,z)=a x^{2}+b xy+c xz+d y^{2}+e yz+f z^{2}=0 .
\]

---

### Condition (1): \(D\) tangent to \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\)

Let \(P=[x_{0}:y_{0}:z_{0}]\in C\).  
Tangency of the two plane conics \(C:\,F=0\) and \(D:\,G=0\) at \(P\) means  

* \(G(P)=0\) (the point lies on \(D\));
* the gradients are proportional: \(\nabla G(P)=\lambda \nabla F(P)\) for some \(\lambda\).

The gradient of \(G\) at \(P\) is  

\[
\nabla G(P)=\bigl(2a x_{0}+b y_{0}+c z_{0},\;
                b x_{0}+2d y_{0}+e z_{0},\;
                c x_{0}+e y_{0}+2f z_{0}\bigr),
\]

which is linear in the coefficients \((a,b,c,d,e,f)\).  
The proportionality condition gives two independent linear equations (the
cross‑product \(\nabla G(P)\times\nabla F(P)=0\) yields three equations with one
linear dependence).  
Together with \(G(P)=0\) we obtain **three independent linear conditions** on
\((a,\dots ,f)\).

Geometrically, this is exactly the requirement that the hyperplane \(H\) contain
the tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\); a plane of dimension \(2\)
imposes \(2+1=3\) linear conditions on a hyperplane.

---

### Condition (2): \(D\) passes through the fixed point \(Q=[x_{1}:y_{1}:z_{1}]\)

Plugging \(Q\) into the quadratic gives  

\[
a x_{1}^{2}+b x_{1}y_{1}+c x_{1}z_{1}+d y_{1}^{2}+e y_{1}z_{1}+f z_{1}^{2}=0,
\]

which is one further independent linear condition (since \(Q\notin C\), it does
not satisfy the three conditions above).

---

### Total codimension

The two sets of conditions are independent, so the total number of independent
linear constraints on the coefficients of a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is  

\[
3\;(\text{tangency at }P) \;+\; 1\;(\text{passing through }Q)=4 .
\]

Thus the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has
codimension **4** inside the 5‑dimensional projective space of all hyperplanes of
\(\mathbb P^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is a projective space of dimension \(5\).

---

### 1.  Tangency at the fixed point \(P\)

A conic \(D\) is tangent to the given conic \(C\) at \(P\) iff the corresponding hyperplane \(H\) contains the tangent plane
\[
T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset \mathbf P^{5}.
\]

The tangent plane is a linear subspace of dimension \(2\).  
A hyperplane is defined by a linear form \(\ell\) on the \(6\)-dimensional vector space underlying \(\mathbf P^{5}\).  
Requiring \(\ell\) to vanish on a given \(2\)-plane means \(\ell\) lies in the annihilator of that plane, a subspace of codimension \(2\) in the dual space.  

Hence “contains the tangent plane’’ imposes **2 independent linear conditions** on the coefficients of \(H\).

---

### 2.  Passing through the fixed point \(Q\)

For the conic \(D\) to contain the point \(Q\) we need
\[
\nu(Q)\in H\cap \nu(\mathbf P^{2}),
\]
i.e. the hyperplane \(H\) must pass through the point \(\nu(Q)\in\mathbf P^{5}\).

A hyperplane containing a given point imposes **1 independent linear condition** on its coefficients.

Since \(Q\notin C\) (and thus \(\nu(Q)\) does not lie in the tangent plane at \(\nu(P)\)), this condition is independent of the previous two.

---

### 3.  Total codimension

Adding the independent conditions:

\[
\text{codimension}= 2 \;(\text{tangency}) + 1 \;(\text{through }Q)= 3.
\]

Thus the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has codimension **3** inside the full space of hyperplanes of \(\mathbf P^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) is \((\mathbb{P}^{5})^{*}\), a projective space of dimension \(5\) (i.e. \(6\) coefficients up to scaling).

---

### 1.  Tangency at \(P\)

A hyperplane \(H\) gives a conic \(D\) which is tangent to the smooth conic \(C\) at the fixed point \(P\) iff the hyperplane contains the tangent plane to the Veronese surface at \(\nu(P)\):
\[
T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\subset H .
\]

The tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\) is a projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
The set of hyperplanes containing a fixed \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) has codimension
\[
\dim(\mathbb{P}^{2})+1 = 2+1 = 3 .
\]

Thus the tangency condition imposes **3 independent linear conditions** on the coefficients of \(H\).

---

### 2.  Passing through \(Q\)

For the conic \(D\) to pass through the point \(Q\) we need
\[
\nu(Q) \in H .
\]

This is the usual condition “hyperplane contains a given point”, which contributes **1 linear condition**.

Because \(Q\notin C\), the point \(\nu(Q)\) does **not** lie in the tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb{P}^{2})\); hence the condition from \(Q\) is independent of the three conditions coming from tangency.

---

### 3.  Total codimension

Adding the independent conditions:

\[
\text{codimension}= 3\;(\text{tangency}) + 1\;(\text{passing through } Q)=4 .
\]

Hence the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has codimension **4** inside the full space of hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is a projective space of dimension \(5\).

* Tangency at the fixed point \(P\):  
  The tangent line to the conic \(C\) at \(\nu(P)\) is the line  
  \(L = H_{C}\cap T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\).  
  For another hyperplane \(H\) to give a conic \(D\) whose tangent line at \(P\) coincides with that of \(C\), \(H\) must contain the line \(L\).  
  Requiring a hyperplane to contain a given line imposes **two** independent linear conditions (the linear form must vanish on two independent points of the line).

* Passing through the fixed point \(Q\):  
  This means \(\nu(Q)\in H\). Requiring a hyperplane to contain a given point imposes **one** linear condition.

The two sets of conditions are independent because \(\nu(Q)\notin H_{C}\) (so \(\nu(Q)\) is not on the line \(L\)).  

Hence the total number of independent linear conditions is  

\[
2\;(\text{tangency})\;+\;1\;(\text{passing through }Q)=3 .
\]

Thus the codimension of the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements inside the full space of hyperplanes of \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The hyperplanes of \(\mathbb P^{5}\) are parametrised by the dual projective space \((\mathbb P^{5})^{*}\); it has dimension  

\[
\dim (\mathbb P^{5})^{*}=5 .
\]

---

### 1.  Tangency at the fixed point \(P\)

A conic \(D\) is tangent to the fixed smooth conic \(C\) at the point \(P\) iff the corresponding hyperplane \(H\) contains the tangent **plane** to the Veronese surface at the point \(\nu(P)\).

The tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\) is a projective plane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\); its vector‑space preimage is a 3‑dimensional subspace  

\[
W\subset V\qquad (V\simeq \mathbf{k}^{6}).
\]

A hyperplane \(H\) is defined by a linear form \(\ell\in V^{*}\).  
The condition “\(H\) contains the plane” is exactly  

\[
\ell|_{W}=0 .
\]

Thus \(\ell\) must lie in the orthogonal complement \(W^{\perp}\subset V^{*}\).  
Since \(\dim W =3\) and \(\dim V =6\),

\[
\dim W^{\perp}=6-3=3 .
\]

Hence the space of hyperplanes containing the tangent plane has projective dimension  

\[
3-1 = 2 .
\]

Therefore the tangency condition imposes  

\[
5-2 = 3
\]

independent linear conditions on the coefficients of \(H\).

---

### 2.  Passing through the fixed point \(Q\)

The condition that the conic \(D\) passes through a given point \(Q\) translates to  

\[
\nu(Q)\in H .
\]

For a hyperplane this is a single linear condition (the linear form must vanish at the vector representing \(\nu(Q)\)).  

Because \(Q\notin C\), the point \(\nu(Q)\) does **not** lie on the tangent plane \(T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\); consequently this condition is independent of the three obtained above and reduces the dimension by one more.

---

### 3.  Total codimension

Starting from the 5‑dimensional projective space of all hyperplanes, we lose \(3\) dimensions for tangency and another \(1\) dimension for passing through \(Q\):

\[
\text{codimension}=3+1=4 .
\]

Thus the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has codimension **4** inside the space of all hyperplanes of \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is the dual projective space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\!*}\cong \mathbf P^{5}\); it has projective dimension \(5\) (i.e. \(6\) coefficients up to scale).

---

### 1.  Tangency at the fixed point \(P\)

A hyperplane \(H\) defines a conic \(D\) that is tangent to the fixed conic \(C\) at \(P\) **iff** the hyperplane section of the Veronese surface is tangent to the surface at the point \(\nu(P)\).  
For the Veronese surface this occurs exactly when \(H\) contains the tangent plane  

\[
T_{\nu(P)}\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset \mathbf P^{5},
\]

which is a linear \(2\)-plane (its underlying vector subspace has dimension \(3\)).

The condition “\(H\) contains a given \(2\)-plane’’ is linear on the coefficients of \(H\).  
The space of linear forms on \(\mathbf k^{6}\) that vanish on a fixed \(3\)-dimensional subspace has dimension  

\[
6-3 = 3 .
\]

Hence the subspace of hyperplanes containing this plane has projective dimension \(2\), i.e. **codimension \(3\)** inside the space of all hyperplanes.

So tangency at \(P\) imposes **3 independent linear conditions**.

---

### 2.  Passing through the fixed point \(Q\)

The condition that the conic \(D\) passes through \(Q\) is simply  

\[
\nu(Q)\in H \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L(\nu(Q)) = 0,
\]

where \(L\) is the linear form defining \(H\).  
This is one linear equation on the coefficients of \(L\), giving **1 independent linear condition**.

Because \(Q\notin C\) (and in particular \(\nu(Q)\) does not lie in the tangent plane at \(\nu(P)\)), this condition is independent of the three obtained above.

---

### 3.  Total codimension

Adding the independent conditions,

\[
\text{codimension} = 3 + 1 = 4 .
\]

Thus the linear subspace of hyperplanes satisfying both requirements has codimension \(4\) inside the full \(5\)-dimensional space of hyperplanes of \(\mathbf P^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{4}
\]

For a plane conic \(C\) let  

\[
H_{C}\subset \mathbf P^{5}
\]

be the hyperplane whose intersection with the Veronese surface \(V\) is \(C\).
If \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) is a smooth conic, the line \(\ell _{D}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) is the tangent line to \(V\) at every point of \(\nu(D)\).

---

### Tangency ⇔ line containment  

A conic \(C\) is tangent to \(D\)  \(\Longleftrightarrow\)  the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) contains the line \(\ell _{D}\).

Indeed, if \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at a point \(p\in D\), then \(\nu(p)\in V\cap H_{C}\) and the tangent line to \(V\) at \(\nu(p)\) (which is \(\ell _{D}\)) lies in the hyperplane \(H_{C}\).  
Conversely, if \(H_{C}\) contains \(\ell _{D}\) then every point of \(\nu(D)\) is a point of \(V\cap H_{C}\) with the same tangent direction, i.e. \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at every point of \(D\).

Hence “\(C\) tangent to \(D\)” is a **linear** condition on the coefficients of the hyperplane \(H_{C}\).

---

### Number of linear conditions

The space of hyperplanes in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is the dual projective space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee}\), a projective space of dimension \(5\) (vector space dimension \(6\)).  

Containing a fixed line \(\ell_D\) imposes two independent linear equations on a hyperplane, because a hyperplane \(H\) is defined by a linear form
\[
a_0x_0+\dots +a_5x_5=0,
\]
and the condition \( \ell_D\subset H\) forces the coefficients to vanish on the two independent linear equations defining \(\ell_D\).

Thus each tangency to a given conic contributes **two** independent linear equations.

---

### Three conics in general position

Let \(D_1,D_2,D_3\) be smooth conics in general position.  
The three tangency requirements give \(3\times 2 = 6\) linear equations on the six coefficients \((a_0,\dots ,a_5)\) of a hyperplane \(H_C\).

For a generic choice of the three lines \(\ell_{D_1},\ell_{D_2},\ell_{D_3}\) these six equations are linearly independent.  
Consequently the only solution of the linear system is the zero vector, which does **not** correspond to a hyperplane (hyperplanes are defined by non‑zero linear forms).

Hence there is **no** hyperplane \(H_C\) that contains all three lines \(\ell_{D_i}\), and therefore there is **no** conic \(C\) tangent simultaneously to the three given conics.

---

\[
\boxed{0}
\]

The Veronese map  

\[
\nu : \mathbf P^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{5},
\qquad 
[x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}] \mapsto 
[x_{0}^{2}:x_{0}x_{1}:x_{0}x_{2}:x_{1}^{2}:x_{1}x_{2}:x_{2}^{2}]
\]

embeds the plane as the Veronese surface \(V=\nu (\mathbf P^{2})\subset\mathbf P^{5}\).
A plane conic \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) is cut out on \(V\) by a hyperplane
\(H_{D}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\); indeed the quadratic equation of \(D\) becomes a
linear equation in the coordinates of \(\mathbf P^{5}\).

For a smooth conic \(D\) the tangent spaces \(T_{\nu(p)}V\;(p\in D)\) all
contain the same line \(\ell _{D}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\); this line is called the
*ruling line* of \(D\).  
Let \(C\) be another conic and let \(H_{C}\) be the hyperplane whose
intersection with \(V\) is \(C\).

---

### Tangency ⇔ containing the ruling line  

\(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at a point \(p\in D\) iff the two curves
\(\nu(D)\) and \(\nu(C)\) have the same tangent line in \(V\) at the point
\(\nu(p)\).  Since the tangent line to \(V\) at \(\nu(p)\) already contains
\(\ell _{D}\), the condition that the two curves be tangent is exactly the
condition that the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) also contain \(\ell _{D}\).  Hence  

\[
C\text{ tangent to }D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 
\ell _{D}\subset H_{C}.
\]

---

### Linear equations imposed by a tangency  

A hyperplane in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is given by a linear form  

\[
a_{0}X_{0}+a_{1}X_{1}+a_{2}X_{2}+a_{3}X_{3}+a_{4}X_{4}+a_{5}X_{5}=0,
\]

with coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\neq 0\) defined up to a common
scalar.  
The condition “\(H_{C}\) contains the line \(\ell _{D}\)” means that the
linear form vanishes on two independent points of \(\ell _{D}\); equivalently
it gives **two independent linear equations** on the six coefficients
\(a_{i}\).  Thus each tangency condition reduces the dimension of the space
of possible hyperplanes by two.

---

### Three conics in general position  

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) be three smooth conics in general position.  
Denote by \(\ell _{i}\) the ruling line of \(D_{i}\).  
A conic \(C\) tangent to all three must satisfy  

\[
\ell _{1}\subset H_{C},\qquad \ell _{2}\subset H_{C},\qquad \ell _{3}\subset
H_{C}.
\]

Each inclusion contributes two independent linear equations; altogether we
obtain **six independent homogeneous linear equations** for the six
coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\).

A homogeneous linear system with as many independent equations as unknowns
has only the trivial solution.  Because the coefficients of a hyperplane are
considered up to a non‑zero scalar, the trivial solution corresponds to no
hyperplane at all.  Hence, for three conics in general position there is **no**
non‑zero solution; i.e. there is **no conic** simultaneously tangent to all
three.

\[
\boxed{0}
\]

**Step 1 – Geometry of the Veronese surface**

The Veronese map  

\[
\nu:\mathbb P^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbb P^{5},\qquad 
[x:y:z]\mapsto [x^{2}:y^{2}:z^{2}:yz:xz:xy]
\]

embeds \(\mathbb P^{2}\) as a smooth surface \(V=\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\subset\mathbb P^{5}\).
A plane conic \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) is cut out on \(V\) by a hyperplane
\(H_{C}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\); conversely every hyperplane section of \(V\) is a
plane conic.

For a smooth conic \(D\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) the image \(\nu(D)\) is a rational
normal curve of degree 2 lying on \(V\).  
All tangent lines to \(V\) along the points of \(\nu(D)\) coincide; we denote
this line by \(\ell_{D}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2 – Tangency ⇔ containing the line \(\ell_{D}\)**  

*If \(C\) is tangent to \(D\).*  
Let \(p\in D\cap C\).  Because \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at \(p\), the
intersection multiplicity \((C\cdot D)_{p}\ge 2\).  In the Veronese picture
this means that the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) meets \(V\) with multiplicity at least
\(2\) at the point \(\nu(p)\).  Consequently the whole tangent line of \(V\) at
\(\nu(p)\) lies in \(H_{C}\).  That tangent line is precisely \(\ell_{D}\); hence
\(\ell_{D}\subset H_{C}\).

*Conversely, assume \(\ell_{D}\subset H_{C}\).*  
Since \(\ell_{D}\) is the tangent line to \(V\) at every point of \(\nu(D)\),
the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) contains the tangent line at each \(\nu(p)\) with
\(p\in D\).  Therefore the intersection \(H_{C}\cap V\) meets \(V\) with
multiplicity at least 2 at each such point, i.e. \((C\cdot D)_{p}\ge2\).  Hence
\(C\) is tangent to \(D\).

Thus  

\[
\boxed{C\text{ tangent to }D\iff H_{C}\supset\ell_{D}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 3 – Linear equations coming from a tangency**

A hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is given by a linear form
\(a_{0}x_{0}+a_{1}x_{1}+ \dots +a_{5}x_{5}=0\); the coefficients \((a_{0}:\dots :a_{5})\)
form a point of the dual projective space \((\mathbb P^{5})^{\vee}\).

The line \(\ell_{D}\) spans a 2‑dimensional vector subspace of the
6‑dimensional space underlying \(\mathbb P^{5}\).  
Requiring the hyperplane to contain this line means that the linear form
vanishes on the whole 2‑dimensional subspace, i.e. it satisfies **two
independent linear equations** in the \(a_{i}\).

Hence each tangency condition contributes exactly two independent linear
constraints on the coefficients of \(H_{C}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 4 – Three conics in general position**

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) be smooth conics in general position and let
\(\ell_{i}:=\ell_{D_{i}}\) be the associated lines in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

The space of hyperplanes is \((\mathbb P^{5})^{\vee}\cong\mathbb P^{5}\) (dimension
5).  
Containing \(\ell_{i}\) imposes two linear conditions, so each \(\ell_{i}\)
cuts out a linear subspace of codimension 2, i.e. a \(\mathbb P^{3}\), inside the
dual \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

Intersecting the three \(\mathbb P^{3}\)’s corresponding to \(\ell_{1},
\ell_{2}, \ell_{3}\) gives, for a generic configuration, a **zero‑dimensional**
intersection: we have six independent linear equations on six homogeneous
unknowns \((a_{0}:\dots :a_{5})\).  The only solution (up to overall scaling)
is a single point of the dual space, i.e. a unique hyperplane \(H\).

That hyperplane \(H\) defines a unique conic \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) (again
up to scaling of its defining equation).  Consequently there is exactly one
plane conic which is simultaneously tangent to the three given conics.

\]

The Veronese embedding  

\[
\nu:\mathbf P^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbf P^{5},\qquad 
[x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}]\mapsto [x_{0}^{2}:x_{0}x_{1}:x_{0}x_{2}:x_{1}^{2}:x_{1}x_{2}:x_{2}^{2}]
\]

maps a plane conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) to the intersection of a hyperplane  
\(H_{C}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) with the Veronese surface \(V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\).
Thus the space of conics (up to scaling) is identified with the dual projective
space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee}\cong\mathbf P^{5}\) of hyperplanes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Tangency to a fixed conic \(D\)

Let \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) be a smooth conic.  
Its image \(\nu(D)\) is a rational normal curve of degree \(4\) lying on \(V\).
A classical property of the Veronese surface is that the tangent line to \(V\)
at any point of \(\nu(D)\) is the same line; denote it by \(\ell _{D}\subset\mathbf
P^{5}\).

*If a conic \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at a point \(p\in D\), then the
hyperplane \(H_{C}\) contains the tangent direction of \(V\) at \(\nu(p)\);
that direction is precisely the line \(\ell _{D}\). Hence \(H_{C}\supset\ell
_{D}\).*

Conversely, if a hyperplane \(H\) contains \(\ell _{D}\) then, at every point
\(\nu(p)\in\nu(D)\), the line \(\ell _{D}\) lies in \(H\) and is tangent to
\(V\). Consequently the plane conic \(C=H\cap V\) meets \(D\) with multiplicity
\(2\) at the corresponding point, i.e. \(C\) is tangent to \(D\).

Thus  

\[
C\text{ tangent to }D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_{C}\supset\ell _{D}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Linear equations coming from a tangency

A line \(\ell\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) corresponds to a \(2\)-dimensional vector
subspace \(L\subset K^{6}\).  
A hyperplane is given by a linear form \(f\in (K^{6})^{\!*}\).  
The condition \(f|_{L}=0\) gives **two independent linear equations** on the
coefficients of \(f\).  
Hence tangency to a fixed smooth conic imposes exactly two independent linear
conditions on the coefficients of the hyperplane \(H_{C}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Three conics in general position

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) be three smooth conics in general position and let
\(\ell_{i}=\ell_{D_{i}}\) be the associated lines in \(\mathbf P^{5}\).
For a conic \(C\) to be tangent to all three we need

\[
H_{C}\supset\ell_{1},\qquad H_{C}\supset\ell_{2},\qquad H_{C}\supset\ell_{3}.
\]

Each inclusion contributes two linear equations; altogether we have six linear
equations for the six coefficients of a hyperplane.  
Because the three conics are in general position, any five of these equations
are independent, while the six‑th one is a linear combination of the previous
five. Consequently the rank of the system is \(5\), leaving a **one‑dimensional**
solution space in the vector space of linear forms.  In projective terms this
means exactly **one point** of \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee}\), i.e. a unique
hyperplane \(H_{C}\).

Therefore there is precisely one (up to scaling) conic \(C\) that is tangent
simultaneously to the three given conics.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

Let  

\[
\nu:\mathbf P^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{5},\qquad 
[x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}]\mapsto [x_{0}^{2}:x_{1}^{2}:x_{2}^{2}:x_{0}x_{1}:x_{0}x_{2}:x_{1}x_{2}]
\]

be the 2‑uple Veronese embedding and let \(V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\) be the Veronese surface.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The line \(\ell _{D}\)

Let \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) be a smooth conic.  
Because \(D\simeq\mathbf P^{1}\) via a degree‑2 map, the restriction  

\[
\nu|_{D}: D\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{5}
\]

is the 4‑uple embedding of \(\mathbf P^{1}\); its image \(\nu(D)\) is a rational
normal curve of degree \(4\) contained in a linear subspace
\(\Lambda_{D}\simeq\mathbf P^{4}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\).

For any point \(p\in D\) the tangent plane to the surface \(V\) at
\(\nu(p)\) is a 2‑dimensional linear subspace \(T_{\nu(p)}V\subset\mathbf P^{5}\).
When \(p\) varies along \(D\) these planes sweep a 3‑dimensional linear
subspace; the intersection of all of them is a line, which we denote by  

\[
\ell_{D}= \bigcap_{p\in D} T_{\nu(p)}V\subset\mathbf P^{5}.
\]

Thus \(\ell_{D}\) is a fixed line depending only on the conic \(D\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Tangency of a plane conic \(C\) to \(D\)

A plane conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) corresponds to a hyperplane
\(H_{C}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) such that  

\[
H_{C}\cap V = \nu(C).
\]

Assume that \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at a point \(p\in D\).  
Then \(\nu(p)\in H_{C}\cap V\) and the curve \(\nu(C)\) has the same tangent
direction as \(\nu(D)\) at \(\nu(p)\).  Consequently the tangent line to
\(\nu(D)\) at \(\nu(p)\) (which is the line \(\ell_{D}\)) is contained in the
hyperplane \(H_{C}\).  Hence  

\[
C\text{ tangent to }D \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ell_{D}\subset H_{C}.
\]

Conversely, if a hyperplane \(H\) contains \(\ell_{D}\) then the
intersection \(H\cap V\) is a plane conic whose restriction to \(D\) has a
double point at every point of \(D\); in particular the curve \(C\) defined
by \(H\) is tangent to \(D\).  Thus we have the equivalence

\[
C\text{ tangent to }D \;\iff\; H_{C}\supset \ell_{D}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Linear equations imposed by a tangency condition

A hyperplane in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is given by a linear form  

\[
a_{0}X_{0}+a_{1}X_{1}+a_{2}X_{2}+a_{3}X_{3}+a_{4}X_{4}+a_{5}X_{5}=0,
\]

up to an overall scalar; the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) form a
point of the dual projective space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee}\).

The condition “\(H\) contains the line \(\ell_{D}\)” means that the linear
form vanishes on every point of \(\ell_{D}\).  Since a line is spanned by two
independent points, we obtain **two independent linear equations** on the
coefficients \(a_{i}\).  Hence each tangency to a fixed smooth conic
contributes exactly two linear conditions on the hyperplane defining \(C\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Simultaneous tangency to three general conics

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) be smooth conics in general
position.  
For each \(i\) the set of hyperplanes containing \(\ell_{D_{i}}\) is a
linear subspace  

\[
\Lambda_{i}= \{ H\subset\mathbf P^{5}\mid \ell_{D_{i}}\subset H\}
\subset (\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee},
\]

which has codimension \(2\) (i.e. \(\Lambda_{i}\cong\mathbf P^{3}\)).

We must find the intersection  

\[
\Lambda_{1}\cap\Lambda_{2}\cap\Lambda_{3}.
\]

* After imposing the first two conditions we have a linear space of
dimension  

\[
5-2-2 = 1,
\]

i.e. a **line** of hyperplanes tangent to both \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\).

* Intersecting this line with the third codimension‑2 subspace \(\Lambda_{3}\)
produces a single point, because a line is not contained in a generic
\(\mathbf P^{3}\) and meets it in exactly one point.

Hence there is **exactly one** hyperplane \(H\) (up to scaling) that
contains all three lines \(\ell_{D_{1}},\ell_{D_{2}},\ell_{D_{3}}\).  The
corresponding conic \(C\) is therefore the unique plane conic tangent to
the three given conics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{1}
\]

Let  

\[
\nu :\mathbf P^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{5},\qquad 
[x:y:z]\longmapsto [x^{2}:xy:y^{2}:xz:yz:z^{2}]
\]

be the degree‑2 Veronese embedding and put \(V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset\mathbf P^{5}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Conics ↔ hyperplanes  

A (plane) conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) is given by a homogeneous quadratic
\[
a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}y^{2}+a_{3}xz+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0 .
\]
The vector \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) defines a linear form on \(\mathbf P^{5}\);
its zero set is a hyperplane  

\[
H_{C}= \{a_{0}X_{0}+a_{1}X_{1}+ \cdots +a_{5}X_{5}=0\}\subset\mathbf P^{5}.
\]

Conversely, intersecting a hyperplane \(H\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) with the Veronese
surface gives a conic in \(\mathbf P^{2}\):
\(C= \nu^{-1}(H\cap V)\).
Thus the space of conics (up to a non‑zero scalar) is the dual projective space
\((\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee}\cong \mathbf P^{5}\); it has projective dimension \(5\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Tangency condition  

Let \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) be a smooth conic.
For any point \(p\in D\) the tangent line to the surface \(V\) at the point
\(\nu(p)\) is the same line; denote it by \(\ell _{D}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\).

\[
\boxed{\;C\text{ is tangent to }D\iff H_{C}\supset\ell _{D}\;}
\]

Indeed, \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) iff the two quadrics defining \(C\) and \(D\)
have a common point of multiplicity \(2\) on \(D\); under \(\nu\) this is
equivalent to the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) containing the line \(\ell _{D}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Linear equations supplied by one tangency  

A line \(\ell\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) has codimension \(4\).  
A hyperplane \(H\) contains \(\ell\) exactly when the defining linear form
vanishes on the two independent points of \(\ell\); this gives **two independent
linear equations** on the coefficients \((a_{0},\dots ,a_{5})\) of \(H\).

Hence the condition “\(C\) is tangent to a fixed conic \(D\)” imposes two
independent linear conditions on the point \([a_{0}:\dots :a_{5}]\in\mathbf
P^{5}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Three conics in general position  

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) be three smooth conics in general position.
For each \(i\) we obtain two linear equations; altogether we have a homogeneous
system of **six** linear equations in the six unknown coefficients
\(a_{0},\dots ,a_{5}\).

Because the three conics are in general position, the six equations are
independent; the coefficient matrix therefore has rank \(5\) (the maximal
possible rank for a homogeneous system in projective space).  
Consequently the solution space is one‑dimensional:

\[
\dim_{\mathbf C}\{[a_{0}:\dots :a_{5}]\mid
L_{ij}(a)=0,\;i=1,2,3,\;j=1,2\}=1 .
\]

Thus there is a **unique** point of \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\vee}\), i.e. a unique
hyperplane \(H\), satisfying all three containment conditions.
The corresponding conic \(C=\nu^{-1}(H\cap V)\) is therefore the only plane
conic (up to a non‑zero scalar multiple of its equation) that is tangent to the
three given conics \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\).

\boxed{1}
\]

The Veronese map  

\[
\nu:\mathbb P^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbb P^{5},\qquad 
[x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}]\mapsto [x_{0}^{2}:x_{0}x_{1}:x_{0}x_{2}:x_{1}^{2}:x_{1}x_{2}:x_{2}^{2}]
\]

 embeds \(\mathbb P^{2}\) as a smooth surface  

\[
V=\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\subset\mathbb P^{5}.
\]

A plane conic \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) is the intersection of a hyperplane
\(H_{C}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) with \(V\):
\[
C = V\cap H_{C},\qquad H_{C}\in (\mathbb P^{5})^{\!*}\cong\mathbb P^{5}.
\]

---

### Tangency condition

Let \(D\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) be a smooth conic.  
For any point \(p\in D\) the tangent line to \(V\) at \(\nu(p)\) is the same
line; denote it by \(\ell_{D}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\).

*If a conic \(C\) is tangent to \(D\), then \(\nu(D)\subset V\) and the
intersection \(V\cap H_{C}\) meets \(V\) along \(C\) with multiplicity 2 at
every point of \(D\).  Hence the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) must contain the whole
tangent line \(\ell_{D}\).*

Conversely, if a hyperplane \(H\) contains \(\ell_{D}\) then the intersection
\(V\cap H\) meets \(V\) along a conic that is tangent to \(D\) (the
multiplicity‑2 contact follows from the fact that \(\ell_{D}\) is the
projectivised tangent space of \(V\) along \(\nu(D)\)).  

Thus

\[
C\text{ tangent to }D\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad H_{C}\supset\ell_{D}.
\]

---

### Linear equations

A line \(\ell_{D}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) is a \(\mathbb P^{1}\); its linear span is a
2‑dimensional vector subspace \(U\subset\mathbb C^{6}\).  
A hyperplane \(H\) is given by a linear form \(L\in(\mathbb C^{6})^{\!*}\).  
The condition \(\ell_{D}\subset H\) is exactly \(L|_{U}=0\), i.e. **two
independent linear equations** on the six coefficients of \(L\).

Hence each tangency to a fixed smooth conic contributes two independent linear
constraints on the hyperplane \(H_{C}\).

---

### Three conics in general position

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) be three smooth conics in general position.
For each \(i\) let \(\ell_{i}=\ell_{D_{i}}\).  
The set of hyperplanes containing \(\ell_{i}\) is a linear subspace  

\[
\Lambda_{i}:=\{H\mid \ell_{i}\subset H\}\subset (\mathbb P^{5})^{\!*},
\]

which is a projective \( \mathbb P^{3}\) (codimension 2).

We must find  

\[
\Lambda_{1}\cap\Lambda_{2}\cap\Lambda_{3}.
\]

Two generic \(\mathbb P^{3}\)’s in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) intersect in a line
(\(\mathbb P^{1}\)).  Intersecting this line with a third generic \(\mathbb
P^{3}\) gives a single point.  Because all conditions are linear, the
intersection is reduced and consists of exactly **one** point.

Consequently there is a unique hyperplane \(H\) (up to scaling) that
contains the three lines \(\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{3}\), and therefore a unique
plane conic \(C\) tangent to the three given conics.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

The Veronese map  

\[
\nu:\mathbf P^{2}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{5},\qquad 
[x_0:x_1:x_2]\mapsto [x_0^{2}:x_0x_1:x_0x_2:x_1^{2}:x_1x_2:x_2^{2}]
\]

embeds the plane as a smooth surface \(V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset\mathbf P^{5}\).  
A plane conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) is cut out on \(V\) by a hyperplane
\(H_C\subset\mathbf P^{5}\); the coefficients of \(H_C\) are the (homogeneous)
coefficients of the quadratic equation of \(C\).

---

### Tangency condition

Let \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) be a smooth conic and let  

\[
\ell_D\subset\mathbf P^{5}
\]

be the line that is tangent to the surface \(V\) at every point
\(\nu(p)\) with \(p\in D\).  
If a conic \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) at some point \(p\in D\), then
\(H_C\) must contain the tangent line \(\ell_D\); indeed,
\(H_C\cap V=C\) and the intersection of a hyperplane with a smooth surface
is tangent to the surface exactly when the hyperplane contains the
tangent line of the surface at the point of contact.  
Conversely, if \(H_C\) contains \(\ell_D\) then the curve
\(H_C\cap V\) meets \(V\) with multiplicity \(\ge 2\) along \(\ell_D\), i.e.
\(C\) is tangent to \(D\).  
Hence  

\[
C\text{ tangent to }D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\ell_D\subset H_C .
\]

---

### Linear equations

A hyperplane in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is given by a linear form
\(L(x_0,\dots ,x_5)=0\); the space of such forms is a 6‑dimensional vector
space \(W\cong\mathbf C^{6}\).  
Requiring that a line \(\ell_D\) (a 2‑dimensional linear subspace of the
underlying vector space) lie in \(H_C\) means that the linear functional
\(L\) vanishes on the 2‑dimensional subspace.  The subspace of functionals
vanishing on a given 2‑dimensional subspace has codimension \(2\) in \(W\);
equivalently, the condition “\(\ell_D\subset H_C\)” imposes **two independent
linear equations** on the coefficients of \(L\).

Thus each smooth conic \(D_i\) contributes two independent linear conditions
on the hyperplane \(H_C\).

---

### Three conics in general position

Let \(D_1,D_2,D_3\) be three smooth conics in general position.  
The three corresponding tangent lines \(\ell_{D_1},\ell_{D_2},\ell_{D_3}\)
are independent, so the six linear equations they impose on \(W\) are
independent.  

\[
\dim_{\mathbf C}W = 6,\qquad
\text{codimension imposed}=2+2+2 = 6 .
\]

Hence the solution space in \(W\) is \(0\)-dimensional; after projectivising
(identifying forms that differ by a non‑zero scalar) we obtain a **single**
point.  That point corresponds to a unique hyperplane \(H_C\), and therefore
to a unique plane conic \(C\) that is simultaneously tangent to the three
given conics.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space \(\mathbb P^{5}\) of coefficients of a homogeneous quadratic form in three variables.  
Via the Veronese embedding \(\nu:\mathbb P^{2}\to\mathbb P^{5}\) a conic \(C\) corresponds to a hyperplane \(H_{C}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) that cuts the Veronese surface \(V=\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\) in \(\nu(C)\).

For a fixed smooth conic \(D\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) the tangent planes to \(V\) along the curve \(\nu(D)\) intersect in a line \(\ell_{D}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\).  
A plane conic \(C\) is tangent to \(D\) iff the hyperplane \(H_{C}\) contains that line \(\ell_{D}\).  
Since a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is given by a linear form \(L=0\), the condition “\(L\) vanishes on \(\ell_{D}\)” is equivalent to the vanishing of \(L\) on two independent points of \(\ell_{D}\); therefore each tangency condition imposes **two independent linear equations** on the coefficients of \(L\).

Consequently, for three smooth conics \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) in general position we must find hyperplanes \(H\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) that contain the three lines \(\ell_{D_{1}},\ell_{D_{2}},\ell_{D_{3}}\).  
Each line contributes two linear conditions, so we have a system of six independent linear equations in the six unknown coefficients of the linear form defining \(H\).  
A homogeneous linear system with a square coefficient matrix has, generically, exactly two solutions up to scaling (the two possible signs of the determinant). Hence there are **exactly eight** distinct conics \(C\) (up to an overall scalar factor) that are simultaneously tangent to the three given conics.

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The Veronese map  

\[
\nu:\mathbf P^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbf P^{5},\qquad
[x:y:z]\mapsto [x^{2}:y^{2}:z^{2}:yz:xz:xy]
\]

embeds the plane as a smooth surface  

\[
V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset\mathbf P^{5}.
\]

A (plane) conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) is cut out on \(V\) by a hyperplane
\(H_{C}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\); conversely every hyperplane cutting \(V\) gives a
conic.  
Thus the space of conics is the dual projective space \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\!*}\),
which is a \(\mathbf P^{5}\) whose points are the coefficients of the hyperplane
\(H_{C}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Tangency condition

Let \(D\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) be a smooth conic and let  

\[
\ell _{D}= \text{the line tangent to }V\text{ at the points }\nu(p),\;p\in D .
\]

For any point \(p\in D\) the tangent plane to \(V\) at \(\nu(p)\) contains the
line \(\ell _{D}\); therefore a hyperplane \(H\) cuts \(V\) in a conic that is
tangent to \(D\) **iff** \(H\) contains the whole line \(\ell _{D}\).

A line in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is a \(\mathbf P^{1}\); the condition “\(H\) contains a
given line’’ is equivalent to the vanishing of the linear form defining \(H\)
on two independent points of that line. Hence it gives **two independent linear
equations** on the coefficients of \(H\).

Consequently each tangency to a fixed conic contributes exactly two independent
linear conditions on the hyperplane \(H_{C}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Three conics in general position

Let \(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}\) be three smooth conics in general position.
Denote by \(\ell_{i}\;(i=1,2,3)\) the corresponding tangent lines on \(V\).

The hyperplane \(H_{C}\) of a conic \(C\) tangent to all three \(D_{i}\) must
contain the three lines \(\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{3}\).  
Each \(\ell_{i}\) gives two linear equations, so we have a system of six linear
equations in the six homogeneous coordinates of a hyperplane in
\(\mathbf P^{5}\).

The space of hyperplanes is a projective \(\mathbf P^{5}\); therefore at most
five independent linear equations can be imposed.  
Because the three conics are in *general position*, the six equations are
linearly dependent with precisely one relation; the rank of the system is
\(5\).

Hence the intersection of the three codimension‑\(2\) linear subspaces
\(\{H\mid \ell_{i}\subset H\}\) inside \((\mathbf P^{5})^{\!*}\) is a single point.
That point corresponds to a unique hyperplane \(H_{C}\), and therefore to a
unique conic \(C\) (up to the overall scalar factor of its equation).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Result

There is exactly **one** conic, up to scaling, that is simultaneously tangent
to the three given smooth conics in general position.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]

problems.skill: Veronese embedding of conics and translation of tangency to hyperplane sections
problems.problem:
Let \(\nu:\mathbb{P}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{5}\) be the degree‑2 Veronese embedding, so that the projective space of plane conics is identified with \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
For a fixed smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\), the locus of conics tangent to \(C\) corresponds, under \(\nu\), to a hyperplane in \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
Similarly, for a fixed point \(P\in\mathbb{P}^{2}\), the locus of conics passing through \(P\) is also a hyperplane in \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
Now let \(C_{1},\dots ,C_{4}\) be four distinct smooth conics and \(P_{1},\dots ,P_{6}\) be six distinct points, all in general position.  
How many independent linear equations (i.e. hyperplane conditions) are imposed on \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) by requiring a conic to be tangent to each \(C_{i}\) and to pass through each \(P_{j}\)?  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
Each condition—“tangent to a fixed smooth conic’’ or “passes through a fixed point’’—defines a hyperplane in the 5‑dimensional projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) of plane conics.  

Hence we have ten hyperplanes in total:

* 4 hyperplanes coming from the tangency to the four conics \(C_{1},\dots ,C_{4}\);
* 6 hyperplanes coming from passing through the six points \(P_{1},\dots ,P_{6}\).

The vector space underlying \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) has dimension \(6\). Consequently, at most six linearly independent hyperplanes can be imposed; any further hyperplane condition must be a linear combination of the previous ones (or make the system inconsistent).  

Since the conics and points are in general position, no non‑trivial linear relation exists among the ten hyperplanes, so the rank of the system of linear equations is the maximal possible, namely the dimension of the ambient vector space.

\[
\text{Number of independent linear equations}= \min\{10,6\}=6.
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space  

\[
\mathbb P^5 = \mathbb P\bigl(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2))\bigr)
\]

whose homogeneous coordinates are the six coefficients \((a_{00},a_{01},a_{02},a_{11},a_{12},a_{22})\) of a quadratic form, defined up to a common factor.

* A fixed smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}\) imposes the **tangency condition**  
  \[
  Q|_{C}\ \text{has a double root}
  \]
  which, when written in the coordinates of \(\mathbb P^5\), is a single linear equation. Hence each \(C_i\) contributes one linear functional on the 6‑dimensional vector space of quadratic forms.

* A fixed point \(P\in\mathbb P^{2}\) imposes the **incidence condition**  
  \[
  Q(P)=0,
  \]
  also a single linear equation in the same six coefficients. Thus each \(P_j\) contributes another linear functional.

Altogether we have \(4+6 = 10\) linear equations on the 6‑dimensional vector space of quadratic forms.  
The rank of a collection of linear equations cannot exceed the dimension of the ambient vector space, which here is \(6\).  

For a generic choice of the four smooth conics \(C_i\) and the six points \(P_j\) (they are assumed to be in general position), the corresponding linear functionals are in general position as well; therefore they span the whole dual space. Consequently the maximal possible rank \(6\) is achieved, and no further linear dependence occurs.

Hence the number of **independent** linear equations imposed by the ten conditions is  

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space  

\[
\mathbb P^5=\mathbb P\bigl(H^0(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2))\bigr),
\]

whose homogeneous coordinate vector space has dimension \(6\).

* For a fixed point \(P\in\mathbb P^{2}\) the condition “the conic passes through \(P\)” is the linear equation  

\[
Q(P)=0,
\]

where \(Q\) is the quadratic form defining the conic. Hence each point gives a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

* For a fixed smooth conic \(C\) the condition “the conic is tangent to \(C\)” also gives a linear equation on the coefficients of \(Q\); therefore each tangency condition is again a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

Thus we have ten linear equations (four from tangency, six from points) in the six‑dimensional vector space of quadratic forms.

Because the six points \(P_{1},\dots ,P_{6}\) are in general position, the six evaluation maps  

\[
Q\longmapsto Q(P_j),\qquad j=1,\dots ,6,
\]

are linearly independent. Consequently the six point conditions already have **full rank 6**; they already determine the zero quadratic form, i.e. they leave no non‑zero conic satisfying all six.

Adding the four tangency conditions cannot increase the rank, since the ambient vector space has dimension only \(6\). Hence the total set of ten equations spans a \(6\)-dimensional subspace of the dual vector space.

Therefore the number of independent linear (hyperplane) conditions imposed is  

\[
\boxed{6}.
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^{5}\); its homogeneous coordinate vector space has dimension \(6\).

* A conic tangent to a fixed smooth conic \(C\) is given by a **single linear equation** in the coordinates of \(\mathbb P^{5}\); i.e. a hyperplane.
* A conic passing through a fixed point \(P\) is also given by a **single linear equation** in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

Thus each of the four tangency conditions and each of the six point‑passing conditions contributes one linear equation, for a total of \(4+6 = 10\) hyperplane conditions.

Linear equations can be independent only up to the dimension of the dual vector space, which is \(6\).  
However, in projective space a non‑zero vector (the conic) must remain in the kernel of the linear forms.  
If we impose more than \(5\) independent linear equations, the only vector satisfying all of them would be the zero vector, which does **not** correspond to a point of \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

Consequently, at most \(5\) of the ten hyperplane conditions can be linearly independent.  
Because the conics \(C_i\) and the points \(P_j\) are in general position, no unexpected linear relations occur among the corresponding hyperplanes, so exactly the maximal number of independent conditions is achieved.

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

Each tangency condition to a smooth conic and each point‑passing condition is a hyperplane in the 5‑dimensional projective space \(\mathbb P^{5}\) of plane conics.  
These hyperplanes correspond to linear functionals on the 6‑dimensional vector space of quadratic forms in three variables.

We have \(4+6 = 10\) such hyperplanes.  
The space of all linear functionals on a 6‑dimensional vector space is itself 6‑dimensional, so at most six of these hyperplanes can be linearly independent.  

Because the conics \(C_i\) and the points \(P_j\) are assumed to be in general position, the ten corresponding linear functionals are generic; consequently they span the whole dual space. Hence the rank of the system of equations is the maximal possible, namely \(6\).

Thus the number of independent linear equations imposed is  

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^5\); its homogeneous coordinate vector space has dimension \(6\).  
Each condition (tangency to a smooth conic or passing through a point) is a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^5\), i.e. a single linear equation on the six coefficients of a conic.

We have  

* 4 hyperplanes coming from the tangency conditions to \(C_1,\dots ,C_4\);
* 6 hyperplanes coming from the point conditions at \(P_1,\dots ,P_6\).

Thus we have ten linear forms in a \(6\)-dimensional vector space.  
For points and conics in general position, none of these hyperplanes coincides or is a linear combination of the others, so they span the whole dual space. Consequently the number of **independent** linear equations among them equals the dimension of that dual space, namely \(6\).

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space  

\[
\mathbb P^5=\mathbb P\bigl(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2))\bigr)
\]

which is the projectivisation of a 6‑dimensional vector space \(V\) of quadratic forms
\(ax^2+by^2+cz^2+dxy+exz+fyz\).

---

### 1.  One point condition  

For a point \(P=[x_0:y_0:z_0]\) the condition “the conic passes through \(P\)” is  

\[
a x_0^{2}+b y_0^{2}+c z_0^{2}+d x_0y_0+e x_0z_0+f y_0z_0 =0 ,
\]

a linear equation on the coordinates of \(\mathbb P^5\).  
Hence each point gives a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^5\).

---

### 2.  Six points in general position  

Take six distinct points \(P_1,\dots ,P_6\) in general position (no conic contains all six).  
The six linear equations are linearly independent **up to one relation**, because the
vector space \(V\) has dimension \(6\).  

Indeed any five of the equations are independent, giving a 1‑dimensional subspace of \(V\)
(i.e. a unique conic through the five points).  
The sixth equation is then a linear combination of the first five; it is not satisfied
by that unique conic, so the intersection of the six hyperplanes is empty.

Consequently the six point conditions impose **exactly 5 independent linear equations** on \(\mathbb P^5\).

---

### 3.  One tangency condition  

For a smooth conic \(C\) the condition “a conic is tangent to \(C\)” is also a linear
condition on the coefficients (it is the pull‑back of a hyperplane via the Veronese
embedding). Thus each tangency gives another hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^5\).

---

### 4.  Four tangencies together with the six points  

The dual space of \(\mathbb P^5\) (the space of linear forms) also has dimension \(6\),
so at most **5** independent hyperplanes can exist in \(\mathbb P^5\) (codimension 5,
leaving a point).  

Since the six point conditions already give the maximal possible rank, adding the four
tangency hyperplanes cannot increase the rank; they must lie in the linear span of the
point hyperplanes. Hence the total number of independent linear equations is still 5.

---

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space  

\[
\mathbb P^5 = \mathbb P\bigl(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2))\bigr),
\]

so its homogeneous coordinate vector space has dimension \(6\) (the six coefficients of a quadratic form).

* For a fixed smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbb P^2\) the condition “the conic is tangent to \(C\)” is linear in the coefficients; it is a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^5\).  
* For a fixed point \(P\in\mathbb P^2\) the condition “the conic passes through \(P\)” is also a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^5\).

Hence each of the ten geometric requirements

\[
\text{tangent to }C_1,\dots ,C_4\quad\text{and}\quad\text{passes through }P_1,\dots ,P_6
\]

gives a linear equation on the six coefficients of a conic.  
All the conics \(C_i\) and points \(P_j\) are assumed to be in general position, so no unexpected linear relation among these ten equations can occur.  

The maximal possible number of linearly independent equations is the dimension of the coefficient space, namely \(6\). Since we have more equations (\(10\)) than that, the rank of the system is limited by this maximum:

\[
\text{rank} = \min(10,6) = 6 .
\]

Thus the ten geometric conditions impose **six independent linear equations** (i.e. six independent hyperplane conditions) on \(\mathbb P^5\).

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

Each conic in \(\mathbb P^{2}\) corresponds to a point of the projective space \(\mathbb P^{5}\) of homogeneous quadratic forms  

\[
V = \{a_{00}x^{2}+a_{01}xy+\dots +a_{22}y^{2}\}\; ,
\qquad \dim V = 6 .
\]

A condition such as “the conic is tangent to a fixed smooth conic \(C\)” or “the conic passes through a fixed point \(P\)” is a **linear** condition on the coefficients \(a_{ij}\); geometrically it is a hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

Hence each of the four tangency requirements and each of the six point‑passing requirements gives one linear equation, i.e. one hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).  
Altogether we have ten hyperplanes, but the space of conics is only a 6‑dimensional vector space (projective dimension 5).  

Consequently the maximum possible rank of the system of linear equations is the dimension of the ambient vector space, namely \(6\). For generic choices of the four conics and six points the ten hyperplanes are in general position, so their defining linear forms are linearly independent up to this maximal rank.

\[
\text{Number of independent linear equations} = \min(10,6)=6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

Each condition (tangency to a fixed smooth conic \(C_i\) or passing through a fixed point \(P_j\)) cuts out a hyperplane in the projective space of conics \(\mathbb P^{5}\).  
Hence we obtain ten hyperplanes

\[
H_{C_1},\dots ,H_{C_4},\;H_{P_1},\dots ,H_{P_6}\subset \mathbb P^{5}.
\]

A hyperplane in \(\mathbb P^{5}\) is given by a single linear form in the six homogeneous coordinates of \(\mathbb P^{5}\).  
Consequently the vector space of all such linear forms has dimension \(6\); after projectivising we obtain the dual projective space \((\mathbb P^{5})^{\vee}\) of the same dimension.

Therefore at most six of the ten linear forms can be linearly independent.  
Because the points \(P_j\) and the conics \(C_i\) are assumed to be in general position, the corresponding hyperplanes are also in general position, so the ten linear forms span the whole 6‑dimensional space of linear forms.

Thus the number of independent linear equations (i.e. independent hyperplane conditions) imposed is

\boxed{6}.
