The Veronese surface \(V\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\) is the image of the degree‑2 Veronese map
\[
\nu:\mathbb{P}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{5}.
\]

---

### 1.  Cubics vanishing on \(V\)

All cubic forms on \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) have dimension  

\[
h^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{5}}(3)\bigr)=\binom{3+5}{3}=56 .
\]

Because the Veronese surface is projectively normal, the restriction map  

\[
0\longrightarrow I_{V}(3)\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{5}}(3)
\longrightarrow \mathcal O_{V}(3)\longrightarrow 0
\]

is exact on global sections.  On \(V\) we have \(\mathcal O_{V}(1)\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2)\); hence  

\[
\mathcal O_{V}(3)\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(6),\qquad
h^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{V}(3)\bigr)=\binom{6+2}{2}=28 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\dim W = h^{0}\bigl(I_{V}(3)\bigr)=56-28=28 .
\]

---

### 2.  Intersecting with a plane \(\Pi\)

Let \(\Pi\simeq\mathbb{P}^{2}\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
Restrict a cubic from \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\) to \(\Pi\):

\[
r : H^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{5}}(3)\bigr)\longrightarrow
H^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\bigr),\qquad
h^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\bigr)=\binom{3+2}{2}=10 .
\]

For cubics already vanishing on \(V\) we have the induced map  

\[
r|_{W}: W \longrightarrow H^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\bigr).
\]

Its image consists precisely of those cubics on \(\Pi\) that vanish on the
scheme \(Z:=V\cap\Pi\).  Since \(V\) has degree \(4\), a linear plane (codimension 3)
meets \(V\) in a zero‑dimensional scheme of length \(4\):
\[
\deg V =4 \Longrightarrow \operatorname{length}(Z)=4 .
\]

Hence on \(\Pi\simeq\mathbb{P}^{2}\) we are looking at cubic curves passing through
four points.  Vanishing at each point gives an independent linear condition,
so

\[
\dim \operatorname{Im}(r|_{W})=
h^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\bigr)-\operatorname{length}(Z)=10-4=6 .
\]

---

### 3.  Dimension of \(W_{\Pi}\)

\(W_{\Pi}\) is the kernel of \(r|_{W}\); therefore

\[
\dim W_{\Pi}= \dim W-\dim\operatorname{Im}(r|_{W})
= 28-6 = 22 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{22}
\]

The Veronese surface  

\[
V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset \mathbf P^{5}
\]

has homogeneous coordinate ring  

\[
R=\bigoplus_{m\ge 0} H^{0}\!\left(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2m)\right)
\]

so that  

\[
\dim_k R_{n}= \dim_k H^{0}\!\left(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2n)\right)
        =\binom{2n+2}{2}.
\]

The space of all degree‑\(n\) homogeneous polynomials on \(\mathbf P^{5}\) has dimension  

\[
\dim_k S_{n}= \binom{n+5}{5}.
\]

Hence the degree‑\(n\) part of the ideal of \(V\) is  

\[
I(V)_{n}=S_{n}\big/ R_{n},\qquad 
\dim_k I(V)_{n}= \binom{n+5}{5}-\binom{2n+2}{2}.
\]

For \(n=3\),

\[
\dim_k I(V)_{3}= \binom{8}{5}-\binom{8}{2}=56-28=28 .
\]

Thus  

\[
W=I(V)_{3},\qquad \dim_k W = 28 .
\]

---

### The plane \(\Pi\)

A plane \(\Pi\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) has ideal generated by three independent linear forms
\(L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}\).  
The restriction map  

\[
\operatorname{res}_{\Pi}\colon S_{3}\longrightarrow H^{0}\!\left(\Pi,\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\right)
\]

is surjective; the target has dimension  

\[
\dim H^{0}\!\left(\Pi,\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\right)=\binom{3+2}{2}=10 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\dim_k I(\Pi)_{3}= \dim S_{3}-10 =56-10=46 .
\]

---

### Cubics vanishing on both \(V\) and \(\Pi\)

Consider the restriction of the cubics in \(W\) to the plane \(\Pi\):

\[
\operatorname{res}_{\Pi}\big|_{W}\colon W=I(V)_{3}\longrightarrow H^{0}\!\left(\Pi,\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\right).
\]

Its kernel is precisely  

\[
W_{\Pi}= I(V)_{3}\cap I(\Pi)_{3},
\]

the space of cubics vanishing on \(V\) **and** on \(\Pi\).

Because \(\dim W =28\) and the target space has dimension \(10\), the map can have rank at most \(10\).  
Since \(\Pi\) is not contained in \(V\), there exist cubics in \(I(V)_{3}\) that do **not** vanish on \(\Pi\); hence the restriction map is **surjective**. Therefore its rank equals \(10\).

Thus  

\[
\dim_k W_{\Pi}= \dim_k W-\operatorname{rank}\big(\operatorname{res}_{\Pi}|_{W}\big)
               = 28-10 = 18 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{18}
\]

The space of all cubic forms on \(\mathbf P^{5}\) has dimension  

\[
h^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{5}}(3)\bigr)=\binom{3+5}{3}=56 .
\]

For the Veronese surface \(V\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) the homogeneous coordinate ring is
\(k[x_{0},\dots ,x_{5}]/I_{V}\cong k[u,v,w]\) with the grading doubled, so  

\[
\dim_k R_{3}= \dim_k \text{ degree }6\text{ polynomials in }u,v,w
          =\binom{6+2}{2}=28 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\dim_k W = h^{0}\bigl(I_{V}(3)\bigr)=56-28 = 28 .
\]

Now fix a plane \(\Pi\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) (a \(\mathbf P^{2}\)).  
Let \(C=V\cap\Pi\).  Since \(V\) is a surface of degree \(4\) in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) and \(\Pi\) is a linear \(\mathbf P^{2}\), their proper intersection is a zero‑dimensional scheme of length \(4\).

Restricting a cubic that vanishes on \(V\) to \(\Pi\) gives a cubic on \(\Pi\) that must vanish on \(C\).  
Thus we have the exact sequence  

\[
0\longrightarrow I_{V\cup\Pi}(3)\longrightarrow I_{V}(3)
   \xrightarrow{\ \text{restriction}\ } I_{C,\Pi}(3)\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\dim_k W_{\Pi}= \dim_k I_{V\cup\Pi}(3)
               = \dim_k I_{V}(3)-\dim_k I_{C,\Pi}(3).
\]

On the plane \(\Pi\simeq\mathbf P^{2}\),

\[
h^{0}\bigl(\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3)\bigr)=\binom{3+2}{3}=10 .
\]

A cubic on \(\Pi\) vanishing on the four distinct points of \(C\) imposes four independent linear conditions, so  

\[
\dim_k I_{C,\Pi}(3)=10-4=6 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\dim_k W_{\Pi}=28-6=22 .
\]

\[
\boxed{22}
\]

The space of cubics on \(\mathbf P^{5}\) has  

\[
\dim_k S_3=\binom{5+3}{3}= \binom{8}{3}=56 .
\]

---

### 1.  Cubics vanishing on the Veronese surface \(V\)

For the Veronese surface \(V=\nu_2(\mathbf P^{2})\) we have  

\[
H^0(V,\mathcal O_V(d)) \cong H^0(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2d)),
\qquad 
\dim_k H^0(V,\mathcal O_V(d))=\binom{2d+2}{2}.
\]

Thus for \(d=3\)

\[
h_V(3)=\binom{8}{2}=28 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\dim_k I(V)_3 = \dim_k S_3- h_V(3)=56-28 = 28 .
\]

So  

\[
\dim_k W = 28 .
\]

---

### 2.  Cubics vanishing on a plane \(\Pi\simeq\mathbf P^{2}\)

A plane \(\Pi\) is cut out by three independent linear forms
\(L_1,L_2,L_3\).  
A cubic vanishes on \(\Pi\) iff it is a linear combination of the
\(L_i\) with quadratic coefficients:

\[
I(\Pi)_3 = L_1\cdot S_2+L_2\cdot S_2+L_3\cdot S_2 .
\]

\(\dim_k S_2 = \binom{5+2}{2}=21\).  
The three linear forms satisfy the Koszul linear syzygies, giving
\(3\cdot 6 =18\) independent relations among the \(L_i\cdot\)quadrics.
Consequently  

\[
\dim_k I(\Pi)_3 = 3\cdot 21-18 = 45 .
\]

---

### 3.  Cubics vanishing on both \(V\) and \(\Pi\)

Consider the restriction map  

\[
\rho : I(V)_3 \longrightarrow H^0(\Pi,\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3))
        \cong k^{10}.
\]

Its kernel is exactly \(W_{\Pi}=I(V)_3\cap I(\Pi)_3\).
A general plane meets the Veronese surface in \(4\) distinct points,
so any cubic in \(I(V)_3\) already vanishes at those four points.
Therefore the image of \(\rho\) consists of the plane cubics that
vanish at those four points.  

The linear system of plane cubics has dimension \(10\); imposing
vanishing at \(4\) independent points leaves a subspace of dimension  

\[
10-4 = 6 .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{rank}\rho =6\) and  

\[
\dim_k W_{\Pi}= \dim_k I(V)_3 - \operatorname{rank}\rho
               = 28 - 6 = 22 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{22}
\]

The space of all cubic forms on \(\mathbf P^{5}\) has dimension  

\[
\dim_k S_3 = \binom{3+5}{5}= \binom{8}{5}=56 .
\]

---

### 1.  Cubics vanishing on the Veronese surface \(V\)

For the Veronese surface \(V=\nu(\mathbf P^{2})\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) we have  

\[
H^{0}(V,\mathcal O_V(d)) \cong H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2d))
\]

so  

\[
h_V(d)=\dim H^{0}(V,\mathcal O_V(d))=\binom{2d+2}{2}.
\]

For \(d=3\),

\[
h_V(3)=\binom{8}{2}=28 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\dim_k I(V)_3 = \dim S_3- h_V(3)=56-28 = 28 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\dim_k W = 28 .
\]

---

### 2.  Cubics vanishing on a plane \(\Pi\)

A plane \(\Pi\cong\mathbf P^{2}\) has  

\[
h_{\Pi}(3)=\dim H^{0}(\Pi,\mathcal O_{\Pi}(3))=\binom{3+2}{2}=10 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\dim_k I(\Pi)_3 = 56-10 = 46 .
\]

---

### 3.  Intersection \(V\cap\Pi\)

A plane meets the Veronese surface in a zero‑dimensional scheme of length \(4\) (the degree of \(V\)).  
For a set of four distinct points the cubics on \(\Pi\) that vanish on them form a subspace of codimension \(4\); therefore  

\[
\dim \{ \text{cubics on }\Pi \text{ vanishing on } V\cap\Pi\}=10-4=6 .
\]

---

### 4.  Cubics vanishing on both \(V\) and \(\Pi\)

Restrict the space \(W=I(V)_3\) to \(\Pi\):

\[
0\longrightarrow W_{\Pi}\longrightarrow I(V)_3 \xrightarrow{\;\text{res}\;}
\{\text{cubics on }\Pi\text{ vanishing on }V\cap\Pi\}\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\dim_k W_{\Pi}= \dim I(V)_3 - \dim(\text{image of restriction})
               = 28 - 6 = 22 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{22}
\]

The Veronese surface  

\[
V=\nu(\mathbb P^{2})\subset\mathbb P^{5}
\]

has homogeneous ideal \(I(V)\subset k[x_{0},\dots ,x_{5}]\) generated by the three \(2\times 2\) minors of the symmetric \(3\times 3\) matrix of coordinates; hence \(I(V)\) is generated by quadrics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Cubics vanishing on \(V\)

Let \(S=k[x_{0},\dots ,x_{5}]\).  
The coordinate ring of \(V\) is  

\[
R_V=S/I(V)\cong k[y_{0},y_{1},y_{2}]^{(2)},
\]

the subring of the polynomial ring in three variables generated by the
quadratic monomials.  
Therefore the Hilbert function of \(R_V\) is  

\[
\dim_k (R_V)_d = \dim_k \bigl(k[y_{0},y_{1},y_{2}]_{2d}\bigr)
               = \binom{2d+2}{2}.
\]

For \(d=3\),

\[
\dim_k (R_V)_3 = \binom{8}{2}=28 .
\]

Since \(\dim_k S_3 = \binom{8}{3}=56\),

\[
\boxed{\dim_k I(V)_3 = 56-28 = 28}.
\]

Thus  

\[
W = I(V)_3,\qquad \dim W = 28 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Cubics vanishing on a plane \(\Pi\)

A plane \(\Pi\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) has codimension \(3\); its ideal is
generated by three independent linear forms \(L_1,L_2,L_3\).
The coordinate ring of \(\Pi\) is a polynomial ring in three variables,
so  

\[
\dim_k (S/I(\Pi))_3 = \binom{3+3-1}{3}= \binom{5}{3}=10 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\dim_k I(\Pi)_3 = 56-10 = 46 } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Intersection \(V\cap\Pi\)

For a **general** plane \(\Pi\) the intersection with the Veronese
surface is a zero‑dimensional scheme of length equal to the degree of
\(V\).  
The Veronese surface has degree \(2^{2}=4\); consequently  

\[
\ell\bigl(V\cap\Pi\bigr)=4 .
\]

Thus the coordinate ring of \(V\cap\Pi\) has Hilbert function  

\[
\dim_k (S/(I(V)+I(\Pi)))_d = \min\{4,\binom{5+d}{d}\},
\]

and in particular for \(d=3\),

\[
\dim_k (S/(I(V)+I(\Pi)))_3 = 4 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{\dim_k (I(V)+I(\Pi))_3 = 56-4 = 52 } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Cubics vanishing on both \(V\) and \(\Pi\)

The subspace we need is  

\[
W_{\Pi}= I(V)_3\cap I(\Pi)_3 .
\]

Using the dimension formula for the intersection of two subspaces,

\[
\dim W_{\Pi}= \dim I(V)_3+\dim I(\Pi)_3-\dim (I(V)+I(\Pi))_3 .
\]

Insert the numbers obtained above:

\[
\dim W_{\Pi}= 28+46-52 = 22 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{22}
\]

problems.skill: Veronese embedding of conics and translation of tangency to hyperplane sections
problems.problem:
Let a general plane conic be written as  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0 ,
\]

and identify its coefficient vector \([a_{0}:\dots :a_{5}]\) with a point of the projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  
Consider the smooth conic  

\[
C:\; xy+yz+zx=0\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}.
\]

Via the degree‑2 Veronese embedding \(\nu:\mathbb{P}^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{5}\), the condition that a conic \(Q\) be tangent to \(C\) becomes a linear condition on the coefficients \(a_{i}\); that is, the set of such \(Q\) is a hyperplane \(H_{C}\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}\).  

Write the linear equation of \(H_{C}\) in the form  

\[
c_{0}a_{0}+c_{1}a_{1}+c_{2}a_{2}+c_{3}a_{3}+c_{4}a_{4}+c_{5}a_{5}=0,
\]

where the integers \(c_{i}\) have no common divisor greater than \(1\).  
Compute the sum  

\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{5}|c_{i}|
\]

and give your answer as the integer \(S\).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
For a conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0 ,
\]

the Veronese map  

\[
\nu:\mathbb P^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb P^{5},\qquad 
[x:y:z]\mapsto [x^{2}:xy:xz:y^{2}:yz:z^{2}]
\]

identifies \(Q\) with the hyperplane  

\[
a_{0}X_{0}+a_{1}X_{1}+a_{2}X_{2}+a_{3}X_{3}+a_{4}X_{4}+a_{5}X_{5}=0
\]

in \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

Let  

\[
C:\; xy+yz+zx=0 .
\]

A line tangent to \(C\) at a point \(p=(x_0:y_0:z_0)\) (with \(x_0y_0+y_0z_0+z_0x_0=0\)) is  

\[
L_{p}= (y_0+z_0)X+(x_0+z_0)Y+(x_0+y_0)Z .
\]

The degenerate conic \(L_{p}^{2}\) is certainly tangent to \(C\) at \(p\).  
Writing \(L_{p}^{2}\) in the basis \(\{X_{0},\dots ,X_{5}\}\) gives the
coefficients  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{0}&=(y_0+z_0)^{2}, &
a_{1}&=2(y_0+z_0)(x_0+z_0), &
a_{2}&=2(y_0+z_0)(x_0+y_0),\\
a_{3}&=(x_0+z_0)^{2}, &
a_{4}&=2(x_0+z_0)(x_0+y_0), &
a_{5}&=(x_0+y_0)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence any linear relation \(\sum c_i a_i=0\) that holds for **all**
points \((x_0,y_0,z_0)\) on \(C\) must satisfy  

\[
c_{0}(y+z)^{2}+2c_{1}(y+z)(x+z)+2c_{2}(y+z)(x+y)
 +c_{3}(x+z)^{2}+2c_{4}(x+z)(x+y)+c_{5}(x+y)^{2}= \lambda (xy+yz+zx)
\]

for some constant \(\lambda\).  
Expanding and comparing coefficients of the monomials
\(x^{2},y^{2},z^{2},xy,xz,yz\) yields the linear system

\[
\begin{cases}
c_{3}+2c_{4}+c_{5}=0,\\
c_{0}+2c_{2}+c_{5}=0,\\
c_{0}+2c_{1}+c_{3}=0,\\
c_{5}=c_{3}=c_{0},\\
c_{4}=-c_{0},\;c_{2}=-c_{0},\;c_{1}=-c_{0}.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus, up to a common factor,

\[
(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5}) = (1,-1,-1,1,-1,1).
\]

These integers have no common divisor larger than \(1\), so they give the
required linear equation of the hyperplane \(H_{C}\).

Finally

\[
S = \sum_{i=0}^{5}|c_{i}| = 1+1+1+1+1+1 = 6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The conic  

\[
C:\;xy+yz+zx=0
\]

has gradient  

\[
\nabla f=(y+z,\;x+z,\;x+y).
\]

A conic  

\[
Q:\;a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0
\]

is tangent to \(C\) at a point \((x,y,z)\) iff  

\[
\begin{cases}
xy+yz+zx=0,\\[2pt]
a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}=0,\\[2pt]
\exists\lambda\;:\;
\begin{aligned}
2a_{0}x+a_{1}y+a_{2}z &=\lambda (y+z),\\
a_{1}x+2a_{3}y+a_{4}z &=\lambda (x+z),\\
a_{2}x+a_{4}y+2a_{5}z &=\lambda (x+y).
\end{aligned}
\end{cases}
\]

Eliminating the variables \((x,y,z,\lambda)\) (the computation is routine) yields the **single linear relation**

\[
2a_{0}+a_{1}-a_{4}-2a_{5}=0 .
\]

Thus the hyperplane \(H_{C}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) is given by  

\[
c_{0}a_{0}+c_{1}a_{1}+c_{2}a_{2}+c_{3}a_{3}+c_{4}a_{4}+c_{5}a_{5}=0,
\qquad
(c_{0},\dots ,c_{5})=(2,1,0,0,-1,-2).
\]

These integers have greatest common divisor \(1\).

The required sum of absolute values is  

\[
S=|2|+|1|+|0|+|0|+|-1|+|-2|=2+1+0+0+1+2=6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The hyperplane of conics tangent to  

\[
C:\;xy+yz+zx=0
\]

is given by a single linear equation  

\[
c_{0}a_{0}+c_{1}a_{1}+c_{2}a_{2}+c_{3}a_{3}+c_{4}a_{4}+c_{5}a_{5}=0 .
\]

Choosing several conics that are clearly tangent to \(C\) (the squares of the tangent lines at
four distinct points of \(C\)) and solving for the coefficients \(c_i\) gives, up to a common factor,

\[
(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(1,0,1,-1,2,-3).
\]

These integers have no common divisor larger than \(1\).  
Hence  

\[
S=|1|+|0|+|1|+|-1|+|2|+|-3|=1+0+1+1+2+3=8 .
\]

\[
\boxed{8}
\]

The hyperplane of conics tangent to  

\[
C:\;xy+yz+zx=0
\]

is given (up to scaling) by  

\[
2a_{0}+a_{1}-a_{4}-2a_{5}=0 .
\]

Thus the integer coefficients with no common divisor are  

\[
(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(2,1,0,0,-1,-2),
\]

and  

\[
S=|2|+|1|+|0|+|0|+|{-1}|+|{-2}|=6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The conic  

\[
C:\;xy+yz+zx=0\subset\mathbf P^{2}
\]

has the symmetric matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
0&\tfrac12&\tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12&0&\tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12&\tfrac12&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
C(x,y,z)=\begin{bmatrix}x&y&z\end{bmatrix} M
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}.
\]

A general conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}
\]

corresponds to the symmetric matrix  

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0}&\tfrac{a_{1}}2&\tfrac{a_{2}}2\\[2pt]
\tfrac{a_{1}}2&a_{3}&\tfrac{a_{4}}2\\[2pt]
\tfrac{a_{2}}2&\tfrac{a_{4}}2&a_{5}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Two conics are tangent somewhere iff the trace of the product of their
matrices is zero (this is the linear condition obtained after applying the
Veronese embedding).  Hence the conics \(Q\) that are tangent to the fixed
conic \(C\) satisfy  

\[
\operatorname{tr}(MA)=0 .
\]

Computing the trace,

\[
\operatorname{tr}(MA)=\frac12\bigl(a_{0}+a_{3}+a_{5}\bigr).
\]

Thus the required hyperplane \(H_{C}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) is given by  

\[
a_{0}+a_{3}+a_{5}=0 .
\]

The coefficients \((c_{0},\dots ,c_{5})\) are therefore  

\[
(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(1,0,0,1,0,1),
\]

which have greatest common divisor \(1\).  Hence  

\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{5}|c_{i}|=|1|+|0|+|0|+|1|+|0|+|1|=3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The conic  

\[
C:\; xy+yz+zx=0
\]

has the symmetric matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
0 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12 & 0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For a general conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}
\]

let  

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0} & \tfrac{a_{1}}2 & \tfrac{a_{2}}2\\[2pt]
\tfrac{a_{1}}2 & a_{3} & \tfrac{a_{4}}2\\[2pt]
\tfrac{a_{2}}2 & \tfrac{a_{4}}2 & a_{5}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) iff there exists a point \(p\neq 0\) with  

\[
p^{T}Mp=0,\qquad Ap=\lambda Mp
\]

for some scalar \(\lambda\).  
Eliminating \(p,\lambda\) gives the linear condition  

\[
\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\operatorname{Adj}(M)\,A\bigr)=0 .
\]

Since \(\det M =\frac14\) and  

\[
M^{-1}= -2I+J\qquad (J\text{ the all‑ones matrix}),
\]

\[
\operatorname{Adj}(M)=\det(M)\,M^{-1}= -\frac12 I+\frac14 J
        =\begin{pmatrix}
          -\tfrac14 & \tfrac14 & \tfrac14\\[2pt]
          \tfrac14 & -\tfrac14 & \tfrac14\\[2pt]
          \tfrac14 & \tfrac14 & -\tfrac14
        \end{pmatrix}.
\]

Computing \(\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Adj}(M)A)\) yields  

\[
-\frac14\,(a_{0}+a_{3}+a_{5})+\frac14\,(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{4})=0,
\]

or, after clearing the denominator,

\[
a_{0}+a_{3}+a_{5}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{4}.
\]

Thus the hyperplane \(H_{C}\subset\mathbb P^{5}\) is given by  

\[
c_{0}a_{0}+c_{1}a_{1}+c_{2}a_{2}+c_{3}a_{3}+c_{4}a_{4}+c_{5}a_{5}=0,
\]

with  

\[
(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(1,-1,-1,1,-1,1).
\]

These integers are coprime, and  

\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{5}|c_{i}| = 1+1+1+1+1+1 = 6.
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The conic  

\[
C:\;xy+yz+zx=0\subset\mathbf P^{2}
\]

has the symmetric matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
0&\tfrac12&\tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12&0&\tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12&\tfrac12&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det M=\frac14\neq0 .
\]

For a conic  

\[
Q(x,y,z)=a_{0}x^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{2}xz+a_{3}y^{2}+a_{4}yz+a_{5}z^{2}
\]

let  

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0}&\tfrac{a_{1}}2&\tfrac{a_{2}}2\\[2pt]
\tfrac{a_{1}}2&a_{3}&\tfrac{a_{4}}2\\[2pt]
\tfrac{a_{2}}2&\tfrac{a_{4}}2&a_{5}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

A conic \(Q\) is tangent to \(C\) iff the polar line of \(Q\) with respect to \(C\) coincides with a tangent line of \(C\).  
Equivalently (see the theory of polar conics) this is the linear condition  

\[
\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}A)=0 .
\]

Since  

\[
M^{-1}= -2I+J
      =\begin{pmatrix}
-2&1&1\\[2pt]
1&-2&1\\[2pt]
1&1&-2
\end{pmatrix},
\]

we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}A)=
-2(a_{0}+a_{3}+a_{5})+(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{4})=0 .
\]

Thus the hyperplane \(H_{C}\subset\mathbf P^{5}\) is given by  

\[
-2a_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}-2a_{3}+a_{4}-2a_{5}=0 .
\]

Multiplying by \(-1\) we may write the equation with integer coefficients having no common divisor larger than \(1\):

\[
2a_{0}-a_{1}-a_{2}+2a_{3}-a_{4}+2a_{5}=0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5})=(2,-1,-1,2,-1,2),
\]

and  

\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{5}|c_{i}|=2+1+1+2+1+2=9 .
\]

\[
\boxed{9}
\]

problems.skill: Lang–Weil point‑count estimate for varieties over finite fields
problems.problem:
Let  

\[
X\subset \mathbf{P}^{3}_{\mathbb{Q}}
\]

be the smooth quadric surface defined by the homogeneous equation  

\[
X_{0}X_{1}=X_{2}X_{3}.
\]

It is a geometrically irreducible projective surface of dimension \(2\).  
Let \(\pi : Y \to X\) be a finite étale morphism of degree \(8\) defined over \(\mathbb{Q}\).  

For each prime number \(p\) at which both \(X\) and \(Y\) have good reduction, denote  

\[
N_X(p)=\# X(\mathbb{F}_p),\qquad N_Y(p)=\# Y(\mathbb{F}_p).
\]

Define  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)},
\]

where the limit runs over all such primes \(p\).  
Using the Lang–Weil point‑count estimate, compute \(\displaystyle\left\lfloor 100\,L\right\rfloor\).  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
**1.  The surface \(X\).**  

The quadric  

\[
X_{0}X_{1}=X_{2}X_{3}\subset \mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Q}
\]

has a rational point, e.g. \((1\!:\!0\!:\!0\!:\!0)\).  
Hence over any field it is a **split smooth quadric surface**, which is
isomorphic to  

\[
\mathbf P^{1}\times\mathbf P^{1}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) of good reduction we obtain  

\[
X_{\mathbb F_{p}}\simeq\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{p}}\times\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{p}},
\qquad 
N_{X}(p)=\#X(\mathbb F_{p})=(p+1)^2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**2.  Étale covers of \(X\).**  

The étale fundamental group of a smooth rational surface over an
algebraically closed field is trivial.  
Consequently a finite étale morphism over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\)

\[
\pi : Y \longrightarrow X
\]

cannot be connected unless it is an isomorphism.  
Since the degree of \(\pi\) is \(8\), the only possibility is that
\(Y_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) is a disjoint union of \(8\) copies of \(X\):

\[
Y_{\overline{\mathbb Q}} \;=\; X\;\sqcup\; X\;\sqcup\;\cdots\;\sqcup\; X
\quad (8\text{ times}).
\]

Thus the geometric fibre of \(\pi\) over any point of \(X\) consists of
\(8\) distinct points, all defined over the base field.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**3.  Point counts modulo a prime.**  

Let \(p\) be a prime of good reduction.  
The reduction \(\pi_{p}:Y_{p}\to X_{p}\) is still a finite étale cover of
degree \(8\).  
Because each geometric component is already defined over \(\mathbb Q\),
the whole fibre over a rational point \(x\in X(\mathbb F_{p})\) consists
of the \(8\) rational points coming from the \(8\) copies of \(X\).

Hence  

\[
\#\pi_{p}^{-1}(x)=8\qquad\text{for every }x\in X(\mathbb F_{p}),
\]

and consequently  

\[
N_{Y}(p)=\sum_{x\in X(\mathbb F_{p})}\#\pi_{p}^{-1}(x)=8\,N_{X}(p).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**4.  The limit \(L\).**  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_{Y}(p)}{N_{X}(p)}
   =\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{8\,N_{X}(p)}{N_{X}(p)}=8.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**5.  Required integer.**  

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L\right\rfloor =\left\lfloor 100\times 8\right\rfloor
                                   =\left\lfloor 800\right\rfloor =800.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\[
\boxed{800}
\]

For the smooth quadric surface  

\[
X\subset \mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Q},\qquad X_0X_1=X_2X_3,
\]

let  

\[
\pi:Y\longrightarrow X
\]

be a finite étale morphism of degree \(d=8\) defined over \(\mathbb Q\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Point counts on a smooth projective surface

For a smooth projective surface \(V\) of dimension \(2\) over \(\mathbf F_{p}\) the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#V(\mathbf F_{p}) = p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right) .
\]

Hence  

\[
N_X(p)=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right). \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Point counts on an étale cover

Because \(\pi\) is finite étale of degree \(d\),

* \(Y\) is also smooth, projective and of dimension \(2\);
* the push‑forward sheaf \(\pi_{*}\mathbf Q_\ell\) is a lisse sheaf of rank \(d\) on \(X\).

Using the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula,

\[
\#Y(\mathbf F_{p}) = \sum_{i=0}^{4} (-1)^i \operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(
\operatorname{Frob}_p \mid H_c^{\,i}(X_{\overline{\mathbf F}_p},
\pi_{*}\mathbf Q_\ell)\bigr).
\]

The contribution of the top cohomology \(i=4\) equals  

\[
\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\operatorname{Frob}_p \mid H_c^{\,4}(X_{\overline{\mathbf F}_p},
\pi_{*}\mathbf Q_\ell)\bigr)= d\;p^{2},
\]

while all lower‑degree terms are bounded by \(O(p^{3/2})\). Consequently  

\[
N_Y(p)=\#Y(\mathbf F_{p}) = d\,p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right). \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The limit of the ratio

From (1) and (2),

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=
\frac{d\,p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}
= d + O\!\left(p^{-1/2}\right).
\]

Hence, as \(p\to\infty\) (over the primes of good reduction),

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = d = 8 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required integer

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 100 \times 8 \right\rfloor = \boxed{800}.
\]

For a smooth geometrically irreducible surface \(V\) of dimension \(2\) over a finite field \(\mathbf{F}_p\), the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#V(\mathbf{F}_p)=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right).
\]

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth projective surfaces of dimension \(2\).  
Because \(\pi:Y\to X\) is finite étale of degree \(8\) and defined over \(\mathbf{Q}\), the reduction \(Y_{\mathbf{F}_p}\to X_{\mathbf{F}_p}\) is also finite étale of degree \(8\) for every prime of good reduction.  

A finite étale cover of a geometrically irreducible variety is again geometrically irreducible (its connected components are permuted transitively by the étale fundamental group). Hence \(Y\) is geometrically irreducible, so the Lang–Weil estimate applies to \(Y\) as well:

\[
N_X(p)=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right),\qquad 
N_Y(p)=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right).
\]

Dividing the two expansions we obtain  

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=1+O\!\left(p^{-1/2}\right)\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=1 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L\right\rfloor =\left\lfloor 100\cdot 1\right\rfloor =100 .
\]

\[
\boxed{100}
\]

The smooth quadric surface  

\[
X:\;X_{0}X_{1}=X_{2}X_{3}\subset\mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Q}
\]

is split: over any field it is isomorphic to \(\mathbf P^{1}\times\mathbf P^{1}\).  
Hence for a prime \(p\) of good reduction  

\[
N_X(p)=\#X(\mathbf F_{p})=(p+1)^{2}=p^{2}+2p+1 .
\]

Let \(\pi:Y\to X\) be a finite étale morphism of degree \(8\).  
Since \(X\) is simply‑connected (its étale fundamental group is trivial), the
geometric fibre of \(\pi\) consists of \(8\) disjoint copies of \(X\).  
Thus over \(\overline{\mathbf F}_p\)

\[
Y_{\overline{\mathbf F}_p}\cong \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{8} X_{\overline{\mathbf F}_p}.
\]

For each rational point \(x\in X(\mathbf F_{p})\) the fibre \(\pi^{-1}(x)\) is a
set of \(8\) geometric points on which Frobenius acts.  The number of
\(\mathbf F_{p}\)-points above \(x\) is the number of fixed points of this
action.  By the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula (or directly by the
Lang–Weil estimate) one obtains  

\[
\#Y(\mathbf F_{p}) = 8\,p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}),\qquad 
\#X(\mathbf F_{p}) = p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=
\frac{8p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}=8+O(p^{-1/2})\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}8.
\]

Hence  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = 8.
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 100\,L \bigr\rfloor = \lfloor 100\times 8 \rfloor = \boxed{800}.
\]

For a smooth projective variety \(V\) of dimension \(n\) defined over \(\mathbf{Q}\) and a prime \(p\) of good reduction, the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#V(\mathbf{F}_p)=p^{\,n}+O\bigl(p^{\,n-\frac12}\bigr).
\]

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth projective surfaces, so \(n=2\).  
Hence for all sufficiently large good primes \(p\),

\[
N_X(p)=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right), \qquad 
N_Y(p)=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right).
\]

(The degree of the finite étale morphism does **not** affect the leading term \(p^{2}\); it only influences the lower‑order terms.)

Therefore

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}
 =\frac{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}
 =1+O\!\left(p^{-1/2}\right)\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = 1.
\]

Finally  

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 100 \times 1 \right\rfloor = 100.
\]

\[
\boxed{100}
\]

For the smooth split quadric surface  

\[
X:\;X_0X_1=X_2X_3\subset\mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Q}
\]

we have an isomorphism over any field  

\[
X \;\cong\; \mathbf P^{1}\times\mathbf P^{1}.
\]

Hence for a prime \(p\) of good reduction  

\[
N_X(p)=\#X(\mathbf F_p)=\#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbf F_p)^2=(p+1)^2
        =p^{2}+2p+1 .
\]

---

### Geometry of the cover \(Y\)

The morphism \(\pi:Y\to X\) is finite étale of degree \(8\) and is defined over \(\mathbb Q\).
Because \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) is simply‑connected (its étale fundamental group is trivial), any finite étale cover of \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) must be a disjoint union of copies of \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\).  
Therefore  

\[
Y_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\;\cong\; \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{8} X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}} .
\]

Consequently, for each prime \(p\) of good reduction the reduction \(Y_{\mathbf F_p}\) is a disjoint union of eight copies of the reduction of \(X\).  
Applying the Lang–Weil estimate to each component gives  

\[
N_Y(p)=\#Y(\mathbf F_p)=8\,p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}) .
\]

---

### The limit

Using the two estimates,

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}
   =\frac{8p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+2p+1}
   =8+\;O(p^{-1/2})\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}8 .
\]

Hence  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=8 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 100\,L \bigr\rfloor = \bigl\lfloor 100 \times 8 \bigr\rfloor = 800 .
\]

\[
\boxed{800}
\]

For a smooth projective variety \(V\) of dimension \(d\) defined over \(\mathbf{F}_p\) the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#V(\mathbf{F}_p)=p^{d}+O\!\left(p^{d-\frac12}\right) .
\]

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth projective surfaces (\(d=2\)) and are geometrically irreducible, so for every prime of good reduction we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_X(p)&=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right),\\[2mm]
N_Y(p)&=p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

(The error term comes from the eigenvalues of Frobenius acting on the middle
cohomology \(H^{2}\); they have absolute value \(p\).)

Hence  

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}
      =\frac{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}
      =1+O\!\left(p^{-1/2}\right)\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = 1 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor 100\cdot 1\right\rfloor = 100 .
\]

\[
\boxed{100}
\]

The surface  

\[
X : X_{0}X_{1}=X_{2}X_{3}\subset \mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Q}
\]

is a smooth quadric, hence over an algebraic closure it is isomorphic to  
\(\mathbf P^{1}\times\mathbf P^{1}\).  
Thus \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) is **geometrically simply‑connected**, so its
geometric étale fundamental group is trivial:

\[
\pi^{\text{ét}}_{1}(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})=1 .
\]

Consequently any finite étale cover of \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) must be a
disjoint union of copies of \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\).  
A degree‑\(8\) étale morphism \(\pi:Y\to X\) defined over \(\mathbb Q\) therefore
has, after base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\),

\[
Y_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\; \cong\; \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{8} X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}} .
\]

Hence \(Y\) is geometrically the union of eight irreducible components,
each isomorphic to \(X\).

---

### Point counts

For a smooth geometrically irreducible surface \(V\) of dimension \(2\) over
\(\mathbb F_{p}\), the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#V(\mathbb F_{p}) = p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}) .
\]

Applying this to \(X\) and to each of the eight components of \(Y\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_X(p) &= p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}),\\
N_Y(p) &= 8\,p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = 
\frac{8\,p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}
\longrightarrow 8\qquad (p\to\infty),
\]

so  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = 8.
\]

---

### Required integer

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 100\times 8 \right\rfloor
= \left\lfloor 800 \right\rfloor = 800.
\]

\[
\boxed{800}
\]

The surface  

\[
X:\;X_{0}X_{1}=X_{2}X_{3}\subset\mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Q}
\]

is a smooth quadric, hence a **geometrically irreducible** projective surface of
dimension \(2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What does a finite étale cover of a quadric look like over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\)?

For a smooth, rationally‑connected variety over an algebraically closed field the
étale fundamental group is trivial.  
A smooth quadric surface over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) (or over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\))
is rational, therefore  

\[
\pi^{\text{ét}}_{1}(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})=0 .
\]

Consequently every finite étale cover of \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) is a **disjoint
union of copies of \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\)**.  
If the cover has degree \(d\), the geometric fibre consists of \(d\) points,
hence the cover splits into exactly \(d\) connected components, each isomorphic
to \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\).

For our morphism \(\pi:Y\to X\) we have \(\deg\pi = 8\); therefore  

\[
Y_{\overline{\mathbb Q}} \;=\; \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{8} X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}} .
\]

Thus **\(Y\) has 8 geometrically irreducible components**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Point counts for a variety with several geometric components

Let a smooth projective variety \(Z\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) have
\(r\) geometrically irreducible components, each of dimension \(n\).
Lang–Weil gives  

\[
\# Z(\mathbb F_p)= r\,p^{\,n}+O(p^{\,n-\frac12}) .
\]

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are surfaces (\(n=2\)).  
Hence, for all sufficiently large primes of good reduction,

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_X(p) &= p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}),\\[2mm]
N_Y(p) &= 8\,p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The limit \(L\)

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}
      =\frac{8p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}
      \longrightarrow 8\qquad(p\to\infty).
\]

Therefore  

\[
L = \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)} = 8 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required integer

\[
\left\lfloor 100\,L\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 100 \times 8 \right\rfloor
                                 = \left\lfloor 800 \right\rfloor
                                 = 800 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{800}
\]

For any such surface over \(\mathbf{F}_p\), the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#X(\mathbf{F}_p)=p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}) .
\]

The morphism \(\pi:Y\to X\) is finite étale of degree \(8\) and defined over \(\mathbf{Q}\).  
For all sufficiently large primes \(p\) (those of good reduction) the reduction
\(\pi_p : Y_{\mathbf{F}_p}\to X_{\mathbf{F}_p}\) is also finite étale of degree \(8\).
Consequently \(Y_{\mathbf{F}_p}\) is again a smooth geometrically irreducible surface of
dimension \(2\). Hence

\[
\#Y(\mathbf{F}_p)=p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}).
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=
\frac{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}=1+O(p^{-1/2})\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1.
\]

Therefore  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_Y(p)}{N_X(p)}=1.
\]

Finally  

\[
\left\lfloor 100L\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 100\cdot 1\right\rfloor = 100.
\]

\boxed{100}

problems.skill: Lang–Weil point‑count estimate for varieties over finite fields
problems.problem:
Let  

\[
C\subset\mathbf{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Q}}
\]

be a smooth plane curve defined by a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(7\).  
For each prime \(p\) at which the reduction \(C_{p}\) remains smooth, denote  

\[
N(p)=\# C_{p}\bigl(\mathbb{F}_{p}\bigr).
\]

The Lang–Weil theorem gives an estimate of the form  

\[
\bigl|\,N(p)-p\,\bigr|\leqslant M\sqrt{p}
\]

for all sufficiently large primes \(p\), where \(M\) depends only on the
dimension and the degree of the variety.  

Determine the smallest possible integer \(M\) that works for this curve \(C\).

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The curve \(C\) is a smooth plane curve of degree \(d=7\).  
For a smooth plane curve the genus is  

\[
g=\frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}= \frac{6\cdot5}{2}=15 .
\]

For a smooth projective curve over \(\mathbf{F}_p\) the Hasse–Weil bound gives  

\[
\bigl|\#C(\mathbf{F}_p)-(p+1)\bigr|\le 2g\sqrt{p}=30\sqrt{p}.
\]

Hence  

\[
N(p)=\#C(\mathbf{F}_p)=p+1+\varepsilon ,\qquad |\varepsilon|\le 30\sqrt{p}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
|N(p)-p| = |1+\varepsilon| \le 1+30\sqrt{p}.
\]

We need an integer \(M\) such that for all sufficiently large primes \(p\),

\[
1+30\sqrt{p}\le M\sqrt{p}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
1\le (M-30)\sqrt{p}.
\]

If \(M=30\) the right‑hand side is \(0\), so the inequality can never hold.  
For \(M=31\) we have \(1\le \sqrt{p}\), which is true for every prime \(p\ge 2\); thus the inequality holds for all sufficiently large \(p\).

Consequently the smallest integer \(M\) that works is  

\[
\boxed{31}
\]

For a smooth plane curve of degree \(d\) the genus is  

\[
g=\frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}.
\]

The Hasse–Weil bound for a smooth projective curve over \(\mathbf{F}_{p}\) says  

\[
\bigl|\#C(\mathbf{F}_{p})-(p+1)\bigr|\le 2g\sqrt p .
\]

Hence  

\[
\bigl|\#C(\mathbf{F}_{p})-p\bigr|
=|1+\varepsilon|\le 2g\sqrt p+1 .
\]

For our curve \(d=7\),

\[
g=\frac{(7-1)(7-2)}{2}=15,\qquad 2g=30 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\bigl|\#C(\mathbf{F}_{p})-p\bigr|\le 30\sqrt p+1 .
\]

To obtain a bound of the required form \(|N(p)-p|\le M\sqrt p\) we need an integer \(M\) such that  

\[
30\sqrt p+1\le M\sqrt p\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }p,
\]

i.e. \(M\ge 30+1/\sqrt p\).  As \(p\) grows, \(1/\sqrt p\) becomes arbitrarily small, so the smallest integer satisfying the inequality for large \(p\) is  

\[
M = 31 .
\]

Thus the minimal integer \(M\) that works for any smooth plane curve of degree 7 is  

\[
\boxed{31}
\]

For a smooth plane curve of degree \(d\) the genus is  

\[
g=\frac{(d-1)(d-2)}2 .
\]

Here \(d=7\), so  

\[
g=\frac{6\cdot5}{2}=15 .
\]

For a smooth projective curve over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) the Hasse–Weil bound gives  

\[
\bigl|\,\#C(\mathbb{F}_p)-(p+1)\bigr|\le 2g\sqrt p =30\sqrt p .
\]

Hence  

\[
\bigl|\,N(p)-p\bigr|
   \le \bigl|N(p)-(p+1)\bigr|+1
   \le 30\sqrt p+1 .
\]

problems.skill: Lang–Weil point‑count estimate for varieties over finite fields
problems.problem:
Let \(k=\mathbb{Z}\) and consider the projective plane \(\mathbf{P}^{2}_{k}\) with homogeneous coordinates \([X:Y:Z]\).
For the six distinct square‑free integers  

\[
a_{1}=2,\; a_{2}=3,\; a_{3}=5,\; a_{4}=6,\; a_{5}=7,\; a_{6}=10,
\]

define the closed subscheme \(X\subset \mathbf{P}^{2}_{k}\) by the homogeneous equation  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}\bigr)=0 .
\]

For a prime number \(p\) let \(X_{p}\) be the reduction of \(X\) modulo \(p\) and denote by \(\#X_{p}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-rational points of \(X_{p}\).
Set  

\[
L \;=\; \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}{p},
\]

where the limit is taken over all sufficiently large primes \(p\) for which the reduction is well defined.
Using the Lang–Weil estimate, determine the value of \(L\).

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The curve  

\[
X:\ \prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}\bigr)=0\qquad (a_{i}=2,3,5,6,7,10)
\]

is a reduced divisor in \(\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z}\) consisting of the six quadratic
hypersurfaces  

\[
C_i:\; X^{2}-a_iY^{2}=0 \qquad (i=1,\dots ,6).
\]

Each \(C_i\) is a smooth conic; over the generic fibre (characteristic \(0\))
it is geometrically irreducible, so the generic fibre of \(X\) has exactly
six irreducible components.

For a prime \(p\) of good reduction the reduction \(X_p\) is the union of the
reductions \(C_{i,p}\).  By the Lang–Weil estimate, for every geometrically
irreducible component \(C_{i,p}\) of dimension \(1\),

\[
\#C_{i,p}(\mathbf F_p)=p+O(\sqrt p).
\]

Since there are six such components, the number of \(\mathbf F_p\)-points on
\(X_p\) satisfies  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p}) = 6p + O(\sqrt p).
\]

Dividing by \(p\) and letting \(p\to\infty\) we obtain  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{p}=6 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The curve  

\[
X\subset \mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z},\qquad 
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_iY^{2}\bigr)=0 ,\qquad 
a_i\in\{2,3,5,6,7,10\}
\]

is the union of the six singular conics  

\[
C_i:\;X^{2}-a_iY^{2}=0 .
\]

Over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) each \(C_i\) splits as the union of the two lines  

\[
L_{i}^{\pm}:\;X=\pm\sqrt{a_i}\,Y .
\]

Hence \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) consists of **12 distinct lines** meeting at the single point  

\[
O=[0:0:1].
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Points over \(\mathbf F_{p}\)

Let \(p\) be a prime that does not divide any \(a_i\).  
For a fixed \(i\) set  

\[
\chi_i(p)=\left(\frac{a_i}{p}\right)\in\{1,-1\}
\]

(the Legendre symbol).  

* If \(\chi_i(p)=1\) then \(a_i\) is a quadratic residue; the conic \(C_i\) splits over \(\mathbf F_{p}\) into the two lines \(L_i^{\pm}\).  
  Each line has \(p+1\) \(\mathbf F_{p}\)-points, they intersect only at \(O\); consequently  

  \[
  \#C_i(\mathbf F_{p}) = 2p+1 .
  \]

* If \(\chi_i(p)=-1\) the conic stays irreducible over \(\mathbf F_{p}\); the only \(\mathbf F_{p}\)-point is the common point \(O\). Hence  

  \[
  \#C_i(\mathbf F_{p}) = 1 .
  \]

Let  

\[
r(p)=\#\{\,i\mid \chi_i(p)=1\,\}
\]

be the number of residues among the six \(a_i\) modulo \(p\).  
Summing the contributions of the six conics and correcting for the multiple
count of the common point \(O\) we obtain  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p}) = \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{6}\#C_i(\mathbf F_{p})\Bigr)-5
                      = \bigl(r(p)(2p+1)+(6-r(p))\cdot1\bigr)-5
                      = 2p\,r(p)+1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{p}=2\,r(p)+\frac{1}{p}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Asymptotics via Lang–Weil

For a projective curve over a finite field, the Lang–Weil estimate says  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p}) = (\text{number of geometrically irreducible
components defined over }\mathbf F_{p})\;p+O(\sqrt p).
\]

The geometrically irreducible components of \(X\) are the 12 lines
\(L_i^{\pm}\).  
A line \(L_i^{\pm}\) is defined over \(\mathbf F_{p}\) exactly when
\(a_i\) is a quadratic residue, i.e. when \(\chi_i(p)=1\).  
Thus the number of components defined over \(\mathbf F_{p}\) equals \(2r(p)\),
and the Lang–Weil estimate yields precisely the formula obtained above:
\(\#X_{p}=2r(p)p+O(\sqrt p)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Limit

For each fixed \(a_i\) the Legendre symbol \(\chi_i(p)\) takes the value
\(1\) for a set of primes of natural density \(1/2\).  
Hence, as \(p\to\infty\),

\[
r(p)=\#\{i\mid\chi_i(p)=1\}\longrightarrow 3 \quad\text{in density}.
\]

Consequently the leading term \(2r(p)\) approaches \(2\cdot3=6\), and the
error term \(1/p\) tends to \(0\).  Therefore

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{p}=6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The scheme \(X\subset\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z}\) is defined by  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_iY^{2}\bigr)=0 ,\qquad 
a_i\in\{2,3,5,6,7,10\}.
\]

For each \(i\) the factor \(X^{2}-a_iY^{2}=0\) is a conic which over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\) splits into the two lines  

\[
X = \pm\sqrt{a_i}\,Y .
\]

Hence, over a finite field \(\mathbb F_p\),

* if \(a_i\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) (\(\bigl(\frac{a_i}{p}\bigr)=1\)), the conic splits into two \(\mathbb F_p\)-rational lines.  
  Each line has \(p+1\) \(\mathbb F_p\)-points; they intersect only in the point \([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\).  
  Thus this component contributes \(2(p+1)-1 = 2p+1\) points, i.e. \(2p\) new points besides the common origin.

* if \(a_i\) is a non‑residue (\(\bigl(\frac{a_i}{p}\bigr)=-1\)), the conic has no \(\mathbb F_p\)-points except the origin \([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\).

All six components share the single rational point \([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\); otherwise they are disjoint.  
Let  

\[
r(p)=\#\{\,i\mid \bigl(\tfrac{a_i}{p}\bigr)=1\,\}
\]

be the number of \(a_i\) that are quadratic residues modulo \(p\).  
Then

\[
\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)=1+2p\,r(p).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)}{p}= \frac{1}{p}+2\,r(p)\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{} 2\,\mathbb{E}[r(p)] .
\]

For a fixed non‑square integer \(a\), the Legendre symbol \(\bigl(\frac{a}{p}\bigr)\) has average \(0\) over the primes, so  

\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1+\bigl(\frac{a}{p}\bigr)}{2}\right]=\frac12 .
\]

Thus each \(a_i\) is a quadratic residue for asymptotically half of the primes, and the expected value of \(r(p)\) is  

\[
\mathbb{E}[r(p)]=6\cdot\frac12 = 3 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)}{p}=2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The equation  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}\bigr)=0 ,\qquad 
a_{i}=2,3,5,6,7,10,
\]

defines the union of the six conics  

\[
C_i:\; X^{2}=a_iY^{2}\qquad (i=1,\dots ,6)
\]

in \(\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z}\).  
Over an algebraic closure each \(C_i\) splits into two distinct lines  

\[
X\pm\sqrt{a_i}\,Y=0 ,
\]

so \(X_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}\) consists of **12** geometrically irreducible
components, all of dimension 1.

For a prime \(p\) let \(r(p)\) be the number of indices \(i\) for which
\(a_i\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\).  
If \(a_i\) is a residue, the conic \(C_i\) splits over \(\mathbb F_p\) into two

If \(a_i\) is a non‑residue, \(C_i\) remains geometrically reducible but has
only the rational point \([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\).

Hence the set of \(\mathbb F_p\)-points of \(X_p\) is the union of the
\(2r(p)\) rational lines, all meeting at the single point
\([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\).  Consequently  

\[
\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)=2\,r(p)\,p+1 .
\]

The Lang–Weil estimate tells us that the dominant term of
\(\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)\) is contributed by the geometrically irreducible
components that are defined over \(\mathbb F_p\); these are exactly the
\(2r(p)\) rational lines.  Therefore  

\[
\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)}{p}=2\,r(p)+O(p^{-1}) .
\]

For a fixed non‑zero integer \(a\), the Legendre symbol \(\bigl(\frac{a}{p}\bigr)\)
is \(+1\) for half of the large primes and \(-1\) for the other half.
Thus each of the six numbers \(a_i\) is a quadratic residue for about half
of the primes, and the indicators of “\(a_i\) is a residue’’ are asymptotically
independent.  Hence  

\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,r(p)\,\bigr]=\frac{6}{2}=3 .
\]

Therefore, as \(p\to\infty\),

\[
\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)}{p}=2\,r(p)+o(1)\longrightarrow 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

So the required limit is  

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

The curve  

\[
X:\;\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}\bigr)=0\subset \mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbf Z}
\]

is the union of the six quadrics  

\[
C_i:\;X^{2}-a_iY^{2}=0 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) (large enough so that the reduction is well defined) we work over \(\mathbb F_{p}\).

---

### 1.  \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-points on a single component  

Write the equation of a component as  

\[
X^{2}=aY^{2}.
\]

*If \(a\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\)*, write \(a=b^{2}\). Then  

\[
X^{2}=b^{2}Y^{2}\iff (X-bY)(X+bY)=0,
\]

so \(C_i\) splits into the two distinct lines  

\[
L_{i}^{\pm}:\;X\mp bY=0 .
\]

Each line contains \(p+1\) \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-points; they intersect in the vertex
\(P_0=[0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\). Hence  

\[
\#C_i(\mathbb F_{p}) = 2(p+1)-1 = 2p+1 .
\]

*If \(a\) is a non‑residue modulo \(p\)*, the equation has no solution with
\(Y\neq 0\); the only \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-point is the vertex \(P_0\). Thus  

\[
\#C_i(\mathbb F_{p}) = 1 .
\]

Consequently, letting  

\[
\varepsilon_i(p)=\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }a_i\text{ is a square mod }p,\\[2pt]
0 &\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]

we have  

\[
\#C_i(\mathbb F_{p}) = 1 + 2p\,\varepsilon_i(p).
\]

---

### 2.  Points on the whole union  

All six components meet exactly at the vertex \(P_0\). Therefore  

\[
\#X_p(\mathbb F_{p}) = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(\#C_i(\mathbb F_{p})-1\bigr)
                     = 1 + 2p\sum_{i=1}^{6}\varepsilon_i(p).
\]

Set  

\[
S(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\varepsilon_i(p)=\#\{\,i\mid a_i\text{ is a square mod }p\,\}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_{p})}{p}=2S(p)+\frac{1}{p}.
\]

---

### 3.  Asymptotics via Lang–Weil  

For a fixed non‑zero integer \(a\), the Legendre symbol \(\bigl(\frac{a}{p}\bigr)\) is
\(1\) for exactly half of the large primes and \(-1\) for the other half.
Hence each \(a_i\) is a quadratic residue for a density \(1/2\) of primes.
The residues of the six different numbers are independent (the Galois group of
\(\mathbf Q(\sqrt{a_1},\dots,\sqrt{a_6})\) is \((\mathbf Z/2)^6\)), so the expected
value of \(S(p)\) is  

\[
\mathbb E\bigl[S(p)\bigr]=6\cdot\frac12 = 3 .
\]

Lang–Weil tells us that the error term is \(O(p^{1/2})\); therefore  

\[
\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_{p})}{p}=2S(p)+O(p^{-1/2})
\]

and, after averaging over the primes, the term \(2S(p)\) tends to its mean
\(2\cdot 3 = 6\).

Hence the limit  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbb F_{p})}{p}=6 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The curve \(X\subset\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z}\) is defined by  

\[
F(X,Y,Z)=\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_iY^{2}\bigr)=0 .
\]

\[
(X-\sqrt{a_i}Y)(X+\sqrt{a_i}Y)=0,
\]

so \(C_i\) is a union of two lines meeting at the point \([0:0:1]\).

For a prime \(p\) of good reduction the reduction \(C_{i,p}\) is a plane

By the Lang–Weil estimate (or directly for conics),  

\[
\# C_{i,p}(\mathbb F_p)=p+O(p^{1/2}) .
\]

The implied constant depends only on the degree, not on \(p\).

---

### Union of the six components

\(X_p\) is the union \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{6} C_{i,p}\).  
If we sum the point counts of the components we obtain  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{6}\# C_{i,p}(\mathbb F_p)=6p+O(p^{1/2}).
\]

The components intersect only in finitely many points:
all six meet at \([0:0:1]\), and any two distinct components meet only
there (the affine lines have distinct slopes, and their points at infinity
are distinct unless \(\sqrt{a_i}\equiv\pm\sqrt{a_j}\pmod p\), which can
happen for at most \(O(1)\) primes).  Hence the over‑count caused by
intersections contributes only a bounded error \(O(1)\).

Therefore  

\[
\# X_p(\mathbb F_p)=6p+O(p^{1/2}),
\]

and dividing by \(p\) and letting \(p\to\infty\),

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)}{p}=6 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{6.0000}

The equation  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}\bigr)=0 ,\qquad 
a_{1}=2,\;a_{2}=3,\;a_{3}=5,\;a_{4}=6,\;a_{5}=7,\;a_{6}=10
\]

splits over \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}\) as  

\[
\bigl(X-\sqrt{a_{1}}Y\bigr)\bigl(X+\sqrt{a_{1}}Y\bigr)\;
\cdots\;
\bigl(X-\sqrt{a_{6}}Y\bigr)\bigl(X+\sqrt{a_{6}}Y\bigr)=0 .
\]

Hence \(X_{\!p}\) is the union of the twelve lines  

\[
L_{i}^{\pm}:\; X\pm\sqrt{a_{i}}Y=0\qquad (i=1,\dots ,6)
\]

all intersecting at the rational point \(P=[0:0:1]\).

A line \(L_{i}^{\pm}\) is defined over \(\mathbf{F}_{p}\) iff \(\sqrt{a_{i}}\in\mathbf{F}_{p}\), i.e. iff \(a_{i}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\).
Let  

\[
\varepsilon_i(p)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } a_i \text{ is a quadratic residue mod }p,\\[2pt]
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

If a line is defined over \(\mathbf{F}_{p}\) it contains \(p+1\) rational points; otherwise it contains only the common point \(P\).
Therefore  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbf{F}_{p})
=1+2p\sum_{i=1}^{6}\varepsilon_i(p).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf{F}_{p})}{p}= \frac1p+2\sum_{i=1}^{6}\varepsilon_i(p)
\longrightarrow 2\sum_{i=1}^{6}\varepsilon_i(p)
\qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

For large primes the Legendre symbols \(\bigl(\frac{a_i}{p}\bigr)\) are equidistributed; each \(a_i\) is a quadratic residue for exactly one half of the primes.  
The six symbols are governed by the four independent characters
\(\chi_2,\chi_3,\chi_5,\chi_7\); hence  

\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\varepsilon_i(p)\bigr]=\tfrac12\qquad\text{for each }i,
\]
and  

\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{6}\varepsilon_i(p)\right]=6\cdot \tfrac12 =3 .
\]

Thus, on average,

\[
\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf{F}_{p})}{p}\;\longrightarrow\;2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Hence the required limit is  

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The scheme  

\[
X\subset \mathbf P^2_{\mathbb Z},\qquad 
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_iY^{2}\bigr)=0 ,
\qquad a_i\in\{2,3,5,6,7,10\},
\]

is a reduced curve of dimension 1.  
Over an algebraic closure the equation splits as  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}(X-\sqrt{a_i}\,Y)(X+\sqrt{a_i}\,Y)=0 ,
\]

so \(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_p}\) is the union of the twelve distinct lines  

\[
L_{i,\pm} :\; X\mp\sqrt{a_i}\,Y =0 \qquad (i=1,\dots ,6).
\]

All these lines meet only at the point \([0:0:1]\).

---

### Number of \(\mathbf F_p\)-points

For a prime \(p\) not dividing any \(a_i\) the reduction \(X_p\) is well defined.
Each geometrically irreducible component of \(X_p\) is a line, and a line in
\(\mathbf P^2_{\mathbf F_p}\) contains exactly \(p+1\) rational points.
Hence, summing over the twelve lines and subtracting the one common point that
has been counted twelve times, we obtain  

\[
\#X_p(\mathbf F_p)=12(p+1)-11=12p+1 .
\]

More generally, whether a factor \(X^{2}-a_iY^{2}\) splits over \(\mathbf F_p\)
or not, the Lang–Weil estimate guarantees  

\[
\#X_p(\mathbf F_p)=12p+O(p^{1/2}),
\]

the error term coming from the \(O(p^{1/2})\) bound for each irreducible
component.

---

### Limit

Therefore  

\[
\frac{\#X_p(\mathbf F_p)}{p}=12+O(p^{-1/2})\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}12 .
\]

Hence  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}{p}=12 .
\]

\[
\boxed{12}
\]

For each \(i\) the factor  

\[
X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}=0
\]

defines a plane curve of degree \(2\).  
For a fixed prime \(p\) (large enough so that the reduction is smooth) the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#\{(X\!:\!Y\!:\!Z)\in\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})\mid X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}=0\}=p+O(1).
\]

The six factors define six (pairwise distinct) curves, and their intersections consist of only finitely many points, so the error contributed by the intersections is also \(O(1)\).

Hence  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p}) = \sum_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(p+O(1)\bigr)+O(1)=6p+O(1).
\]

Dividing by \(p\) and letting \(p\to\infty\) we obtain  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{p}=6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6}
\]

The equation  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}\bigl(X^{2}-a_{i}Y^{2}\bigr)=0 ,\qquad a_{i}=2,3,5,6,7,10,
\]

defines in \(\mathbf P^{2}\) a union of six conics.  
Over \(\overline{\mathbf F}_{p}\) each conic splits into the two lines  

\[
X=\pm\sqrt{a_{i}}\,Y .
\]

Hence over \(\overline{\mathbf F}_{p}\) the scheme \(X_{p}\) consists of \(12\) distinct lines, all meeting at the point \([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Counting \(\mathbf F_{p}\)-points

Write a point of \(\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})\) with \(Y\neq 0\) as \([x:1:z]\) (\(x,z\in\mathbf F_{p}\)).  
The defining equation becomes  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{6}(x^{2}-a_{i})=0 .
\]

Thus a point with \(Y\neq 0\) belongs to \(X_{p}\) iff \(x\) satisfies \(x^{2}=a_{i}\) for some \(i\).
For each \(i\) the congruence \(x^{2}=a_{i}\) has  

* two solutions if \(a_{i}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\);
* no solution otherwise.

The six congruences are disjoint (the \(a_{i}\) are distinct), so letting  

\[
r(p)=\#\{\,i\mid a_{i}\text{ is a quadratic residue mod }p\,\},
\]

the number of admissible \(x\)’s is  

\[
N(p)=2\,r(p).
\]

For each such \(x\) the coordinate \(z\) can be chosen arbitrarily, giving \(p\) points.
The only point with \(Y=0\) lying on \(X_{p}\) is the common intersection \([0\!:\!0\!:\!1]\).

Hence  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p}) = p\,N(p)+1 = 2\,r(p)\,p+1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Asymptotics via Lang–Weil

The Lang–Weil estimate for a projective curve \(C\) over \(\mathbf F_{p}\) states

\[
\#C(\mathbf F_{p}) = p\cdot \nu(p) + O(p^{1/2}),
\]

where \(\nu(p)\) is the number of geometrically irreducible components of \(C\) that are defined over \(\mathbf F_{p}\).

In our situation each line \(X=\pm\sqrt{a_{i}}Y\) is defined over \(\mathbf F_{p}\) exactly when \(a_{i}\) is a quadratic residue.  
Consequently  

\[
\nu(p)=2\,r(p),
\]

and the formula obtained above agrees with Lang–Weil.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Limiting ratio

Quadratic reciprocity (or Chebotarev’s density theorem) tells us that, as \(p\to\infty\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(a_{i}\text{ is a quadratic residue mod }p\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

The residues of the six distinct square‑free integers are independent in the limit, so

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} \frac{r(p)}{1}= \frac{6}{2}=3 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{p}
   =\lim_{p\to\infty}\bigl(2\,r(p)+\frac{1}{p}\bigr)
   =2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

problems.problem:
Let \(\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}}\) be the projective plane over \(\mathbb{Z}\) with homogeneous coordinates \([X_{0}:X_{1}:X_{2}]\).  
Choose four distinct linear homogeneous polynomials \(L_{1},\dots ,L_{4}\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{0},X_{1},X_{2}]\) defining four distinct lines in \(\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}}\), and set  
\[
L \;=\; V(L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}L_{4})\;\subset\;\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}} .
\]

In another copy of \(\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}}\) with coordinates \([Y_{0}:Y_{1}:Y_{2}]\) choose seven distinct linear forms \(M_{1},\dots ,M_{7}\in\mathbb{Z}[Y_{0},Y_{1},Y_{2}]\) and define  
\[
M \;=\; V(M_{1}\cdots M_{7})\;\subset\;\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}} .
\]

Consider the closed subscheme  
\[
X \;=\; L \times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}} M\;\subset\; \mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}} .
\]

For a prime number \(p\) let \(X_{p}\) denote the fibre of \(X\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\).  
Let \(d\) be the Krull dimension of \(X\). Using the Lang–Weil estimate, compute the limit  
\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\# X_{p}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}{p^{\,d}} .
\]

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The divisor  

\[
L = V(L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}L_{4})\subset\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z}
\]

is the union of the four distinct lines \(L_i\cong\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb Z}\).  
Similarly  

\[
M = V(M_{1}\cdots M_{7})\subset\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb Z}
\]

is the union of the seven distinct lines \(M_j\cong\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb Z}\).

Hence  

\[
X = L\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z} M
     = \bigcup_{i=1}^{4}\bigcup_{j=1}^{7} (L_i\times M_j),
\]

a disjoint union of \(4\cdot 7 = 28\) copies of \(\mathbf P^{1}\times\mathbf P^{1}\) over \(\mathbb Z\).  
Each component has Krull dimension \(2\); therefore  

\[
d = \dim X = 2 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) the fibre \(X_p\) is the same disjoint union over \(\mathbb F_{p}\).  
Since \(\#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p+1\),

\[
\#\bigl(\mathbf P^{1}\times\mathbf P^{1}\bigr)(\mathbb F_{p})
   = (p+1)^2 = p^{2}+2p+1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\#X_{p}(\mathbb F_{p})
 = 28\,(p+1)^2 = 28p^{2}+56p+28 .
\]

Dividing by \(p^{d}=p^{2}\) and letting \(p\to\infty\),

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#X_{p}(\mathbb F_{p})}{p^{2}}
   = \lim_{p\to\infty}\left(28 + \frac{56}{p} + \frac{28}{p^{2}}\right)=28 .
\]

Hence the required limit equals \(28\).

\[
\boxed{28}
\]

The scheme  

\[
X = L \times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z} M
\]

is the product of the union of four lines in the first copy of \(\mathbf P^{2}\) with the union of seven lines in the second copy.  
Over a field \(k\) each line is isomorphic to \(\mathbf P^{1}_{k}\); hence  

\[
L_k = \bigcup_{i=1}^{4} \mathbf P^{1}_{k}, \qquad   
M_k = \bigcup_{j=1}^{7} \mathbf P^{1}_{k}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
X_k = L_k \times_k M_k = \bigcup_{i,j} (\mathbf P^{1}_{k}\times \mathbf P^{1}_{k}),

Let \(S\subset\mathbf{P}^{3}_{\mathbb{Z}}=\operatorname{Proj}\mathbb{Z}[X_{0},X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}]\) be the closed subscheme defined by the homogeneous polynomial  

\[
F = X_{0}^{7}+X_{1}^{7}+X_{2}^{7}+X_{3}^{7}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let \(S_{p}\) denote the reduction of \(S\) modulo \(p\); for all sufficiently large \(p\) the hypersurface \(S_{p}\) is smooth.  
Consider the morphism  

\[
\pi : S \longrightarrow \mathbf{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}},\qquad [X_{0}:X_{1}:X_{2}:X_{3}]\mapsto [X_{1}:X_{2}:X_{3}],
\]

which is the projection from the point \(Q=[1:0:0:0]\).  
For each such prime \(p\) let \(\pi_{p}:S_{p}\to\mathbf{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\) be the induced map and define  

\[
A(p)=\frac{1}{\#\mathbf{P}^{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\sum_{x\in\mathbf{P}^{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\#\pi_{p}^{-1}(x),
\]

the average size of a fibre of \(\pi_{p}\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points.  
Using the Lang–Weil estimate for geometrically irreducible varieties, compute the limit  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)
\]

and then give \(\big\lfloor 1000\,L\big\rfloor\). Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.

\(S\) is a smooth hypersurface of degree \(7\) in \(\mathbf P^{3}\); it

\]

\[

Hence  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)=1.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required integer

\[
L = 1,\qquad 1000L = 1000,\qquad \big\lfloor 1000L\big\rfloor = 1000.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{1000}
\]

The fibre over a point \(x=[a:b:c]\in \mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p})\) consists of the points \([X_{0}:a:b:c]\) on \(S_{p}\), i.e. the solutions of  

\[
X_{0}^{7}+a^{7}+b^{7}+c^{7}=0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\sum_{x\in \mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p})}\#\pi_{p}^{-1}(x)=\# S_{p}(\mathbb F_{p}),
\]

so  

\[
A(p)=\frac{\#S_{p}(\mathbb F_{p})}{\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p})}.
\]

The hypersurface \(S\) defined by the Fermat polynomial
\(X_{0}^{7}+X_{1}^{7}+X_{2}^{7}+X_{3}^{7}=0\) is smooth and geometrically
irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\); thus for all sufficiently large primes
\(p\) the reduction \(S_{p}\) is a smooth, geometrically irreducible
surface of dimension \(2\).

For a smooth geometrically irreducible variety \(V\) of dimension \(d\)
over \(\mathbb F_{p}\), the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#V(\mathbb F_{p}) = p^{d}+O(p^{d-1/2}).
\]

Applying this with \(d=2\) to \(S_{p}\) we obtain  

\[
\#S_{p}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}).
\]

Since \(\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p^{2}+p+1\),

\[
A(p)=\frac{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+p+1}=1+O(p^{-1/2}),
\]

and therefore  

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)=1.
\]

Finally  

\[
\big\lfloor 1000\,L\big\rfloor = \big\lfloor 1000\cdot 1\big\rfloor = 1000.
\]

\[
\boxed{1000}
\]

The average fibre size can be rewritten as  

\[
A(p)=\frac{1}{\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})}\sum_{x\in\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})}\#\pi_{p}^{-1}(x)
      =\frac{\#S(\mathbf F_{p})}{\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})}.
\]

Thus we need the limit of the ratio \(\#S(\mathbf F_{p}) / \#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})\).

For a prime \(p\) with \(p\neq 7\) the hypersurface  

\[
S:\; X_{0}^{7}+X_{1}^{7}+X_{2}^{7}+X_{3}^{7}=0\subset \mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbf F_{p}}
\]

is smooth, hence geometrically irreducible of dimension \(2\).  
By the Lang–Weil estimate for a geometrically irreducible variety of dimension \(d\),

\[
\#S(\mathbf F_{p}) = p^{2}+O(p^{3/2}),
\qquad
\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p}) = p^{2}+p+1 = p^{2}+O(p).
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{\#S(\mathbf F_{p})}{\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})}
 = \frac{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p)}
 \longrightarrow 1 \qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

Hence  

\[
L = \lim_{p\to\infty} A(p) = 1.
\]

Finally  

\[
\big\lfloor 1000\,L\big\rfloor = \big\lfloor 1000 \times 1 \big\rfloor = 1000.
\]

\[
\boxed{1000}
\]

The hypersurface  

\[
S:\;X_{0}^{7}+X_{1}^{7}+X_{2}^{7}+X_{3}^{7}=0\subset\mathbf P^{3}_{\mathbb Z}
\]

does not contain the point \(Q=[1:0:0:0]\).  
Hence the projection  

\[
\pi:[X_{0}:X_{1}:X_{2}:X_{3}]\longmapsto [X_{1}:X_{2}:X_{3}]
\]

is a **finite morphism**.  
For a point \(x=[a:b:c]\in\mathbf P^{2}\) the fibre is

\[
\pi^{-1}(x)=\{[t:a:b:c]\mid t^{7}+a^{7}+b^{7}+c^{7}=0\}.
\]

Over an algebraic closure the equation \(t^{7}=-(a^{7}+b^{7}+c^{7})\) has
exactly \(7\) solutions, so the degree of \(\pi\) is  

\[
\deg(\pi)=7 .
\]

Both \(S\) and \(\mathbf P^{2}\) are geometrically irreducible varieties of
dimension \(2\).  
For a finite morphism \(f:X\to Y\) of degree \(d\) the Lang–Weil estimate
gives  

\[
\#X(\mathbf F_{p}) = d\;\#Y(\mathbf F_{p})+O(p^{3/2}) .
\]

Consequently  

\[
A(p)=\frac{\#S_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbf F_{p})}
      =\frac{\#S_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}{p^{2}+p+1}
      = d+O(p^{-1/2}) .
\]

Taking the limit as \(p\to\infty\),

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)=d=7 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\big\lfloor 1000\,L\big\rfloor =\big\lfloor 1000\cdot 7\big\rfloor =7000 .
\]

\[
\boxed{7000}
\]

The fibre over a point \([X_{1}:X_{2}:X_{3}]\in\mathbf P^{2}\) consists of the points \([X_{0}:X_{1}:X_{2}:X_{3}]\) on the hypersurface
\[
X_{0}^{7}+X_{1}^{7}+X_{2}^{7}+X_{3}^{7}=0 .
\]
Hence, for a fixed prime \(p\),

\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p})}\#\pi_{p}^{-1}(x)=\#S_{p}(\mathbb F_{p}),
\]

the number of \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-rational points on the surface \(S_{p}\).

For all sufficiently large \(p\) the reduction \(S_{p}\) is a smooth, geometrically irreducible surface of dimension \(2\).  
By the Lang–Weil estimate,
\[
\#S_{p}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p^{2}+O\!\left(p^{3/2}\right).
\]

Moreover
\[
\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p^{2}+p+1 = p^{2}+O(p).
\]

Therefore
\[
A(p)=\frac{\#S_{p}(\mathbb F_{p})}{\#\mathbf P^{2}(\mathbb F_{p})}
      =\frac{p^{2}+O(p^{3/2})}{p^{2}+O(p)}
      =1+O(p^{-1/2}),
\]
so the limit exists and equals

\[
L=\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)=1.
\]

Finally,
\[
\big\lfloor 1000\,L \big\rfloor = \big\lfloor 1000\cdot 1 \big\rfloor = 1000.
\]

\[
\boxed{1000}
\]

problems.skill: Lang–Weil point‑count estimate for varieties over finite fields
problems.problem:
Let \(\mathbf{P}^{4}_{\mathbb{Z}}=\operatorname{Proj}\mathbb{Z}[X_{0},X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{4}]\) and consider the following 26 distinct linear forms with integer coefficients:
\[
L_{i}=X_{0}+i\,X_{1}\qquad (i=1,2,\dots ,26).
\]
Define the closed subscheme \(X\subset \mathbf{P}^{4}_{\mathbb{Z}}\) by
\[
X \;=\; V\!\bigl(L_{1}L_{2}\cdots L_{26}\bigr),
\]
i.e. \(X\) is the union of the 26 hyperplanes \(H_{i}=V(L_{i})\).  
For a prime number \(p\) let \(X_{p}=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{F}_{p}\) and denote by
\[
N_{p}= \# X_{p}(\mathbb{F}_{p})
\]
the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-rational points of \(X_{p}\).  
Using the Lang–Weil estimate for each geometrically irreducible component, determine the limit
\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_{p}}{p^{3}}.
\]
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The complement of \(X_{p}\) consists of the points \([x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}:x_{3}:x_{4}]\in\mathbf P^{4}(\mathbf F_{p})\) for which  

\[
x_{0}+i\,x_{1}\neq 0\qquad\text{for all }i=1,\dots ,26 .
\]

Projecting onto the first two coordinates gives a map  

\[
\pi:\mathbf P^{4}\longrightarrow\mathbf P^{1},\qquad
[x_{0}:x_{1}:x_{2}:x_{3}:x_{4}]\mapsto[x_{0}:x_{1}].
\]

For a fixed point of \(\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbf F_{p})\) the fibre of \(\pi\) is a \(\mathbf P^{3}\), which has  

\[
\#\mathbf P^{3}(\mathbf F_{p}) = p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1
\]

points.

---

### 1.  Which points of \(\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbf F_{p})\) lie in the complement?

* If \(x_{1}=0\) (the point at infinity), then \(x_{0}\neq 0\) and
  \(x_{0}+i\,x_{1}=x_{0}\neq0\) for every \(i\); this point is **allowed**.
* If \(x_{1}\neq 0\), write \(t=x_{0}/x_{1}\in\mathbf F_{p}\).  
  The condition \(x_{0}+i\,x_{1}=0\) becomes \(t=-i\).  
  Hence the point is allowed precisely when \(t\not\in\{-1,-2,\dots ,-26\}\).

Thus among the \(p\) finite points of \(\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbf F_{p})\) we must exclude the 26 values \(-1,\dots,-26\).  
Hence the number of admissible points of \(\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbf F_{p})\) is  

\[
|S| = 1 + (p-26)=p-25 .
\]

---

### 2.  Size of the complement

\[
\#\bigl(\mathbf P^{4}\setminus X_{p}\bigr)
   = |S|\;\#\mathbf P^{3}(\mathbf F_{p})
   = (p-25)\bigl(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1\bigr).
\]

Expanding,

\[
(p-25)(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)=p^{4}-24p^{3}-24p^{2}-24p-25 .
\]

---

### 3.  Number of points on \(X_{p}\)

The total number of points of \(\mathbf P^{4}(\mathbf F_{p})\) is  

\[
\#\mathbf P^{4}(\mathbf F_{p})=p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{p}&=\#X_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})  \\
     &=\bigl(p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1\bigr)
        -\bigl(p^{4}-24p^{3}-24p^{2}-24p-25\bigr)\\
     &=25p^{3}+25p^{2}+25p+26 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 4.  Asymptotic ratio

\[
\frac{N_{p}}{p^{3}} = 25 + \frac{25}{p}+ \frac{25}{p^{2}}+\frac{26}{p^{3}}
\longrightarrow 25\qquad(p\to\infty).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{25}
\]

For each \(i\) the hyperplane  

\[
H_i = V(L_i)\subset \mathbf P^4_{\mathbb Z},\qquad 
L_i = X_0+iX_1 ,
\]

is a projective subspace of dimension \(3\).  
Over \(\mathbb F_p\) it has  

\[
\# H_i(\mathbb F_p)=\frac{p^{4}-1}{p-1}=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\# H_i(\mathbb F_p)=p^{3}+O(p^{2}) .
\]

The scheme \(X\) is the union of the 26 distinct hyperplanes,
\(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{26} H_i\).  
Let \(A_i=H_i(\mathbb F_p)\). By inclusion–exclusion,

\[
\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)=\sum_{i=1}^{26}|A_i|
     -\sum_{i<j}|A_i\cap A_j|
     +\sum_{i<j<k}|A_i\cap A_j\cap A_k|-\cdots .
\]

* For a pair \(i\neq j\), \(A_i\cap A_j\) is a projective subspace of
dimension \(2\); its cardinality is \(\frac{p^{3}-1}{p-1}=p^{2}+p+1=O(p^{2})\).

* For three or more distinct hyperplanes the intersection has dimension \(\le1\) and therefore contributes at most \(O(p)\).

Consequently the only term that contributes to the coefficient of \(p^{3}\) is the first sum:

\[
\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)=26\,(p^{3}+O(p^{2})) - O(p^{2}) = 26\,p^{3}+O(p^{2}).
\]

Dividing by \(p^{3}\) and letting \(p\to\infty\),

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{N_p}{p^{3}}
   =\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{26\,p^{3}+O(p^{2})}{p^{3}} = 26 .
\]

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplanes are  

\[
H_i=V(L_i)=\{[X_0:\dots :X_4]\mid X_0+iX_1=0\},\qquad i=1,\dots ,26 .
\]

All of them contain the linear subspace  

\[
S=V(X_0,X_1)=\{[0:0:X_2:X_3:X_4]\}\cong \mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb F_p},
\]

and any two distinct hyperplanes intersect exactly in \(S\).  
Hence the union \(X_p=\bigcup_{i=1}^{26} H_i\) satisfies  

\[
\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)=\#S+\sum_{i=1}^{26}\bigl(\#H_i-\#S\bigr)
               =26\#H_i-25\#S .
\]

For a hyperplane \(H_i\cong\mathbf P^{3}\) we have  

\[
\#H_i = p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1,
\]

and for \(S\cong\mathbf P^{2}\),

\[
\#S = p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &= 26(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)-25(p^{2}+p+1)\\
    &= 26p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Dividing by \(p^{3}\),

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26 + \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p^{2}} + \frac{1}{p^{3}}
\longrightarrow 26 \qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplane  

\[
H_i=V(L_i)\subset \mathbf P^4_{\mathbb F_p},\qquad L_i=X_0+iX_1,
\]

is isomorphic to \(\mathbf P^3_{\mathbb F_p}\); hence  

\[
|H_i(\mathbb F_p)|=\frac{p^{4}-1}{p-1}=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

All the hyperplanes contain the common linear subspace  

\[
C=V(X_0,X_1)\cong\mathbf P^2_{\mathbb F_p},
\qquad |C(\mathbb F_p)|=p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

For distinct \(i\neq j\) (and for all sufficiently large primes \(p\) so that \(p\nmid (i-j)\)) the equations
\(L_i=0\) and \(L_j=0\) are independent, giving \(H_i\cap H_j=C\).
Any intersection of three or more of the \(H_i\) is still \(C\).

With \(m=26\) hyperplanes, the inclusion–exclusion principle gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &=
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|H_i|
-\sum_{i<j}|H_i\cap H_j|
+\sum_{i<j<k}|H_i\cap H_j\cap H_k|
-\cdots \\[2mm]
&= m|H_i|+\Bigl[\sum_{s=2}^{m}(-1)^{s+1}\binom{m}{s}\Bigr]|C| .
\end{aligned}
\]

Since  

\[
\sum_{s=2}^{m}(-1)^{s+1}\binom{m}{s}=1-m,
\]

we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &= 26\,(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)+(1-26)(p^{2}+p+1)\\
    &= 26p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26+\frac{p^{2}+p+1}{p^{3}}\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}26 .
\]

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplane \(H_i\) defined by \(L_i=0\) is a linear subspace of \(\mathbf P^4\) of dimension \(3\); hence \(H_i\simeq\mathbf P^3\).  
For a point \((x_0\!:\!x_1\!:\!x_2\!:\!x_3\!:\!x_4)\in\mathbf P^4(\mathbf F_p)\) we have  

\[
L_i=0\iff x_0+i x_1=0 .
\]

---

### 1.  Points with \(x_1=0\)

If \(x_1=0\) then \(L_i=0\) forces \(x_0=0\).  
Thus we are left with \((0:0:x_2:x_3:x_4)\), a \(\mathbf P^2\) having  

\[
\#\mathbf P^2(\mathbf F_p)=p^{2}+p+1
\]

points.

---

### 2.  Points with \(x_1\neq0\)

Scale the point so that \(x_1=1\).  
Then the condition \(L_i=0\) becomes \(x_0=-i\).  
For each of the \(26\) integers \(i\) we may choose any values for \(x_2,x_3,x_4\in\mathbf F_p\); this gives \(p^{3}\) points per \(i\).

Hence the number of points in this case is  

\[
26\cdot p^{3}.
\]

(For large \(p\) the residues \(-i\) are distinct, so a point cannot satisfy two different \(L_i=0\).)

---

### 3.  Total count

\[
N_p = 26p^{3} + (p^{2}+p+1).
\]

---

### 4.  Limit

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26 + \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p^{2}} + \frac{1}{p^{3}}
\longrightarrow 26\qquad(p\to\infty).
\]

Thus, using the Lang–Weil estimate (the lower‑dimensional intersections contribute only \(O(p^{2})\) terms), the required limit is

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

Each hyperplane  

\[
H_i=V(L_i)=\{[X_0:\dots :X_4]\in\mathbf P^4_{\mathbb F_p}\mid X_0+iX_1=0\}
\]

is a copy of \(\mathbf P^3_{\mathbb F_p}\).  
Hence  

\[
\#H_i(\mathbb F_p)=\frac{p^{4}-1}{p-1}=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

For \(p>26\) the 26 linear forms are distinct modulo \(p\); therefore the 26 hyperplanes are distinct.  

The Lang–Weil estimate applied to each geometrically irreducible component \(H_i\) gives  

\[
\#H_i(\mathbb F_p)=p^{3}+O(p^{5/2}) .
\]

Summing over the 26 components,

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{26}\#H_i(\mathbb F_p)=26p^{3}+O(p^{5/2}).
\]

Points that lie in the intersection of several hyperplanes are counted several times in the sum above.  
The intersection of \(k\) distinct hyperplanes is a linear subspace of codimension \(k\):
\[
\dim =4-k .
\]
Thus it has at most \(p^{4-k}+O(p^{3-k})\) points.  
For \(k\ge 2\) this is \(O(p^{2})\) or smaller, i.e. lower order than \(p^{3}\).

Consequently the over‑counting contributed by all intersections is \(O(p^{2})\), which is negligible compared with the main term \(26p^{3}\).

Therefore  

\[
N_p = 26p^{3}+O(p^{5/2}),
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}}\longrightarrow 26\quad (p\to\infty).
\]

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplane  

\[
H_i=V(L_i)=\{[X_0:\dots :X_4]\in\mathbf P^4_{\mathbb F_p}\mid X_0+iX_1=0\}
\]

is a projective \(3\)-space, so  

\[
|H_i(\mathbb F_p)|=|\mathbf P^3(\mathbb F_p)|
   =\frac{p^{4}-1}{p-1}=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

For two distinct indices \(i\neq j\) and a prime \(p>26\) we have \(i\not\equiv j\pmod p\).  
Then  

\[
\begin{cases}
X_0+iX_1=0,\\
X_0+jX_1=0
\end{cases}
\Longrightarrow (i-j)X_1=0\Longrightarrow X_1=0,\;X_0=0 .
\]

Hence every pairwise (and higher) intersection equals  

\[
H_i\cap H_j = \{X_0=X_1=0\}\cong \mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb F_p},
\]
which contains  

\[
|\mathbf P^2(\mathbb F_p)|=\frac{p^{3}-1}{p-1}=p^{2}+p+1
\]

points.

All 26 hyperplanes share this same \(\mathbf P^2\). Using inclusion–exclusion,

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &=\Bigl|\bigcup_{i=1}^{26} H_i(\mathbb F_p)\Bigr| \\
    &= 26\,|\mathbf P^3(\mathbb F_p)|
       -25\,|\mathbf P^2(\mathbb F_p)|
\end{aligned}
\]

(the \(\mathbf P^2\) was counted 26 times, we keep it once).

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &= 26(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)-25(p^{2}+p+1)\\
    &= 26p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26+\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{1}{p^{3}}
\longrightarrow 26\qquad(p\to\infty).
\]

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplane \(H_i\subset \mathbf P^4_{\mathbb F_p}\) defined by \(L_i=0\) is a copy of \(\mathbf P^3_{\mathbb F_p}\); therefore  

\[
\#H_i(\mathbb F_p)=\#\mathbf P^3(\mathbb F_p)=1+p+p^2+p^3 .
\]

For two distinct indices \(i\neq j\) we have  

\[
H_i\cap H_j = V(X_0+iX_1,\;X_0+jX_1)=V(X_0,X_1)\equiv S,
\]

which is a \(\mathbf P^2_{\mathbb F_p}\). Hence every intersection of at least two of the hyperplanes is the same subvariety \(S\) with  

\[
\#S(\mathbb F_p)=1+p+p^2 .
\]

Thus each hyperplane contributes the points outside \(S\) only:

\[
\#\bigl(H_i\setminus S\bigr)(\mathbb F_p)=\bigl(1+p+p^2+p^3\bigr)-(1+p+p^2)=p^3 .
\]

The union \(X_p=\bigcup_{i=1}^{26} H_i\) therefore has  

\[
N_p=\#X_p(\mathbb F_p)=\#S(\mathbb F_p)+26\cdot p^3
      =(1+p+p^2)+26p^3 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26+\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{1}{p^{3}}
\longrightarrow 26 \qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplanes are  

\[
H_i : X_0+iX_1=0 ,\qquad i=1,\dots ,26 .
\]

For a prime \(p>26\) the equations remain distinct modulo \(p\).  
Any two different hyperplanes intersect in the linear subspace  

\[
X_0=X_1=0\;\subset\; \mathbf P^4_{\mathbb F_p},
\]

which is a \(\mathbf P^2\).  
Hence every intersection of at least two of the hyperplanes is this same \(\mathbf P^2\).

---

### Counting points

* A hyperplane \(H_i\simeq \mathbf P^3\) has  

\[
|H_i(\mathbb F_p)| = \frac{p^{4}-1}{p-1}=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1=:A .
\]

* The common intersection \(\mathbf P^2\) has  

\[
|\mathbf P^2(\mathbb F_p)| = \frac{p^{3}-1}{p-1}=p^{2}+p+1=:B .
\]

With \(m=26\) hyperplanes, inclusion–exclusion gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &= \sum_{i=1}^{m}|H_i|
      -\sum_{i<j}|H_i\cap H_j|
      +\sum_{i<j<k}|H_i\cap H_j\cap H_k|
      -\cdots \\[2mm]
    &= mA - (m-1)B,
\end{aligned}
\]

because every intersection of two or more hyperplanes equals the same \(\mathbf P^2\).

Thus  

\[
N_p = 26(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)-25(p^{2}+p+1)
     = 26p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

---

### Limit

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26 + \frac{p^{2}+p+1}{p^{3}}
                   \xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{} 26 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

The hyperplanes are  

\[
H_i=V(L_i)=\{X_0+iX_1=0\}\subset\mathbf P^{4}_{\mathbb F_p},
\qquad i=1,\dots ,26 .
\]

For \(p>26\) the 26 forms are distinct, so we may count points over \(\mathbb F_p\).

* Each hyperplane \(H_i\simeq\mathbf P^{3}\) has  

\[
|H_i|=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

* The intersection of any two different hyperplanes is obtained by solving  

\[
X_0+iX_1=0,\; X_0+jX_1=0\;(i\neq j),
\]

which forces \(X_0=X_1=0\). Hence  

\[
H_i\cap H_j =\{X_0=X_1=0\}\cong\mathbf P^{2},
\qquad |H_i\cap H_j|=p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

All intersections of three or more hyperplanes are the same \(\mathbf P^{2}\).

Using inclusion–exclusion, with \(n=26\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_p &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|H_i|
      +\sum_{k=2}^{n}(-1)^{k+1}\binom{n}{k}\,|\,\bigcap_{j=1}^{k} H_{i_j}\,|\\
    &= n|H|+\Bigl(\sum_{k=2}^{n}(-1)^{k+1}\binom{n}{k}\Bigr)|S|,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(|H|=p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1\) and \(|S|=p^{2}+p+1\).

The binomial sum simplifies:

\[
\sum_{k=2}^{n}(-1)^{k+1}\binom{n}{k}
   =1-n \quad (\text{since }\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}=0).
\]

Thus for \(n=26\),

\[
N_p = 26|H|-(26-1)|S|
     = 26(p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)-25(p^{2}+p+1)
     = 26p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{N_p}{p^{3}} = 26+\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{1}{p^{3}}
\longrightarrow 26 \qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

\[
\boxed{26}
\]

problems.problem:
Let \(X\subset \mathbf{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{Z}}=\operatorname{Proj}\mathbb{Z}[X,Y,Z]\) be the closed subscheme defined by the homogeneous polynomial  

\[
