problems.problem:
Let \(X=\mathbf{P}^{5}\) be the projective space that parametrises plane conics in \(\mathbf{P}^{2}\), and let \(H\in A^{1}(X)\) denote the hyperplane class.  
It is known that  

* the divisor \(\Sigma_{C}\subset X\) of conics tangent to a fixed smooth conic \(C\) has class \([\,\Sigma_{C}\,]=6H\);  
* the divisor \(\Sigma_{P}\subset X\) of conics passing through a fixed point \(P\in\mathbf{P}^{2}\) has class \([\,\Sigma_{P}\,]=H\);  
* the discriminant divisor \(\Delta\subset X\) of singular conics has class \([\Delta]=3H\).

Fix two general smooth conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\) and three general points \(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) in \(\mathbf{P}^{2}\).  
Consider the closed subscheme  

\[
Z \;=\; \Sigma_{C_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{C_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{3}}\;\subset\;X .
\]

For a general choice of the five conditions the scheme \(Z\) consists of finitely many reduced points, and the natural map sending a conic to the five‑tuple \((C_{1},C_{2},P_{1},P_{2},P_{3})\) is finite étale over the open locus of such tuples.  

Compute the number of points of \(Z\); equivalently, determine the degree of this finite étale map.  
Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The space of plane conics is  

\[
X=\mathbf P^{5}= \mathbb P\bigl(H^{0}(\mathbf P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2))\bigr) ,
\qquad 
A^{*}(X)=\mathbf Z[H]/(H^{6}),
\]

where \(H\) is the hyperplane class.  
For a fixed smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) the divisor of conics tangent to \(C\) is  

\[
\Sigma_{C}\sim 6H,
\]

and for a fixed point \(P\in\mathbf P^{2}\)

\[
\Sigma_{P}\sim H .
\]

Hence for two conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\) and three points \(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\)

\[
[Z]=[\Sigma_{C_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{3}}]
   =(6H)^{2}\,H^{3}=6^{2}H^{5}=36 .
\]

If we intersect the five divisors transversally we would obtain \(36\) points.
However the product \(36H^{5}\) counts also the **singular** conics that lie on the
discriminant divisor  

\[
\Delta\subset X ,\qquad [\Delta]=3H .
\]

The divisor \(\Delta\) is singular along the Veronese surface \(V\) (the double
lines) and its generic point corresponds to a union of two distinct lines.
Because the five conditions are not transverse along \(\Delta\), an excess
intersection occurs.  
The characteristic numbers of plane conics (see e.g. Eisenbud–Harris,
*3264 & All That*) give the correct numbers after removing the contribution of
the singular locus:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{points }a & \text{tangencies }b\\ \hline
5 & 0 \\
4 & 1 \\
3 & 2 \\
2 & 3 \\
1 & 4 \\
0 & 5
\end{array}
\qquad
N_{a,b}= \begin{cases}
1,2,5,10,16,24 \text{ respectively}.
\end{cases}
\]

In our situation we have \(a=3\) point conditions and \(b=2\) tangency
conditions, so the characteristic number is  

\[
N_{3,2}=5 .
\]

Thus among the \(36\) points counted by the product \((6H)^{2}H^{3}\) the
singular conics contribute \(36-5=31\) (with the appropriate multiplicities);
the remaining reduced points correspond exactly to smooth conics satisfying
the five prescribed conditions.

Consequently the finite étale map that sends a conic to the five‑tuple
\((C_{1},C_{2},P_{1},P_{2},P_{3})\) has degree

\[
\boxed{5}
\]

The space of plane conics is  

\[
X=\mathbf P^5 ,\qquad H=c_1(\mathcal O_X(1)).
\]

For the five imposed conditions we have the divisor classes  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_1}]=6H,\qquad [\Sigma_{C_2}]=6H,\qquad 
[\Sigma_{P_i}]=H\;(i=1,2,3).
\]

The intersection of these five divisors in \(\mathbf P^{5}\) is a zero‑dimensional cycle whose degree is the product of the coefficients of \(H\):

\[
\deg\bigl(\Sigma_{C_1}\cap\Sigma_{C_2}\cap\Sigma_{P_1}\cap\Sigma_{P_2}\cap\Sigma_{P_3}\bigr)
   = 6\cdot 6\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 1 = 36 .
\]

A possible extra contribution could come from singular conics, i.e. points lying on the discriminant divisor \(\Delta\) (class \(3H\)).  
For a singular conic to satisfy the five generic conditions it would have to be a union of two lines, one of which is tangent to \(C_1\) and the other to \(C_2\), while the three given points lie on the two lines. Because the points and the conics are chosen generically, no such configuration occurs; hence none of the 36 intersection points lie on \(\Delta\).

Therefore all 36 points of the intersection correspond to smooth conics, and the finite map that records the five conditions is étale of degree \(36\).

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(X=\mathbf P^{5}\) with hyperplane class \(H\).  
The divisor of conics tangent to a fixed smooth conic has class \(6H\), the divisor of conics through a fixed point has class \(H\).  

For two fixed conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\) and three fixed points \(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) we intersect the corresponding divisors:

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{3}}]
   =(6H)\,(6H)\,H\,H\,H = 36\,H^{5}.
\]

In the Chow ring of \(\mathbf P^{5}\) we have \(H^{5}=1\); therefore the intersection number is  

\[
\int_{X} 36\,H^{5}=36 .
\]

For a general choice of the five conditions the intersection is transverse and none of the resulting conics is singular, so the enumerative count equals the intersection number.

Hence the finite étale map has degree  

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is  

\[
X=\mathbf P^5 ,\qquad H\in A^{1}(X)
\]

with  

\[
[\Sigma_{C}]=6H ,\qquad [\Sigma_{P}]=H ,\qquad [\Delta]=3H .
\]

For two general smooth conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\) and three general points
\(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) we intersect the corresponding divisors:

\[
Z=\Sigma_{C_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{C_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{3}} .
\]

Since \(\dim X =5\), the class of a point is \(H^{5}=1\) in \(A^{5}(X)\).
Hence the degree of the zero‑dimensional cycle \(Z\) is  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{1}}]\cdot
[\Sigma_{P_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{3}}]
= (6H)^{2}\, H^{3}=6\cdot6\cdot 1\cdot1\cdot1\, H^{5}=36 .
\]

It remains to check that no singular conic (a point of the discriminant
\(\Delta\)) satisfies the five conditions, because such a conic would
contribute with multiplicity to the intersection number.

A singular conic is either a double line \(L^{2}\) or the union of two
distinct lines \(L_{1}+L_{2}\).

* A double line would have to contain the three general points
\(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\); this is impossible because the points are not
collinear.

* For a reducible conic \(L_{1}+L_{2}\) each of the three points must lie
on one of the two lines, so (up to ordering) one line contains two of
the points and the other line contains the remaining point.  
For a general choice of the points none of the three lines determined
by the pairs \(\{P_{i},P_{j}\}\) is tangent to either \(C_{1}\) or
\(C_{2}\).  A line through a given point is tangent to a given smooth
conic in at most two directions; a line through the remaining point can
be tangent to at most one of the two conics, and it is never tangent to
both for general data.  Consequently the two lines cannot together give
a tangent to each of \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\).  Hence no reducible singular
conic satisfies the five conditions.

Thus every point of the intersection \(Z\) corresponds to a smooth conic,
and the total number of such conics equals the intersection number
computed above.

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is  

\[
X=\mathbf P^{5},\qquad \dim X =5 ,
\]

and the hyperplane class is \(H\in A^{1}(X)\).

The divisor classes of the imposed conditions are  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_i}]=6H \qquad (i=1,2),\qquad 
[\Sigma_{P_j}]=H \qquad (j=1,2,3).
\]

Hence the class of the closed subscheme  

\[
Z=\Sigma_{C_1}\cap\Sigma_{C_2}\cap\Sigma_{P_1}\cap\Sigma_{P_2}\cap\Sigma_{P_3}
\]

is  

\[
[Z]=(6H)^2\cdot H^3 = 6^2\,H^5 = 36\,H^5 .
\]

In \(\mathbf P^{5}\) we have \(H^5=1\); therefore the intersection number is  

\[
\int_X 36\,H^5 = 36 .
\]

For general choices of the two smooth conics and the three points, no singular conic (a double line or a pair of lines) can satisfy the five independent conditions, so the intersection is transverse and consists of reduced points only.

Thus the finite étale map sending a conic to the five‑tuple \((C_1,C_2,P_1,P_2,P_3)\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{36}.
\]

The space of plane conics is  

\[
X=\mathbf P^{5},\qquad H=c_{1}(\mathcal O_{X}(1)).
\]

For the given conditions we have the divisor classes  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_i}]=6H,\qquad [\Sigma_{P_j}]=H .
\]

Hence the class of the intersection  

\[
Z=\Sigma_{C_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{C_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{3}}
\]

is  

\[
[Z]=(6H)\cdot(6H)\cdot H\cdot H\cdot H = 36\,H^{5}.
\]

In \(\mathbf P^{5}\) we have \(H^{5}=1\); therefore the intersection number (the degree of the finite étale map) is \(36\).

It remains to check that no singular conic (i.e. a reducible or double line) satisfies the five general conditions.  
A singular conic is the union of two distinct lines \(L\cup M\).  
Because the three points \(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) are general, they are not collinear; consequently one of the lines must contain exactly two of the points and the other line the remaining point.  
For a line determined by two general points the probability of being tangent to a given smooth conic is zero, so neither line can be tangent to \(C_{1}\) or \(C_{2}\). Hence no singular conic meets all five conditions.  

Thus every solution of the five conditions is a smooth conic, and the number of solutions equals the intersection number computed above.

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(X=\mathbf P^{5}\) with hyperplane class \(H\).
For a smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^{2}\) the divisor of conics tangent to \(C\) has
class \([\Sigma _C]=6H\); for a point \(P\) the divisor of conics passing through \(P\) has
class \([\Sigma _P]=H\).

Impose the three point conditions first.  
The three linear conditions cut out a linear subspace  

\[
L = \Sigma_{P_{1}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{2}}\cap\Sigma_{P_{3}}\subset X ,
\qquad \dim L = 2 ,
\]

so \(L\simeq\mathbf P^{2}\).  
Inside this \(\mathbf P^{2}\) the restriction of \(\Sigma_{C}\) is a plane curve of degree
\(\deg(\Sigma_{C}|_{L}) = (\,6H\cdot H^{2}\,) = 6\).  
Hence each tangency condition to a fixed smooth conic gives a plane curve of degree \(6\) in
\(L\).

Therefore the required conics are the intersection points of two degree‑\(6\) plane
curves in \(L\).  By Bézout’s theorem the number of intersection points, counted with
multiplicity, is

\[
6 \times 6 = 36 .
\]

For a general choice of the two conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\) and the three points
\(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) the two degree‑\(6\) curves intersect transversely, so all
intersection points are reduced and correspond to smooth conics.  Consequently the
finite étale map described in the statement has degree \(36\).

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is  

\[
X=\mathbf P^5 ,\qquad \dim X =5 ,\qquad H=c_1(\mathcal O_X(1)).
\]

For a smooth conic \(C\subset\mathbf P^2\) the divisor of conics tangent to \(C\) has class  

\[
[\Sigma_C]=6H .
\]

For a point \(P\in\mathbf P^2\) the divisor of conics passing through \(P\) has class  

\[
[\Sigma_P]=H .
\]

Hence for two fixed smooth conics \(C_1,C_2\) and three fixed points
\(P_1,P_2,P_3\) the class of the intersection

\[
Z=\Sigma_{C_1}\cap\Sigma_{C_2}\cap\Sigma_{P_1}\cap\Sigma_{P_2}\cap\Sigma_{P_3}
\]

is  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_1}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_2}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_1}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_2}]
\cdot[\Sigma_{P_3}]
   =(6H)^2\cdot H^3 = 36\,H^{5}.
\]

On \(\mathbf P^5\) we have \(H^{5}=1\); therefore the top‑degree intersection number is  

\[
\int_X 36\,H^{5}=36 .
\]

For a general choice of the two conics and the three points no singular conic satisfies the five conditions (a singular conic would have to be a union of two lines, which would require a line through two of the points to be tangent to one of the given conics, a condition that does not hold for general data). Consequently all points of \(Z\) correspond to smooth conics, and the intersection is transverse, giving a reduced zero‑dimensional scheme.

Thus the fibre of the natural map over a general tuple consists of \(36\) reduced points, i.e. the map has degree \(36\).

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(X=\mathbf P^{5}\) with hyperplane class \(H\).

* Passing through a fixed point \(P\) imposes a hyperplane condition, so  
  \([\Sigma_{P}]=H\).

* Being tangent to a fixed smooth conic \(C\) gives a divisor of class  
  \([\Sigma_{C}]=6H\).

Hence for two conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\) and three points \(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) the
intersection class of the corresponding divisors is  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{2}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{P_{3}}]
   =(6H)\,(6H)\,H\,H\,H = 36\,H^{5}.
\]

In \(X=\mathbf P^{5}\) we have \(H^{5}=1\); therefore the degree of the
zero‑dimensional cycle obtained by intersecting the five divisors is \(36\).

For a general choice of the two conics and three points the intersection is
proper and transverse, so the 36 points are reduced and distinct. Consequently
the finite étale map sending a conic to the five‑tuple \((C_{1},C_{2},P_{1},
P_{2},P_{3})\) has degree \(36\).

\[
\boxed{36}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(X=\mathbf P^{5}\) with hyperplane class \(H\).  
For a fixed smooth conic \(C\) the divisor of conics tangent to \(C\) has class \(6H\); for a fixed point \(P\) the divisor of conics through \(P\) has class \(H\).

We intersect the following five divisors in \(X\):

\[
\Sigma_{C_{1}}\;(6H),\qquad 
\Sigma_{C_{2}}\;(6H),\qquad 
\Sigma_{P_{1}}\;(H),\qquad 
\Sigma_{P_{2}}\;(H),\qquad 
\Sigma_{P_{3}}\;(H).
\]

Since the five conditions are independent and are chosen generically, the intersection is transverse and consists of a finite reduced set of points.  
In a projective space the number of points obtained by intersecting hypersurfaces of degrees \(d_{1},\dots ,d_{5}\) is the product \(d_{1}\cdots d_{5}\).

Hence

\[
\# Z = 6\cdot 6\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 1 = 36 .
\]

Thus the finite étale map that sends a conic to the five‑tuple \((C_{1},C_{2},P_{1},P_{2},P_{3})\) has degree  

\[
\boxed{36}.
\]

problems.skill: Degree of the finite étale map counting conics tangent to five general conics
problems.problem:
Let \(U\subset \mathbb{P}H^{0}\bigl(\mathbb{P}^{2},\mathcal{O}(2)\bigr)\) be the open subset parametrising smooth plane conics.  
For a smooth conic \(C\) write \(\Sigma_{C}\subset U\) for the divisor of conics tangent to \(C\); for a line \(\ell\) write \(\Lambda_{\ell}\subset U\) for the divisor of conics tangent to \(\ell\); and for a point \(P\) write \(\Pi_{P}\subset U\) for the divisor of conics passing through \(P\).  

Fix two general smooth conics \(C_{1},C_{2}\), two general lines \(\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\) and a general point \(P\in\mathbb{P}^{2}\).  
Define the incidence variety  

\[
Z \;=\; \bigl\{\, (C,C_{1},C_{2},\ell_{1},\ell_{2},P)\in U^{5}\times (\mathbb{P}^{2})^{2}\times \mathbb{P}^{2}\mid 
C\in \Sigma_{C_{1}}\cap \Sigma_{C_{2}}\cap \Lambda_{\ell_{1}}\cap \Lambda_{\ell_{2}}\cap \Pi_{P}\,\bigr\}.
\]

Projection onto the last five parameters \((C_{1},C_{2},\ell_{1},\ell_{2},P)\) yields a morphism \(\pi: Z \to V\), where \(V\) is a dense open subset of the product of the parameter spaces.  For general choices the map \(\pi\) is finite étale.  

Compute the degree of \(\pi\); equivalently, determine how many smooth conics are simultaneously tangent to the two given conics, tangent to the two given lines, and passing through the given point, for general data.  

Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.
all_solutions:
The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^5\).  
For a fixed point the condition “the conic passes through the point’’ is a linear condition, i.e. a hyperplane of class \(H\).

For a fixed line \(\ell\) the condition “the conic is tangent to \(\ell\)” is given by the vanishing of the discriminant of the quadratic polynomial obtained by restricting the conic to \(\ell\); this is a quadric hypersurface, hence its class is \(2H\).

For a fixed smooth conic \(C\) the condition “the conic is tangent to \(C\)” is a hypersurface of degree 6 in \(\mathbb P^5\) (the discriminant of the resultant of the two quadrics). Its class is therefore \(6H\).

Hence, for general data the intersection class on \(\mathbb P^5\) is  

\[
(6H)^2\cdot (2H)^2\cdot H
   = 6^2\cdot 2^2\cdot 1 \; H^{5}
   = 144\, H^{5}.
\]

Since \(H^{5}=1\) on \(\mathbb P^{5}\), the degree of the finite étale map \(\pi\) equals \(144\).

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^5\).  
For a fixed smooth conic \(C\) the condition “\(Q\) is tangent to \(C\)” is a hypersurface of degree \(6\) in \(\mathbb P^5\) (a pencil of conics meets a given conic in a quartic; tangency means the quartic has a double root, giving a discriminant of degree 6).  

For a fixed line \(\ell\) the condition “\(Q\) is tangent to \(\ell\)” is a hypersurface of degree \(2\) (the restriction of a conic to \(\ell\) is a quadratic polynomial; its discriminant is quadratic in the coefficients).  

Passing through a fixed point \(P\) is a hyperplane, i.e. degree \(1\).

Thus the classes of the five divisors in \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb P^5)=\mathbb Z\) are  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_1}]=6h,\qquad [\Sigma_{C_2}]=6h,\qquad 
[\Lambda_{\ell_1}]=2h,\qquad [\Lambda_{\ell_2}]=2h,\qquad 
[\Pi_{P}]=h,
\]

where \(h\) denotes the hyperplane class.  

The number of smooth conics satisfying all five conditions is the intersection number

\[
(6h)^2\,(2h)^2\,(h)=6^2\cdot 2^2\cdot 1\;h^{5}=144.
\]

For general choices the intersection is transverse, so each solution is counted once and all are smooth. Hence the finite étale map \(\pi\) has degree \(144\).

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The linear system of plane conics is  

\[
|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2)|\simeq \mathbf P^{5},
\qquad H =\text{hyperplane class}.
\]

For a fixed geometric condition we obtain a divisor in \(\mathbf P^{5}\); its class is a multiple of \(H\).

---

### 1.  Passing through a point  

\(P\in\mathbf P^{2}\) gives the linear condition \(Q(P)=0\).  
Hence  

\[
[\Pi _{P}]=H .
\]

---

### 2.  Tangency to a line  

Let \(\ell\) be a line.  Restrict a quadratic form \(Q\) to \(\ell\); we obtain a binary quadratic
\(q(t)\).  Tangency means the discriminant of \(q\) vanishes, which is a quadratic condition in the
coefficients of \(Q\). Thus  

\[
[\Lambda _\ell]=2H .
\]

---

### 3.  Tangency to a smooth conic  

Let \(C_{0}\) be a fixed smooth conic with equation \(Q_{0}=0\).  
A conic \(Q=0\) is tangent to \(C_{0}\) iff the two quadrics have a common point with a common
tangent line, i.e. the intersection scheme of \(Q\) and \(Q_{0}\) contains a double point.  
Eliminating the point gives the discriminant of the resultant of the two quadrics; this
discriminant is a homogeneous polynomial of degree **6** in the coefficients of \(Q\). Consequently  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{0}}]=6H .
\]

---

### 4.  Intersection of the five divisors  

We have two conic‑tangency conditions, two line‑tangency conditions and one point condition.
Their classes add up to  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{1}}]+[\Sigma_{C_{2}}]+[\Lambda_{\ell_{1}}]+[\Lambda_{\ell_{2}}]+[\Pi_{P}]
=6H+6H+2H+2H+H = 17H .
\]

Since we intersect five hypersurfaces in \(\mathbf P^{5}\), the expected dimension of the
intersection is \(0\).  For general choices the intersection is transverse, so the number of
points equals the product of the degrees of the hypersurfaces:

\[
\deg \pi = 6\cdot 6\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 144 .
\]

All the points are smooth conics because the discriminant hypersurface (degree 3) does not meet a
general transverse complete intersection of the above five hypersurfaces.

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space \(\mathbb P^{5}\).  
Let \(H\) denote the hyperplane class on \(\mathbb P^{5}\).

* A conic through a fixed point is a hyperplane section, so  
  \([\Pi_{P}]=H\).

* A conic tangent to a fixed line \(\ell\) is given by the vanishing of the discriminant of the quadratic polynomial obtained by restricting the conic to \(\ell\); this is a quadric hypersurface. Hence  
  \([\Lambda_{\ell}]=2H\).

* A conic tangent to a fixed smooth conic \(C\) is a quartic hypersurface (the condition that the resultant of the two quadrics has a double root). Thus  
  \([\Sigma_{C}]=4H\).

The five conditions we impose are therefore represented by the class  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{1}}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_{2}}]\cdot[\Lambda_{\ell_{1}}]\cdot[\Lambda_{\ell_{2}}]\cdot[\Pi_{P}]
   =(4H)^{2}\,(2H)^{2}\,H = 4\cdot 16\,H^{5}=64\,H^{5}.
\]

Since \(H^{5}=1\) on \(\mathbb P^{5}\), the intersection number equals \(64\).  
For general choices of the data the intersection is transverse, so there are exactly \(64\) smooth conics satisfying all the conditions.

\[
\boxed{64}
\]

The space of (smooth) plane conics is the open subset \(U\subset \mathbf P^{5}\).  
For a fixed line \(\ell\) the condition “\(C\) is tangent to \(\ell\)” is a quadratic
hypersurface in \(\mathbf P^{5}\); its class is \(2H\) where \(H\) is the hyperplane
class.  

For a fixed smooth conic \(C_{0}\) the condition “\(C\) is tangent to \(C_{0}\)’’
is a quartic hypersurface; its class is \(4H\).  

Passing through a fixed point is a linear condition; its class is \(H\).

Hence the five conditions imposed on a conic have total class  

\[
(4H)\cdot(4H)\cdot(2H)\cdot(2H)\cdot(H)=4\cdot4\cdot2\cdot2\cdot1\,H^{5}=64\,H^{5}.
\]

Since \(H^{5}=1\) on \(\mathbf P^{5}\), the intersection consists of \(64\) points.
For general choices of the two conics, two lines and the point none of these
conics is singular, so all 64 solutions lie in the open set \(U\).

Therefore the morphism \(\pi : Z \to V\) is finite étale of degree  

\[
\boxed{64}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^{5}= \mathbb P H^{0}(\mathbb P^{2},\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{2}}(2))\).
For a fixed smooth conic \(C_{0}\) the set  

\[
\Sigma_{C_{0}}=\{\,Q\in\mathbb P^{5}\mid Q\text{ is tangent to }C_{0}\,\}
\]

is a divisor of degree \(6\) in \(\mathbb P^{5}\); indeed, restricting a variable conic to the fixed conic gives a degree‑\(4\) divisor on the latter, and the discriminant of a degree‑\(4\) divisor is a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(6\) in the coefficients of the variable conic.

For a fixed line \(\ell\) the divisor  

\[
\Lambda_{\ell}=\{\,Q\in\mathbb P^{5}\mid Q\text{ is tangent to }\ell\,\}
\]

has degree \(2\) (the discriminant of the quadratic obtained by restricting the conic to \(\ell\)).

Finally, for a fixed point \(P\) the divisor  

\[
\Pi_{P}=\{\,Q\in\mathbb P^{5}\mid P\in Q\,\}
\]

is a hyperplane, i.e. has degree \(1\).

Hence in the Chow ring \(A^{*}(\mathbb P^{5})=\mathbb Z[h]/(h^{6})\) we have  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_{0}}]=6h,\qquad
[\Lambda_{\ell}]=2h,\qquad
[\Pi_{P}]=h .
\]

The required number of smooth conics is the intersection product of the five divisor classes:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\deg \pi
&= \int_{\mathbb P^{5}} (6h)\;(6h)\;(2h)\;(2h)\;(h) \\
&= 6^{2}\,2^{2}\,\int_{\mathbb P^{5}} h^{5} \\
&= 36 \times 4 \times 1 \\
&= 144 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus for general data there are exactly **144** smooth conics that are tangent to the two given conics, tangent to the two given lines, and pass through the given point.

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The space of plane conics is the projective space \(\mathbf P^{5}\).  
For a general condition we have the following divisor classes in \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^{5})\):

* passing through a fixed point                     \(H\) (degree 1);
* being tangent to a fixed line                     \(2H\) (degree 2);
* being tangent to a fixed smooth conic              \(6H\) (degree 6).

These degrees are the numbers of solutions when the condition is imposed on a one‑dimensional linear system (a pencil) of conics.

Hence a smooth conic satisfying

* \(p\) point conditions,
* \(\ell\) line‑tangency conditions,
* \(c\) conic‑tangency conditions

is counted by the intersection product  

\[
H^{p}\,(2H)^{\ell}\,(6H)^{c}=2^{\ell}\,6^{c}\,H^{5}.
\]

Since \(H^{5}=1\) (a point in \(\mathbf P^{5}\)), the number of such conics is  

\[
N(p,\ell,c)=2^{\ell}\,6^{c}.
\]

In the problem we have \(p=1,\;\ell=2,\;c=2\). Therefore  

\[
N(1,2,2)=2^{2}\,6^{2}=4 \times 36 = 144.
\]

Thus for general choices of the two conics, two lines and a point there are exactly **144** smooth conics that are tangent to both given conics, tangent to both given lines, and pass through the given point.

\[
\boxed{144}
\]

The space of plane conics is \(\mathbb P^5=\mathbb P H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O(2))\); denote its hyperplane class by \(H\).

* Passing through a fixed point \(P\) is a linear condition, hence \([\Pi_P]=H\).

* Being tangent to a fixed line \(\ell\) is a quadratic condition on the coefficients of the conic, so \([\Lambda_\ell]=2H\).

* Being tangent to a fixed smooth conic \(C\): restrict a variable conic to \(C\).  
  The restriction map \(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O(2))\to H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(4))\) is surjective with a one‑dimensional kernel, so the linear system \(|\mathcal O_C(4)|\) is a \(\mathbb P^4\).  
  On \(\mathbb P^4\) the discriminant of a binary quartic (the condition that the divisor on \(C\) has a double point) is a hypersurface of degree \(2\cdot4-2=6\).  
  Pulling this hypersurface back to \(\mathbb P^5\) gives a divisor of degree \(6\); thus \([\Sigma_C]=6H\).

Hence the class of the intersection we need is  

\[
[\Sigma_{C_1}]\cdot[\Sigma_{C_2}]\cdot[\Lambda_{\ell_1}]\cdot[\Lambda_{\ell_2}]\cdot[\Pi_P]
 = (6H)\,(6H)\,(2H)\,(2H)\,(H)=6\cdot6\cdot2\cdot2\cdot1\; H^{5}.
\]

On \(\mathbb P^5\) we have \(H^{5}=1\). Therefore  

\[
\deg \pi = 6\cdot6\cdot2\cdot2\cdot1 = 144 .
\]

For general choices of the two conics, two lines and the point, all solutions are smooth conics, so the morphism \(\pi\) is finite étale of degree \(144\).

\[
\boxed{144}
\]
